Author: Śivayogiśivācārya Commentator: Maritoṇṭadārya Description: The Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi of Śivayogiśivācārya with the commentary Tattvapradīpikā by Maritoṇṭadārya.

Publisher: Śaivabhāratī Publication Year: 2006
Place of publication: Vārāṇasī;
Country of publication: India. First Chapter.

Victorious is Śrīnātha, the embodiment of the Moon, the supreme Śiva, the Three-eyed Lord in the form of the *Tāra* (Om), situated within the pure and beautiful *brahmarandhra* in a white lotus arising from the water,
in a triangle, consisting of the threefold script known as Will, Knowledge, and Action, with the phonemes *ha*, *kṣa*, *la*, and *ra* at its tips and sides.

In the bindu that is oriented toward the entire ocean [of manifestation], he is enriched by the two feet of vision and action, which bring about the emergence of both consciousness and the unconscious.
The flawless crest-jewel of manifold philosophical systems,
the Śrī Vīraśaiva Siddhānta consisting of one hundred and one stages (sthala).
The King of Śiva-yogins illuminates the conversation between Reṇukā and Agastya, renowned in the Vedas and Āgamas, by extracting its hidden meaning.
In this *Śivastuti*, it is stated that after the onset of the Kali age, Revana Siddheśvara— renowned as Reṇukagaṇeśvara for the welfare of the world—
instructed the Vīraśaiva scriptures to Agastya (Kumbhasambhava).
Following that,

there was a certain devotee of Maheśvara named Śivayogīśvara, who was renowned in the tradition of Siddharāmeśvara— which originated from the vision of Revanasiddheśvara— and who possessed the essence of all the Vedas and Āgamas.
In order to instruct his own disciples without obstacle, he composes this dialogue between Reṇukā and Agastya in seven verses.

For the sake of instructing his disciples, he first performs an auspicious salutation (*maṅgala*)—in the form of a prostration to his chosen deity—which consists in internalizing within his own mind the unification of all the preeminent Siddhāntas, Nigamas, and Āgamās. He does so as follows:
Salutation to Śiva, to Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who serves as the wall for painting the prosperity of the three worlds. (1)

The meaning is: "Salutations to Śiva—the Supreme Śiva well-known in the Śiva-siddhānta, who is the Brahman propounded by the Vedāntas, who is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), whose essential nature is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, and who serves as the foundational wall for the variegated depiction of the illusory manifestation of the world. || 1 ||
I bow to that Supreme Śiva, the root of the universe, whom the Vedāntins declare to be the object designated by the term "Brahman. || 2 ||

The meaning is: "I bow to that Supreme Śiva, the cause of the universe, who is the well-known Paramaśiva according to the Śaiva Siddhānta; he whom the Vedāntins designate by the term 'Brahman' and refer to as the object—the Supreme Self—denoted by the word 'Parabrahman'. || 2 ||
I bow to that great ocean of consciousness, named Śiva, which is stainless, and whose appearance as waves and bubbles is the collection of the thirty-six principles.

I bow to that great ocean of consciousness named Śiva— pure and free from the three impurities— who is the supreme ocean of consciousness known as Paraśiva, within which the aggregate of the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth appears like waves and bubbles, manifesting in one part like ripples upon the surface of clarified butter due to its inherent solidity.
The meaning is "I pay homage. || 3 ||
Salutations to that Supreme Self, whose splendor illumines the universe and whom one rejoices in through bliss, for his majesty transcends all attributes.
By the scriptural testimony, "By its light all this shines" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 2.5.15),

it is understood that the universe shines by the illumination of that Supreme Brahman; and by the scriptural testimony, "Other beings live on but a fraction of this bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32), it is understood that one rejoices through the happiness of that Supreme Brahman.
The meaning is: "Obeisance to that Śiva, the Supreme Self, whose majesty transcends the qualities of illusion—sattva, rajas, and tamas. || 4 ||
Salutation to Śambhu, the peaceful one, whose nature is stainless, who brings about the manifestation of all the principles beginning with Sadāśiva through his mouth. (5)

According to the analogy of the peacock’s egg-fluid (*mayūrāṇḍarasanyāya*): just as the body of this bird named the peacock—consisting of variegated plumage—is contained within its fluid and remains hidden, only to manifest outwardly in the course of time; even so, in the state of Śiva transcending the universe, everything [remains latent].

The world, consisting of manifold variety, exists hidden within the Supreme Śiva and manifests in the course of time. [Salutations] to Him who brings about the unfolding of the thirty-six principles—from Sadāśiva down to the Earth—through His state of aesthetic equilibrium with the power of self-reflection (*svavimarśaśakti*); whose essential nature is free from all defects; and who is the enjoyer of bliss.
The meaning is: "Obeisance to the source of happiness, the bringer of auspiciousness. || 5 ||
Salutations to Śambhu accompanied by Ambā, who possesses a body according to his own will, who acts according to his own will, and who created the three worlds by his own will.

The meaning is: "Salutations to Paraśiva, the Lord of Pārvatī, who possesses a divine, auspicious form fashioned by His own will for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees—according to the Vedic scripture, 'He of many forms, the fierce one with firm limbs'—who moves according to His own desire, and who has created the three worlds by the power of His own will. || 6 ||
Salutations to that Maheśa, the Great God, the wielder of the trident, in whom the supreme, innate lordship finds its rest.

In that Supreme Śiva, known as the Supreme Brahman and renowned through the Vedas and Āgamas, there rests the unsurpassed, all-surpassing, innate, and non-illusory lordship— the state of Umāmaheśvara— wherein His form, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, is like the solidity of clarified butter.
She indeed exists under the name Śivā, for she is always Śiva himself.
To that Maheśvara, who possesses identity [with all] according to the statement in the *Sūtagītā*;
to Mahādeva, the cause of Brahmā and the other lords, as stated in the *Śruti*: "The supreme Maheśvara among the lords";
to the one whose form is immeasurable light; to the trident-bearer, whose trident consists of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.

The meaning is "salutation to Paramaśiva. By this, one should understand that this established conclusion (siddhānta) is characterized by the non-duality of Brahman devoid of distinctions (nirviśeṣabrahmādvaita).
The reality propounded by these seven verses is that Supreme Brahman; He is the One, He is the One Rudra. He...

"He is Īśāna, he is the Blessed One, he is Maheśvara, he is Mahādeva" (Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad 2.3); in accordance with this statement from the Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad, those proficient in the Śivādvaita scriptures should understand that [Śiva] is indeed one alone. || 7 ||
p. 4) Thus, having paid homage to Śiva with seven verses in accordance with the Vedas and the Āgamas, [the author proceeds] with the praise of Śakti.
He introduces Śiva and Śakti, who are eternally inherent and well-known from the Vedas, Āgamas, and other sources, through five verses:
"I bow to that supreme Śivā, the follower of Dharma, whom those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures declare to be the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all worlds. (8)
Those who possess knowledge of Śiva and have mastered the scriptures such as the Vedas and Āgamas describe her as the power inherent in Paraśiva,
the primordial nature of all worlds,
whose essence consists in the equilibrium of knowledge and action that serves as the fundamental cause. Her—
The meaning is: "I bow down to Śivā Bhavānī, the companion in dharma of Śambhu, whose nature is dharma, who is supreme and most excellent. || 8 ||
Salutation to that supreme Śakti, whose nature is Māyā, by whom Maheśvara Śambhu is endowed with name, form, and the rest.

In accordance with the statement of the *Tattvaprakāśa*, "By which power inherent in Himself, Śambhu— Śiva, the Lord of all causes such as Brahmā and others— is empowered; by which Śambhu is capable regarding both the enjoyment and liberation of this multitude of bound souls (paśus)," [He exists as] characterized by name, form, and activity, [and as that which] "exists, shines, and is dear."

Name and form constitute the fivefold division; the first three are of the nature of Brahman, while the latter two are of the nature of the world. [Pañcadaśī] May he be the bestower of enjoyment and liberation upon living beings.
To her, whose nature is Māyā—one should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad]

According to the Śruti [Upaniṣad 4.10], the meaning is: "Salutation to the Supreme Power (paramaśakti), who is known as Mūlaprakṛti—consisting of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—and who, by way of being the source of manifestation, serves as the material cause of the universe; she is the eternal power inherent in Paramaśiva. || 9 ||
I bow to that auspicious Mother Śivā, who is born from the primordial source beginning with Śiva, who transcends peace, who is supreme among all, and who bestows auspiciousness upon everyone. (10)

From Śiva, the primordial Paraśiva, [the kalās] beginning with Nivṛtti— just as whiteness exists in the first cloth— arose previously; and in relation to the supreme Kuṇḍalinī-Śakti consisting of the kalās of Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatīta, [Nivṛtti is] the subsequent and superior one.
The meaning is: "I bow to her who is the mother of all, the bestower of auspiciousness, the bringer of welfare, the auspicious Śivā, and the source of all blessings. || 10 ||
I praise that auspicious Śivā, who, in the form of will, knowledge, and the rest, brings forth the universe for Śambhu; she is a wave of the awakening of supreme bliss. 11.

That inherent power of Śambhu, the Supreme Lord—which exists in the form of will, knowledge, and so forth; which is His supreme, stainless, and pure power; which is free from conceptual construction and is natural; and which possesses qualities equal to Rudra, manifesting in thousands of forms such as knowledge, action, and will—may that mind of mine be intent upon the resolve for Śiva. [Śiva-saṃhitā]

Thus, according to scripture, the meaning is: "I bow to that auspicious Śivā, who, in the form of will and the rest, is the source of the universe and the illuminator of the universe—the wave of the awakening of supreme bliss, overflowing with the bliss of consciousness. || 11 ||
I daily and nightly revere that goddess, who is as enchanting as Īśāna, who bestows true knowledge upon those who have sought refuge for the sake of immortality. 12.

According to the *Sūtasamhitā*, which states: "For those who have surrendered and sought refuge for the sake of the nectar of immortality and liberation, that power inherent in Śiva which bestows excellent knowledge is the wisdom born from the statements of Vedānta"—
it refers to the wisdom regarding the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) as revealed by the great Vedāntic mahāvākyas such as *tat tvam asi*.

The meaning is: "I praise" and "I bow down day and night to her, the bestower [of all], who is the beloved life-breath of Śiva. For according to the Pauṣkara scripture, 'She alone is Śivā; she is in reality the sovereign form (mūrti)'; thus, one should [worship] this Śakti, as propounded in these five aphorisms, precisely as non-different from Śiva."
One should reflect upon it. || 12 ||
(p. 6) Having thus paid homage to Pārvatī and Parameśvara in brief, [the author] next describes the lineage of the author in eight verses.

He reveals the teachers who belong to the lineage of Śiva-yogins: "There was a certain one, the foremost among the Śiva-yogins perfected in conduct, renowned as Śivayogī, a great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva. (13)

Among the Śiva-yogins, he was the foremost and most excellent, a great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva— a veritable sea of Śiva-knowledge. Born from the womb of the vision of the Siddha Revaṇeśvara, he was the Siddha Rāmeśvara,
renowned as a Śiva-yogin within the lineage of those perfected in conduct who were endowed with virtuous behavior.
The meaning is "there was. || 13 ||

The speech of that [author], which was like the pure moonlight causing the ocean of the nectar of devotion to Śiva to swell, generally brought about the festival of the blue water-lily (the world). 14.
The speech of that Siddharāmeśvara, renowned as Śivayogin,

which is like the stainless moonlight that increases the ocean of the nectar of devotion to Śiva, has brought about— exceedingly— the festival of the blue lily (kuvalaya), meaning it has caused the festival of the blue lotus (nīlotpala) known as the earth-mandala. || 14 ||
He explains that very point:
"Born in his lineage, the teacher named Muddadeva, stainless like a pearl-jewel, was the foremost among the Śiva-yogins. (15)

In the lineage of that Siddharāmeśvara, among those who know Śiva—that is, among the knowers of Śiva—there arose, like a spotless pearl, the preceptor named Muddadeva, the foremost and most excellent; this is the meaning of "he was born. || 15 ||
Because she awakens all living beings who bow down to her with devotion, her renowned title is celebrated as Muddadevī. (16)

Because she grants satisfaction to all living beings and awakens those who bow before her, she is renowned by the name "Mudradevi" (the Goddess of Joy), which is well-known through both its etymological meaning (*anvartha*) and its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); that is to say, it is famous and established in the world.
He had a son named Siddhanātha, who was peaceful, pure, a teacher of Śiva (Śivācārya), whose very self was Śiva, and who was the definitive expounder of the Śiva-siddhānta. || 17 ||
The preceptor of Śiva (Śivācārya) for that Muddadeva was pure, sanctified, tranquil, free from attachment and aversion,
of the nature of Śiva, identical with Śiva, the determiner of the Śiva-siddhānta, the one who ascertained the meaning of the Śivāgamas endowed with the three categories and four feet.
The preceptor who established the Śiva-samaya, named Siddhanātha, was joined with the name Siddharāmeśvara; he was the son known as Siddhanāthācārya, meaning that he became Kumāra. || 17 ||
The crest-jewel of the Vīraśaivas, possessed of the excellence of distinguished conduct, he whom the teachers praise as a great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva. (18)

The meaning is that the teachers (deśikas), the preceptors (ācāryas)— who are the crest-jewels of the Vīraśaivas and the crown-gems of the Vīraśaiva community— praise and speak of this Siddhanāthācārya, who is endowed with distinguished conduct, perfected in virtuous behavior, and is a great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva. || 18 ||
From whose teacher’s family arose the manual of conduct for the virtuous, and in whom was born firm devotion to Śiva, free from all disturbance. (19)

The manual of conduct for the virtuous, the noble persons, was born from the lineage of teachers—that is, from the family of teachers—of that Siddhanātha Ācārya. In him, the eightfold devotion to Śiva, free from disturbances and free from defects, became firmly established; "jajñe" means it was born. || 19 ||
To that crest-jewel of the Vīraśiva Ācāryas was born a son named Śivayogin, who was like the moon arising from the ocean.
The son of that Siddhanāthācārya, the crest-jewel of the Vīraśaivas, was born as a youth known as Śivayogī, just as the moon is to the ocean; the meaning is that he became famous. || 20 ||
(p. 8) Now, this Śivayogin, the compiler of this treatise, describes the sequence of the introduction of the scripture by means of twelve aphorisms, preceded by a praise of his own name:
Because of his union with the experience of Śiva, who is the supreme space of consciousness and bliss,
the name "Śivayogī" is truly appropriate for him.

The meaning is that for this teacher, because of his yoga of experiencing Śiva—who is of the nature of the supreme ether of consciousness and bliss according to such Vedic texts as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) and "Brahman has the ether as its body" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.6.2)—the designation "Śivayogī" (Yogi of Śiva) is endowed with its true significance; that is to say, it becomes consistent with the actual reality. || 21 ||
The face of the quarters has been perfumed by the flower of his fame, which is fragrant with the full maturity of his thorough knowledge of the Śiva-āgamas.

The face of the green directions— that is, the quarters— was perfumed and nourished by the flower of the fame of that Ācārya, a flower made fragrant by the full maturity of his thorough knowledge of the Śiva-āgamas whose characteristics have been previously described. || 22 ||
By him, who possesses a garland of rays that dispel the great darkness of the heterodox doctrines of the Buddha and others, eternal devotion to Śiva was brought forth in Rakṣāvatī.

The meaning is that by this Ācārya—who is like a fierce sunbeam to the darkness of doctrines hostile to the Śiva-samaya of the Buddhists and others—the eternal devotion to Śiva became protected; that is to say, it was preserved. || 23 ||
He was the promoter of the path of dharma for the Mahāvīra-Śaivas,
a moon enveloped by the moonlight of the thorough knowledge of the Śiva-tattva.

(9) That Śiva-yogi, whose moon is veiled by the moonlight of the knowledge of the Śiva-tattva, is the one who sets forth the path of dharma for the Mahāvīra-Śaivas; the meaning is that he alone abides on the path of his own conduct. || 24 ||
Having respectfully examined the Śaiva Tantras beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula, as well as all the Purāṇas belonging to the Śaiva tradition; 25.
Having examined with affection all the Śaiva Tantras, beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula, as well as all the Purāṇas. || 25 ||
For the sake of establishing distinguished conduct without contradicting the path of the Vedas, for the purpose of rejecting the wrong path, and for the delight of the discerning; (26)

It is for the sake of establishing virtuous conduct without contradicting the Vedic path, for the purpose of refuting the systems and paths of wicked people such as the Jains and Buddhists, and for the satisfaction of those who can distinguish between the Vedas and the Āgamas.
The *Sarvasva* of the Vīraśaivas illuminates all matters;
it is untouched by any defects and is honored by those of pure mind. (27)
It is the very essence of the Vīraśaivas, illuminating all meanings, untouched by any defects, honored by those of pure mind who know the Nigamas and Āgamas, and it brings satisfaction. || 27 ||
In all those Āgamas and in all the Purāṇas without exception,
this was told of old by the Lord to the Goddess and to Nandana.
This was graciously narrated by Śiva to the Goddess and to his son, the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), within the aforementioned Āgamas and Purāṇas. || 28 ||
It was then told again on earth by the high-souled Gaṇeśvara Reṇuka, who was established in that tradition, to Agastya. (29)
This was further related on earth by the high-souled Reṇukagaṇādhīśvara, who was perfected in that tradition, to Agastya. || 29 ||
The best among the wise proclaimed this Vīraśaiva Mahātantra, consisting of one hundred and one topics, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world.

For the benefit of the world, the preceptor renowned as the Śivayogin— the most excellent among those of stainless knowledge— concisely expounded the Vīraśaiva Siddhānta, which consists of one hundred and one stages, beginning with the knowledge of the *piṇḍa* and ending with *śūnya*.
The meaning is that he has made it manifest. || 30 ||
Because it is the highest among all Śaiva tantras, it is known in the world by the name *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, meaning "The Crest-Jewel of the Siddhāntas. (31)

Since it is the most supreme among all Śaiva tantras, this Vīraśaiva tantra—being "niruttara" (without superior) because there is nothing higher than itself—is known in the world by the name *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*; the meaning is that it shines forth [as such]. || 31 ||

May the distinguished Vīraśaivas apply their minds to this [work], which encompasses all objects of knowledge and in which the grace of the non-dual state of Śiva-consciousness has been revealed by all the Śaiva Tantras.
In the *Paśupatimatāsāra*, which is worthy of praise by the learned. || 32 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi. || 1 ||

In this *Śivasiddhāntasāra*, which conforms to the entire secret meaning of all the Vīraśaiva Tantras and is endowed with the clarity of the state of aesthetic rapture (*samarasa*) arising from the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva;

While this Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi is being praised by the learned, let the distinguished, excellent Vīraśaivas and Vīraśaiva teachers apply their minds—that is, let them compose it—such is the meaning. || 32 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Contents," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 1.
The Second Chapter.
Now, the teacher Śivayogin pays homage to Pārvatī and Parameśvara by means of two aphorisms, in accordance with the consensus of the Vedas and Āgamas:

Salutations to Śiva, who is of the nature of Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss; the cause of the manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent; who is accompanied by Ambā, attended by his Gaṇas, and is self-born. || 1 ||

The meaning is: "Salutation to Śiva—the Lord of Bhavānī, who is accompanied by the hosts of Pramathas, who is self-born, not born from a womb, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and who is the cause for the manifestation of the world-expansion consisting of the spheres of existence and non-existence, and the cause for the manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent. || 1 ||

I salute the Śakti of Maheśvara, who is the mother-of-pearl shell for the pearls of all the principles (tattvas) issuing from the mouth of Sadāśiva, and who takes the form of Mahāmāyā and other powers. (2)

I bow to and praise Bhavānī—the power (śakti) inherent in Śiva—who is the mother-of-pearl oyster shell from which the thirty-six principles (tattvas), beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the earth, arise as pearls; she whose nature is the Great Māyā known as Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). This is the meaning. || 2 ||

Now, in order to establish the process of universal creation, he provides a description of the reality through four aphorisms: "There exists that which has the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; which is the abode of the state beyond defining characteristics; which is free from conceptual construction, formless, and devoid of all affliction. (3)
It is the very nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss; it is the abode of the state devoid of marks; it is free from duality, devoid of form, and has warded off all disturbances.
(13) Devoid of the discourse of conceptual differentiation, possessing a majesty that transcends all proliferation,
it abides in a state that is beyond the range of the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception.

Being devoid of any disconnected contingency and lacking the nature, flavor, and other qualities of extraordinary majesty, it is inaccessible to the means of knowledge known as direct perception; for this very reason, it is also inaccessible to inference and the like, since those too are rooted in perception and are themselves limited in scope. || 4 ||
Self-luminous, resplendent, free from affliction, incomparable, omniscient, all-pervading, peaceful, omnipotent, and unrestrained. || 5 ||
Shining by its own self-luminosity— [self-luminosity being defined as the state of illuminating itself while simultaneously illuminating others]— it is free from defects such as birth and death,
beyond comparison, omniscient, all-pervasive, devoid of attachment and aversion, and possesses unrestrained, universal capacity.
That is to say, it is devoid of cessation. || 5 ||
The eternal Supreme Brahman, designated by such names as Śiva, Rudra, Mahādeva, and Bhava, is non-dual and indefinable.

The second void, designated by various terms such as Śiva and Rudra, which is ineffable, eternal, and the supreme Brahman, must be accepted as "it exists," for otherwise the consequence would be the blindness of the world;
as it is said: "He indeed becomes non-existent if he knows Brahman as non-existent."
"If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing"—so says the Śruti (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1). || 6 ||

Now, he demonstrates the manner of the universe’s creation from the Supreme Brahman— which possesses a single power of action— in accordance with the scriptural statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), using the analogy of the seed and the sprout: "In that [Brahman], the world of sentient and insentient beings was previously dissolved."
The world, which is his effect, is dissolved within his own self; that it is yet manifest by him is truly marvelous.

In that aforementioned Supreme Brahman, the entire universe consisting of the moving and the non-moving was previously dissolved before creation; existing in a state of identity with it beyond the range of both types of sense organs, that is truly wonderful and marvelous.

The word "immediately" (*anantaram*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The meaning is that the universe—merged in its own self, merged in the power of its own self, and being self-luminous due to the absence of any other suitable material cause and the non-existence of a second entity—became capable of being manifested by itself alone, and thus fit to be made an object of both types of sense organs. 7.
Now, by means of six aphorisms, he demonstrates the nature of Śiva and Śakti as they become oriented toward the creation of the universe, according to the analogy of the solidity of clarified butter:
"The Supreme Brahman, designated as Śiva, through the desire to create the world..."
He assumed a certain form, which was a manifestation of the non-manifestation of bliss.
The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman, known as Śiva, by his own will, for the purpose of creating the universe, assumed a certain form that was swollen with an abundance of bliss. || 8 ||
Regarding its nature, the *Kulaka* states in two verses: "A *yugmaka* is to be known as consisting of two [verses], a *viśeṣaka* is to be known as consisting of three;
a *kapālaka* consists of four, and that which follows is remembered as a *kulaka*. (Stuti-kusumāñjali-ṭīkā).
He speaks [further] regarding the *viśeṣaka*:
Free from any connection with defects, unconditioned,
immutable, divine, non-material, eternal, blue-throated, and three-eyed.

The meaning is that [He] is devoid of all connection with defects such as old age and death; He is empty of adjuncts (upādhi) such as ignorance (avidyā) other than Himself; He is without destruction, and therefore eternal, being unassailable throughout the three periods of time. He is non-material (aprākṛta), free from association with primordial nature (prakṛti), blue-throated, and three-eyed. || 9 ||

(15) One should worship him who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, who is pure, resembling pure crystal, shining like a pure pearl, and who is served by the forms of the [three] qualities. 10.

He who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, who is pure, holy, resembling pure crystal, possessing the luster of stainless pearl-jewels, and who is worshipped by Brahmā and others through their embodiments of the qualities (guṇas). || 10 ||
The object of all yogins, which is the means for producing pure knowledge,
resembles ten million suns and possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons.

The abode of extraordinary qualities, the locus of infinite majesty, divine and worthy of praise, possessing a manifold array of instruments such as eyes composed of pure knowledge, perceptible to yogins,
shining with the brilliance of ten million suns and the luster of ten million moons, and transcendentally infinite—

"Assume some nature that is the locus of auspicious qualities and the substratum of manifold greatness, such as performing what is extremely difficult to accomplish"—this is the connection with the preceding [verse]. || 11 ||
Now he reveals the nature of Śiva’s power: "His supreme power is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. (12)

The supreme power belonging to Him—that is, related to Paraśiva—is the power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*), whose nature is the totality of the manifestation of all worlds; she is of the highest form, characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). This is the sense of the remaining portion [of the verse]. || 12 ||
By His will, she became manifest, conforming to His very nature.

From the Vedic revelation, "I am," there arises within this Light a supreme manifestation in the form of the non-arising of the play of impurity and the absence of action— expressed as "I rejoice"— which,

despite being the creator of all worlds in the manner previously described, does not exist as a positive entity for that which is non-existent, according to the teaching: "The being of the non-existent does not exist" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.16).

Because of the Lord’s teaching that, by way of the analogy of the juice within a fruit, it is experienced within one's own self as the non-dual reflective awareness of "I," which is not within the range of either of the two types of sense organs.

Having established the identity-in-difference through her own sovereign majesty within the playful act of creation— which consists of the reflective awareness of the divisions characterized by "this-ness" (idantā) regarding the established universe— she again becomes the material cause, whose nature is inherence (samavāya), remaining free from modification according to the analogy of fruits and flowers on a tree.

Through her will, by means of the play of withdrawal characterized by drawing [all things] into herself, she drew everything into her own self— like a female tortoise withdrawing its limbs— via the two powers of knowledge and action which act as her own rays; thus, manifest and immediate, she became one whose nature conforms to that [universal] "I" and whose essence is non-different from Śiva.

This is the meaning: nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction between difference and non-difference, because that [conceptual] difference is imagined through independence; for contradiction exists only between natural difference and non-difference—that is to say, between those things that possess equal ontological status—since the Lord’s power is capable of effecting the impossible.
This will become clear in various places further on, so there is no need for elaboration here. "Dev" means one whose nature is playfulness. || 13 ||

Having thus described the nature of Śiva and Śakti, he now sets forth the sequence of creation in the manner stated in such scriptural passages as, "Then He thought: 'Let me create the worlds'" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1–2) and "He fashioned them as before" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3): [The text continues with the description of the creation process.]
Desirous of creating the world, the Lord of the Universe first appointed Brahmā as the creator of all embodied beings and of all the worlds. (14)

"Of the worlds" means of the fourteen worlds; "of embodied beings" means of the living creatures existing by depending upon their respective worlds—the rest is clear. On this point, there is the Yajurvedic scripture: "Rudra, the great seer, who is superior to the universe, generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning. (14)
17) Now, he elucidates the meaning of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.18): "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him."
To that first-born son, the omnipotent, all-knowing Śaṅkara imparted all the sciences along with his grace.
"Endowed with power" means possessed of inherent power. The meaning is that he taught all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, in such a way that they were accompanied by grace. || 15 ||
He became intent on the effort to create all the worlds;
yet, despite his exertion in the creation of the worlds, he remained shrouded by Māyā, as he was unaware of the means for its accomplishment due to the command of Śaṅkara. || 16 ||
This is clear. || 16 ||
Desiring to obtain the means to create all the worlds,
he once again petitioned that God of gods, Tryambaka.

Now, he shows the manner of that prayer: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O mine of compassion, who are capable of the method of creating the entire world beginning with ourselves. (18)
"O Śambhu! O Creator of the world! O Lord of the world! Tell me the means [to liberation].
You are omniscient, omnipotent, the eternal creator of all. (19)
In this context, regarding the statement of the means, the phrase "the omniscient one" and so forth are qualifiers containing the logical reason (hetugarbha).
Thus entreated by Brahmā, Śambhu, the leader of the universe,
explained to him the means for setting in motion the creation of the worlds.
Even after obtaining the method taught by Īśvara, the four-faced one was not capable of creating this world in its manifold forms.

Even Brahmā, though he had obtained the means for the creation of the universe from Śiva, was not capable of it. Why? Here, the answer lies in the qualifying epithet: "of manifold forms. The sense is that this is because the world possesses manifold forms. || 21 ||
Then he describes that manner [of prayer]: "Again Brahmā, his mind agitated, entreated him:
'O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O primordial cause of the universe! (22)
Therefore, with a distracted mind and a mind filled with fear, he again prayed for auspiciousness; this is the meaning:
"Salutations to you, O Saccidānanda, resplendent with a form manifested by your own will!
O Bhava, Śarva, Maheśāna, the cause of all causes! (23)
Indeed, the means spoken by you is not understood by me at all now.
O Bhava, creator of all worlds; O Śarva, destroyer of all; O cause of all causes—meaning, the cause of all causes such as Bindu, Māyā, and so forth. || 23 ||
p. 19) To the question "What, then, should be done?", he says:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, first perform the act of creation."
"Therefore, O Lord of Umā, having known the means, I shall perform the creation of the world."
This is clear. || 24 ||
Then, commanded by Viriñci to "create progeny," the moon-crested Lord created from his mind the Rudras, great lords equal to himself—
blue-throated, three-eyed, and adorned with crowns of matted locks.

In accordance with such statements from the Āditya Purāṇa, he says that [Śiva] created: "Thus requested by Brahmā, the source of the universe, Śambhu created beings equal in splendor to himself, all-pervading, and possessed of all powers. (25)
This is clear. || 25 ||
Their minds were perpetually immersed in the supreme bliss of awakening;
they were the Pramathas, capable of bringing about both the creation and the dissolution of the entire universe.
This is clear. || 26 ||
When those hosts of Pramathas had been created by the Supreme Self, two became dear to Śiva: Reṇuka and Dāruka.
This is clear. || 27 ||
(p. 20) Now, he reveals the majesty of those two lords of the Gaṇas with five verses:
"They are knowers of the distinctions of all sciences and are expert in all undertakings."
They are liberated from the impurity of illusion and resplendent with supreme majesty. || 28 ||
This is clear. || 28 ||

They were greedy for the savor of relishing the manifestation of the bliss of the Self, and they had cast off the disease of worldly existence through the thorough knowledge of the principle of Śiva. (29)
"Free from the impurity of *māyā*" means being devoid of the connection with the three impurities, beginning with *āṇava*, which are conceptualized by the power of *māyā*. || 29 ||
They were intent on expounding the various paths of the great Śaiva tantras, and were experts in discerning the entire essence of Vedānta. || 30 ||
This is clear. || 30 ||
Beholding those two highly fortunate ones, who were eternally perfected, free from fear, and possessed of unrestrained prowess, the Supreme Lord [spoke]. (31)
If [the self] were eternally established, then it would possess the eternal establishment of the elements; the rest is clear. || 31 ||
The omnipresent Lord appointed two gatekeepers for the inner apartments, who were capable in all tasks, relied upon with supreme trust, and strictly disciplined.

The omnipresent, independent Supreme Lord created—meaning he fashioned—the two doorkeepers of the inner apartments as the two atoms, Renuka and Dāruka, whose selves were thus purified by their destiny. || 32 ||
21) Now, it is said that both Reṇuka and Dāruka performed service to Śiva:
"Both Reṇuka and Dāruka were lords of the Gaṇas."
Having become objects of trust for the one who bears the new moon on his crest,
those two always performed service to the Lord of the Universe while stationed at the gate of the inner apartments.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Incarnation of Reṇuka and Dāruka," in the *Śrīsiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*.
This is clear. || 33 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Incarnation of Reṇuka and Dāruka," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter. Now, for the purpose of narrating the account of Śivayogin Reṇuka’s descent to the world of mortals,
he first describes Kailāsa with eight verses:
Once, moreover, on Mount Kailāsa, which consists of silver-white rocks and serves as a pearl mirror for the playful glances of the Gandharva women; (1)
Then, following the descent of Reṇukā, once upon a time, at a place of silver-stone, in a pearl-mirror within the pleasure-garden of Gandharva women; || 1 ||
In that place where the trees consisted mostly of *mandārava*, *kula*, *aśoka*, and *mākanda* blossoms, and where the bees were swollen with drinking the flowing nectar of the *mallī* flowers; (2)
It abounds with various trees such as the *mandāra* and *mākanda*, and its bees are nourished by drinking the flowing nectar of *mallikā* blossoms.
On the banks of the Harinīmukha river, which were washed by the fragrance of saffron clusters and made lovely by the immediate warbling of flocks of sweet-voiced cuckoos; (3)

In that place where the currents of the river touch the banks filled with the fragrance of clusters of saffron flowers, and which is enchanting with the fifth musical note arising from the abundance of the warbling of flocks of cuckoos; || 3 ||
(23) In the mountain cave whose depths resound with the sweetness of the songs of kinnarīs, and whose interior is adorned by joyful throngs of the best of yogis; (4)
O Goddess, whose mountain caves are made resonant by the sweetness of the songs of Kinnara women, and whose regions are adorned by a multitude of Śiva-yogīs headed by the joyful Gaṇeśa! || 4 ||
O you whose mind is like the fragrant nectar of a golden lotus bud, resplendent with hundreds of lofty pillars made of gold! || 5 ||
In the Mānasa lake, which is filled with the fragrance of the interior of golden lotus buds and shines with the towering height of hundreds of golden pillars; || 5 ||
Its interior was illuminated by the rays from the flames of ruby lamps,
and at its gateway stood two erected gate-arches in the form of the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures.
In the inner apartments, illuminated by the rays of the crest-jewel resembling the flame of a gem-lamp,
there were two treasures, a conch and a lotus, fixed upon the door-arch and the pillars.
Its vast canopy was adorned with a sky-like expanse studded with pearls like stars,
and it possessed a succession of walls made of vaidūrya gemstone, discernible by their touch.
It was adorned with a great canopy-cloth like a forest of stars fashioned from pearls and gems, and possessed rows of walls made of beryl jewels characterized by touch-sensitive surfaces. || 7 ||
(24) In the jeweled pavilion atop the coral gables, where the anklets were set in motion by the footsteps of the moving ranks of Pramathas; || 8 ||
In the jeweled pavilion of the primary decorative gables, where the mountain ridges resounded with the footsteps of wandering Pramatha spirits.
He describes the Supreme Lord seated upon the throne with fifteen verses:
"The Supreme Lord is seated upon a divine jeweled throne, perfumed by the nectar of the *mandāra* flowers from the crowns of the gods who bow before him. (9)

In the center of that pavilion shines a lion-throne made of nine jewels, enchanting with the essence of celestial flowers from the crowns of the thirty-three crores of deities who are inclined to bow [before it]. || 9 ||
To that god who had taken his place on the throne, the Great Lord of all the worlds,
who is like a swan sporting in the lotus-forest of the Vedāntas— || 10 ||
Regarding the nature of the Supreme Lord who exists therein, he says "the Divine" and so forth:
He is playful by nature, the Lord of all worlds, and the royal swan sporting in the cluster of lotuses consisting of the Vedāntas. (10)
The syllable Om is a pearl within the oyster-shell of its own sublime qualities;
it is the abode of the entire collection of all auspiciousness and good fortune.
He is characterized by the virtue of renunciation, a pearl within the shell of the syllable *oṃ*, and the locus of the entire collection of all auspiciousness and good fortune. || 11 ||
It is the life-restoring medicine for living beings fainting from the poison of saṃsāra; it is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree of eternal luminosity, purity, and absolute liberation. (12)

He is the life-restoring medicine for living beings fainted by the poison of saṃsāra; he is the stainless wish-fulfilling tree that bestows supreme liberation through his own self-luminosity. || 12 ||
He is the bee for the nectar of infinite supreme bliss;
he is the flower-bud of the three worlds blooming upon the creeper of his own power.

He is a honey-bee tasting the nectar of the flavor of boundless supreme bliss; he is the bud-like flower of the three worlds, blossoming from the wish-fulfilling vine of the powers inherent within himself. || 13 ||
He is the expert in condensing the multitude of the jar-like cosmic eggs,
established in the position of the sovereign emperor over the entire circle of deities.
He is skilled in merging the entire multitude of cosmic eggs and is the sovereign emperor over the assembly of all deities, beginning with Nārāyaṇa. || 14 ||
His body possessed a luster that surpassed the combined radiance of ten thousand moons,
and his garments were turned golden-brown by the clusters of light from his ruby crown.
His splendor rivals the radiance of ten thousand moons;
his garments are variegated with the clusters of light from the fresh jewels set in his crown. || 15 ||
(26) Adorned with a crest by means of a digit of the moon, as delicate as a lotus fiber, and enchanting with an ear-ornament of auspicious flower buds. (16)
Adorned with a crest-jewel resembling a digit of the moon upon a tender stalk, he is enchanting with ear-ornaments like exquisite, most auspicious flower buds. || 16 ||
Adorned with a garland of severed heads strung together like a string of pearls,
his splendorous face rivals the beauty of the full moon.
He is resplendent with a garland of skulls interspersed with strings of pearls, and the beauty of his face rivals that of the full moon. || 17 ||
His three eyes are like a cluster of lotuses in full bloom at dawn;
his sprout-like lower lip is sweet with gentle smiles and measured speech.
In the morning, his three eyes are like a cluster of blossoming lotuses, and his sprout-like lower lip is enchanting with the playful grace of words accompanied by a gentle smile. || 18 ||
His makara-shaped earrings play against the region of his cheeks,
while his throat is stained by the blackness of the *kālakūṭa* poison.
His makara-shaped earrings swayed against the full expanse of his cheeks, and the stalk of his throat was stained by the blackness of the *kālakūṭa* poison. || 19 ||
He shone brilliantly with four arms that were like coral-tree branches, their sprout-like hands radiant with the luster of jewels, bracelets, and armlets.
His four sprout-like hands shine with jeweled bracelets and armlets, while his arms gleam like celestial kalpa-trees. || 20 ||
His arms were rendered meaningful by the embrace of Gaurī’s breasts;
he was marked by a golden sacred thread and wore garments of fine silk. (21)
His chest was fulfilled by the embrace of Umā’s breasts; he was marked by a golden sacred thread and wore garments of exceedingly fine silk. || 21 ||
He was embraced by a necklace of nine pearls hanging down from the region of his navel,
as if by the Gaṅgā descending from the crown of his head.
They were embraced by a necklace of nine pearls reaching down to their navels, as if by the Gaṅgā descending from their heads.
With his feet, whose beauty was made to bud by the radiance of jeweled anklets,
he stood before him, covering the crystal pedestal like the moon.
The meaning is that he stands covering the moonstone pedestal in front of the throne with his foot, whose splendor is made to blossom by the light of his jeweled anklets. || 23 ||
Having thus described Maheśvara, he now describes Bhavānī, who is seated upon his left lap,
in thirteen verses:
"By her who dwells on the left side, whose attire is dear to Maṅgala..."
By her whose essential nature is the collective union of the creation of all worlds. || 24 ||
Situated at her left side was she who is auspicious, of enchanting form, and the material cause for the creation of all worlds. || 24 ||
(28) [She is] one who manifests through the play of many powers in the form of will, knowledge, and action;
she illumines the principle of *vidyā*, and is devoid of separation [from Him]. (25)
She is the one who manifests the play of many powers such as will, knowledge, and action; she illumines the knowledge of the Self and is inseparable from Śiva. || 25 ||
With a line of forest fires burning the poisonous wilderness of saṃsāra, and with swarms of bees humming in delight at the fragrance of jasmine flowers in her braided hair; || 26 ||
She is a row of forest fires for burning the poisonous grove of saṃsāra,
and she makes the swarms of bees hum with the fragrance of the jasmine flowers in her braided hair.
With a lotus-face that rivaled the beauty of the full moon, and with the splendor of her smile that eclipsed the luster of her pearl-like nose-ornament; (27)
Her lotus-face rivals the splendor of the full moon, and she possesses the beauty of a gentle smile suffused with the abundant luster of her pearl-like nose. || 27 ||

With the playful movement of her outer corners of the eyes, which were framed by the luster of jeweled earrings, and with the beauty of her two eyes that put to shame the splendor of blue lotuses; (28)
Her playful sidelong glances, dancing in the midst of a pavilion formed by the movement of her jeweled earrings, surpass the beauty of blue lotuses with the splendor of her two eyes. || 28 ||
(29) With the playful arching of her eyebrows like the bow of the flower-armed god [Kāma],
and with the beauty of her lower lip that was a kinsman to the hue of the bandhūka flower; (29)
She is playful with the curved creeper-like brows of Māra’s bow,
and the beauty of her lower lip is as lovely as a bandhūka flower.
She surpassed the beauty of the conch of the bodiless god (Kāma) with the graceful movements of her throat,
and she outshone the garland of blue lotuses with the splendor of her two arms.
Her throat possesses the resonance of a victory-conch for the God of Love,
and the beauty of her two arms surpasses that of a garland of blue lotuses.
Her body was adorned with the beauty of perpetual youth,
and she bore the weight of breasts that were exceedingly firm, lofty, and full.
Her body was adorned with the beauty of perpetual youth, and she bore the weight of exceedingly firm and elevated breasts. || 31 ||
With her waist bound by a girdle resembling the fibers of a lotus stalk,
she bore the weight of hips like the high sandbanks of the river of passion.
Her waist region is exceedingly slender, resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk; she is resplendent with the weight of her hips, which are like the high sandbanks of the river of passion. || 32 ||
With the beauty of her delicate garments, which possess the hue of safflower blossoms;
with thighs like the trunks of plantain trees, full of the passion of a garden of love (33).
She shone with soft garments possessing the luster of safflower blossoms, and her thighs were like plantain trunks agitated by the passion of love in a garden. || 33 ||
Her lotus-feet were as delicate as the beauty of mango sprouts,
and her limbs were adorned with ornaments of steadfast auspiciousness and passion.
Her lotus-feet are delicate and charming like mango sprouts, and her limbs are adorned with ornaments that are auspicious and enduring.
Her body was made radiant by necklaces, anklets, and armlets;
she was a creeper of bliss for the eyes, the family lore of good fortune. (35)
Her body was adorned with pearl necklaces, anklets, and armlets; she was a creeper of delight for the eyes and the personified ancestral lore of good fortune. || 35 ||
His attendants from all sides beheld him of unprecedented form, seated together with Umā, the mother of the world’s web of beings.

The meaning is that the thirty-three crores of deities, beginning with Nārāyaṇa, worshipped the Supreme Lord of unprecedented form as he sat upon a divine throne together with this celestial maiden, the wife of the multitude of worlds, who was of such a nature. || 36 ||
Having thus described Pārvatī and Parameśvara, [the author] next describes, in twenty sūtras, the service being performed for them by those deities:
The Great Goddess Mahālakṣmī held over him a white sunshade, shaped like a lotus, translucent, and as radiant as the full moon.
The meaning is that Mahālakṣmī held the white parasol of that Supreme Lord—a parasol as stainless as a white lotus and a sibling to the full moon. || 37 ||
And at his side, Sarasvatī attended upon Mahādeva with the nectar-like lore of music, resplendent with the ringing of her lute.

The meaning is that Sarasvatī served Mahādeva in the presence of [the Lord], her hand adorned with a multitude of tinkling bracelets made of precious gems, and possessing the art of the essence of music, which was beautified by the resonant humming of the strings of the *upaniṣad*-radiant mandala-lute. || 38 ||
With her hand, from which bracelets produced a tinkling sound,
the wife of Upa-niṣad fanned Śaṅkara with the fan of the syllable Oṃ.
The meaning is that the bride, the Upaniṣads, fanned Śiva with the fan of the syllable *oṃ*, using her hand adorned with a multitude of jingling bracelets made of precious gems. || 39 ||
Divine maidens, with chowries waving in their hands and jeweled bracelets tinkling, attended upon that Lord from all sides.
"Divine maidens" means the wives of the gods, such as Indrāṇī and others; the rest is clear. || 40 ||
In the midst of those waving yak-tail whisks, his round face shone like a lotus amidst a flock of wandering royal swans.
The meaning is that Śiva’s countenance shone like a lotus in the midst of swaying chowries, as if it were a lotus in the midst of wandering royal swans. || 41 ||
The Vedas, along with their auxiliary branches and manifestations, served him through mantras,
as if bearing upon their crests that beloved crest-jewel with devotion. (42)

The meaning is that the Veda-purushas— the Rigveda and others— endowed with their limbs such as the phonetics (śikṣā) and possessing the glory of their ancillaries, carry upon their heads, which are in the form of the Upanishad portions, that beloved Supreme Lord like a crest-jewel, and thus they worshipped Him with devotion through the Praṇava mantra. || 42 ||
Certain women, who were like his very limbs, bearing his weapons and adorned with ornaments identical to his, waited upon that Lord.
The presiding deities of the limbs, bearing weapons identical to those of the Veda-Purusha and possessing ornaments similar to his, served that Śiva; such is the meaning. || 43 ||
Certain authorized officials, including Ananta and others, as well as the eight Vidyeśvaras, worshipped the God from all sides. (44)

The meaning is that certain supreme authorized officials— the eight Vidyeśvaras known by the names Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin— were worshipping the Supreme Lord on all sides. || 44 ||
Then Nandi, Mahākāla, Caṇḍa, Bhṛṅgin, and Riṭi;
then Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Puṣpadanta, Kapālī, and Vīrabhadraka. || 45 ||
Thus, these and other highly fortunate ones, possessing great strength and prowess, and endowed with unrestrained great courage, took refuge in that Maheśvara. (46)
This is clear. || 45-46 ||
Now he describes the hosts of Pramathas with five verses:
Those from whom the sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis] is withdrawn by their power;
those whose commands even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, fear to transgress. (47)

The meaning is that for those hosts of Pramathas, even the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) beginning with atomization (aṇimā) are insignificant compared to their spiritual perfection; and as for the gods such as Brahmā and others, they are characterized by fear at the mere thought of transgressing their commands. || 47 ||
Those who rejoice in their inner self at the embrace of the glory of liberation, for whom the conceptualization of the creation and destruction of the universe is an easy task; 48.

Those who, with their intellects turned inward, rejoice in the embrace of the Goddess of Liberation—for whom the conceptualization of the creation of the universe and so forth is easy, meaning it is trivial—[are the ones described]. || 48 ||

Those for whom the supreme power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which illuminates all things, [shines]— [the power of knowledge of Maheśa blazes in the form of the sun] (Svacchanda Tantra)— and for whom the riches of Hari, Brahmā, and the others are but mere droplets of bliss; 49.
Those whose supreme and most excellent power of knowledge illuminates all things, and for whom the riches of Brahmā and others are but mere fragments—meaning, drops—of bliss. || 49 ||
Those yogins devoted to yoga who long for their station, whose every resolve is a wish-fulfilling tree bearing the fruits they desire— (50) p. 34).

Those yogis who are intent on the yoga of Śiva long for and desire their state; the meaning is that their resolve is like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) endowed with the fruits of all desired objects. || 50 ||
For those in whom there exists no thought of wretchedness regarding their actions, time, and so forth;
for those whose preparations for valor are death-dealing even unto Death himself. (51)
Having attained the state of conformity, those Pramathas entered into Śiva.

Those for whom thoughts of wretchedness arising from accumulated karma, the elements, time, desire, and so forth do not exist; those whose engagement in valor is death unto even Death itself; having attained the state of similarity (sārūpya), those Pramathas approached Hara. The verbal root *bhaja* is used in the sense of "to serve. || 51 ||
Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra, and the others, their borders adorned with weapons, attended upon him from all sides as he held authority over the entire universe.
The meaning is that the thirty-three crores of deities, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra,
each adorned with rows of their own respective weapons, attended upon Śiva from all sides— he who possesses the authority over the creation of the universe. || 52 ||
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Dānavas,
Rākṣasas, Daityas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas,
with their unbounded hosts, took refuge in Mahādeva.
The twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the Yakṣas headed by Kubera, the Gandharvas headed by Hāhā, the Kinnaras headed by Aśvamukha, and the Dānavas headed by Bāṇa.
The meaning is that Rāvaṇa and other rākṣasas, Tāraka and other daityas, Ādinātha and other siddhas,
Maṇibhadra and other vidyādharas, and Śeṣa and other uragas, remaining with their armies unbroken, devoted themselves to Mahādeva. || 53 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Pulastya, Agastya, Śaunaka, Dadhīci, Gautama, as well as Ānanda, Śuka, and Nārada; || 54 ||
Upamanyu, Bhṛgu, Vyāsa, Pārāśara, Marīci,
and all such sages as these worshipped Nīlakaṇṭha.
Reflected in the stainless limbs of his attendants standing at his sides,
he shone as if displaying his own self, which is present within all.
Now, he demonstrates the sovereign activity of the Supreme Lord through ten aphorisms:
"For a moment, that Śambhu determines the share of the work for the gods;
for a moment, [for the kings of the Gandharvas... [according to the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*].
From the word *rājan*, with the addition of the suffix *ṭac* following the rules for compound endings, [the form is *rājñaḥ*]; thus, manifesting the science of music. || 57 ||
For a moment he engaged in conversation with the gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
for a moment he indulged in the playful charms of the dance of the fawn-eyed goddesses.
For a moment, he shows reverence for the recitation of the Vedas by Vyāsa and others;
for a moment, he fixes his gaze upon the bimba-fruit-like lower lip of the Goddess’s mouth. [Compare *umāmukhe*]
She directed her eyes toward her lower lip, which was like the fruit of the bimba. [Kuṭṭanīmata 59]
This is clear. || 59 ||
For a moment he watched the comic dance performed by Bhṛṅgin,
while Nandin stood with a staff in hand, the one authorized over all the Tantras.
He never left his side, being ever cognizant of his own intentions;
he would settle some who were urged by him, dismiss others with a movement of his eyebrows,
honor some in such a manner, and likewise direct others toward their duties.
He dismissed some with a gesture of his brow, sent others away, honored some by speaking kind words, restrained others, and instructed still others; the rest is clear. (60–61)
His commands are cherished by the crowns of all the lords of the worlds;
his power is unimpeded, and his form is charming with natural loveliness. 62.

The meaning is: he is the sovereign lord of all worlds, possessing the power of omniscience established upon the head of Brahmā, with unimpeded power, and a form captivating through his own innate beauty. || 62 ||
His body was adorned with the fragrance of perpetual youth,
and his mind was gladdened by the savor of tasting the nectar of his own spiritual power.

His body is adorned with the exuberance of youth, free from both increase and decay; his inner being is blossomed by the tasting of the essence of supreme bliss, characterized by the power inherent within himself. || 63 ||
(37) He is the ultimate limit of repose in innate, great sovereignty;
he has assumed manifold forms fashioned from stainless, great being. (64)

Regarding the term *svābhāvikī* (intrinsic): it refers to the ground culminating in the repose of supreme sovereignty (*mahaiśvarya*), characterized by omniscience that is free from adventitious conditions (*anaupādhika-sarvajñatā*) and so forth. As stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "The knowers of the sacred injunctions declare that the six limbs of the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) are omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, independence, eternally undiminished power, and infinite power. This is the stage reaching the ultimate limit of resting in great sovereignty.
He possesses many divine and auspicious forms created by his stainless and great power.
The Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha is the wish-fulfilling gem for those who have sought refuge; he is expert in severing the itching pride of the unbroken enemy’s staff-like arms. 65.

Skilled in lopping off the itching arms of countless enemies of the virtuous, and for that very reason the bestower of desired objects upon those with pure hearts, the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha shone forth—this is the ellipsis. || 65 ||
Having thus described the majesty of Śiva, he now indicates, through eleven verses, the greatness of Reṇukagaṇeśa’s devotion to Śiva:
"The leader of the Gaṇas, Reṇuka, who had entered into the assembly..."
He invited him to take betel-leaf, which is easily obtained as a mark of favor.

That Śiva, in the midst of the assembly, called out with his head—that is, he summoned—the principal or well-known Tantra, in order to grant a gift of betel-leaf easily obtained from that Reṇuka. This is the meaning.
Due to the agitation caused by his joy at being summoned by Śambhu,
Reṇuka bypassed Dāruka and went to the side of the Lord of the World.
“Pārśvam” means the left side. || 67 ||
Beholding him there, having leaped over the wooden barrier, the Lord, illuminating the majesty of his own devotees, spoke this: (68)
"Vibhuḥ" means "independent"; the rest is clear. || 68 ||
"O Renukā, you evil-minded woman! How is it that you have now transgressed [the rules] in the midst of this assembly? For Dāruka is indeed my devotee. (69)
Neglecting me is the cause of supreme misfortune for my devotees;
indeed, it destroys the lifespan, prosperity, lineage, and fame of embodied beings. (70)
The meaning is that it is well-known. || 70 ||
In ancient times, Yama, having disregarded my devotee Mārkaṇḍeya, found his body rendered subject to remembrance [as a corpse] due to being struck by my foot. (71)
Because his body had perished, the meaning is that he was one whose body was now only to be remembered; the rest is clear. || 71 ||
Because those two, Bhṛgu and Śaṅkukarṇa, were devoted to me,
Viṣṇu incurred their displeasure and became one with disheveled hair, passing through ten births.
"Vikeśaḥ" means one who has hair produced on the front part of the head. || 72 ||
(39) Having fought with my devotee Dadhīca, Janārdana previously suffered defeat, his wheel-weapon shattered. (73)
In former times, even Dakṣa, though he had performed the horse sacrifice, became goat-faced in the midst of the assembly for having insulted my devotees, the lords of the Gaṇas.
"Having disregarded" means "having cast aside. || 74 ||
In the past, even Time itself was consumed by me through my indifference, for I am Śveta, a devotee whose splendor is difficult to overcome. (75)
"Of irresistible splendor" means of blameless splendor. || 75 ||
In this way, many others as well were humiliated and slain for transgressing against my devotees; yet my devotees are difficult to overcome.
Having thus described the greatness of devotion, he points out the fruit of the fault of transgressing it:
"Because you disregarded my devotee Dāruka by transgressing him, O Renukā, you shall be born again on the surface of the earth. (77)
"This is Dāruka"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. || 77 ||
Then Reṇuka, being afraid regarding his birth, addressed Śiva with five verses:
40) "Thus was he addressed by the Supreme Lord, who proclaims the greatness of devotion..."
Having prostrated himself, that Reṇuka made a request to the Lord of Gods.

Having been addressed thus for the sake of the world's welfare, he said: "I have transgressed this [command] out of ignorance, through the confusion of being summoned by you; protect me!"—this is the meaning of his prayer. || 78 ||

Having entered a human womb that increases great suffering, [one encounters] that which brings about karma as the cause for the inequality of birth, lifespan, and experience; [as it is said in the *Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra*: "When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience"]. 79.
The birthplace of the servitude and wretchedness of all the gods,
beset by the three great miseries, and constrained by the rules of caste and stage of life.
Having abandoned service to your lotus feet, what else could I possibly dwell upon? (80)
The meaning is: "Having abandoned service to your lotus feet, am I worthy to remain having attained such a human birth? (79-80)
O Lord of Gods, O Ocean of Compassion, grant such grace that my human nature may no longer exist upon the circle of the earth. 81.

Having ascertained that Reṇuka, who had thus petitioned him, was his very own self, and having granted him fearlessness, the Lord Maheśvara demonstrates the purpose by means of six aphorisms: "Thus entreated by Reṇuka, the God Maheśvara..."
"Do not fear; for my devotees, whence shall there be any fear here? (82)
On the northern side of Śrīśaila, in the auspicious region of Triliṅga,
there is a certain very great village named Kollipāka. (83)
In the region of Trilinga, in the land of Andhra, there is a great village named Kollipāka. || 83 ||
"From the linga of me, who dwell there under the name Someśvara,
you shall manifest, untouched by human nature."
The meaning is that you shall manifest from my linga named Someśvara, located there in Vāsava, without being touched by human nature. || 84 ||
"Born from my own liṅga and the protector of my devotees—let all humans, filled with wonder, worship you by my command. (85)
You shall establish in the world of mortals this scripture devoted to my non-dualism, which is in accord with the Vedas and Vedānta, and which brings benefit to all. (86)
"O portion of the earth, manifest my incomparable majesty, and especially that of my devotees, in accordance with the path of the Vedas. (87)

Now, the words of the compiler, Śivayogin: Having spoken thus, the Blessed Supreme Lord rose from His auspicious seat and dismissed the gods, headed by Brahmā and Upendra, with a mere sign of his eyebrows.
Accompanied by Pārvatī and his beloved attendants, Reṇuka reached his own inner apartments and descended to the surface of the earth at the command of Paśupati.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Reṇuka’s Realization of the Earthly Realm," in the venerable *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*. 3.

The Blessed One reached his own inner apartments with his beloved and most trusted attendants, such as Nandi and others. Now, the meaning is that Reṇuka arrived at the region by the power of the command of Śiva, the Lord of Brahmā;
thus [it was stated] by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is a leader across the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Descent of Reṇuka to the World of Men," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, with eight verses, he describes the true nature of the Śiva-yogin Reṇukagaṇeśvara: Now, in the city named Kollipāka, within the region of the three lingas (Triliṅga)...
From the great liṅga Someśvara, that Reṇuka appeared.
Beholding him manifested from the Śiva-liṅga, all living beings born of the three liṅgas were struck with wonder at his exceeding splendor. || 2 ||
His entire body was smeared with ashes, adorned with excellent rudrākṣa beads,
crowned with matted locks, and his forehead marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra).
By the word "essence" (sāra), abundance is expressed. || 3 ||
He bore a mass of patched rags draped over his hips,
as well as a yogic staff, a vessel for ashes, and a water-pot.
It is gladdened by the supreme bliss of the thorough knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva,
and it has shaken off the cage of defects consisting of the latent impressions of all worldly existence.
[He is] the moon that causes the nectar-ocean of the Śiva-āgamas to swell,
and whose two lotus feet are hidden within the lotus of his own heart. (6)
He who knows the *Yāmādi* and *Yogatantras*, who is independent in all ritual actions,
and who is the crest-jewel of the entire assembly of the lineage of accomplished masters (*siddhas*).
It is the binding of the seal that accomplishes the Vīra-siddhānta;
it shatters the slaughter of all living beings by means of mere light alone.
By the term *vīrasiddhānta*, the *vīraśaiva-siddhānta* is meant; the rest is clear. || 8 ||
Then, having arrived at the mortal realm, this Reṇuka, being questioned by the people, gave an answer and went to the Malaya mountain; this is related in the five verses beginning with "tamapṛcchan":
"All the people, bowing down, asked him: 'Who are you?'"
Thus was the great yogi questioned by people whose minds were filled with wonder.
The lord of the Gaṇas named Reṇuka, who stood by the side of the wielder of the Pināka bow and was devoted to the great bliss of the non-duality of Śiva, replied.
For a certain reason, I have come here from the Śivaliṅga;
I am known by the name Reṇukasiddha, the leader of the lineage of Siddhas.
Wandering at will in this world, he is a protector of the Śiva-siddhānta, refuting the false scriptures of the Jains, Cārvākas, Buddhists, and others. (12)
Having spoken thus, while they looked on with eyes fixed upon the object,
he rose up and departed for Mount Malaya by way of the sky.

Now, with three verses, he describes Mount Malaya: "Where the gentle breeze causes the sprouts of the groves of fresh sandalwood to tremble, and which is filled with the essence of the unceasing songs of female serpents. (14)
It possesses a gentle breeze capable of breaking fresh śrīcandana trees and is permeated by the essence of the music performed by very thick-skinned female serpents. || 14 ||
The cave was scented by cardamom seeds shimmering as they were pulled out by young elephants,
and its interior was fragrant with nut-grass uprooted by the tusks of wild boars.
It was perfumed by the fragrance of cardamom seeds scattered by young elephants as they pulled them out,
and its riverbanks were made fragrant by the *bhadramusta* roots uprooted by the tusks of wild boars.

[The forest] where pairs of hunters were fast asleep, reclining upon beds of sandalwood petals, and which was colored by the pollen of the clusters of *mādhavī*, *mallikā*, and *jātī* jasmine flowers. || 16 ||
The couple of Kirātas were asleep upon a couch of camphor and plantain leaves;
[the wind] was colored by the pollen from clusters of flowers such as the *sevantī*; it went to the Malaya mountain—such is the connection with what precedes. (16)
46) Then, with eight verses, he describes the hermitage of Agastya:
There, in a certain place, amidst trees that provide space and bear flowers of all seasons—
He beheld the divine hermitage of the great sage Agastya.

On that Malaya mountain, which was filled with trees consisting of the blossoms of all seasons beginning with spring, he beheld—in some particular place—divine and enchanting hermitage of Agastya; "beheld" is the meaning. || 17 ||
It was adorned with groves of trees consisting mostly of Mandāra and sandalwood,
whose branches and treetops were covered with clusters of blossoms resembling the stars.

It was adorned—that is, beautified—by clusters of blossoms in the form of groups of stars merged at the tips of the branches, and by groves of trees such as the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), the sandalwood tree, and others. || 18 ||
[The groves] where herds of female deer rejoice at the taste of the water in their basins, which has been increased by the water from the jars brought by the daughters of sages. || 19 ||
Fragrant with the nectar trickling from golden lotuses, and enchanting with garlands of waves made resonant by the warbling of swans; || 20 ||
The faces of the directions were blinded by the light of the finest blue lotuses,
and the banks were marked by the traces of Lopāmudrā’s footsteps, which had fulfilled their purpose.
With waters as white as necklaces, camphor, and the laughter of Śiva, intended for the daily, occasional, and ritual baths of ascetics; (p. 47) 22.
Surrounded by lakes with steps made of exquisite jewels,
it was like another world of Brahmā, free from the enmity of living beings.
The great courtyard was fragrant with the smoke from the continuous stream of clarified butter being offered as oblations,
while the assembly of parrots commenced the expansion of the Vedic scriptures and the Shastras.
The meaning is "having approached the assembly of parrots. The rest is clear; the sense is that he saw such a hermitage of Agastya.
Then, he describes the sage Agastya with nine verses: seated in its midst, at the foot of a sandalwood tree...
The splendor of the sun was eclipsed by the shadow of his delicate petals. || 25 ||
With masses of matted hair tawny like lightning, their foreheads marked with the triple-ash line (tripuṇḍra), all their limbs smeared with ashes, and adorned with shimmering rudrākṣa beads; || 26 ||
It was surrounded by hosts of sages clad in garments of fresh bark and observing various religious observances, like Śaṅkara surrounded by the Pramathas.
With their intensely blazing masses of matted hair, which were like the tender sprouts of the tree of asceticism,
they resembled a fire with its flickering nets of flames that are like flashes of lightning. (28)

The meaning is that he was blazing like fire with masses of matted hair, which were like sprouts on the tree of asceticism produced by the grace of Śiva and resembled flickering streaks of lightning. || 28 ||
With a line marked by a triple-crested sectarian mark made from pure ashes,
he resembled the Himalaya mountain, whose rocky slopes are joined by the triple-streamed Ganges.

The meaning is that it was like the Himalaya mountain—marked on its summit with three white sectarian lines (tripuṇḍra)—with a portion of its rock surface connected to the flowing Gaṅgā by means of one-third [of its height]. || 29 ||
With all his limbs adorned with ashes like the moon fallen to the earth,
he was wearing fresh bark garments with a luster equal to the morning sun.
Like an ocean enveloped by the mass of flames from the submarine fire,
it was the abode of the entire collection of all sciences.
"Samālīḍha" means pervaded; such is the meaning. || 31 ||
Having humbled ordinary egoism, firmly established in the contemplation of Śiva,
and having rendered the web of the world as insignificant as a blade of grass, he was the ground for the arising of supernatural powers.
The meaning is: one who possesses an ego that has transcended the ordinary body and so forth;
"of the siddhis" means of the siddhis such as aṇimā and the rest. || 32 ||
The great yogi beheld the sage born from a water-jar, who was like the sun dispelling the darkness of delusion and the great tree of primordial awakening. (33)
The meaning is that [he saw] the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) of fundamental awakening, which is the knowledge of one's own true nature.
The meaning is that the teacher Reṇukācārya beheld—that is, he saw—Agastya, who was born from a water-jar (*kalaśasambhava*) and distinguished by such epithets as these. || 33 ||
Now, with four verses, he explains how Agastya honored that teacher Reṇuka upon his arrival:
"Having beheld that great adept who had arrived, the one born from a jar (Agastya)..."
He perceived with the eye of knowledge that leader of the Gaṇas known as Reṇuka.
Recognizing its power, he rose up suddenly with the exceedingly purifying water brought by Lopāmudrā in her hands.
He washed the feet of that Śiva-yogin.
Having observed the majesty and power of that Reṇuka, Agastya rose at that very moment, bowed, and seated him upon a seat; such is the meaning. || 35 ||
Having worshipped him according to the scriptures and following his instructions,
the sage, endowed with humility, sat down upon another seat.

The word "atha" (then) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having worshipped that Reṇuka according to the method prescribed in the scriptures, the sage Agastya, being endowed with devotion, sat down upon another seat in accordance with his command; such is the meaning. || 36 ||
Revaṇa, the crest-jewel of the Siddhas, addressed with peaceful words the best of sages, the lord of all radiant beings, as he sat there; this was the dialogue between Reṇukā and Agastya.

50) Then, with eight verses, the venerable Reṇuka initiates the discourse by first inquiring after Agastya’s welfare: "Are you proceeding without obstacles? Is your practice of daily observances constant?"
Or rather, O radiant Agastya, how could there be any obstacles for you? (38)

"O radiant Agastya, you proceed with auspiciousness and without obstacle; does your constant performance of religious observances continue without interruption?"—this is the meaning. "From where could there be those who cause hindrances or create obstacles for you?"—the sense is that there would be none. || 38 ||
The Vindhya mountain, which possessed the power to overstep the universe, has been restrained by you;
and Nahuṣa, through even a slight trace of your anger, immediately attained the state of a serpent. (39)
Vindhya, who possesses the playful grace of leaping over great mountains such as Mahāmeru, displays the sport of transcending the entire universe.
The Vindhya mountain was checked; the meaning is that it was made to fall to the ground. O Agastya, by even a mere fragment of your anger, Nahuṣa immediately attained the state of a serpent. || 39 ||
Previously, when you had merely sipped water, the oceans were reduced to mere mud;
the arrogant Dānava Vātāpi was digested in the fire of your stomach. (40)

Previously, when you had performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the oceans were reduced to nothing but mud; the meaning is that the arrogant and haughty Dānava Vātāpi, an asura named Vātāpi, was digested by the fire of your stomach. || 40 ||
O Agastya, you who possess a radiance equal to that of Agastya, who is your equal as the performer of such diverse deeds that surpass all the world? 41.

The meaning is: you are the creator of such diverse works that surpass all people; thus, while performing these deeds, who is there, O Agastya, whose power is equal to yours? The meaning is: none at all. || 41 ||
They praise you alone as being devoted to the manifestation of the supreme bliss of non-dual Śiva, and as being by nature free from attachment.
p.
52) Here, the people regard you alone as one who is intent upon manifesting the light of supreme bliss through the realization of the non-duality of Śiva.
The meaning is that they declare it to be devoid of any connection with primordial nature (prakṛti). || 42 ||
To the question "How so?", he says here:
"In the past, the six-faced son of Himavat spoke to you the scripture named Śivadharmottara, which was uttered by the Lord. (43)
The son of Haimavatī means the delight of Pārvatī. || 43 ||
O great sage Agastya, through you, the devotion to Śiva— which removes the fear of this most terrible saṃsāra— has become established in the world, O King.

The meaning is that, through the greatness of the teaching on the *skandhas*, devotion to Śiva—which destroys the fear of this exceedingly cruel saṃsāra—has become perfectly manifest in the world of mortals by you, O King. || 44 ||
