The words of Sage Agastya:
Now Agastya describes his own good fortune arising from the sight of his teacher Reṇukācārya in ten aphorisms:
Having heard these words of the Siddha, the bull among sages spoke with deep-toned speech and full of devotion.
I alone am always to be cherished by the lords of sages; for whom else could the attainment of the arrival of you all be possible, were it not for me? (46)
"I alone am always to be cherished and praised by the lords of sages; the reason for this is your arrival.
The excellence of your coming belongs to no one other than me; thus, the sense is that I alone am to be praised by all. (46)
Today the knowledge of Śiva has become firm; my ascetic practice has become firm;
by the merit of beholding you, my status as a king among sages has become firm. (47)
For embodied beings bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra and rendered unconscious, your glance is the auspicious medicine for their complete restoration to life. (48)

For living beings who have been bitten by the serpent of the threefold suffering and have consequently fainted, His glance is a beneficial, auspicious medicine for restoration to life; that is to say, it is the *sañjīvana* elixir.
The great fire of the threefold afflictions that scorches all the world is extinguished for embodied beings by tasting even a drop of water from your lotus feet. (49)
Then, in response to the inquiry "Who am I?", he says: "I know you as Reṇuka, the Lord of Gaṇas, beloved of Śiva, who has descended to this earth with the desire to bestow grace upon me. (50)
For perfected beings such as you, whose births have been destroyed by awakening, such activity in the world serves to bring about the welfare of others. (51)
"Activity" (pravṛtti) means movement; the meaning is that it is precisely of such a nature as consisting in the favoring of others. || 51 ||

(54) O Omniscient One, I desire to hear from your own mouth that which is in accordance with the sacred tradition of the Siddhānta; tell me directly the Śaiva doctrine that accomplishes all goals. (52)
It brings immediate success to men, is served by all the lords of yogis, is untouched by those of evil conduct, and is accepted by the knowers of the Vedas;
it is the propagator of the great tradition of the supreme awakening into the identity of Śiva and the Self. (53)
"Unsmelled by those of evil conduct, such as the Jains and Buddhists" means not accepted by them.
"The direct identity with Śiva" means obtained through the tradition of knowledge regarding the oneness of the individual soul and Śiva, which is perceptible to all the world.

"I wish to hear from your own lips, O Omniscient One, the Śaiva Siddhānta distinguished by such specific characteristics as these; please tell it to me out of compassion—this is the meaning. || 52-53 ||
Having spoken this compendium of the Siddhāntas, which brings great benefit to all the world and disregards external tantras, you,
O divine yogin, ought to immediately grant us our purpose.
To me, whose doubts have arisen from hearing various scriptural traditions.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Episode of the Vision of Reṇukā and Agastya," in the illustrious Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi.
O divine yogin, O Revanasiddheśvara, who are endowed with the captivating yoga of Śiva, you have disregarded external tantras and refuted the systems of the Jains,
Buddhists, and others; this compendium of the Siddhānta is a source of great benefit for all the world and a benefactor to all living beings.

Having stated and taught the essence of the doctrines approved by the Vedas, you ought to instantly fulfill my purpose— meaning that you are worthy to do so— for I am one whose doubts have arisen from hearing various scriptures, having encountered uncertainty through listening to many Āgamas beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula. || 54 ||

Thus ends [the section] in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Śrīmaritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. (p.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Vision of Reṇukā and Agastya. || 4 ||

The Fifth Chapter: Thus, immediately after hearing the words of Agastya’s petition, the venerable Reṇukācārya, the sovereign lord of Śiva’s hosts, descended to the world of mortals solely for the purpose of propagating that scripture.
For a moment, with an unswerving mind,

he performed in his heart the auspicious rite consisting of meditation on Śiva— which has the power to pacify the host of obstructive deities that hinder the commencement and completion of the Śiva scriptures— and then spoke the following reply.
Although the meaning of this is already clear from the introductory statement that "Śivayogin explains," a slight distinction is indicated by way of the formal interpretation:
"Then, having heard the words of Agastya, Reṇuka, the leader of the Gaṇas..."
Having meditated for a moment upon Mahādeva together with Ambā, he, being composed in mind, spoke.
Having heard the words of Agastya, Reṇuka, the leader of the Gaṇas, for a moment became one-pointed in mind; he [beheld] Sāmba together with Ambā, the Mother of the World,
by means of the Power of the Sky of Consciousness— characterized by the state of equilibrium between consciousness and action inherent in his own self, whose primary form is the Praṇava of Śakti.

The meaning is that, having meditated upon Mahādeva—who is present together [with her], who is a mine of many jewels of qualities such as playfulness and the desire for victory, and who is the Supreme Brahman in the form of a radiant *liṅga*—she articulates his reply. || 1 ||
O Agastya, tiger among sages, you who have reached the further shore of all the scriptures;
I shall declare the Siddhānta which bestows the knowledge of Śiva—listen with reverence.

O Agastya, tiger among sages, supreme among munis, who has reached the further shore of all Āgamas and has mastered the entirety of the Nigamas and Āgamas— by virtue of your mastery of the Śiva-śāstras—
I shall proclaim the Siddhānta, the Siddhānta-śāstra, which imparts the knowledge of Śiva and illuminates the independent non-dual knowledge of Śiva.
The meaning is: being respectful and full of affection, you should listen. || 2 ||
57) Now, in order to demonstrate the superiority of his own system, he states that there are indeed many systems, owing to differences in preference:
"O Agastya, there are indeed many well-known systems according to the diversity of tastes."
They are characterized by divergent conduct and propound divergent meanings. || 3 ||

O Agastya, it follows that there are many established doctrines (siddhāntas) which, due to differences in perspective and the diverse inclinations of sages such as Kapila, Patañjali, and others, teach different systems of conduct and different objects of knowledge; the meaning is that these are indeed renowned and well-known. || 3 ||
To the question "Which are they?", he says:
"Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are authoritative and are not to be undermined by logical arguments. (4)

Sāṃkhya is the system of Kapila, which establishes two categories of reality characterized by primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*); in that system, there is no acceptance of a Lord (*īśvara*). Yoga is the science of Yoga composed by Patañjali;
in that system, there is the acceptance of a Lord, and it sets forth the eight limbs beginning with the difficult-to-perform restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*).
The Pāñcarātra, composed by Vāsudeva, is Vaiṣṇava;

it establishes the three categories—consciousness, the unconscious, and the Lord—by means of teaching such practices as the wearing of the heated seal (*taptamudrā*), which are constituent parts of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Viṣṇu. The Pāśupata, composed by Śiva, is...
It elucidates the three categories characterized as the individual soul (*paśu*), the bond (*pāśa*), and the Lord (*pati*). The Vedas are His breath;

thus, the Vedas—consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—are the effortless, natural breath of Śiva, and for that reason, they are uncreated. Following the first section (*pūrva-kāṇḍa*) of those [Vedas], there is the system known as Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, proclaimed by Jaimini.

These scriptures—which establish the primacy of rituals such as sacrifice and are devoid of a Lord—are authoritative, they are valid means of knowledge, and they are not subverted by reasonings; they cannot be refuted by logical arguments. They are: the Three Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Paśupati-mata, and Vaiṣṇava.
The meaning is that this is because it is well known from the *Mahimnaḥstotra*. || 4 ||
(58) Now, one might ask: "How is the authority of these [scriptures] established? To this he replies:
"O Great Sage, the Veda is the primary authority for all [systems], such as Sāṃkhya and the rest."
It is certain that their authority derives from their conformity with the Vedas. || 5 ||

The meaning is that among all those systems such as Sāṃkhya and others whose characteristics have been described, the Veda is the primary and principal authority because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). It has been determined by those learned in the scriptures that the validity of these doctrines of Sāṃkhya and others is established through their conformity with the Veda and their being rooted in the Veda.
Now, one might ask: "Since the Sāṃkhya and other scriptures also have the Veda as their source, what is the distinction of the Śaiva scripture from them?
To this, he says: "O Sage, [the same applies] to the Pāñcarātra, the Sāṃkhya, and likewise to Yoga."
The Śaiva doctrine, which abides in a single portion of the Veda, is considered to be composed of the Veda.
Here, by the word "and" (ca), the two [other systems] that are not distinct [from the Pāñcarātra] are included.
Thus, it is held that the five established doctrines, such as the Pāñcarātra defined by the aforementioned characteristics, are based on a single portion of the Veda;
and that the Śaiva Śiva-śāstra consists of the Veda and has the nature of the Veda itself.
The meaning is that it has been accepted by those who know the scriptures and traditional lore. || 6 ||
This being the case, he states that because it consists of all the Vedas, the Śaiva Tantra is superior to Sāṃkhya and the other systems:
"O Great Sage, because it follows all the Vedas, the Śaiva Tantra excels over Sāṃkhya and the others, which abide in only a single portion of the Vedas. (7)
59) Here, by the word *tantra*, the treatise (*śāstra*) is meant. The rest is clear. || 7 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since it is perceived that the Śaiva Tantra was merely imagined by someone, how can it possess authority? To this, he says:
"That which is called the Śaiva Tantra, known as the Siddhānta, was uttered by Śiva."
Because it embodies the meaning of all the Vedas, its authority is always equal to that of the Vedas themselves.

The Śaiva Tantra is that which was spoken by Śiva; it is proclaimed as being called the Siddhānta because it is the very essence of the meaning of all the Vedas and the essential nature of the meaning of all the Upaniṣads. The meaning is that, like the Veda, it is an authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa) due to its being free from temporal distinctions at all times. || 8 ||
The Āgamas have been proclaimed in many ways by Śiva, the Supreme Self, according to their divisions as Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula. (9)
By the Supreme Self, Śiva, many scriptures have been proclaimed through various divisions, such as the Śaiva, the Pāśupata, the Soma, and the Lākula. || 9 ||
Now, one might ask: since the Tantras spoken by Śiva are so numerous, why are they all authoritative like the Vedas? To this he says:
"Among them, the Śaiva Tantra, which is divided into four parts, is determined to be the most excellent of all."
The Left (vāma), the Right (dakṣiṇa), and the Mixed (miśra), which is designated as the Siddhānta. || 10 ||

Among those, it is certain to all who know the Āgamas that the Śaiva Tantra consists of four divisions. To the question "What are those divisions?", he says: "Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Miśra, and that which is called Siddhānta. (10)
Now, he reveals its essential nature with the words beginning "śakti": (p.
60) "The [aspect] called Vāmā is dominated by Śakti; Dakṣiṇa consists of Bhairava."
The Siddhānta, which is beyond the seven Mothers, is a synthesis approved by the Vedas.

The Vāmākhya-tantra is centered on Śakti; the Dakṣiṇa-tantra is centered on Bhairava; the Miśra-tantra is centered on the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī; and the Siddhānta—known as the Śaiva-tantra—is in accord with the Vedas. By this [it is shown that] it is indeed the Śaiva-tantra called Siddhānta that is in accord with the Vedas.
Because it is accepted by the Vedas, it is authoritative like the Veda; because it is not accepted by the learned (śiṣṭa), it is indicated that it does not possess such authority. || 11 ||
Now, one might ask: how can the Śaiva tantra known as Siddhānta be considered consistent with the Veda? To this, he says:
"Because it proclaims the dharma of the Veda, the Śiva-āgama known as Siddhānta is said to be consistent with the Veda, since it does not contradict what is outside the Veda. (12)

The meaning is that the Śiva-āgama, known as the Siddhānta, is said to be in accord with the Vedas because it establishes dharmas such as the wearing of the ash-mark (bhasma-liṅga) as declared in the Vedas, and because it refutes the views of those outside the Vedic fold, such as the Jains and the Cārvākas. || 12 ||
Thus, because it is authorized by the Veda, the Siddhānta is an authoritative means of knowledge just like the Veda; so he says:
"The identity of the Veda and the Siddhānta exists because they both set forth the same subject matter;
the wise should always recognize that the authority of these two is equal. (13)

The meaning is that because of the statement in the *Vīrāgama*, "Whatever is seen in all the Vedas, all that is in the Śiva-āgama," the Siddhānta is also authoritative just like the Veda, since the Siddhānta and the Veda have the same objective. || 13 ||
Now, as to what is propounded in this Śiva-āgama known as Siddhānta, he says:
"In the great Tantra called Siddhānta, beginning with the Kāmika and proclaimed by Śiva, the supreme Vīraśaiva doctrine is set forth in its northern section. (14)

In the great Tantra called Siddhānta spoken by Śiva—which begins with the Kāmika and ends with the Vātula—in its Uttarabhāga (latter part), the supreme and most excellent Vīraśaiva doctrine is set forth and taught. By this, it is indicated that the [ordinary] Śaiva doctrine was taught in the Pūrvabhāga (former part). || 14 ||
(p. 61) Now, he also demonstrates the term *vīraśaiva* in the *Vedaśiras*:
"Because there is a special delight (*viśeṣād ramaṇam*) in the knowledge (*vidyā*) whose nature is Śiva."
Therefore, these highly fortunate ones are remembered as Vīraśaivas. || 15 ||

Because there is a special delight (*rati*) in that knowledge which is to be known through the Vedānta— according to the *Sūtagītā* statement, "Knowledge born from the Vedāntic texts [is established] in that Vidyā which is of the nature of Śiva and of the nature of Brahman"—
therefore, these fortunate ones (*mahābhāgāḥ*) who possess such delight therein are the most excellent Vīraśaivas.
The meaning is that they are remembered. || 15 ||
Now, he demonstrates the etymological derivation of the term *vīraśaiva* even according to the Vedas and Āgamas:
"By the word *vī* is meant *vidyā*, which brings about the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*).
Those Śaivas who delight in that [knowledge] are considered *vīraśaivas*. (16)

The knowledge (*vidyā*) that brings about the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*), which illuminates the identity of Śiva and the *jīva* in the form of the *liṅga* and the body (*aṅga*), is called "Vī" by the learned; this is the meaning. Since the verbal root *vī* is used in the senses of movement, pervasion, procreation, beauty, existence, and eating, those devotees of Śiva (*śaiva*) who take delight (*ramante*) in that knowledge are called Vīraśaivas.
"Matāḥ" means "saṃmatāḥ," that is, they are approved or esteemed. || 16 ||
Now he provides the etymological derivation of the term *vīramāheśvara*:
"Because he delights in knowledge (*vidyā*) and abandons the delusion (*māyā*) to be discarded like a dog, by this very definition he is known as a *vīramāheśvara*. (17)

Because, for the purpose of establishing the connection between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, one should delight in the *vidyā* that reveals the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*), and should abandon— like a dog— one should ward off *māyā*, which takes the form of the world and is to be discarded; this is precisely according to the etymological derivation (*nirukta*) through the utterance of the initial syllables found in the words "one," "two," "three," and so forth.
The meaning is that he is remembered by the name Vīramāheśvara, which is significant according to its literal sense. || 17 ||
In this way,
[it applies] to the words *veda-anta-siddha* (established by the Vedānta), *vīra-śabda-siddhānta-prasiddha* (renowned in the Vīra-śabda-siddhānta), and the words *śaiva* and *maheśvara*.

Having thus distinguished [the subject], he clarifies the nature of Siddha-Vīraśaiva and Vīramāheśvara—established in the crest of the Vedāgamas—through six aphorisms. Therein, first, he explains how the word "Vīra" is well-known in the Vedānta: [The text continues with the following: vīra iti śabdo vedānte prasiddhaḥ | yathoktaṃ śrutiṣu— "vīro vai nāma eṣa yo 'yaṃ dakṣiṇe 'kṣan puruṣaḥ |" iti | tathā ca— "vīro vai nāma eṣa yo 'yam uttare 'kṣan puruṣaḥ |" iti | evam ādiṣu śrutivākyeṣu vīraśabdena paramātmano 'bhidhānād asau vedāntaprasiddha iti jñeyam ||1|| The word "Vīra" is well-known in the Vedānta. As it is stated in the Śrutis: "The one who is this person in the right eye is indeed named Vīra. And likewise: "The one who is this person in the left eye is indeed named Vīra. Since the Supreme Self is denoted by the word "Vīra" in such scriptural passages, it should be understood that this term is well-known in the Vedānta. ||1||
The knowledge produced by the Vedānta is celebrated as "Vidyā" (wisdom);
he who delights in that Vidyā is called a "Vīra" (hero). || 18 ||

The meaning is that, according to the statement in the *Sūtagītā*, "knowledge born from the Vedānta texts," knowledge is that which is revealed by the Vedānta texts; he who delights in that is a hero (*vīra*). || 18 ||

Thus, by means of a half-verse, he clarifies both the Śaivas— who are established in the knowledge of the principle of Śiva according to the Siddhānta and preceded by the word "vīra" as well-known in the Vedānta— and the Māheśvaras— who are established in the ritual acts pertaining to the principle of Maheśvara.
The rites of the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras should be performed according to the sequence of internal and external [levels];
for Śiva and Maheśvara are not absolutely different here. (19)

By the Śaivas—that is, by the Vīraśaivas, so the meaning is—and by the Māheśvaras—that is, by the Vīramāheśvaras—the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is to be performed both internally and externally; this is the remainder [of the sense] that ought to be done. This being the case, Śiva is the partless (niṣkala), while Maheśvara is the manifest (sakala) Śiva.

And [the term] "Sadāśiva" is used in the sense of persistence. Here, in the list of names and qualities such as "Śiva," "the Trident-bearer," and "Maheśvara," just as there is no difference whatsoever between them, so too there is no absolute distinction between those two. || 19 ||
Now, regarding the question of what kind of internal and external worship of the *liṅga* is prescribed for the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras, he says:
"In whatever manner they exist, the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras are not different."
Those men who take refuge in Śiva and are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge are called Śaivas. || 20 ||

Likewise, the Śaivas—those connected with Śiva—and the Vīraśaivas, as well as the Māheśvaras—those connected with Maheśvara—and the Vīramāheśvaras do not differ; they are not distinct. Here, although Sadāśiva possesses adjuncts (upādhi), according to the manner that will be explained, those adjuncts...
The sense is that because the quality of *sattva* predominates, there is no absolute difference between those two, as they are not distinct from one another.
Among those who have taken refuge in Śiva, those men who are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge...
The meaning is that those Śaivas who possess devotion toward the worship of the *cilliṅga* situated within the heart-lotus are Vīraśaivas. || 20 ||
Those on earth who are devoted to ritual sacrifices are known as Māheśvaras;
therefore, the Śaivas should remain within, while the Māheśvaras stay outside.

Those devoted to ritual sacrifice (*karmayajña*), who take delight in the worship of the *kriyā-liṅga* held in their lotus-like hands, are known on earth as *Māheśvaras* and *Vīramāheśvaras*; this means they are well-renowned. Therefore, the *Śaivas* and *Vīraśaivas* should perform [the worship] within the lotus of the heart.

The meaning is that they should practice the dharmas taught in the stage of oneness with Śiva (śivaikyasthala), which is described in the section on refuge (śaraṇa) for those who bear the mark of the vital breath (prāṇaliṅgin) as expounded in the Jñānakāṇḍa. As for the Māheśvaras and Vīramāheśvaras, they should practice the dharmas taught in the stage of grace (prasādisthala) for the devoted Māheśvaras who abide in the external Karmakāṇḍa.
The ellipsis "they should perform" is to be supplied. Knowledge is primary, but not devoid of action; action is primary, but not devoid of consciousness.
Therefore, success arises only from both together, for a bird does not fly on only one wing.
Knowledge devoid of action does not exist, nor does action devoid of knowledge;
the blind man was burned without seeing, and the lame man was burned even while seeing.
From such statements as these, it should be understood that the knowledge and ritual action of the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras are identical;
however, they differ merely in their preference for external versus internal worship. || 21 ||

The Vīraśaivas, however, are of six divisions according to the distinctions in their ritual practices (*sthaladharma*); they are described by those who have mastered the scriptures through the conventional designations of *bhakta* and so forth. (22)

Now, those known as Vīramāheśvaras—meaning the well-known Vīraśaivas—are said by those who have mastered the scriptures to possess six divisions, being of six kinds; this is because they differ according to the distinctions of their local duties (*sthaladharma*) ranging from the stage of the devotee (*bhakta*) up to the realization of oneness with Śiva, and because of the differences in their internal conduct (*sthalācāra*) ranging from the physical body (*piṇḍa*) up to the state devoid of objective cognition (*jñānaśūnya*). This is the meaning. || 22 ||
(p. 64) Now, he shows the divisions of that scripture: "But the scripture of the Vīraśaivas is sixfold according to the distinction of the *sthala*s."
Due to the connection with different categories of dharma and due to the distinction among those entitled [to practice]. || 23 ||

The scripture of the Vīraśaivas, however, is distinguished by six types [of divisions]: by the distinction of *sthala* (locations/contexts), by the association with different *dharma*s according to the distinction of *sthala*, by the connection with the differences in the right conduct (*sadācāra*) prescribed for each *sthala*, and by the distinction of the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), such as the difference between devotees (*bhakta*) established in the various *sthala*s. The meaning is that it is "sixfold," i.e., consisting of six modes. Of this...

The qualified seeker (adhikārī) is a devotee established in the dharma of Vīraśaivism who desires liberation; the purpose (prayojana) is supreme liberation in the form of oneness with Śiva, attainable through devotion to Śiva; the subject matter (viṣaya) is the knowledge of the one hundred and one stages (sthalas); and the relationship (sambandha) between this knowledge and the scripture is that of the revealed and the revealer.
Thus, this treatise possesses the fourfold connection.
Now he defines the sequence of the stages:
"First the stage of the devotee (bhakta-sthala) is proclaimed, then the stage of the Great Lord (māheśvara-sthala);
the stage of grace (prasādi-sthala) is another, and after that the stage of the vital-organ-liṅga (prāṇaliṅga-sthala). (24)
This is clear. || 24 ||
O Agastya, I shall first describe the Bhaktasthala;
listen with a concentrated mind to its various subdivisions as well. (25)
p.

65) Now, regarding the aforementioned topics, the connection [of the verse] is as follows: "I shall speak of the stage of the devotee (bhakta-sthala) which follows in sequence, as well as its intermediate subdivisions; listen. || 25 ||
Now, he defines the stage of the devotee (bhaktasthala):
"He in whom devotion to Śiva has arisen is called a devotee (bhakta). Liberation through the duties to be performed by him is considered the stage of the devotee. (26)

He in whom devotion related to Śiva has arisen is called a devotee (*bhakta*). Regarding that devotee, the statement concerning the duties to be performed—the Vīraśaiva duties to be practiced—is as follows:
"Good conduct, devotion to Śiva, and single-mindedness toward the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*."

"Devotion to the mark and the refuge is the unsurpassed stage of the devotee (bhaktasthala). Such instruction and so forth is considered, that is to say, agreed upon as the "stage of the devotee. || 26 ||
Now, having stated that there are fifteen intermediate stages within the stages of *piṇḍa* and so forth, he enumerates them:
"The excellent teachers declare that there are fifteen intermediate stages here:
the state of *piṇḍa*, the knowledge of *piṇḍa*, and the worthlessness of the qualities of transmigratory existence. (27)

Initiation, the wearing of the *liṅga*, as well as the application of sacred ash, followed by the wearing of *rudrākṣa* beads and likewise the recitation (*japa*) of the five-syllabled mantra. || 28 ||
The practice of the path of devotion, the worship of the Guru and the Linga, as well as the acceptance of the grace (prasāda) of these [deities] and of the Jaṅgama. || 29 ||

In this regard, those who have reached the further shore of all the scriptures have declared that three kinds of giving are taught: that which is conditioned, that which is unconditioned, and that which is innate.
These [stages] must be diligently practiced by a devotee of Śiva.
Regarding this "place of devotion" (bhaktasthala), they say there are fifteen excellent sub-locations (avāntarasthala).
As to what those are, it says: "Piṇḍata," and so forth. These are Piṇḍasthala and Piṇḍajñānasthala.
The stage of what is to be abandoned in saṃsāra; the stage of the guru’s compassion characterized by initiation; the stage of wearing the liṅga; the stage of wearing sacred ash;
the stage of wearing rudrākṣa beads; the stage of the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra; the stage of the path of devotion;
and the stage consisting of both the worship of the guru and the liṅga.
66) This is the stage characterized by the threefold perfection consisting of the worship of the mobile [deity];
it is the stage of the fourfold essence characterized by the acceptance of the grace of these three. Herein lies the stage of the devotee (*bhakta*).

The meaning is that these three aforementioned stages— namely, the stage with attributes (*sopādhika*), the stage without attributes (*nirupādhika*), and the innate stage (*sahaja*)— constitute the fifteen internal stages which must be practiced by a devotee of Śiva. || 30 ||

Piṇḍasthala is the pinnacle of all the Vedas and Āgamas; it is the locus of the six limbs of the Siddha [system], and within the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), it encompasses the one hundred and one stages beginning with the state of being a physical body (piṇḍatā) and ending with the state of being devoid of knowledge (jñānaśūnyatā), which are to be practiced accordingly.
He defines the primary state of being established in the body (piṇḍastha): "When the cage of sins has been worn away by merits accumulated over many births... (31).
The embodied soul with a purified internal organ is designated by the word "piṇḍa" (body).

The meaning is that when the accumulation of sins committed through the actions of mind, speech, and body has been destroyed by the merits performed over many lifetimes, the Self possessing a stainless internal organ is called by the term "piṇḍa."

"Because of the connection with karma in another future birth, that very same individual soul [remains]," according to the Śruti. In the manner described, that very same individual soul, whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified, is what is designated as the "body" (*piṇḍa*). Here, the state of the body (*piṇḍasthala*) is the means (*sādhana*), while the hundred states beginning with the knowledge of the body (*piṇḍajñāna*) to be described hereafter are the goals (*sādhya*). Both eyes also...

Just as seeing is one and both feet are one in the act of walking, so too, there is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self; the meaning is that the physical locus (piṇḍasthala), which is taught by the Śruti and Āgama as "there is no deity higher than the Self," should be known as one through the instruction of the Guru and one's own experience. || 31 ||
(67) Now, as to whether this entity denoted by the word *piṇḍa* is common to the world or distinct from it, he says: "In this phenomenal world produced from Śiva and Śakti, it is conceptualized. (32)

"One who has an abundance of merit, whose sins are exhausted, and whose self is pure is called *piṇḍa*. Behold this world, produced from Śiva and Śakti, marked with the *liṅga* and the *bhaga*," according to the words of Vyāsa;
thus, in this phenomenal world produced from Śiva and Śakti, [one becomes pure] through the preponderance of merit and the destruction of sin.
The meaning is that the person designated as the "body" (piṇḍa), whose inner organ is pure and stainless, becomes distinguished—that is, superior—compared to other people. || 32 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is this [deity] named Piṇḍa Śiva himself, or is he something else? To this, he says:
"Śiva alone is directly composed of consciousness and bliss, and is all-pervading. (33)
It is free from conceptual construction, formless, devoid of qualities, and beyond phenomenal proliferation;
yet, due to its connection with beginningless ignorance, a portion of it is called the "individual soul" (jīva).

Consisting of consciousness and bliss, he is autonomous light; for this very reason, he is directly manifest to all the world as "I," untouched by space, time, and so forth, according to such Vedic texts as, "The cowherds saw him" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 16.7). He is all-pervasive, full, free from conceptual construction, and devoid of duality; therefore, he is beyond the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañca*).

The Supreme Self (Paramātman) alone is Śiva—devoid of the illusory expansion (māyika-prapañca), formless (nirākāra) meaning devoid of forms such as blue or yellow, qualityless (nirguṇa) meaning devoid of the illusory qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, and full of many auspicious attributes such as unimpeded will; for the Śruti states: "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). There is nothing other than Śiva.
The meaning is that there is no separate ontological entity. Nevertheless, due to the connection with beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*),

and like the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, it is a portion [of that] resulting from the connection with *māyā*— which is imagined as beginningless by its own power of self-reflection (*svavimarśaśakti*)— as will be explained hereafter.

The meaning is that the "individual soul" (jīva)—named after the act of living—is a portion of Śiva, whose nature is the equilibrium of knowledge and action, characterized by consciousness and activity. This is because of the Lord’s statement: "In the world of living beings, My own eternal portion has become the individual soul" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.7), and because of the Sūtra: "A portion [of the Lord], on account of the various designations" (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.43).
And because of the abiding within the Brahman-thread (Brahma-sūtra). 33–34.
Now, as to how Śiva abides within that inner self, he says:
"Established in the various distinctions of species such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth...
The illusory Maheśvara, residing within their hearts, is their impeller.
That living soul (jīva), though situated within the distinctions of various species such as gods, animals, and humans, [is as follows]:
there are sixteen hundred thousand gods, nine hundred thousand humans;
likewise, aquatic creatures, birds, and wild beasts each number one million.
Reptiles, both mobile and immobile, number eleven lakhs;
and eight lakhs are those that take seven births.

Here, "sarīsṛpas" refers to reptiles and "sarpas" to snakes; the rest is clear. Thus, according to the statement of Skanda, the meaning is that he resides amidst the various distinctions of species such as gods, humans, and serpents. Maheśvara is the Supreme Śiva characterized by the aforementioned definition, as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.10): "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara."
From scripture: being accompanied by the power of *māyā* characterized as previously described, He is the impeller of those aforementioned individual souls;
being the impeller of the mental modifications regarding merit and demerit, He "resides in the heart," meaning He abides within their innermost core. || 35 ||

In such a state, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are not distinct from Brahman; rather, he states that the status of being a soul and the status of being a Lord are merely superimposed upon Brahman.
Just as water is present in the moonstone, as fire in the sunstone,
and as a sprout is established within a seed, so too does Śiva abide within the self.
The meaning is that Śiva exists within the individual soul (jīva) by way of the relation of identity (tādātmya). || 36 ||

An objection may be raised: "Since the status of being a reflection belongs to the reflection because it is produced by limiting adjuncts such as a mirror, and since the status of being the original object (bimba) relative to that reflection is likewise superimposed upon the sun, it would be more appropriate to say that in the case of Brahman there is no limiting adjunct distinct from it; therefore, this illustration is inappropriate and the two cases are dissimilar. To this, he replies:

The nature of the self and the nature of the Lord are both conceived as one within Brahman; as it is said: "Just as fire, though one, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form, so too the single inner self of all beings assumes a form corresponding to every form, both within and without" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.5.9).
Just as the state of being an image and the state of being a reflection are imagined in the sun. || 37 ||
"Ekatra" means "in one"; the rest is clear. || 37 ||

Within the supreme reality, which is the conscious self, the states of being the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller are conceptualized through the differentiation of the three qualities (guṇas).

The meaning is that, through the distinction of the three qualities beginning with *sāttvika*, the states of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), the object of enjoyment (*bhojyatva*), and the impeller (*prerakatva*) are superimposed upon the Supreme Reality, which is the conscious Self, pure consciousness. || 38 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated that there is no connection with the three qualities, such as sattva, in the Supreme Śiva whose nature is pure consciousness, how can the aforementioned point be established? To this, he says:
"The eternal Power, consisting of the three qualities, is grounded in Brahman."
Due to that very imbalance, the designation of the three entities arises within it. (39)
Since conjunction is preceded by action, the conjunction resulting from the action of either one or both [of two bodies] is distinct from the conjunction with Brahman.

It is established that [this] occurs only between two things situated in space; for since there is no external space outside of Brahman, conjunction is impossible, and because a conjunction not preceded by action is unestablished, and because Viṣṇu, having an uninterrupted pervasion, is devoid of any separation, there is no opportunity for the joining of joints. "I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī."
As stated by the Blessed One: "I am the radiance in the moon and the sun" (Bhagavad Gītā 7.8), just as heat exists in fire, coolness in the moon,
and softness in beds, so too does hardness exist in stones.
"Indeed, just as there is delusion among outsiders, so too is there awakening among yogis; for my great sovereignty as the Controller exists.
According to this statement by the learned, identity—characterized by the non-duality of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) [while remaining distinct from that]—[exists].

Identity (*tādātmya*) is the state of being perceived as non-different from that [the object]. Since they exist through a relationship [of identity], there is no universal contradiction between difference and non-difference. The eternal, constant power (*sanātanī śaktiḥ*), whose nature is the equilibrium of knowledge and action, is the innate power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*); "it exists" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Otherwise, even though Brahman is of the nature of light,
it would be like the light of a crystal gem or a mirror, due to its lack of self-reflection regarding its own essential nature and its incapacity for reflection.

Since the state of insentience is unavoidable due to the absence of self-reflection upon one’s own nature—which consists of *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda*—that supreme power of his is heard of as being manifold:
"His supreme power is declared to be indeed manifold; it is innate, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
Thus, it possesses various forms such as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).
Because the particle *ca* (and) illuminates a meaning not explicitly stated: therein, since consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are indivisible, there is an absence of agitation;
whereas, because the powers of will (*icchā*) and so forth possess objects, agitation is possible.
Thus, there arises a manifestation of both difference and non-difference, according to the maxim of the variegated colors of the feathers within a peacock’s egg.

Consisting of the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings embraced within her own identity, the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), being of such a nature, remains established in herself during the state of undivided self-reflection; yet, in the state of divided self-reflection, she becomes composed of the three qualities (*guṇatrayātmikā*). If it is asked how this is so, it is said:

When only a fraction of that power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) remains— according to the analogy of the solidity of clarified butter— due to the dissociation of the aspect of action from the state of being a knower and the dissociation of the aspect of knowledge from the state of being an agent, the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), whose nature is the quality of purity (sattva-guṇa), arises from that aspect of knowledge which is thus divested of supreme agency.

From that portion of activity which is devoid of such subjectivity, there emerges the power of the quality of *rajas*, mixed with a slight degree of the qualities of *sattva* and *tamas*. This is because, in the conventional usage "I know," knowledge is distinct from activity;
likewise, in the usage "I act," agency is also [distinct].

Although knowledge and action are in reality one due to their flashing nature, by the power of the reflective awareness of their differentiation, there arises the cognition of mutual non-existence— namely, that "knowledge is not action" and "action is not knowledge"— and this very cognition is the power of the quality of *tamas*. Thus, being composed of the three qualities (*guṇatrayātmikā*), it exists.

71) Due to that imbalance—that is, due to the variation in the three *guṇas*—within that Supreme Śiva whose nature is pure consciousness, [the power] comes to possess names, forms, and functions characterized as the three entities: the object of enjoyment (*bhojya*), the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and the impeller (*preraka*).
The meaning is that the established sense of the statement is that [the world] has arisen and manifested through the process called "illusion" (*māyā*), which functions by way of reflection.

By this, it is indicated that the entire universe exists in the manner of the analogy of the juice within a mango; thus, there is no room for doubt based on the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*).

For it is said in the venerable *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "The Lord, whose very self is consciousness, manifests the multitude of objects existing within Him externally by the power of His will, without any material cause, just like a yogi. Furthermore, because the arising of the non-existent is impossible and would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [the effect] does not arise from the non-existent.

And because it is sung [in the Bhagavad Gītā 2.16]: "The being exists. Now, if this were so, since the universe would attain reality, there could be no cessation of bondage; for it is sung [in the Bhagavad Gītā 2.16]: "The non-being does not exist for that which is real.

If this is argued, we say no; because the two extremities—the beginning and the end—are of the single nature of Consciousness (citi), they lack causal efficiency, and thus [the world is merely a manifestation of] will.

Just as with a jar that has entered the [fired] stage, there is no further bondage even for one who is liberated, because the will of the Lord (*īśvara*) acts as the regulator in that regard. Now, since it was previously introduced that [bondage arises] from the connection with beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), [one might ask] whether this occurs through an indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) connection...

There exists the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyāśakti*), which is established in Brahman, eternal, equal in essence to Brahman, composed of the three qualities (*guṇatrayamayī*), and characterized by superimposition (*adhyāsarūpinī*).
Due to its inequality— that is, due to the inequality of those qualities— there is the designation of three entities within that Brahman.
If it is asked, "Since it can be explained that the designation 'the triad of realities' has arisen [from Him], why such an effort?", we reply:
His supreme power is characterized by Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (saccidānanda).
She, whose nature is the collective synthesis of the creation of all worlds,
became manifest as his very self, directly imitating his own form.
Thus, because it contradicts even the statement previously introduced, [it is said]:

"That reflective awareness (vimarśa) which serves as the locus for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of hundreds of millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) is called the 'place of the vessel' (bhāṇḍasthala)."
Possessing the fullness of reflective awareness through immersion in the supreme I-consciousness,
he is the omniscient, omnipresent witness and the great lord who is the creator of all.

They call the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the Supreme Self that which is the support of all, filled with the light of the Great Consciousness, and consisting of the supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā).
Just as the steady moonlight residing in the moon illuminates all things,
so too does Śakti, whose essence is reflective awareness (vimarśa), abide within the various manifestations of Brahman.

Furthermore, this contradicts the statements regarding the vessel, the container, and the locus that are to be explained below. In this context, since Śakti is non-different from Śiva and is therefore partless (*niravayava*), how can she be the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of a manifold universe (*prapañca*) consisting of constituent parts?
It should not be suspected that [the world] cannot arise; for just as it is accepted that atoms, despite being partless,
serve as the material cause of the universe because their effects— such as dyads (dvyaṇuka)— possess parts,
so too is it accepted for the power of Māyā imagined through His sovereignty.

The status of being the material cause of the universe is possible because it is possible for [Brahman] to possess parts, owing to the power [of Śakti] which is expert at accomplishing the impossible. Now, even the acceptance of *avidyā* as you yourself admit is not possible;
for since *avidyā* is of the nature of a defect (*doṣa*), if Brahman were its substratum, it would follow that Brahman itself is defective. But surely—

If it is argued that, just as there is no contact between silver appearing in a fragment of mother-of-pearl and the pearl itself, so too there is no contact with Brahman for the ignorance appearing within it— and thus the aforementioned defect does not apply— then in that case, there would be no distinction at all between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), because of the absence of contact with ignorance. Nor can this be maintained by means of a reflection (*pratibimba*).

It must be stated that such a distinction is possible; for it is impossible to accept the existence of ignorance— which would occupy the place of a mirror— in a location external to Brahman, the original object (bimba), just as a face or other objects exist externally to a mirror.

Because there is no location outside of Brahman, it is impossible for that which has already merged into Brahman—like a face entered into water or a line drawn on a mirror—to reflect back from that very same place; furthermore, in comparison to Brahman, ignorance (avidyā) lacks transparency. Nevertheless, it is like the earth and other objects reflected in a mirror.
Since a reflected object is devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it follows that the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and so forth would have no substratum.

Nor can it be argued that this is possible—just as the sun reflected in a mirror possesses the power to blink with the eyes—for in that case, the status of being an enjoyer and so forth is likewise absent in Brahman, which is the original form (*bimba*). And not...
It should be said that, just as the appearance of redness in something that is neither [red nor not-red] occurs through the application of turmeric powder,

so too— in the case of ignorance and its reflection— because they lack substantial reality in themselves and because there is no other factor to join them, the primary Light (prakāśa) remains unattached precisely for this reason.
Since even the analogy of iron and the gem has been set aside,

and because the reflection is ascertained to be dependent upon limiting adjuncts such as a mirror and is therefore false as an effect of *māyā*, its identity with the inner self (*pratyagātman*) would be impossible; thus, the instruction "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) would indeed be entirely meaningless.
If it is argued that its cessation also occurs through the door of the cessation of ignorance, and that this alone constitutes identity with the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*),
then— since the destruction of the self would be a non-purpose (*apuruṣārtha*)— no one at all would ever engage in the effort for liberation as you conceive it;
this is the summary.

Now, even that distinction is not possible, because it has already been stated that Brahman cannot come into contact with it, as that would entail the consequence of Brahman being subject to defects. Furthermore, does this occur partially or in its entirety? It cannot be the first, because Brahman is partless and devoid of distinctions such as above, below, or across.

Nor is a division of imagined parts possible, because it is impossible to determine where ignorance (avidyā) resides while performing its imagining, since there is no space external to Brahman. Nor should it be argued that this is possible even in partless space, as in the case of the residence of stars and so forth; for that [residence] has air as its substrate, and not space itself.
Because it is admitted that [the atom] possesses parts by virtue of being a produced substance (*janyadravyatva*),
and because that example is not established for both parties; and if it is argued that "it is exceedingly capable of non-connection," that is true,
but since the existence of that [non-connection] depends on the strength of the substratum of consciousness, it is impossible according to the aforementioned method, otherwise...

Consciousness would necessarily be fragmented, and there would be the undesirable consequence of falling into the Sāṃkhya doctrine; nor is the second [alternative] possible, because the distinction between the pure and the impure would be impossible.

If it be objected that impurity exists during the state of saṃsāra and purity exists in the state of liberation, we say no; for the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), pure consciousness (viśuddhā cit), the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, nescience (avidyā), and the connection between that nescience and consciousness—these six are, according to us, beginningless. [Pañcadaśī]

Thus, because the distinction between the pure and the impure is accepted as existing precisely during the state of saṃsāra. Now, if it is argued that even though it is impossible to define it in such a way, ignorance (avidyā) must nevertheless be accepted on the strength of scriptural authority such as "Darkness existed" (Ṛgveda 10.129.3), then [we reply]: regarding those [scriptures],...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*), such as scripture, would themselves be real, because one must admit a difference in nature between the means of cognition and its object, just as the eye and other senses differ from a jar. Nor should it be argued that this rule does not apply because the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is admitted to be a valid means of cognition with respect to the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*).
Because cognition rests upon the knower, it never remains fixed in the status of an object of knowledge— such as "this"— and thus, through the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*),
it is capable of making the heart of the object of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), such as a jar, its own. Otherwise...

There would be the loss of established order, the fallacy of infinite regress, and the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that even a pot would become the object of another pot; thus, the example [cited by the opponent] is not admitted by both parties. Furthermore, there is the consequence that ignorance (avidyā) would be real, because it is accepted as being an unbeginning entity (anādibhāva); nor is this reason (hetu) inconclusive.
If reality were not present, then beginningless existence as an entity would also not be present, just like a jar;

for there exists even a negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore, because it is accepted as being distinct from Brahman, it would result in its becoming equivalent to a non-entity. This is because [it is] different from that [Brahman].

There is no proof for the restriction that [the Self] is external to that [Great Light], because it is external to the Great Light which is the remainder of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is the example of color and so forth residing in a jar applicable, because [the Self] does not reside in that [Light] in the same manner. Nor is the example of the space within a jar applicable, because "from the Self, space was produced."

This is because, according to such scriptural passages as *Tai. U. 2.1*, air and the other elements—being its effects either directly or through a succession of causes—can be considered included within it; however, this is not the case here with consciousness (*caitanya*), owing to its being unattached (*asaṅga*) and lacking any similarity to "Being" (*sat*). Even if one were to somehow grant that inclusion, it would still follow that [consciousness] is an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Since it must be accepted that the object of knowledge (prameya) finds its rest in the knower (pramātṛ) by way of the act of knowing (pramā), ignorance (avidyā) would simply not exist as such; otherwise, there could be no memory regarding a destroyed jar. Nor can it be argued that this [memory] arises from a latent impression (saṃskāra), for even that [impression], having an object, must likewise reside in the self (ātman).

Thus, since the ignorance (avidyā) favored by you lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and even if it were accepted, it would be untenable due to a lack of explanatory consistency and the emergence of subverting arguments, one must necessarily accept the power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) as the very nature of Brahman in order to eliminate its insentience; therefore, of that [power]...
This effort is meaningful in order to establish that [Brahman] has the nature of *māyā*, which serves as the material cause of the universe.
Now, if this is so, what is the proof for Brahman? Since there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) distinct from itself, otherwise—
If it is argued that Brahman must be an object [of cognition], we say no;
for it is self-luminous, and its existence is established by the means of valid knowledge consisting in one's own direct experience, which is composed of the reflective awareness "I.
Due to the state of vigilance, although the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is non-different from the Light (*prakāśa*), it possesses the capacity to bring about the impossible; thus,

through the existence of non-duality in the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) imagined by its own sovereignty, the conventional operation of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) occurs.

Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. If it were cognizable by another means of knowledge (pramāṇa) distinct from itself, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*), like a jar; however, according to the authority of the Śruti and other sources—specifically the Vedic verse, "Four are the measured steps of speech" (*Ṛgveda* 1.164.45)—it consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya*) in the form of the utterances of intention, commencement, desire to speak, and determination.
In the state of deliberating upon the distinctions [between the views], since the intent is to manifest the greatness of that [Lord],
it is entirely consistent that words such as "avidyā" (ignorance) and others, which are well-known from the Śrutis and other sources, can possibly refer to Māyā conceived as independent. || 39 ||
The individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), pure consciousness (viśuddhā cit), as well as the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord,
nescience (avidyā), and the connection between that [nescience] and consciousness— these six are, for us, beginningless.
Now, by what quality does what entity arise? To this he says:
"That which consists of the qualities of *sattva* and *rajas* is called the 'enjoyer' (*bhoktṛ*);
that which has the quality of *tamas* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is designated as the 'object of enjoyment' (*bhojya*)."
The Lord (Īśvara) is the consciousness of Brahman, whose limiting adjunct (upādhi) consists of the supreme reality (paratattva). || 40 ||

As stated by the Blessed One: "The fourfold varṇas were created by Me according to the divisions of qualities and actions, because the quality of rajas is slightly mixed with sattva and tamas" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.13).

The meaning is that consciousness mixed with such a quality of *rajas* is the consciousness of the *jīva* as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Consciousness qualified by an extremely *tāmasa* limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the object of enjoyment (*bhojya*) in the form of taste and so forth; the limiting adjunct consists of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), which is superior to these two.

The meaning is: the Great Lord (Maheśvara) who acts as the impeller of consciousness, which is qualified by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the quality of existence (sattva-guṇa) whose nature is the supreme reality (paratattva).
Now, he confirms the point already stated:

"The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—these three things are traditionally taught to be imagined within the indivisible consciousness of Brahman due to the differentiation of the qualities. (41)
This is clear. || 41 ||
In this context, Śambhu, the Great Lord whose adjunct is pure, is the impeller;
all those with mixed adjuncts are known as the experiencing subjects, the bound souls (paśus). || 42 ||
Now, he states their other names and qualities: "The object of enjoyment is called the Unmanifest (avyakta), whose nature is pure tamas;
Śambhu is the omniscient impeller, while the individual soul (jīva) is said to be possessed of limited knowledge."
That which is extremely hidden consciousness is called the insentient unmanifest. || 43 ||

Maheśvara is omniscient, the enjoyer of bliss, and Śambhu, because he has *sattva* as his predominant limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); yet, due to being mixed with a small amount of *tamas*, he is skilled in the act of dissolution and is endowed with wrath. Individual souls (*jīvas*), however, possess limited knowledge and are a mixture of knowledge and ignorance, because they have *rajas* as their limiting adjunct, which is itself mixed with a small amount of *sattva* and *tamas*.

For this very reason, they are the experiencers of pleasure and pain. The meaning is that the unmanifest (avyakta), which is Prakṛti, is the object of experience when it is conditioned by the pure quality of tamas. To the question "What is this unmanifest?", he says: "absolutely...
Although trees and the like are for the most part merely insentient due to being largely devoid of senses, vital breaths, and so forth— (End of sentence fragment)

Because thirst exists and because growth is observed in crops and stones, there is the conventional usage of the term "unmanifest consciousness" (*avyakta-caitanya*). Unmanifest (*avyakta*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and illusion (*māyā*) are synonyms. || 43 ||

77) Having thus demonstrated the triad of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the differentiated forms of the qualities of *māyā*, [the author] subsequently divides the previously mentioned *māyā*-adjunct into two types in order to clearly define the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is Śiva in the form of the subtle body (*liṅga-aṅga*).
He shows [this] by analyzing it: "Furthermore, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is declared to be divided into pure and impure.
The pure adjunct is supreme Māyā, which does not cause delusion within its own locus. (44)
The previously mentioned adjunct (*upādhi*), which is *māyā*, further becomes twofold through the distinction between the pure (*śuddha*) and the impure (*aśuddha*).

Among these, the pure adjunct is supreme *māyā* (*parā māyā*), which causes delusion within its own locus; this is the meaning of "upper *māyā*" (*ūrdhvamāyā*). The impure adjunct is likewise the ignorance (*avidyā*) that causes delusion within its locus.
Due to the differentiation of the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti), living beings (jīvas) are said to be of many kinds. || 45 ||

Impure limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is ignorance (*avidyā*), which deludes the substratum; this means it is *māyā* directed downwards. By the differentiation of the power of ignorance—that is, by way of its various parts—the individual souls (*jīva*) are said to be manifold. (45)
By the power of his illusory energy (māyā-śakti), the Lord, the Sovereign, assumes manifold forms;
he is the omniscient creator of all, the Great Lord who is eternally liberated.

The Lord (Īśa) is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) characterized by pure adjuncts; by the power of Māyā-śakti and the power of Mahāmāyā-śakti, he assumes various forms such as Sadyojāta and others, is the impeller of the intellect of living beings, the sovereign Lord capable of acting,
not acting, or acting otherwise, and is omniscient.

He possesses the power of primordial knowledge whose object is the totality of all things, both existent and non-existent; He is the creator of all, the instrumental cause for the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world; eternally liberated, devoid of connection with the beginningless impurities such as *āṇava*, He is omniscient and the maker of all—omniscient indeed.
"He who is endowed with the fivefold functions is the Lord of all and rules," according to the Vṛddha-Jābāla Śruti. || 46 ||
The individual soul is an agent of limited action, a knower of limited knowledge, bound, and possessed of a beginningless body;
such souls are deluded by ignorance and devoid of the knowledge of their identity with Brahman. (47)

Now he describes the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*): "The doer of little," etc. The doer of little, the knower of little, bound—bound by the fetters of beginningless impurities such as *āṇava* and the rest, impelled by the Lord—that *jīva* possesses a beginningless body;
that is, from time immemorial, it has possessed the conceit of identifying with a body.
"There are two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord; for the one who is unborn is joined with the object of enjoyment, the experiencer.
The non-lordly self is bound by virtue of its state as an experiencer; but by knowing God, it is released from all fetters.
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.9)
Thus, according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Because of its connection with beginningless impurity, [the self] is declared to be a limited knower and atomic;
because it is liberated from beginningless impurity, this same [self] is remembered as the omniscient Śiva."

And because it is stated thus in the *Kiraṇāgama*: "Individual souls (*jīva*) of such a nature, being deluded by ignorance (*avidyā*), are devoid of the knowledge of Brahman as the one reality; they are destitute of the knowledge of identity [expressed as] 'I am Brahman'."
They wander through saṃsāra according to their own karma, distinguished by various types of births such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth. (48)

The meaning is that [beings] wander through saṃsāra, having attained various distinctions of birth—such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth—in accordance with their own karma. Here, one should not raise the objection, "How can this be, since karma did not exist prior to creation? For, according to the principles of the Satkāryavāda (the doctrine of pre-existent effect), the entire cosmic egg exists [in a latent state], like the juice within a mango.
Because it is accepted that [the world] exists by virtue of being of the nature of a non-differentiated reflection within the Supreme Brahman. || 48 ||
(p. 79) Now, as to how they wander, he says:
"Indeed, embodied beings wander precisely by the sequence of the rim of a wheel."
Karma alone is the cause of the inequality of birth, lifespan, and experience; for when the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.13) 49.
The meaning is that they whirl about like iron rings placed upon the rims of chariot wheels. || 49 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated that living beings wander about according to their karma, and that karma alone is the cause of the diversity in their birth, lifespan, and experience, for what purpose should a Lord (Īśvara) be accepted? To this, he says:
The Supreme Lord is the witness and the impeller of these embodied beings, who wander eternally under the constraint of the machine of karma. (50)

For these diverse embodied beings who are constantly wandering on the wheel of saṃsāra bound by the thread of karma—the word "of these karmas" is to be understood as the ellipsis—the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is the impeller; for since karma is insentient, it cannot itself possess the capacity to impel. Thus, the meaning is that the Lord must be accepted as the impeller and the witness. || 50 ||
Alternatively, he states that his excellence is not merely this much, but there is even more:
"Śambhu is the impeller of embodied beings and the instructor of the path to welfare;
he is the instructor of the path to liberation, which is devoid of rebirth. (51)
This is clear. || 51 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
Through the ripening of his own karma, with the impressions of impurity destroyed by the grace of Śiva, this individual soul (jīva) becomes pure-minded. (52)

According to the teaching of the Śiva-āgamas, "The destruction of karma occurs for this individual soul (jīva) through the ripening of its own karma, or through the enjoyment [of its fruits], or through the application of knowledge and renunciation"; thus, having had the impressions of impurity destroyed by the ripening of its respective karma,
[the soul attains liberation] through the grace of Śiva.
One becomes pure in inner disposition. || 52 ||
When the individual soul (jīva) has a purified inner organ due to the ripening of pure karma, divine devotion arises through the compassion of Śiva. (53)

In that regard, by virtue of the ripening of pure karma—that is, through the power of the maturation of pure karma as taught in the scriptures and traditions—Śiva’s grace arises; devotion directed toward Śiva becomes manifest, and by means of that, there is instruction on the path to liberation; such is the meaning. || 53 ||
Thus, one who possesses devotion to Śiva that has arisen in this way, even while in his final body, is designated by the term *piṇḍa*; with these words, he concludes the section on the *piṇḍa*:
"This living being in his last body is what is denoted by the word *piṇḍa*. (54)

This living being (jantu), having thus developed devotion to Śiva, is a soul in its final body; "this is his third birth," according to the Śruti. Thus, possessing his last body, he is denoted by the word *piṇḍa*;
that is to say, he bears the designation of the word *piṇḍa*. || 54 ||
Now, regarding the section on the knowledge of the aggregate (piṇḍajñāna):
one might ask, "Why is the discrimination between the body and the self required? To this, he says:
"By means of the discrimination between the body and the self"—[discrimination meaning the knowledge of difference, having the form: 'this is distinct from that'].
He who possesses knowledge of the aggregate (piṇḍa) is so described;
indeed, the Cārvākas proclaim the body itself to be the self (ātman). || 55 ||

The meaning is that one who possesses knowledge of the body through the discrimination between the body and the self— that is, through the discrimination between the body and the embodied— is called a "knower of the physical aggregate" by those learned in the scriptures. Since the true nature of the self remains doubtful due to such disputants, and because the authors of the treatises have accepted that reasoning (*nyāya*) proceeds regarding a doubtful matter, [this inquiry is undertaken] concerning the identity of the body and the self.
The meaning is that discernment (viveka) is necessary. || 55 ||

By those who hold that the self is of the nature of the sense faculties, it is designated as such; by the Buddhists who abide in the principle of consciousness (buddhi), consciousness is proclaimed to be the self. (56)

To the question "How is there its isolation?", he says: "Neither the senses, nor the body, nor the intellect can be the Self, because they are known through the notion of 'I' and also because of the recollection of what was previously experienced. (57)
He who is distinct from the body, the senses, and the intellect, who is eternal, established in the Self, and possessed of discernment—he is called a knower of the body (piṇḍajñānī). || 58 ||

The point is this: because people perceive suffering when houses, fields, and so forth are destroyed, and because they experience an excess of pleasure when those same things increase, worldly people who maintain the doctrine that the object is the self (viṣayātmavādinaḥ) believe that the house, field, and such are themselves the self.
Even more than that, those possessing superior discernment [realize] that houses, fields, and so forth...

The Cārvākas maintain that the body alone is the self, because there is no such distinction [between the self and its environment] as exists between the body and animals, birds, rivers, mountains, villages, and so forth; whereas such a distinction does exist for the body itself. [Others hold that] since consciousness does not arise when the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) ceases within the body, the body is not the self, but rather the vital breath alone is the self.

Some say that because there is an absence of sensory activity and a lack of cognition during sleep—despite the continued vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the senses are the self. Others hold that here, due to the multiplicity of the senses, either the aggregate of the senses is called the self, or the individual form of the self is being described; such is the dilemma.
Not the first [alternative], because if even one or two of those [atoms] were destroyed, it would follow that knowledge could not arise due to the destruction of the aggregate.

Not the second, because there would be no such cognition as "this water is clear and sweet," since the individual [atoms] (*vyaṣṭi*) manifest only their respective objects. Thus, [the body] and so forth would be devoid of knowledge.

Since insentience precludes the possibility of being the self, the intellect (*buddhi*) alone is the self. Here, one should not raise the objection that because the intellect is produced by instruments such as the eyes, and because instruments like axes are dependent upon an agent, some agent transcending the intellect must be admitted; for [this does not apply] to that which is produced by instruments.

If it is argued that there is no undesirable consequence because the intellect (*buddhi*) would become insentient due to the rule of insentiency, and thus would lack the capacity to apprehend objects, we reply:

this is not so. For if the intellect were insentient, it would be impossible to avoid the conclusion that the Self (*ātman*) is also insentient, which would result in the collapse of worldly transactional activity (*lokavyavahāra*).
Therefore, since the intellect must be accepted as being self-established—just like the Self as you yourself maintain—it must first be admitted [as such].

First is the experience of the jar, then the conceptualization of the jar, immediately after which, from the latent impression produced by that, arises a memory directed toward the actual object; and through this memory, worldly transaction occurs. Thus, the self is merely a stream of momentary cognitions, characterized by different times, different forms, and different objects.

The Buddhists, who maintain the primacy of consciousness (*buddhi*), say this. To this, the reply is: because it is known through the cognition "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), and because there is also the recollection of what was previously experienced, there exists an eternal Self (*ātman*) distinct from the body, the senses, and the intellect—[as evidenced by such thoughts as] "my body," "my sense organ," "my intellect," and "mine."

Memory and so forth also appear as dependent upon the notion of "I" which transcends the body, the senses, and the intellect— as in "I am the embodied one," "I am possessed of clear senses," "I know," and "I remember"— and therefore they are distinct from those [faculties].
The meaning is that it must be admitted that some self exists.

Now, [one might object]: since we have admitted that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is included within the two types of cognition characterized as non-conceptual and conceptual, it is not something distinct from those; nor is it...
If it is argued that this [self] is established because it does not conceptualize anything other than itself, we reply: it is not so,
for it conceptualizes the body and so forth by being in contact with the continua of form and sensation, such as "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am happy," and "I am suffering."

Therefore, even the notion of "I," which is the preeminent among the series of the body and so forth, cannot be the self, because it transcends the fivefold continuum characterized by form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as accepted by us,
and because it is impermanent due to its contact with the continua of form and sensation.

Furthermore, because [the self] is absent during states such as sleep and fainting; nor should it be argued that the notion of "I" conceptualizes the self alone, on the grounds that in the cognition "I know the jar," the self appears as transcending both the manifestation of the object of knowledge (in the form of the jar) and the manifestation of the knowledge itself (in the form of the act of knowing).
Because that [self] is not perceived apart from the notion of "I," and because the notion of "I" is impermanent;

if the self distinct from that notion is inferred on the grounds that the notion cannot otherwise have an object, then who is this inferrer—is it the notion of "I" or something distinct from it? It cannot be the former.

If you accept that the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) has a cognizer when it is impermanent, you fall into our own position, because no cognizer distinct from that [notion] is perceived. If you argue that if it were perceptible,
it would follow that it is identical to the intellect (buddhi), and therefore the intellect alone is the Self— do not say so, because the intellect is momentary.
Because they are accepted as being distinct in terms of time, distinct in terms of object, and distinct in terms of form, blue is different from yellow,
yellow is different from blue, "I know blue," "I know yellow," and "I who experienced my parents in childhood am that very same I now [in youth or old age]."
Because consciousness is fixed upon a single [perceptual] unity— such as "I am experiencing my son and wife"—

there is no possibility of connecting the external with the internal; because two moments cannot be encompassed by a single consciousness, and because a memory of taste does not arise from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a form, since memory [requires such a connection].

Since the latent impression (saṃskāra) has fulfilled its purpose by establishing the determination of an object-field identical to its own, we do not perceive anything that generates memory; thus, memory would be like a flower in the sky, and there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of all worldly activity rooted in it. Therefore, there must be some eternal self as the synthesizer.

He must be accepted as possessing the power of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance], because this was indeed intended by the Blessed One when he sang: "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal. Furthermore, it has been well said that He is of the very nature of the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃpratyaya), because anything distinct from that is imperceptible. Thus, of Him...

One should not suspect its impermanence on account of its absence during sleep, fainting, and so forth; for at those times, it is submerged in the state of emptiness (*śūnya*), whereby its own self-luminosity is concealed. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that one who has awakened would have no recollection of pleasure in the form "I slept happily," since recollection is rooted in prior experience.

In brief, because the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), which has become a constituent part of [the body], exists, that [memory]—being of the nature of taking up and discarding—is defined by an agent, since it is preceded by the knowledge of an agent. Now, one might object: "By this much, some embodied individual soul (*jīvātman*) is established, but not a Lord (*īśvara*) who impels him."

If [it is argued that] in the world, actions such as splitting are accomplished by means such as axes, and since those instruments are dependent upon the organs of action (karmendriya), [the sense organs must exist].

It should be understood that the followers of Vyāsa (the Vaiyāsikas), who argue that [the Lord] is established by the very fact that worldly activity would otherwise be inexplicable— since such activity depends on place, time, and other factors, and thus cannot occur without an independent agent— are thereby refuted. || 56–58 ||
(15.15) From Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
Bodies, which perish and take on various forms through karma, [are likewise from Me].
The discernment of a living being consists in realizing that this [self] is indeed eternally dependent. (59)

The discernment that the various bodies obtained through the power of karma are perishable is the "discernment of the body" (piṇḍaviveka). The discernment that the living being (jīva) residing in such a body is eternal is the "discernment of the knower of the body" (piṇḍajñaviveka). || 59 ||
To the objection that this discernment has become similar to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, he says:
"He who knows the Self as distinct from the body, and the Lord as distinct from the Self and as the impeller, is called a knower of the aggregate. (60)

This is clear. This very discernment between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), characterized by the eternal and the non-eternal, exists through identity (*tādātmya*) with the Lord (*īśvara*) as the impeller within the individual soul (*jīva*), according to the aforementioned illustration: "as water [is present] in a moonstone," and so forth. And it is said in the *Gītā*:
This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field (kṣetra).
He who knows this is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) by those who understand that.
The knowledge of both the field and the knower of the field—that, in my view, is true knowledge.
"And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.1–2).
This Self is indeed to be attained through truth and austerity.
"By means of right knowledge and constant celibacy,
they behold within the body that which is luminous and pure, which ascetics whose sins have been destroyed perceive. [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.5]
Thus says the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
"When one perceives the bodiless Self with the eye of knowledge,
then one becomes tranquil in soul, free from longing for everything."
