Thus, from the statement of the *Devikālottara*, the nature of the body and the embodied one, as well as the nature of the limbs and the possessor of limbs—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—should be understood. || 60 ||
Now, regarding the stage where that which is to be abandoned in saṃsāra arises:
next, he describes the stage where that which is to be abandoned in saṃsāra arises for one who possesses knowledge of the body (*piṇḍa*) of such a nature—(p.
For one whose mental impurities have been cast off and who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal,
the realization that worldly existence is to be abandoned arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā).

The meaning is that, by the aforementioned process, for one whose internal organ is purified through the destruction of sins resulting from merit accumulated over many births, and who possesses discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, a sense of renunciation toward saṃsāra arises due to an abundance of merit and the power of virtuous impressions (*saṃskāra*). || 61 ||
To the question "Why?", he says:
For what discerning person could there be a desire for the fleeting pleasures of this world arising from sons, wives, and the like, or for a heaven characterized by decay and other such defects? (62)
The perishable nature of the happiness arising from children, wife, and so forth is experienced through direct perception.
Even regarding the happiness of heaven produced by sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is said:
"Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven, they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted" (Bhagavad Gītā 9.21).
From these words spoken by the Blessed One, it is understood that [worldly existence] is impermanent.
For one who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal regarding such pleasures of this world and the next, who could possibly have a desire for them? None indeed.
The meaning is "of anyone. The intention is that because it is perishable, there would only be the thought of it as something to be abandoned. || 62 ||
Now, since worldly pleasure is impermanent, its renunciation is indeed appropriate; however, as to why saṃsāra itself should be abandoned, he points out its defects:
"For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain" (cf. Bhagavad Gītā 2.27).
A living being revolves like a wheel through death and birth.
The meaning is: because there is an absence of rest. || 63 ||
87) Regarding this point, he also provides the example of the person dependent on karma: "By means of the forms of the fish, tortoise, boar, Nṛsiṃha, man, and so forth..."
Even the high-souled Viṣṇu, once born, met with death.

The meaning is that even by the Great Soul, the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa— who, though subject to karma, took incarnations such as the Fish and the Tortoise for the sake of destroying wicked Daityas and for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees— death, that is, destruction, was attained. || 64 ||
This being the case, he says that a living being, dependent on others, is indeed scorched by the threefold suffering:

"Having come into existence among castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and others through the power of karma, the living being is intensely scorched by the heat of the great fire of the threefold suffering. (65)
"It is burned" means "it is tormented. || 65 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is there ever, even at some time, an interruption in the persistence of the threefold suffering within this cycle of existence? To this, he says:
"For the embodied being who is constantly tormented by suffering rooted in karma—consisting of the internal and other types—where is rest desired? (66)
For a living being who is constantly afflicted by suffering— whether internal or otherwise— rooted in karma, where, in what locus,
is rest (viśrānti)— that is, repose— sought or made the object of desire? Nowhere.
The meaning is "somewhere. || 66 ||

Now, as to what those three types of suffering are, he says: "The first is internal (ādhyātmika), the second is external due to other beings (ādhibhautika), and the third is due to divine or supernatural causes (ādhidaivika); these are remembered as the threefold suffering. (67)
Now, he defines its nature:
"The internal [suffering] is said to be twofold, through the distinction of external and internal.
Suffering born from wind, bile, and so forth is considered external; that which is internal is considered *ādhyātmika*. (68)
This is clear. || 68 ||
That which is characterized by passion, hatred, and so forth is proclaimed as internal;
for this suffering arising from kings and other such beings is indeed of a physical nature (ādhibhautika). (69)
That which arises from planets, yakṣas, and so forth is declared to be of a divine nature.
For the embodied being bound by karma who is beset by these sufferings, not even a trace of happiness exists, whether in heaven or on earth. (70)
Now, regarding whether or not happiness exists in the prosperity of kingship and the like, he says "it does not exist," preceded by an illustration:
89) "In flashes of lightning, in rows of waves, and in the radiance of a lamp..."
When prosperity has its roots in karma, who indeed could possess a steady mind? (71)

The meaning is that just as there is no notion of stability in flashes of lightning, in waves, or in the flames of lamps, so too the man of discrimination has no notion of stability even toward prosperities rooted in karma. || 71 ||
To the objection that the body may indeed be an object of desire because it is distinct from lightning and the like, and because it is a means to pleasure,
[the author replies]: "O Blessed One, [it is] defiled by bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, phlegm, and tears."

In accordance with the Maitreyī Śruti— “What is the use of the enjoyment of desires in this body, which is a mass of feces, urine, wind, bile, and phlegm, foul-smelling and devoid of essence” (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 1.2)— he says: “In this body, which is a receptacle of filth and an increaser of great suffering...”
Like a flash of lightning, two defects reside in this sprout: first, its momentariness;

second, that upon contact, it burns the body. Similarly, the body appears delightful at first sight, yet in its enjoyment, it becomes the cause of falling away from one's desired goal. What wise person, then, would take delight in such a thing? (72)

In this momentary body, which is a vessel for impurities such as filth and urine—a mere lump of sin—what person of discernment would feel affection? The meaning is that no one at all would do so. || 72 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the body alone is the object of supreme love, let your attachment be directed toward it. To this he replies:
"Abandoning the reality of the Self, which has the form of eternal bliss and consciousness, what discerning person would take delight in the perishable body, that vessel of suffering? (73)

Since the reality of the Self, whose nature is eternal bliss, exists, and since that alone is the object of supreme love, what discerning person would take delight in the perishable body, which is a vessel of suffering? The meaning is: no one at all would take delight in it. || 73 ||
Now, it is said that for the discerning one, detachment is directed only toward the perishable body alone, and not toward all things related to it:
"The discerning one, whose heart is pure and who has attained certainty regarding the arising of the bliss of the Self..."
In this body which is the cause of suffering, and likewise in one's wife and children. || 74 ||

One whose heart is pure, whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is stainless, and for that very reason one in whom the arising of the bliss of the Self has been ascertained— meaning one who possesses the manifestation of the realization of the eternal and the non-eternal through scripture, the teacher, and one's own experience [as stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"From scripture, from the teacher, and from oneself"]— is a discerning person (*vivekī*), one who discriminates between eternal and non-eternal realities regarding the cause of suffering.
In this body, which is the cause of all suffering as previously described, and in wife, women, and sons, [he attains supreme detachment]—thus connects with the subsequent verse. || 74 ||

Regarding friends, kinsmen, wealth, and family lineage, one should maintain the perception of their impermanence. In the Vedānta, for the purpose of the inquiry into Brahman—which is the cause of the bliss of Brahman—the four prerequisites (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*) have been stated: 1. discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal; 2. ... [text continues] ... *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Vedāntasāra*, specifically concerning the first prerequisite.*
Dispassion toward the enjoyment of the fruits of goals here and hereafter; 3. the attainment of the means such as tranquility and self-control; 4.
the desire for liberation—[in all these, one attains supreme dispassion]. 75.

The meaning is that, through the perception of impermanence regarding friends, allies, circles of kinsmen, family lineage, ancestral tradition, wealth such as cattle and property, and indeed everywhere including all things other than these, he attains— that is, takes refuge in— supreme detachment. || 75 ||

Now, he states that for one who is thus detached from impermanent things, who is attached to the permanent reality, and whose intellect is directed toward the cause of the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra:
"For the discerning person who is detached from sense objects and attached to the Self..."
The intellect is directed toward the cause for severing the suffering of saṃsāra. || 76 ||
This is clear. || 76 ||

Now, regarding the question of what is the cause for cutting off the suffering of saṃsāra, he states it in verse, incorporating the essential meaning of the stages of knowledge concerning the body and that which is born of the body: "For the self who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal, who is meritorious and of pure intention..."
For one who perceives the instability even in the preeminent splendors of Brahmā, Upendra, and Mahendra,
[there remains only] the state of eternal bliss, wherein the arising of the world’s cycle of suffering has been utterly cast out.
May devotion toward Sāmba, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, arise—devotion that destroys worldly existence. || 77 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Discussion on the Stages of the Body, Knowledge, and the World to be Abandoned," within the section on Devotion in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a definitive exposition of the Śrī Vīraśaiva Dharma. 5.
Of the virtuous one who performs the righteous deeds prescribed by the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*, whose disposition is pure and whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is stainless,
who is the Self denoted by the word "body" (*piṇḍa*), who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal,
who discriminates between the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Field (*kṣetra*), and who possesses knowledge of the body.

For one who perceives and knows the instability and momentariness within the prosperity of all the gods, headed by Brahmā, Upendra, and Mahendra; and for that very reason, one who possesses the discernment that saṃsāra is to be abandoned, [there is liberation] in the state of eternal bliss—
the refuge of eternally perfect Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda)— wherein the arising of the worldly suffering of saṃsāra has been dispelled, and which is accompanied by Ambā.

The meaning is that devotion—eightfold in nature and destructive of worldly existence—arises and shines forth toward the Great Liṅga, which is the cause of the various playful forms (līlāvigraha) such as the one bearing the moon, based on the Atharvaṇa Śruti: "Obeisance, obeisance to Umā’s consort, whose crest-jewel is the moon, whose forehead is the moon, who is clothed in an elephant hide. In this regard:
For one whose internal organ is purified and who discriminates between eternal and non-eternal entities,
through the door of dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to this world and the next,
there arises an aversion toward external and internal objects of the senses, such as sound and the like, including attachment, aversion, and so forth.

It is thus stated that, through the perfection of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, and by virtue of the desire for liberation, devotion arises toward the Great Liṅga, which serves as the means for the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra. || 77 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Section on the Knowledge of the Body and the Abandonment of Saṃsāra," within the *Bhaktasthala* of the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences.
Chapter Five.
The Sixth Chapter:

Now, for the sake of knowing that [Reality], one should approach a true guru with sacrificial fuel in hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman; thus says the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* (2.1.2).

Having attained the aforementioned stages of the piṇḍa and the knowledge of the piṇḍajas, and being desirous of knowing the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga) which effects the destruction of saṃsāra, he approaches the venerable Guru; thus,
Śrī Reṇuka describes to Kumbhaja the stage of the Guru’s compassion characterized by initiation (dīkṣā).
Then, endowed with solitude, free from passion, and pure in mind, he became desirous of knowing Śiva, who destroys all the defects of saṃsāra. (1)
He approaches one who is world-renowned, free from greed and delusion,
a knower of the investigation into the reality of the Self, and liberated from the error of sense-objects.
One who knows the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta, whose doubts and delusions have been severed, who is skilled in the application of all tantras, righteous, and truthful in speech. || 3 ||
One who follows the conduct inherited through family lineage, avoids the paths of evil, is devoted to the meditation on Śiva, is tranquil, and discerns the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). || 4 ||
One who is proficient in smearing himself with ashes, who discerns the true nature of ashes, who is eager to wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads. || 5 ||
One who is joined with the wearing of the *liṅga*, devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*,
who knows the reality of the yoga of the *liṅga* and the body, and whose latent impression of non-duality is firmly established.
[One should approach] the venerable Guru, the proclaimer of Śiva, who knows the distinctions between the *liṅga*, the *aṅga*, and the *sthala*.
93) Thereupon, after the arising of the realization that *saṃsāra* is to be abandoned, one whose mind is purified and whose inner being is stainless—

By virtue of being the instrument [of realization], that which is denoted by the word *piṇḍa* is the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who is endowed with discernment—possessing knowledge of the body through the discrimination between the body and the Self; who is dispassionate, having turned away from impermanent pleasure; and who possesses the conviction that cyclic existence is to be abandoned because its defects are faults, the meaning of which is suffering. This is the instrument for the destruction of all the defects of cyclic existence.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: desiring to know the Great Liṅga of Paraśiva—the supreme Brahman, which is another synonym for Śiva and the remover of all worldly suffering—one approaches the venerable Guru, a proponent of Śiva, who is the instructor regarding the true nature of the Great Liṅga. Of what nature is he?

To this, he replies with the words "renowned in the world" and so forth. [He is] well-known to all the world, free from greed and delusion— where "delusion" means ignorance— and a knower of the investigation into the true nature of the Self,
meaning one who knows the reality of the Self's essential nature as distinct from the body, senses, and so on, and whose confusion regarding sense objects has been liberated.

"Whatever power is proclaimed to belong to whatever object, that is the Goddess who is the Sovereign of All; he is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) who is everything. This is established in the *Sarvamaṅgalāgama*.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*: "The beloved of Śarva sustains the entire collection of sounds, while the one whose crest is the charming moon sustains the entire collection of meanings. Thus, because the entire universe consists of Śiva and Śakti, there is no difference between the two.

The meaning is that the delusion regarding the distinction between objects has dissolved. For this very reason, he is one whose latent impression of non-duality is firmly established—distinguished by a solidified saṃskāra of advaita; one who knows the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta, being proficient in the tenets of the Śiva-āgama; and one whose doubts and delusions have been severed.

The meaning is: one who has eliminated doubt and error; one who knows the application of all systems (tantras), that is, one who knows the application of the sixty-four tantras; one who is righteous, devoted to the dharma of Śiva; a speaker of truth;
one whose conduct follows the traditional lineage of his family; one whose conduct conforms to the succession of the lineage of gurus; and one who avoids the practices of false paths.
One who has abandoned the conduct of his family and attained the observances [of the tradition], who is devoted to meditation on Śiva, intent on contemplation of the Śivaliṅga,
tranquil, free from passion and hatred, a discerning knower of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), one who knows the nature of Śiva and Paraśiva, and who is proficient in the smearing of ashes—
this means one who is skilled therein; that is, one who discerns the true nature of the ashes.
One who possesses discernment regarding the true nature of the sacred ash, who is eager to wear the *tripuṇḍra*— the meaning being that he is intent upon it—
and who wears a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads, is one joined with the wearing of the *liṅga*, possessing both the external and internal *liṅga*.

Devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*, intent upon the external and internal worship of the *liṅga*, he knows the reality of the union of the *liṅga* and the body (*aṅga*), knows the reality of the connection between the seed of Śiva (*śivabīja*) and [the *liṅga*], and knows the distinctions between the locations of the *liṅga* and the body; that is to say, he possesses knowledge of the one hundred and one distinct locations situated within the *liṅga* and the body. He is a proponent of Śiva (*śivavādī*).

One who employs auspicious words— a mature disciple, that is to say, one who possesses the discernment that worldly existence is to be abandoned and who desires liberation— should approach, meaning he should go to, the illustrious Lord True Guru, who is endowed with such excellent marks, while carrying an offering in his hand. || 1-7 ||
Having thus found a true guru, one should perform service to him; so it is said:
"The disciple, endowed with devotion and fear, should serve the supreme teacher. (7)
For six months or even for a year, until he becomes gracious;
the meaning is that one should serve him through [attaining] the status of a trusted person, the limbs [of the practice], and true being. The rest is clear.
Now, he describes the manner of requesting that [grace] with two aphorisms:
To the gracious supreme teacher, the one who reveals liberation, with devotion.
The disciple, endowed with humility, should pray before him with palms joined in reverence:
"O auspicious one, O highly fortunate one, O great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva! (9)
O most excellent Teacher, protect me, who am afflicted by the disease of worldly existence;

with humility, I approach you— the supreme Guru and Great Master, who has attained [realization], whose mind is pleased by devotion and service, who is intent on bestowing grace, and who reveals liberation, showing both the higher and the lower paths to release.

Endowed with fear and devotion, the disciple, with palms joined and hands folded like buds, should pray before him, in his presence: "O auspicious one, O you whose nature is blessing and well-being, O highly fortunate one, O most excellent one, O ocean of the knowledge of Śiva, O preeminent teacher, O supreme guru! [Please save] me, who am afflicted by worldly existence, a patient suffering from the disease of *saṃsāra*."
"Protect me, save me, who have arrived and come before you! || 8-9 ||

The teacher should unite the disciple who has thus made this request with the initiation that constitutes a limb of the instruction; so he says: "Thus requested by the pure disciple, the supreme teacher... (10).
"Having observed the descent of power (śaktipāta), one should unite this person with initiation.
Thus, having been requested by a disciple who is pure and whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is purified in such a manner, [the teacher acts].

The supreme teacher, the great teacher— of whom it is understood that [the disciple] has made a request— having thoroughly observed, that is, having clearly perceived, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), specifically the most intense descent of power, should unite, meaning he should connect, this disciple standing before him with initiation (*dīkṣā*). || 10 ||
Regarding the question "What indeed is initiation?", he says: "Śiva-knowledge is bestowed (dīyate) and the bondage of the fetters (pāśabandhana) is destroyed (kṣīyate). (11)
Therefore, this is declared as "dīkṣā" by the wise; for,
according to the root *dā* meaning "to give," the knowledge of Śiva—
the knowledge of the Great Liṅga known as the Supreme Brahman and Paraśiva— is given, that is, it will be bestowed as non-different from one's own self.
The bond of fetters (*pāśabandhana*)—the bondage of impurity (*mala*), illusion (*māyā*), and karma—is destroyed (*kṣīyate*) according to the verbal root *kṣi* meaning "to perish.
Therefore, the meaning is that this very power (*śakti*), consisting of knowledge and action, is rightly declared by the wise who know the scriptures to be initiation (*dīkṣā*). || 11 ||
Now, he states that this initiation is threefold:
"That initiation is declared to be of three kinds by those proficient in the Śiva Āgamas. (12)
O ascetic, [initiation] consists of the form of piercing (vedhā), the form of ritual action (kriyā), and the form of mantra.
Now he states the characteristics of those three types of initiation:
"By the mere glance of the guru, or by the joining of his hand with the head... (13).

The meaning is as follows: that immersion (*samāveśa*) into the reality of Śiva, which consists of both knowledge and action, that occurs through the mere glance of the venerable Guru or through the contact of his hand with the head, is considered "piercing initiation" (*vedhā-dīkṣā*). It is remembered as such.

The essential meaning is that *vedhadīkṣā* is the instruction on the nature of the Self as consisting of consciousness, which arises in the lotus-like hand of the Guru while [the disciple] remains within the core of the Guru’s vision. || 13 ||
The initiation of the mantra is said to be that which consists solely of the instruction in the mantra.

(96) The instruction on the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*) alone is given for the sake of Śaivas— that is, for living beings whose nature is the *praṇava* mantra "So 'ham" (I am He)— as an instruction on the five-syllabled mantra alone.
For those belonging to other traditions, there is the instruction of the mantras current in their respective traditions;

for example, for the Vaiṣṇavas, there is the instruction of the twelve-syllable mantra: *oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*. That which possesses the nature of both reflecting (*manana*) and protecting (*trāṇa*) is the *māntrī* [power].
The meaning is that it is called "initiation" (dīkṣā). || 14 ||
The *kriyādīkṣā* (initiation through ritual action) is that which is accompanied by the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala; it is the *kriyottarā* (superior ritual action).

It is the *kriyāparā* (supreme ritual action) conjoined with the jar (*kalaśa*), the binding (*bandha*), the svastika, and the mandala; it is the initiation (*dīkṣā*) characterized by the ritual of wearing the sectarian mark (*liṅgadhāraṇa*). This is the meaning.
Now he demonstrates that method with five verses:
"In an auspicious month, on an auspicious lunar day, at an auspicious time, on an auspicious day... (15)
Having bestowed prosperity upon the devotees of Śiva, preceded by the offering of betel-leaf,
the preceptor should, according to the rules and as is appropriate, bring the disciple forward.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, and having first performed the cleansing of the teeth,
the teacher, facing north, should place the disciple facing east within the mandala.

One should cause the name, the fame, and even the contemplation of Śiva to be performed in an auspicious month— such as Māgha or other favorable months— and on an auspicious lunar day, such as Bhadrā or others [the lunar days are, in order: Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā], that is,
on an auspicious lunar day and an auspicious day.
On an auspicious day such as Monday or Friday, at a favorable time and during a propitious *muhūrta* joined with the *amṛta*-yoga,

the preceptor— having first given sacred ash (*vibhūti*) along with betel leaves to the devotees of Śiva according to the method prescribed by the *Vidhi* and the sequence taught in the scriptures— and having himself performed the cleansing of the teeth and bathed;
Having summoned a disciple wearing white garments to his side and having made him face the east,

he himself, facing north, should place him upon a svastika mandala. Immediately thereafter— whether it be even a caṇḍāla, one should dwell with him who utters the word "Śiva," one should lie down with him, and one should sit together with him.

Based on the scriptural injunction "one should eat," the meaning is that one should cause the recitation of Śiva’s name—which constitutes the entirety of expiatory rites—and meditation upon Śiva to be performed. || 15–17 ||
Immediately thereafter,
having bestowed the fillet of sovereignty in front, according to the proper place and according to the prescribed rite. (18)
There, with the water from the ritual jars established and consisting of the five Brahmans,
the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should sprinkle the disciple three times.

First, having performed the wearing of the *vibhūti* according to the rules and in the proper places, [the ritual is performed] by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with the water from the jars— which consist of the five Brahmās, being of the nature of the five Brahmās beginning with Īśāna— namely, the jar-water consisting of the five-syllabled mantra.

Together with officiating priests who follow the tradition of the five world-renowned teachers, the Guru— the venerable teacher who has been consecrated upon the seat of the teacher (ācārya-paṭṭa) within that very same tradition— should sprinkle the disciple three times. || 18–19 ||

Now, it is said that one should impart the instruction of the mantra in order to establish the *māṃsapiṇḍa* and the *mantrapiṇḍa*: "The Guru, having consecrated the pure disciple who is seated all around him, [should then impart] the five-syllabled Śaiva mantra which delivers one from the fear of saṃsāra. (20)
One should whisper into his right ear its meter, form, seer, deity, and the manual for its ritual placement (nyāsa), even if they are secret.
Then, immediately after the consecration, the Guru [should impart] to the pure disciple standing nearby,
into his right ear, the five-syllabled Śaiva mantra— namely, "Namaḥ Śivāya"— which delivers one from the fear of saṃsāra and is the knowledge renowned in the Śrī Rudra.

One should proclaim—that is, one should instruct—the form of this five-syllabled [mantra] in such a way that it reveals the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and does not remain hidden, but becomes the object of the supreme hearing (*paraśruti*). This is the meaning. Its form is as follows:
The intrinsic nature, the meter, the seer—the great sage who perceived the mantra—and the procedure for the deity-installation;

the names of the five Brahmans and the five Sadas as synonyms for the forms of the presiding deities (adhidevatā) and counter-deities (pratyadhidevatā); and the method of the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) characterized by the fivefold three-fold marks, such as conduct and so forth.
The meaning is "the sequence of nyāsa"; the verb "should proclaim" (kīrtayet) is to be supplied.

In order to place the great liṅga consisting of the praṇava situated in the ājñācakra upon the palm of the hand, one first [places] the five liṅgas beginning with Ācāra, which consist of the seed-syllables beginning with *na*, within the five cakras beginning with the ādhāra.
"One should instruct according to the method taught in the Śiva-āgamas; this is the secret. || 20-21 ||
Thus ends the section on the Compassion of the Guru;
now follows the section on the Wearing of the Liṅga.
Now, this [rite] establishes the universal liṅga of Soma and Sūrya as the purifying mantra for the hand.
He describes the locus for wearing the *liṅga* as ordained by the venerable Guru according to the method stated in the Śruti.
The meaning of "pāṇimantra" is that which protects (*trāyate*) through meditation (*mananāt*) in the hand (*pāṇau*). Here, at the outset, he indicates the nature of the *liṅga* to be worn:
One should procure a single liṅga made either of crystal, or of stone, or of moonstone, or of bāṇa-lapis lazuli, or of sunstone.
"Born of stone" (śailaja) means produced from the rocks of great mountains such as Śrīśaila and others; the rest is clear.
The meaning is that one should examine one of these [stones] and then take it. || 22 ||
Then he says that one should invoke the digit of Śiva (Śivakalā) into that liṅga:
"When that liṅga, endowed with all auspicious characteristics, has been purified, established upon its pedestal, consecrated, and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (23)
The Guru should, according to the prescribed rite, unite the Śiva-kalā within that [image] which has been purified by mantras,
endowed with all the characteristics described in the treatises on iconography (śilpa-śāstra), thoroughly cleansed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and consecrated with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

When that *liṅga*, which has been fully worshipped with fragrant flowers and other offerings, consecrated by the root five-syllable mantra (*mūlapañcākṣarī*), and placed upon the palm of the hand, the Guru— the Preceptor— [bestows] the Śaiva *kalā*, the power of Śiva, which resides upon the head of the disciple.

The meaning is that one should invoke [the deity] in the manner prescribed by the injunctions. That procedure is as follows: having drawn a five-spoked wheel with fragrant paste on the head of the disciple, one should visualize the *praṇava* (om) in the center and the five syllables on the five petals.

To her who is eternal bliss, the incomparable state, partless and devoid of distinctions; whose form is fashioned from the upward-moving *māyā* through artlessness; who is supreme and worshipped by the universe; the foundational primordial power, immeasurable by any multitude of qualities—the Goddess of gods known as Śivā.
I bow to the venerable one known as Ūrdhvā, who dwells upon the seat of the heart-lotus and whose state is that of Supreme Śiva.
Thus, having meditated upon the digit of Śiva (śivakalā)— which is the form of the consciousness-light of all moving and non-moving beings and which causes the engagement in all worldly activities—

and having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, one should draw her forth from the lamp into another lamp as it were, by means of the *aṅkuśa* mudrā while uttering "Kroṃ," and having invoked her, one should contemplate her as being within that [lamp].
One should worship again with offerings of fragrance and so forth. || 23 ||
Then, having brought about the state of equilibrium between the *liṅga* and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should place that *liṅga* in the hand of the disciple; thus it is said:
"Having taken the disciple's vital breath, one should deposit it there in the *liṅga*. One should then establish that *liṅga* within his vital breath through a state of single-minded identity. (24)
Having done this, the preceptor should cause the liṅga to be placed in the hand of the disciple. || 25 ||

There, in that *liṅga*— the *liṅga* filled with the *kalā* of Śiva— one should take and draw forth the disciple’s vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the *kalā* of the individual soul (*jīva*), and install it; one should establish that *liṇga*, which is filled with the *kalā* of Śiva, within the vital breath of that disciple, which is of the nature of the *kalā* of the individual soul in the form of the *praṇava*.

"Establishing as a single entity" means one should cause it to abide through identity (*tādātmya*). The meaning is that the Guru, having thus rendered the *liṅga* as consisting of the state of aesthetic union (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva, the individual soul (*jīva*), and *kalā*, should place it in the lotus-hand of the disciple. || 24-25 ||
(100) He instructs the disciple:
"This *liṅga* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must be maintained by you as if it were your own life."
Never, nor anywhere, separate me from my body.

O disciple! This very *prāṇaliṅga* must be maintained by you as your own life-breath; never separate it from your body—the meaning is that you must not let it be parted from the physical frame. || 26 ||
If, through negligence, the *liṅga* should become separated from the body upon the surface of the earth, what then should be done? To this he says:
"If the *liṅga* falls from the body onto the ground due to negligence, one should suddenly renounce the vital breaths in order to attain the wealth of liberation. (27)

It is clearly stated here—“for the attainment of the wealth of liberation”—lest there be a miserable death (*durmaraṇa*) through the loss of life due to childish conduct; otherwise, the implication is that one would surely end up in hell. || 27 ||
Thus instructed by the teacher who is learned in the scriptures, the disciple should bear the Śaṅkara-liṅga upon his body through the yoga of the vital breaths. || 28 ||

The meaning is that as long as the vital breath remains in the body, for that long the disciple, instructed by a Guru who is a knower of the Vīraśaiva scriptures, should wear the Śāṅkara Liṅga. || 28 ||

Now, as to what purpose is served by its wearing and by whom it is accepted, he says: "The wearing of the *liṅga* is meritorious and destroys all sins; it is honored by all sages who are experts in the meaning of the scriptures. (29)
The meaning is that this has been accepted by all the sages who are experts in the Vīraśaiva Āgamas. || 29 ||
101) Now, regarding the fact that the wearing of the *liṅga* has been accepted in two ways by sages desiring liberation, he says:
"The wearing of the *liṅga* has been declared to be twofold by those who accomplish all goals."
Both external and internal [meditation] is practiced by sages who desire liberation. || 30 ||
The meaning is that it accomplishes all goals and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. The remainder is clear. || 30 ||
Regarding the question "What is this internal [meditation]?", he says:
"The supreme Śiva-liṅga, whose nature is consciousness and which is the cause of all;
the holding of that within the mind is declared to be the internal. (31)
The supreme form of consciousness, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, is therefore transcendent of space and time;
it is the cause of all, the cause of the universe characterized by space, time, and form.
Within the mind of that Great Liṅga—the Śāṅkara Liṅga pertaining to Śiva—which exists in the lotus of one's own heart—...

Alternatively, that which is wearing [the liṅga] in the form of meditation—that is, maintaining it internally—is declared to be "internal wearing of the liṅga" (antarliṅgadhāraṇa); this is the meaning. || 31 ||
Now, he reveals this essential nature in many ways:
"The supreme reality, called Śiva, is the cause of the universe; its nature is consciousness, it is free from all worldly impurities, partless, and beyond conceptual construction. (32)
Consisting of the digit of radiance that causes the manifestation of the bliss of existence,
it is immeasurable, indescribable, and worshipped by those seeking liberation.

The Supreme Brahman is the Great Liṅga, transcending the phenomenal world and imperishable. Because it is distinct from the insentient, it is of the nature of consciousness; because it is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), it is supreme. For this very reason, it is the cause of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, devoid of all defects, partless, and free from differentiation.

Indeed, the Great Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman known as Śiva; it functions as the nature of the seventeen kalās beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), consisting of the essence of eternal bliss and light; it is inaccessible to perception and other means of valid knowledge, inexpressible, worthy of worship by those desiring liberation, transcendent to the universe, and uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.
The meaning is that it is well-known as the "Mahāliṅga. || 32-33 ||
(102) Now, one might ask: "Since such a Great Liṅga is devoid of a specific location or visualization, how can it be worshipped? To this, he says:
That very [Self] is within all beings, its range being the three abodes.
In the mūlādhāra, in the heart, and between the eyebrows of all embodied beings, the jyotirliṅga shines eternally; that is what the Āgamas call Brahman. (35)

Thus, that very Great Liṅga mentioned previously exists within all living beings, occupying three locations; the meaning is that it possesses three stations. That reality of the Great Liṅga, well-known in the Śiva Āgamas—the one which the Āgamas and Upaniṣads call "Brahman"—is the Jyotirliṅga for all embodied beings, for all living creatures.

The meaning is that [the Self] shines eternally through the instruction of the Guru as something to be known in the front of the heart, at the mūlādhāra, in the middle of the heart, in the heart, in the upper heart, and between the eyebrows. || 34-35 ||
To the question, "How can there be fragmentation of the Great Liṅga which is itself undivided? he says:
"The eternal Brahman is the Liṅga, which is unlimited and unmanifest;
for the sake of meditation, it is made limited and situated within by its own Māyā. (36)

Although it is the one, indivisible, unmanifest, eternal Brahman— denoted by the word "Brahman" and situated within— the single *liṅga* is, for the sake of the devotion, meditation, and worship of its devotees, rendered limited by its own *māyā* (whose synonym is its own sovereignty) according to different locations.
The meaning is that it is known in the form of the three genders. || 36 ||
To the question, "How is it that the Supreme Brahman is designated by the form of the *liṅga*? he says:
103) "Into this very [liṅga] this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, goes to its dissolution."
The eternal Brahman is that sign characterized by repeated rebirth.
In that Brahman this world of moving and non-moving beings goes to dissolution and undergoes repeated rebirth; thus, the meaning is that that eternal Brahman is the *liṅga*. || 37 ||
He concludes the meaning already stated:
"Therefore, that which is known as the *liṅga* consists of existence (*sattā*), bliss (*ānanda*), and consciousness (*cit*);
because of its vastness (*bṛhatva*) and its capacity to expand (*bṛṃhaṇatva*), it is denoted by the word *brahman*. (38)

Therefore, the Liṅga consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss is known as the Mahāliṅga; because of its vastness, its greatness, its nourishing nature, and its orientation toward the creation of the universe, it is designated by the term "Brahman"—meaning it is well-known and celebrated as such. Thus, the Supreme Brahman itself is the Mahāliṅga, and the Mahāliṅga itself is [the Supreme Brahman].
The sense is that it is the Supreme Brahman. || 38 ||
Now, he states that the continuous contemplation of the *jyotirliṅga* within one of the aforementioned locations is the internal wearing of the *liṅga*:
"Whether in the *ādhāra*, in the heart, or in the middle of the eyebrows, the uninterrupted contemplation of the *jyotirliṅga* is the internal wearing of the *liṅga*. (39)
This is clear. || 39 ||

Now, as to the manner in which it should be contemplated, he says: "The yogi should visualize the *liṅga* in the *ādhāra* as resembling gold, in the heart as having the luster of coral, and between the eyebrows as having the brilliance of crystal. (40)
This is clear. || 40 ||
104) Now, he states that this internal wearing of the *liṅga* is superior to the external wearing of the *liṅga*:
"The internal wearing of the *liṅga* is declared to be free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*)."
It is a million times more distinguished than the wearing of external sectarian marks. || 41 ||
This is clear. || 41 ||
Those who hold in their hearts the Lord’s linga, whose nature is consciousness, shall have no further return to the terrible cycle of worldly existence. 42.
The meaning is that it is indeed the supreme liberation. || 42 ||

To the question "How so?", he says: "The internal contemplation of the signs, diligent application to the knowledge of the Self, and the power of service to the Guru are the causes for the attainment of liberation. (43)

Based on the scriptural authority (śruti/smṛti) that "there is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self," the internal contemplation of the *liṅga* serves both as the means to dispel the ignorance that one is not the Lord— wherein the mastery of the knowledge of the Self consists of either sharpness (*naiśityam*, meaning keenness or intense longing)— and as the capacity for service to the Guru.
The meaning is that it is the cause of the attainment of liberation. || 43 ||
Therefore, he says that for Śiva-yogins whose hearts are unwavering, the inclination is toward the internal liṅga alone and not toward the external:
"For yogins endowed with dispassion and knowledge, whose minds are steady..."
When there is a continuous contemplation of the internal sign, no interest arises in the external.
This is clear. || 44 ||
105) How much more so, then, do even those such as Brahmā who are fully matured perceive the *jyotirliṅga* through the yoga of right knowledge? To this he says:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the world-protectors beginning with Vāsava..."
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Dānavas, and likewise human beings. || 45 ||
And all, through the yoga of knowledge, behold within their hearts the Linga, the cause of all causes, characterized by supreme bliss. 46.

In this context, based on the scriptural statement, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra are produced here," it should be understood that the Rudra intended is the one who has entered the category of the effected (kārya), and not the Great Liṅga Rudra who is the cause of the three forms (trimūrti). || 45-46 ||
Therefore, for the sake of ceasing the sufferings of saṃsāra, one should indeed practice the contemplation of the internal *liṅga*; thus he says:
"Therefore, with every effort, the wise man should contemplate within the supreme *liṅga* of Śaṅkara, for the sake of liberation from all afflictions. (47)
This is clear. || 47 ||
If this is so, then one might ask: for what purpose is the wearing of external signs? In response to this expectation, he says:
Whether incapable or indeed capable of maintaining the internal sign, one should wear the external sign as well, because of the certainty that it is of that same nature. (48)

Whether one is incapable or indeed capable of wearing the internal liṅga, one should [worship] an external liṅga made of crystal, stone, or other materials, perceiving it as having that same form— namely,
as being identical in nature to the Great Liṅga consisting of consciousness (cinmaya) residing in the heart-lotus— through a firm conviction free from doubt.

One should maintain the Linga of consciousness, which is established in the lotus of the heart; its pure root-pedestal is the nature of the Bindu, its radiant upper pedestal is the nature of Nāda, and it is enriched by the Gomukha [principle] extending crosswise as the Kalās.
According to this statement from the *Śivāloka*, the meaning is that a Vīraśaiva should wear an external liṅga of that form for the purpose of recollecting the internal liṅga. || 48 ||
106) Now he defines the classification of the great *liṅga*: "The *liṅga* is said to be threefold: gross, subtle, and beyond the supreme."
This gross external linga which is worn upon the body is the "desired linga. (49)
This subtle *prāṇaliṅga*, which consists of internal meditation, is said to be that which is higher than the highest; it is called the *tṛptiliṅga*.
The term *liṅga* refers to the *mahāliṅga*. It is threefold: gross (*sthūla*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and beyond the supreme (*parātpara*).

Among these, that which is worn externally on the body is this *iṣṭaliṅga*, which is gross. That *liṅga* which exists internally within the heart-lotus, consisting of meditation and having the form of the contemplation of pure Being (*sanmātra*), is the *prāṇaliṅga*.
The meaning is that whatever subtle sign is proclaimed as "beyond the beyond," that is called the "sign of satisfaction."

To the question, "For what purpose should this gross liṅga be worn?", he says: This cherished liṅga is the unmanifest Supreme Brahman named Śiva, transcending all mental cultivation; it is so because it directly wards off that which is undesirable.
The wise person should always wear it upon their body with focused attention. || 51 ||

The unmanifest Supreme Brahman, known as Śiva and renowned in the Vedas and Āgamas, is beyond the reach of the external senses due to the absence of form and other qualities; it is beyond the sphere of the impure mental functions and transcends all conceptualization, precisely because it is the cessation of all that is undesirable.
Because it wards off the undesirable characteristics of the snares of *saṃsāra* and bestows liberation— which is superior even to the most desired forms—

it is the manifest, directly perceptible *iṣṭaliṅga*. As established in the *Atharvaśiras*, "One who bestows the desired vigor through austerity"— the wise person, proficient in the scriptures and traditions, should with vigilance [worship] this *liṅga* within the body.
The meaning is that one should always wear [it]. || 51 ||
Now, regarding where this desired liṅga should be worn on the body, he says:
One should wear the Lord’s liṅga either on the head, or in the region of the throat, or in the armpit, or even on the chest; or in the belly, or even on the surface of the hand. (52)
This is clear. || 52 ||
107) Now, he states the grounds for prohibition:
"Wearing [the *liṅga*] below the navel is a cause of sin."
One should not wear it on the tip of the matted hair, nor in the three parts [of the head], nor in a place of impurity. || 53 ||
The "triangular portion" means the back portion; the rest is clear. || 53 ||
Now, regarding where this *liṅga* should be worshipped, it is said here:
"The bearer of the *liṅga*, ever pure, should worship his own beautiful *liṅga* upon the palm of his hand with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, being fully concentrated. (54)
This is clear. || 54 ||
Compared to the worship of external seats, this worship of the hand-seat is superior for all Vīraśaivas who desire liberation, and it should be performed continuously. (55)
This is clear. || 55 ||
Now, regarding the question of by whom this wearing of the *liṅga* has been accepted, he says:
"The gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the sages, such as Gautama and others, always wear the *liṅga* specifically upon their heads. (56)
All the powers, such as Lakṣmī and the others, being permeated by devotion to Śiva,
bear the Śiva-liṅga upon the tips of their foreheads day and night.
By this, the wearing of the marks by both women and men is also stated. || 56-57 ||
108) Now, as to where this wearing of the *liṅga* is taught, he says:
"In the Vedas, the Śāstras, and the Purāṇas, as well as in the Āgamas such as the Kāmika."
The wearing of the *liṅga* has been declared to be the definitive characteristic of a Vīraśaiva. || 58 ||
Now, to show where this is well-known in the Śruti, he says:
"The Ṛgveda says: 'O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out.
Therefore, that purifying, healthy Śaiva liṅga should be worn. (59)

"The Rigveda says: 'O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out. O Brahmaṇaspati, the remainder [of the sense] is: 'your linga'—it is spread out, extending from Śiva down to the earth; it is a purifier, meaning it is sanctifying.
Therefore, one should wear that auspicious linga, which is free from disease and devoid of defects. || 59 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of wearing this?
To which he replies: "The *liṅga* is declared to be Brahman; its Lord is the Sovereign (*Īśvara*).
For it is renowned as pure, and through contact with it, the body becomes purified. (60)
"That is pure" means that through contact with it, the body—the physical frame—becomes pure. || 60 ||
Now, he says that one who is devoid of initiation should not wear such a *liṅga*:
"One whose body has not been heated by austerity, who is ignorant, raw, and devoid of purificatory rites—such a person, lacking initiation, shall certainly not attain the supreme *liṅga*. (61)

One whose body is unrefined (*ataptatanuḥ*) means one whose body is devoid of austerity (*tapas*); "unripe" (*āmaḥ*) means immature, meaning one whose nature is lacking in dispassion (*vairāgya*). "Devoid of refinement" (*saṃskāravarjitaḥ*) means lacking the purificatory rites of Śiva; "ignorant" (*ajñaḥ*) means devoid of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal realities;

"devoid of initiation" (*dīkṣayā rahitaḥ*) means lacking the compassion of a Guru. [Such a person] [does not perceive] the supreme [reality] directly (*sākṣāt*), that is, through direct perception (*pratyakṣam*).
One should not obtain nor wear the supreme *liṅga*. In this regard, it is said: "One whose body has not been heated by austerity does not enjoy that, being raw" (Ṛgveda).
"Thus says the Śruti. The word *tad* (that) is to be separated as *tad-āma* (that raw/unripe), meaning that very sign (*liṅga*).
By this, it is indicated that the very sign bestowed by a perfectly gracious Guru alone grants enjoyment and liberation; whereas [a sign] worn according to one's own whim is fruitless. || 61 ||
Now, he states that there is also a Vedic revelation from the Yajurveda regarding the wearing of the *liṅga*:
"Because that auspicious form of yours, O Rudra, which is non-terrible and does not cause sin, is sung in the *Yajus*, therefore the devotee of Śiva is free from evil. (62)
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and does not appear as evil— O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with that most peaceful form.

[This is] the Śrī Rudra-śruti [Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 16.2]. The meaning of this scripture is as follows: O Rudra, that body (*tanū*) of yours which is auspicious (*śivā*), having the nature of blessing—according to the scriptural statement, "the *liṅga* is the body of Śiva and Śakti"—that form of the *liṅga*, consisting of Śiva and Śakti, is non-terrible (*aghorā*), peaceful (*śāntā*), and not shining upon the sinful (*apāpakāśī*), [but rather] upon those who are sinless (*apāpeṣu*).

Because he shines among his devotees, he is called "Apāpakāśī" (the one who shines sinlessly). Since it is proclaimed in the *Yajuṣ*—that is, the Yajurveda—that he resides there in the form of the desired *liṅga*, he is therefore "Śaiva," meaning related to the Śiva-liṅga;
the sense is that he is "aghavarjita," which means free from sin. || 62 ||
Now, having concluded the section on the wearing of the *liṅga*, he indicates the section on the wearing of ashes for one who has accomplished that:
"He who wears the *liṅga* with a restrained inner self..."
With his mind constantly fixed on the worship of Śiva,
he should apply pure and beautiful ashes according to the prescribed method for the sake of destroying all impurities.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Occasion for Wearing the Guru’s Compassion-Liṅga in the Section on Devotion," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, the Determination of the Śrī Vīraśaiva Dharma.

That person who bears the *liṅga*, who is perfected in the wearing of the *liṅga*, whose inner self is restrained, whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is stainless, and whose mind is constantly fixed on the worship of Śiva— he is the bearer of the Śiva-liṅga.

The meaning is that one should wear the beautiful, captivating, stainless, and pure ash for the sake of removing all impurities and for the cessation of all defects, according to the application prescribed by the scriptures. || 63 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Occasion for Wearing the Liṅga through the Guru’s Compassion in the State of Devotion," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the illustrious scriptures, sentences, and means of valid knowledge.
The Seventh Chapter: The Place for Wearing Ashes.
Now, regarding the wearing of ashes: "One should not neglect prosperity" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1).
Śrī Reṇuka describes the locus of the application of ash as established in the Śruti. Herein, he first describes the unconditioned application of ash with two aphorisms:
"One who is joined with the application of ash is pure and of restrained intent."
That which is called Śiva is likewise called bhasita because of its shining (bhāsana). || 1 ||
Having conceived of Mahādeva as the great ash, which is composed of light, those fortunate ones who abide [in him] are the foremost wearers of ash. || 2 ||
One who is engaged in the wearing of ashes, who bears the Śiva-linga, and whose intention is disciplined—through meditation on the ashes, union [with Śiva] occurs;

through meditation on the ashes, the remembrance of the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) occurs; from that meditation, one attains the state of Sthāṇu (Śiva). He is indeed the light of ashes; he is indeed the light of ashes.

In the *Bhasmajābālaśruti*—this extracted portion is not found in the *Bhasmajābālopaniṣad*—one whose mind is restrained [thinks]: "The ash-light-liṅga (*bhasmajyotirliṅga*) is this; being pure and purified, that which is the ash-light-liṅga is named Śiva, the designation of Paraśiva, the Supreme Brahman."

"It is said" refers to that Mahādeva whose nature is a *jyotirliṅga* consisting of light; because he shines and illuminates, he is "ash" (*bhasita*), and thus [the term] *mahābhasma* (great ash) is used. Having reflected thus, those who are highly fortunate and the most excellent among the wearers of the *liṅga* are the primary ones who wear the primary ash.
The meaning is: one who wears ashes without any external adjuncts. || 1-2 ||
112) Now he defines the nature of ash that possesses an adjunct (sopādhika):
[Ash] produced from the fire of Śiva and so forth, through the application of mantra-installation and other such means.
Those proficient in the Bhasma-tantra say that it is conditioned by that [impurity]. || 3 ||

That ash which, through the application of mantras such as the *pañcabrahma-mantra-nyāsa*, arises from the fire of Śiva and is consecrated by the mantras of Śiva— that ash is called "qualified" (*sopādhika*) by those experts in the Tantras who are proficient in the Śiva Āgamas.
The meaning is that they say, "It is ashes. || 3 ||
Now, he states that this ash has five names according to its different causes:
"Vibhūti, bhasita, bhasma, kṣāra, and rakṣā—these are the five names of ash, [given] emphatically according to five reasons. (4)
This is clear. || 4 ||

Having given names that correspond to their respective causes, he explains them: "It is *vibhūti* because it is the cause of prosperity (*bhūti*); it is *bhasita* because it illuminates reality (*tattva*);
it is *bhasma* because it terrifies (*bhartsanā*) evils; and it is *kṣāra* because it wears away (*kṣaraṇa*) calamities. (5)
Because it protects all beings, it is celebrated as "Rakṣā" (the Protector).

Because it is the cause of the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with *aṇimā*, it is "Vibhūti" (Prosperity). Because it reveals the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*), it is "Bhasita" (the Illuminator).
Because it censures and strikes fear into sins born of mind, speech, and body, it is "Bhasma" (the Ashes).

The meaning is that it is celebrated as "Kṣāra" because it neutralizes—that is, causes the destruction of—calamities, which are misfortunes arising from the three types of suffering; and it is called "Rakṣā" because it protects all beings, including those afflicted by planets, yakṣas, and other such spirits. || 5 ||
To the question, "What is the basis for the distinction between these various types of activity?", he says that it is rooted in the *go* (cow):
"Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā. (6)
Five cows were born from the faces of the All-pervading Lord, beginning with Sadyojāta.
From Śiva’s mouth, Sadyojāta, Nandā was born; from the face of Vāmadeva, Bhadrā; and from the mouth of Aghora, Surabhi.
From the mouth of Tatpuruṣa came Suśīlā, and from the face of Īśāna came Sumanā; thus five cows were born.
The meaning is that this distinction in their functions is produced by them. || 6 ||
In response to the question "What then is their form?", he says:
"Tawny, black, white, smoky, and likewise red. (7)
The colors of the cows beginning with Nandā have been proclaimed in sequence;
the connection is that they are likewise [described] in that same order. || 7 ||

Now, as to which cow [the ash was produced from] and what kind of ash arose, he states the very meaning of the Bṛhajjābāla Śruti: "From Sadyojāta comes the Vibhūti (sacred ash), and from Vāmadeva comes the bhasita (ash). (8)
From Aghora, the sacred ash (bhasma) was produced; from Tatpuruṣa, it received the name "alkali" (kṣāra);
protection came from the face of Īśāna; and [the fourfold nature] arose from the gates beginning with Nanda.
The ash is produced by Nandā arising from the Sadyojāta face; it is smeared with Bhaṭṭārikā born from the Vāmadeva face;
that ash is fragrant due to Surabhi produced from the Aghora face;
it is well-disposed due to Suśīlā manifested from the Tatpuruṣa face; and it provides protection through Sumanas emerging from the Īśāna face.
The meaning is that "abhavat" signifies "was. || 8-9 ||
Now he states their respective applications:

"One should diligently apply the *vibhūti* (ash) during daily obligatory rites (*nitya-kārya*), the *bhasita* (ash) during occasional rites (*naimittika*), and the *kṣāra* (alkali/ash) always during rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*). (10)
In all rites of expiation, as well as in matters of protection and liberation, the wise should always employ that which is called "ashes" according to the prescribed rule.
(114) It should be employed—that is, worn—by the wise, meaning by those learned persons who have entered the Vīraśaiva doctrine.
The rest is clear. || 10–11 ||
Now, he describes the colors of such ashes:
"The colors of Nanda and the others which have been proclaimed as tawny (kapila) and so forth—those very same colors are renowned for Bhūti and the others, respectively. (12)
This is clear. || 12 ||
Now, he states that the production of this ash is fourfold:
"The production of ash is declared by those who know the Tantras to be of four kinds:
the primary method (kalpa), the secondary method (anukalpa), the approximate method (upakalpa), and the method-less method (akalpaka). (13)
Of these, the first is the most excellent; all the others are non-existent.
Among the four kinds of ash known as *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, *upakalpa*, and *akalpa*, the first—the initial *kalpa* ash—is the most excellent;
all the other remaining three kinds of ash are non-existent [in comparison].
The meaning is that it must be accepted because of the attainment of the ashes of the eon (kalpabhasma). || 13 ||
Now he describes their essential nature in sequence:
having taken fresh cow dung according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures... (14)
One should fashion the unsurpassed *piṇḍa* with the *Sadyojāta* and *Vāmadeva* [mantras];
one should dry it with *Puruṣa* alone, and burn it with the *Ghora* fire of Śiva.
That ash is to be known as a *kalpa*; now the *anukalpa* is being described:
likewise, cow dung found in forests that has been dried and ground into powder.
That which is called the secondary (anukalpa) ash is what has been burnt in marketplaces and similar places;
it is strained through a cloth and formed into a ball bound with cow urine. || 17 ||
That which has been burnt according to the previously mentioned procedure shall become the prepared ash;
it is certain that even ash brought by others is unfit for ritual use. (18)

In accordance with the method prescribed in the scriptures, Nanda and the others took fresh cow dung that had appeared [naturally], held it in their hands with the *sadyojāta* mantra (*sadyena*), formed it into a ball with the *vāmadeva* mantra, dried it with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra,
and [cooked it] with fire consecrated by the *śiva* mantra, starting from the *aghora* mantra.

"Burns" means one should reduce it to ashes. "Then, by means of the Īśāna mantra, that ash placed in a vessel such as one made of *bilva* is fit to be known as the *kalpa*"—this is the meaning. "In the forests, whatever dried cow-dung has been powdered and burnt as before, that ash is called the *anukalpa*"—this is the meaning. Here...

There is an omission of the three mantras. The meaning is that if the ash found in marketplaces and such places is purified with a cloth, then formed into a ball with cow urine, and subsequently burnt according to the previously mentioned procedure, it becomes what is called *upakalpa* ash. [This applies to] that which has been prepared by others who are ignorant of the mantras.
The meaning is that the prepared ash, though actually beyond conceptualization (*akalpa*), is said to be "conceptualized" (*kalpita*) because it has been described [as such]. || 14-18 ||
Now, he says that one should perform a bath with such ashes as follows:
"Having taken any one of these into vessels such as jars and the like, one should perform the bath at the three junctions of the day, or whenever possible. (19)

The meaning is that when these ashes have been placed separately in vessels such as a *kalaśa* and others, one should take one of those ashes and perform the bath either at the three times of day or at a single time. || 19 ||
To the question of how it should be performed, he says:
At the time of bathing, having washed one's hands and feet with pure water...
Having sprinkled ashes on the palm of the left hand and covered it with the other hand, || 20 ||
Then, having consecrated the ashes eight times with the root mantra while observing silence,
he should apply it to the head with the Īśāna mantra and likewise to the face with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should sprinkle the heart region with the Aghora mantra, the secret parts with Vāmadeva,
the feet with Sadyojāta, and all the limbs with the Praṇava alone.

At the time of the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), having washed one's hands and feet with clear water, one should place the ash in the palm of the left hand, cover it with the right hand, and rest it upon the right thigh; then, remaining silent according to the injunctions of the Śiva-āgamas, one should consecrate the ash with mantras. Thus, becoming silent—

Having consecrated [the water] eight times with the root mantra, one should touch the head, face, heart, navel, and feet while bowing, using the mantras beginning with Īśāna: "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām | Brahmādhipatir brahmaṇo'dhipatir brahmā śivo me 'stu" (Īśāna is the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings; the overlord of Brahman, the overlord of the sacred word, the Brahman—may Śiva be auspicious to me).

Sadāśiva: *Om*. Tatpuruṣa: We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us. Aghora: From the non-terrible ones, and from the terrible ones, and from those more terrible than the terrible; from all, from every one of them...
Salutations be to those who have the form of Rudra!

To Vāmadeva— salutations to Vāmadeva, salutations to the Eldest, salutations to the Most Excellent, salutations to Rudra, salutations to Kāla, salutations to the Transformer of Time, salutations to the Transformer of Strength, salutations to Strength.

Salutations to the Subduer of Strength; salutations to the Tamer of All Beings; salutations to the One who Transcends the Mind. To Sadyojāta: I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations, salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. In every birth, O Bhava, protect me from further becoming; salutations to the Source of Birth.
[One should sprinkle with water while reciting the *praṇava*.]
The meaning is that one should sprinkle all the limbs. || 20-22 ||
Now, he says that this is superior to bathing in water:
"This bath performed with ashes is the supreme Agneya (fiery) bath."
Among baths such as the Vāruṇa and others, this is the primary means for removing impurity.

Among the baths such as those with the waters of the Gaṅgā, divine waters, or wind, this bath prescribed with ash is the supreme "fiery" (āgneya) bath. Because fire reduces everything to ash, this fiery bath removes all impurities; thus, it is the primary one—this is the meaning. || 23 ||

Now, as to whether bathing in water and so forth possesses the power to remove all impurities or not, he says: "For men who perform the ash-bath day after day as appropriate, there is no need for baths such as those with water, which only remove external defects. (24)

The meaning is this: for those men who daily perform the ash-bath according to the method prescribed in the scriptures as appropriate, there is no need for baths with water and other substances that merely remove external impurities; since ash is a limb of knowledge (*jñāna-aṅga*), it removes both internal and external stains. Thus, what is the purpose of [ordinary] baths? || 24 ||
For this very reason, he states that since the fire-related (āgneya) bath is superior to bathing in water, the ash-bath alone is prescribed for ascetics:
"The fire-related bath with ashes is indeed prescribed for ascetics."
After bathing while the body is still wet, one must apply ashes; otherwise, the killing of living beings certainly occurs. || 25 ||

The practice of bathing with ashes is prescribed by ascetics as "fiery" (*āgneya*), because fire, through its luminosity, bestows knowledge. For ascetics, bathing with ashes is superior to bathing with water; for it is a certain certainty that in a wet bath involving water, there is the killing of living beings due to the suffering caused to aquatic creatures by the cold.
And it means that it does not cause injury to living beings; for in this case, such a defect is absent. || 25 ||
118) Now he brings forth another defect of water: "One should know that moisture is its nature; they know that nature is bondage."
However, for the sake of abandoning material nature (prakṛti), bathing with ashes is prescribed. || 26 ||
One should know that "moist" (*ārdra*) refers to water, which is the nature of dwelling in the womb, because blood and semen consist of water;

for the Śruti says: "This very person consists of the essence of food" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1). The wise know and understand that this "nature" (*prakṛti*) is bondage—a snare for the person (*puruṣa*) in the form of the enjoyed and the enjoyer. The person...

The meaning is that, because the person (puruṣa) is bound by primordial nature (prakṛti)— as stated by the Blessed One in Bhagavad Gītā 13.21, "For abiding in nature, one experiences the qualities born of nature"— one desires bathing with ashes for the purpose of abandoning that nature, just as one bathes with water to remove the impurity arising from bathing in water.
Now, regarding the question of who has accepted this bath with ashes, he says:
"All the gods beginning with Brahmā, the sages beginning with Nārada, the yogins beginning with Sanaka, and even the Dānavas beginning with Bāṇa. (27)
All those who have performed ten million ash-baths become devoted solely to Śiva;
indeed, freed from the impurities of defects, they are eternally pure. 28.
"Kalilāḥ" means multitudes; the rest is clear. || 27-28 ||
Now, it is said that the smearing with ashes and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) must be performed:
"Having consecrated the ashes seven times with the mantra 'Namaḥ Śivāya', one should smear the body with it and also wear the triple mark. (29)

The meaning is that, having consecrated the ashes seven times with the mantra "Bhasma Namas Śivāya" for the purpose of removing the defects committed in seven previous births, one should smear the body with those ashes and also fashion the *tripuṇḍra* on the body. || 29 ||
119) Here, he states that the *tripuṇḍra* is superior to the smearing (*uddhūlana*) [of ashes] over the entire body: "Even the smearing of all limbs is not equal to the *tripuṇḍra*s."
Therefore, one should apply only the single triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra), without the application of sacred ash.
This is clear. || 30 ||

Now, regarding when, how, and where the *tripuṇḍra* should be worn, it is said here: "The best of practitioners should always wear the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes and water on fifteen locations of the body. (31)
This is clear. || 31 ||
To the question "Which ones are they?", he says here:
on the head, on the forehead, likewise on the pair of ears, on the throat, on the two arms, on the heart, on the navel, and on the back. (32)
Practitioners should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes on both arms, on the region of the shoulders, and likewise on the two wrists, using the root mantra.

One should wear [the marks] on the head, forehead, throat, shoulders, and chest using the *triyāyuṣa*, *tryambaka*, *praṇava*, and *pañcākṣara* mantras; one should draw three lines with the *triyāyuṣa* and *tryambaka* mantras.
For it is stated in the Śruti: "This is the *śāmbhava* vow. (32–33)
120) Now, preceded by the method of consecrating that [ash], he states the fruit of wearing the *tripuṇḍra* with mantras:
Having sprinkled ashes on the palm of the left hand and covered it with the other hand,
one should touch it while reciting the mantra beginning with "Agnis" and consecrate it by sprinkling water.
In places where the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has been removed, one should apply wet ashes;
he attains Śiva, the auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the peaceful one—of this there is no doubt. || 35 ||

"Agni is ashes, Vāyu is ashes, water is ashes, earth is ashes, space is ashes; indeed, all this is ashes. The mind and these senses are ashes"—with this mantra from the *Bhasmajābāla Upaniṣad*, while touching it seven times with water, one should consecrate it with the root mantra; such is the meaning. (34)
Now he describes the method for applying the Tripuṇḍra:
"With the three middle fingers of one's own right hand, [the mark] should be six finger-breadths in length, or else the measure of the forehead. (36)
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead with a measurement equal to the span of both eyes;
this is clear. || 36 ||
Now, he describes the application of the *tripuṇḍra* in another manner:
"With the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, in both direct and reverse order. (37)
He who wears the mark of the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
One should fashion two lines with the middle and ring fingers, moving in the natural direction (anuloma) and clockwise (pradakṣiṇa).
Between them, one should fashion a single line with the thumb, moving in the reverse direction (viloma) and counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa). Thus.
The meaning is that by saying "Rudra is he who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)," there is a distinction compared to what preceded. || 37 ||
(p. 121) Now he describes its characteristics:
straight, white, pervasive, smooth, and equal in length to the ear. || 38 ||
Thus, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) endowed with these characteristics bestows all accomplishments;
it should be straight, upright, white, bright, pervasive, unbroken, smooth, thick, and measured by the ear—the meaning being that its extent is limited by the ears. || 38 ||
Now, he indicates the greatness of this *tripuṇḍra* with two verses:
"The *tripuṇḍra* [should be applied] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. (39)

Sometimes one may apply it with ashes; he is indeed Rudra, there is no doubt about this. The Śruti declares that he who thus applies the Tripuṇḍra with sacred ash (vibhūti) is endowed with the nature of Rudra and consists of the three Vedas.

He who, with ashes and with such splendor, applies the *tripuṇḍra* endowed with such auspicious characteristics as being straight and white—he, being joined with the *raudra-dharma*, that is, being joined with the *rudra-sambandhī dharma*, which is the practice of Śiva, is "consisting of the three," meaning his nature is the three Vedas; such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). He who this...
He who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) becomes a bearer of the three Vedas; he constantly becomes the three sacred fires (tretāgni);
he becomes one who has bathed in the three lotuses (puṣkara). That man who wears the triple mark is Rudra; he is the Supreme Lord (parameṣṭhī).
Whoever beholds this man wearing the triple mark is liberated from all sins.

"He becomes possessed of the fruit arising from the study of all the Vedas" [this citation is not found in the Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad]. Thus, this matter is established by many scriptural authorities such as the Vṛddhajābāla. Therefore, at some time during the three periods beginning with morning—
The meaning is that he who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is Rudra, indeed Śiva himself; there is no doubt about this. || 39-40 ||
Now, to answer the question of by whom such a *tripuṇḍra* is worn, he says:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the gods headed by Indra...
They indeed wear the triple mark fashioned with sacred ash.
The highly fortunate sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, who are experts in the Vedas,
always wear the Tripuṇḍra mark made with sacred ash.
This is clear. || 41-42 ||
Now, as to where this is prescribed, he says:
"The sacred ash mark (bhasmapuṇḍraka) is ordained in the Śaiva Āgamas, in the Vedas, in all the Purāṇas, and in the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Kalpas."
It is to be upheld by all [followers], and especially by the Śaivas. || 43 ||
"In the Kalpas" means in the Kalpasūtras; such is the meaning. || 43 ||
Then, having stated that "by this wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), there is the destruction of all sins," he concludes the section on the application of ashes:
"One who is an atheist, one who has transgressed the bounds of conduct, and one who is devoted to wicked behavior— "
If one wears the triple mark of ashes, one is liberated from all sins.

The meaning is that even one who is devoted to conduct contrary to the Vedas— a nihilist such as a Cārvāka and the like, who asserts that there is no self distinct from the body, senses, and intellect— and who is thus intent on wicked behavior, is liberated from all taints, that is, from every sin, if he wears the triple mark of ashes. || 44 ||
Now, the section on the wearing of Rudrākṣas.
Next, he describes the proper manner of wearing Rudrākṣas:
"Having performed his bath with sacred ash, and having marked his forehead with the Tripuṇḍra..."
One who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva should also wear rudrākṣa beads. || 45 ||
"Head" (mastaka) means the forehead; the rest is clear. || 45 ||
To the question "What is the purpose of this?", he says:
"By the mere wearing of rudrākṣas, even men who are evil-minded, of wicked conduct, and of poor intellect, are liberated from all sins. (46)
This is clear. || 46 ||
Now, how were these rudrākṣas produced? From where does such power as this arise? To this he says:
"In the past, during the destruction of Tripura, the three-eyed Lord of the worlds, his eyes opened wide, beheld the union of the cities. (47)
Many drops of water fell from his eyes;
from those were born the rudrākṣas, which are thus celebrated as "rudrākṣas. (48)

The Rudrākṣas, which purify the world, were produced from the eyes of Rudra. Formerly, during the occasion of the destruction of Tripura, the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the universe, the three-eyed Śiva—
whose eyes are the Moon, the Sun, and Fire— opened his eyes at the very time of universal dissolution.

With his three eyes blossomed due to the opening of the eye on his forehead, he beheld the union—the connection—of the three cities (Tripura) from above; from his eyes, many drops of water, droplets of moisture, fell and landed upon the earth, and from those water-drops, the rudrākṣas were born. Indeed.

Because they were produced from the eyes of Rudra, for that reason they are celebrated as *rudrākṣas*; the meaning is that for this very reason they are the purifiers of the world. In this regard, formerly, at the time of the destruction of Tripura, my eyes were opened;
the drops of water that fell from them onto the earth became these *rudrākṣas*.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon all, by the utterance of their names, the fruit of giving away a thousand cows is obtained;
through seeing and touching them, the fruit becomes twofold and threefold. Beyond this, it is impossible to describe. (Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad, Seventh Brāhmaṇa, Eighth Khaṇḍa)
"The description of the Rudrākṣa is heard [in various texts], yet the sequence [of its qualities] differs"—thus says the Bṛhajjābāla and other Śrutis. (47–48)
(124) Thus, because they have arisen from the eyes of Rudra, they undergo origination in thirty-eight ways through the differentiation of his creative powers (*kalā*); so he says:
They become thirty-eightfold through the distinction of their modes of arising. || 49 ||
This is clear. || 49 ||
Now, as to why so many [mantras] have arisen from the eye, he says here:
"From the eye of Śambhu, which is of the nature of the Sun, twelve Kapilas have emerged;
sixteen Śvetas were born from the eye that is of the form of the Moon. (50)
The black variety arose from the eye in the form of fire;
thus, due to the differences in their origin, the rudrākṣas are remembered as being of many kinds.

From the eye of Śiva, whose nature is the Sun, twelve *kapila*—meaning tawny-colored—rudrākṣas, possessing twelve varieties, are said to have arisen or been produced; this is because the eye of the Sun consists of the twelve digits (*kalās*) beginning with *Tāpinī*. From the eye that is the Moon, the lunar eye, the white ones [arose].
