Sixteen white-colored ones, possessing sixteen varieties, were born and produced,

because that [third] eye consists of the sixteen digits (kalās) beginning with Amṛtā. From the fire-form eye, the eye of fire, ten black-colored ones, possessing ten varieties, were born and produced.

Because that eye consists of ten digits (kalās), beginning with Dhūmrārcis; thus, the meaning is that Rudrākṣas are remembered as being of many kinds and many varieties according to their different origins. || 50-51 ||
125) Now, he states the characteristics of the rudrākṣa beads to be worn:
"One that is flawless, resembling gold, not worn by another, is the most excellent."
A wise person devoted to the worship of Śiva should wear rudrākṣa beads. || 52 ||
The meaning is that it is "without flaws" (acchidra), i.e., not kissed by worms; the rest is clear. || 52 ||

Now, as to where, how, and how many [beads] are to be worn, he says here: "I shall describe the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads according to their place, according to their face, according to their application, and according to the rule, for the sake of attaining union with Rudra. (53)
This is clear. || 53 ||
Having made this promise, he stated the positions and the numbers:
"A wise man should wear one Rudrākṣa with a single face on the top-knot (śikhā);
he should wear three on the head—those having two, three, and twelve faces. (54)
One should always wear thirty-six eleven-faced [deities] upon the head;
one should bear ten, seven, and five-faced [deities], six on each of the two ears.
One should always wear thirty-two [faces] with six or eight faces around the neck;
the wise man should wear fifty four-faced [liṅgas] upon his chest.
One should wear thirteen on the face and sixteen on each of the two arms. [Compare: Rudrākṣajābālopaniṣad.]
Twelve [channels] flow from each [of these], and nine [flow] from the wrists. || 57 ||
A worshiper of Śiva should always wear a hundred and eight Rudrākṣas, including one with fourteen faces, as a sacred thread (yajñasūtra).

Regarding the phrase "here, ten, seven, and five-faced [deities], six, six, and two ears," the meaning is that one should place two ten-faced, two five-faced, and two seven-faced [deities] upon the two ears, each consisting of six; this is according to the maxim "it should be equal, as there is no scriptural statement to the contrary. Thus, there are six and six.

"One on each ear," according to the *Rudrākṣajābāla-śruti*. Alternatively, one may wear one on each of the two ears. Likewise, one should wear six or eight-faced [rudrākṣas] equally upon the neck. The rest is clear.
This is the intended meaning:

The purification of the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhva*) is accomplished by wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) in a number corresponding to the Śivas who are lords of the pure, mixed, and impure worlds, the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), and the hundred Rudras;
the purification of the path of phonemes (*varṇādhva*) is accomplished by a garland of beads on the chest in a number corresponding to the phonemes.
The purification of the path of the foot (padādhva) is performed by means of a necklace for the wrists, arms, and neck consisting of a number of beads equal to the number of words [of the mantra];

the purification of the path of the mantra (mantrādhva) is performed by means of an ear-ornament consisting of a number of beads equal to the number of the six limbs, the five Brahmans, and the Praṇava mantra, or alternatively, by means of an ear-ornament whose essence is Śiva and Śakti.
The purification of the path of principles (*tattvādhva-śuddhi*) is by means of the garland of heads numbering the [twenty-five] principles;

the purification of the path of aspects (*kalādhva-śuddhi*) is by means of the garland of the cranial aperture characterized by the moon, sun, and fire, which are filled with the thirty-eight aspects (*kalā*).
By wearing a single rudrākṣa located on the crest, which consists of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman—the cause of the six paths of such a nature—one becomes the very essence of Paraśiva;
for the scripture declares: "He who wears the rudrākṣa is truly the supreme Śiva; he is truly the supreme Śiva. (54–58)
127) Now, he says that through the wearing of rudrākṣas in this manner, there is the destruction of all sins:
"He who, in this way, wears rudrākṣas at all times..."
For him there is no talk of evil, even for a fool; of this there is no doubt. || 59 ||

In the manner thus described, for one who always wears rudrākṣas in these places, there is not even talk of sin for the fool; how much less, then, can there be any connection with sin? This is the meaning. || 59 ||
Now, it may be asked: is it being said that there is no connection with minor sins (*kṣudrapāpa*), or is it being said that there is no connection with mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*)? To this he says:
"The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the stealer of gold, and the violator of the Guru’s bed..."
Even a killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of an embryo, or an ungrateful person is liberated from all sins merely by wearing Rudrākṣa beads. || 60 ||
It should be understood that by the word "all" (*sarva*) here, those sins not explicitly mentioned are included. || 60 ||
Now he states the specific benefits: "By seeing, by touching, by even remembering, and by worshipping, as well as by wearing rudrākṣas, people in this world are liberated from their sins. (61)
This is clear. || 61 ||
Regarding the question of who is intended here by the word *jana*, he says (p.
"Whether a Brāhmaṇa or even an outcaste, whether a fool or even a scholar."
Merely by wearing rudrākṣas, one is liberated from all sins. || 62 ||
By this, it is stated that all persons whatsoever are qualified for the wearing of rudrākṣas. || 62 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is there merely the destruction of evil, or is there also some merit? To this he says:
"Whatever fruit is obtained on earth from the gift of ten million cows, that fruit a mortal obtains by the constant wearing of rudrākṣas. (63)
This is clear. || 63 ||
Now, [the author] states that there is not only this much [merit], but there is another wonder as well due to the difference in action:
"And at the time of death, he who squeezes a rudrākṣa together with water and drinks it while meditating on Rudra goes to the world of Rudra. (64)
This is clear. || 64 ||
Having thus determined, he says that those who wear ashes and rudrākṣas are indeed Rudras themselves:
"Those great-souled ones whose entire bodies are smeared with ashes and who wear garlands of rudrākṣas are Rudras; there is no doubt about this. (65)
This is clear. || 65 ||
Now, he states that even the daily, occasional, and other rites performed by a twice-born man who is devoid of the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads are futile:
"The obligatory, the optional, and those arising from specific occasions..."
Even while constantly performing all ritual actions, if one should be a wearer of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, (p. 129) [he attains liberation].
For that twice-born man, there is no attainment of the fruit [of his actions]. || 66 ||
"Rebirth" (upapatti) means "attainment" (prāpti). The remainder is clear. || 66 ||
Therefore, he says that among those devoted to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life, the wearer of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads alone is most venerable:

"Among all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life who are constantly devoted to virtuous conduct, the wearer of the sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads is equal [to them all], even as he is enjoined here by both the Śruti and the Smṛti. (67)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Occasion for Wearing Vibhūti and Rudrākṣa," in the *Bhaktasthala* of the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a definitive exposition of the Vīraśaiva Dharma composed by the venerable Śivayogin, the Brahmin of the Six Stages (*Ṣaṭsthala*). || 7 ||

Among all those in this world who belong to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas and to the stages of life beginning with studentship, the wearer of rudrākṣas is equal in prosperity; yet the wearer of ashes and rudrākṣas alone is praiseworthy, as he is enjoined by both the Śruti and the Smṛti. || 67 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Wearing of Ashes and Rudrākṣas," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences.
The Eighth Chapter:

Now, having thus become perfected through the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga and Rudrākṣa beads, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) for the sake of illuminating the reality of Śiva; thus [the author] describes to Agastya the locus for the muttering of the *pañcākṣarī*.
Śrīreṇuka said:
Holding sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, self-restrained, and bearing the liṅga, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra which awakens the reality of Śiva. (1)
Having adorned himself with auspicious ashes and purified by rudrākṣa beads, and bearing the liṅga of Śiva,

he should mutter the five-syllabled vidyā— *namaḥ śivāya*— which awakens one to the reality of Śiva and illuminates the reality of Paraśiva, namely the five-syllabled mantra renowned in the Śrī Rudra.
One should perform the recitation (japa) in the form of mental, whispered, or vocal [utterance]; this is the meaning derived from the verbal root *jap*, which signifies "inarticulate speech. || 1 ||
Now, one might ask: since there are many mantras that reveal the Śiva-principle, why is this five-syllabled mantra alone to be recited? To this he says:
"Just as there is no other great principle greater than the Śiva-principle," [so too there is no mantra greater than this].
Likewise, there is no other mantra greater than the five-syllabled mantra. (2)

Based on such scriptural passages as "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon," the meaning is that just as there is no other great (mahat) or vast (bṛhat) principle distinct from and separate from the Śiva-principle, so too there is no other mantra greater than the five-syllabled mantra, *namaḥ śivāya*.
Among the sciences, the Vedas are supreme; within the Vedas, the Rudraikādaśinī is supreme;
therein, the five-syllabled mantra is supreme; and within that, the two syllables "Śi-vā" are supreme.

Thus, according to the statement of the Paurāṇikas, the two syllables "Śi-va" constitute the essence of the Vedas; therein, the letter *a* takes the form of a compendium of the *Ṛg* and *Sāman* Vedas because those two begin with the letter *a*, while the letter *i* takes the form of a compendium of the *Yajus* (p.

Because it begins with the letter *i*, it is the essence of the *Atharva-veda*; because it begins with the letter *śa*, it is the essence of the *Atharva-saṃgraha*; because it begins with the letter *va*, it is the essence of *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar); and because it begins with the letter *ya*, it is the essence of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*). Thus, by virtue of being composed of such auspicious (*śiva*) syllables, this is the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*).
The meaning is that it is thus the most excellent of all mantras. || 2 ||
When the five-syllabled mantra and Śiva have been thus known, one might ask: "What is the purpose of other mantras or other deities? To this, he says:
"Once the five-syllabled mantra is known, what fruit is there in other mantras?"
When Śiva, the root of the universe, is known, what is the use of other deities?
When it is known that Paraśiva is the root of the entire universe— including Viṣṇu and all others— based on the Vedic scripture stating, "Verily, Nārāyaṇa was alone" [Nārāyaṇopaniṣad 2],
what is the use of other deities such as Viṣṇu, who are subject to birth and death as they are included within His creation?

What is the fruit? The meaning is that there is no fruit whatsoever. For it is according to the maxim: "A beggar does not beg from another beggar when there is another donor who is not a beggar. But [one might object]: "In the passage 'Verily, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed' [Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad], and in 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone' [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1]," [is there not a result?]

If it is argued that because of the hearing of similarity with such Vedic passages as those establishing Brahman, how can there be a focus on origination? We say no; for, just as in the case of "From the red [goat] he was born, from power (śakti) Parāśara was born," a focus on the existence of origination is logically possible. Nor should it be said that, due to the absence of a statement of a cause (*hetu*) like that, how can there be a focus on origination.

Because of the statement in the Śikhā Upaniṣad, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced," and because the birth of Viṣṇu is heard therein, it is possible that [the passage] intends to convey his origination according to that [scriptural authority]. Nor is it the case that the birth of Nārāyaṇa is not heard here; rather, it is indeed Viṣṇu who is meant, since he is a constituent part of Nārāyaṇa.
It should not be said that, because of the statement in the *Bhagavad Gītā* (10.21), "Of the Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu," the word *viṣṇu* refers only to a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*),
for it is impossible that the word *viṣṇu*, which is recited here between the primary [deities] Brahmā and Rudra, should refer to a partial incarnation.

Because it contradicts the general reading [of the scriptures] and because the scripture, "Thus Viṣṇu, the highest knower of this, being born great, protects the third," declares the birth of Mahāviṣṇu himself, some timid person resorts to the view that He is "unborn."
O Rudra, with that face of yours which is auspicious, protect me forever. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.21)
This is because the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (p. 132) declares that the Great Rudra, who is the cause, is unborn; such is the direction of the argument.
Now, as to whether there exists any mantra equal to this among the seventy million great mantras, he says:
Among the seventy million mantras, the five-syllabled mantra is the great one;
just as Śambhu is the greatest among the gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having abandoned everything else, including the gods such as Viṣṇu who are subject to rejection,
Śiva alone— the destroyer of the entire cycle of worldly existence— should always be meditated upon.

Thus, based on the Pippalāda-śruti and the Śruti stating "He is called the Unborn," and because He is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation as the Unborn, the meaning is that just as Śiva is the greatest among Brahmā and the other gods, so too the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara-mantra) is the greatest among the seventy million great mantras, owing to its being the essence of the Vedas. || 4 ||
Now, one might object: "Since Śiva is the root of the entire universe, including Viṣṇu and all others, let him be the supreme;
but how can the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) be the supreme? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The Supreme Self, Maheśvara, is the cause of all worlds without exception."
This mantra is its expressive formula (vācaka), the sole cause of all mantras.
Just as Śiva is the cause of the entire universe, so too the mantra that denotes him is the cause of all mantras; this is the meaning. || 5 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
"This is its mantra as the designator, and it is remembered as the designated;
through the relationship of designator and designated, the supreme Śiva is realized from the mantra. (6)
This mantra is the *abhidhāna-mantra* (denotative mantra) of that Śiva; the meaning is that it is the mantra of His name.

That Śiva is the *abhidheya* (the denoted), and He is traditionally held to be fit to be expressed by that mantra because of the relationship between the denoter and the denoted—that is, because of the relationship between the denoter and the denoted consisting of the name "Śiva" and [the deity] Śiva. From this mantra, Śiva is established as being beyond the mantra.
It has been revealed that [these mantras] serve to manifest the deities to be worshipped; in the absence of these mantras, there would be no manifestation of Śiva at all.

One should not even suspect what this might mean; for since Śiva is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of all principles (*tattva*), it is logical that he consists of the fifty phonemes which express him. Because he is the root of all mantras, his nature as the cause of all mantras follows from his being their illuminator. If one asks how that is so, it is said:
Now, all the initial lunar days (tithis) consist of vowels ending with the bindu;
within them, through the conjunction of time, the Moon and Sun are proclaimed.
O virtuous lady, the principles beginning with earth and ending with the Puruṣa reside respectively in the consonant groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
The fourfold set of concentrations (dhāraṇās) on air, fire, water, and earth.
Above that, the five Brahmans beginning with Īśa are renowned;
from the root upwards, this sequence ending in *kṣa* is declared to be the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
This illustrious one is declared to be the source of all mantras and vidyās at all times in all tantras. [Pañcarakṣā 5.8]

Thus, according to the established doctrine of the *Śrī Parātriṃśikā-śāstra*, in the word "Śiva," the letter Śa denotes the five Brahmans beginning with Brahmā, while the letter Va denotes the principle of Māyā;
since [Māyā] consists of the thirty principles beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth— which are its effects— in this way, [the meaning of] the letters Śa and Va [is established].

Because the letter *a* denotes the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), because the letter *i* consists of the sixteen vowels which are the forms of the *kalās* of the principle of Śiva, and because the letter *i* denotes the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the Mātṛkā and so forth possess the nature of the cause of all mantras; this is due to their inclusion within both the phenomenal world of words and their meanings, and because they are the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the entire expansion of the phenomenal world of sound.

This universe [is filled] with infinite, diverse elements born from the fifty letters of her own body— elements possessing manifold meanings, which generate words and sentences, which are inseparable from their referents, and which bestow the bliss of the fruits of purposeful, virtuous actions.
Pervading all through your conscious self, you manifest as "I, I" within the Mother.

They are the very nature of the knowledge transmitted through the oral tradition of the Guru, which effects the manifestation of the web of reality by uttering the manifold sounds of the fifty-fold garland of phonemes;
they are the various and manifold established doctrines of the Vedas that existed prior to the creation of the Creator and others.
Since she alone manifests various languages through her actions, she is indeed your Sāṅga Veda.
Thus [it is] from the words of the Lord Dūrvāsas. || 6 ||

(134) If this is so, it would be more appropriate for it to consist of only two syllables; why then does this mantra appear in the form of five syllables, residing at the head of all the Vedas? Here, by means of the salutation (*namaskāra*)—
Regarding the nature of the living being, he says here:
"One should first utter the word 'namaḥ' and thereafter 'śivāya';
for this is the five-syllabled mantra that resides at the head of all the Vedas. (7)

This mantra shines forth as the crest-jewel of all the Vedas, appearing in the form of five syllables—preceded by the word *namaḥ* and consisting of the essence of consciousness (*cit-tattva*)—for the purpose of revealing the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva-aiikya*).

Here, by the word *namaḥ*, the state of being the individual soul (*jīvatva*) is indicated; by the word *śiva*, the state of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmatva*); and by the root *aya* (in *āya*), their unity, according to the rule that *aya* means "to go" or "to attain."
The meaning is "from the root. || 7 ||
Now, as to how the Supreme Brahman, which is a mass of Being-Consciousness, is designated as "Śiva," he says:
"Because of being pure from the beginning and because of being free from the three impurities, the Lord, who is a mass of Consciousness and Bliss, is called Śiva and Śambhu. (8)

The Lord Śambhu is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose essential nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss; he is independent and the Supreme Brahman because he both enjoys happiness and bestows happiness. From the beginning (i.e., always), due to his separation from the three impurities—being perfectly pure through the absence of connection with the three impurities such as *āṇava* and the rest—[he remains so].
Because of its stainlessness, it is called *śiva*; the sense is that, according to the verbal root *vaś* meaning "to desire," it is so called because its nature is pure luminosity. || 8 ||

Now, because it is the abode of all auspiciousness, he states that Brahman is denoted by the word "Śiva": "For the God of gods, the Three-eyed One, is indeed designated by the word 'Śiva', as he is especially the locus of all auspicious things without exception. (9)

(135) Here, by the word *triyambaka*, the Supreme Brahman—the cause of creation, maintenance, and so forth—is denoted, because [the Supreme Brahman] is the cause of the creation and other states of the sun and the rest; [as it is said]: "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, dark and tawny..."
According to the Śruti, "He is the one with upward-flowing vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) and three eyes" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.12.1). Tryambaka, the God of gods,
the Supreme Lord who is the deity even of Brahmā and the others, is the preeminent abode and refuge of all auspicious things without exception, being superior even to Viṣṇu and the other deities.
For that which is designated by the word "Śiva" is well known as being auspicious, blessed, and propitious. || 9 ||
Now, since there exist many names [for the Supreme], why is the Supreme Brahman designated specifically by the word "Śiva"?
To this he says:
"The pair of syllables 'Śi-va' reveals the Supreme Brahman."
In the primary sense, all other words function as figurative expressions (guṇavṛtti). || 10 ||

The two syllables "Śi-va" primarily reveal the Supreme Brahman; the meaning is that other words—words such as "Bhava" and so forth, distinct from the word "Śiva"—reveal the Supreme Brahman through secondary application (guṇavṛtti), by association with its qualities, just as in the expression "the boy is a lion. || 10 ||
Now he concludes the point already stated:
"Therefore, the two syllables 'Śi-va' are the most primary name for Śambhu, who is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and whose splendor is immeasurable. (11)
By relying on this name, the five-syllabled mantra is remembered;

the word "great" is the understood remainder. The two syllables "Śi-va" constitute the most primary, indeed the absolute primary, name of Śambhu—the Supreme Brahman—who is the mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and whose nature is immeasurable light.
The meaning is that by virtue of depending upon this name—that is, by virtue of being composed of this name—the five-syllabled mantra is remembered as "great. || 11 ||
Now, as to what should be done with this and what its fruit is, he says here by means of an illustration:
136) "Therefore, it should always be recited by those who desire liberation for themselves. (12)
Just as the Great God is beginningless, perfected, and the liberator from saṃsāra, so too is the five-syllabled mantra the destroyer of saṃsāra. || 13 ||

Since the five-syllabled mantra is great by virtue of being composed of the name of Śiva, for that reason it should always be recited with devotion by persons desiring liberation. Herein is the illustration: having abandoned everything else, including the gods such as Viṣṇu who are to be discarded.
Śiva alone, the destroyer of all saṃsāra, should always be meditated upon.

Thus, according to the Pippalāda-śruti, just as the supreme Śiva, who is beginningless, is renowned as the liberator from the bonds of saṃsāra, so too the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara-mantra) is renowned as the cause of the destruction of the bonds of saṃsāra; for the severing of all bonds, there are the two syllables "Śi-va."
This mantra, joined with the act of salutation, is sufficient and conducive to liberation.
Thus, according to the statement from the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa. || 12-13 ||

Now, if this mantra, like Śiva, is the cause of the destruction of saṃsāra, one might ask why its being the cause of the universe is not likewise [evident]; to this he says: "All five gross elements and the five subtle elements..."
The five organs of cognition and the five organs of action. || 14 ||
In the five Brahmans, all five activities along with their causes are to be understood through the five syllables of the great mantra of five syllables.
The five elements beginning with earth; the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with odor;
the five organs of cognition (buddhīndriyas) beginning with the nose, which are of the nature of the power of knowledge;
and the five organs of action (karmendriyas) beginning with the organ of procreation, which are of the nature of the power of action.
The five lingas, beginning with Ācāra, which are synonymous with the five Brahmans known as Pañcasāda;
the fivefold creative acts, beginning with creation, performed by the causal lords beginning with Bhava, Mṛḍa, and Hara—
all these are to be understood through the five syllables of the great five-syllabled mantra.
The meaning is that they are to be manifested. || 14-15 ||
137) Now, one might ask: are these things to be manifested by light like a jar and so forth, or are they to be manifested like a gold earring and so forth?
To this, he says:
All those things which are specifically established in fivefold ways—indeed, all such entities consist of the five syllables. (16)

By the mention of the five powers and the five fingers, there are the objects of the five organs of action, such as speech and grasping; and those fivefold categories— mind, intellect, ego, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the person (puruṣa)— which are specifically well-known, all of these, according to the analogy of the golden earring, consist of the five syllables.
The meaning is that the fivefold activities and their manifestations are [to be understood] as such, because the phonemes (varṇa) are of the nature of power (śakti).
Now, one might ask: "Since the *praṇava* is the cause of liberation, how can the five-syllabled mantra bestow liberation in its absence? To this, he says:
"This supreme mantra consisting of five syllables is preceded by the syllable *oṃ*."
In the Śaiva Āgamas and in the Vedas, it is remembered as the six-syllabled mantra (ṣaḍakṣara). || 17 ||

Furthermore, this mantra consisting of five syllables is considered the most excellent in the manner described; it is recorded as a six-syllable mantra preceded by *oṃ* in the Śiva Āgamas and the Vedas, because in the Śrī Rudra [Upaniṣad], following the mantra of Īśāna— "Salutation to Tāra, salutation to Śambhu"— the words "may Sadāśiva be mine" (*me astu sadāśivom*) are heard at the end.

The supreme Śiva, who transcends the state of quiescence, shines as the very essence of the syllable Oṃ; Śiva is declared to be the Praṇava, or the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva. For there is never any absolute distinction between the signified and the signifier.

Because of these scriptural statements and the declarations of the Purāṇas, there is no difference between Śiva and the Praṇava; therefore, the meaning is that [the mantra] consists of six syllables because it begins with the syllable *oṃ*. || 17 ||
Now,
the first is said to be the form of a star, the second a staff;
the third is the shape of an earring, and the fourth is a half-moon.
The fifth is mirror-shaped, the sixth has the nature of light;
the letter *na* is the form of the star, and the letter *ma* is called the staff.
The letter Śa is shaped like an earring; Va is like a half-moon;
Ya is shaped like a mirror; and Oṃ is the sovereign of five colors.

Thus, based on the statement of the Śivāgama, he describes the majesty of the syllable *oṃ*, which serves as the seed of the wish-fulfilling tree of the five-syllabled mantra, by means of three aphorisms: "By means of the *praṇava*, which constitutes the placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth of the great mantra..."
Mahādeva, who is exclusively of the nature of consciousness and bliss, is awakened.

The meaning is that by means of the *praṇava*, which is the first element of this five-syllabled mantra—the form of the Great Mantra—Paraśiva, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), is revealed. This is based on the passage beginning with "He who is Rudra is the Blessed Lord," followed by: "That which is Oṃ is the *praṇava*; that which is the *praṇava* is all-pervading; that which is all-pervading [is Paraśiva]."
That which is infinite is the syllable *tāra*; that which is *tāra* is subtle; that which is subtle is white; that which is white is the lightning-like (*vaidyuta*);
that which is lightning-like is the Supreme Brahman. He is the One; He is the One Rudra; He is Īśāna; He is the Blessed Lord; He is Maheśvara; He is Mahādeva. (Atharva Upaniṣad 2.3)
Thus, because the *Atharvaśiras* Upaniṣad declares that the *praṇava* alone is the Supreme Brahman, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 18 ||

Now, as to whether Śiva is revealed by anything other than the *praṇava*, he says: "By the single-syllabled *praṇava*, the Supreme Brahman is revealed—That which is non-dual, supreme bliss, named Śiva, and devoid of phenomenal expansion. (19)

According to the statement in the Śivāgama, "Śiva is beyond the beyond, subtle, eternal, all-pervading, and immutable," that which is named Śiva is supreme bliss, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), non-dual, and indeed one without a second; for the Śruti says, "One alone, without a second," and "There is not even the slightest diversity here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19). Thus, it is devoid of a second.

Therefore, by means of the single syllable *praṇava*— that is, by the *praṇava* itself which consists of the single syllable— the Supreme Brahman, which is beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcaka*) and devoid of worldly distinctions (*prapañcikabhedaśūnya*),
is revealed and awakened; [this occurs] through the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, which constitute the parts of the *praṇava*.

"Because it denotes *saccidānanda* (Being-Consciousness-Bliss). And thus, the five syllables of "namaḥ śivāya" are the seed-syllables (*bījākṣaras*) of Ācāra, Guru, Śiva-carana, Prasāda, and Liṅga; and since the *oṃkāra* is the seed of the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga*), the *praṇava* consisting of these five syllables—which is itself the form of the seed-tree—is indeed the seed of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*).
The intended meaning. || 19 ||

May there be the manifestation of Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, through the *praṇava*, which is the cause of the yoga of the six stages of the limbs of the *liṅga* for the sake of the new [initiate].

To explain how it establishes the non-conceptual Brahman (*niṣprapañca-brahma*), he demonstrates its essential nature preceded by the application of the *ajapā-gāyatrī* mantra: "The Supreme Self-mantra is to be known as the eternal form of 'I am He' (*so'ham*)."
Through the elision of the two *ja* sounds, there arises the single-syllable mantra *om*.

The *paramātmamanu* (the mantra of the Supreme Self) is the *paramātmamantra*; it should be understood as being of the nature of "I am He" (*so'ham*), which is the nature of self-recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
It is fit to be realized through the teachings of the scriptures and the guru, and through one's own direct experience, in the form: "I am that very Person.
Thus, every day, [it should be recited] twenty-one thousand six hundred times.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*), because this [mantra] is composed of distinct parts, through the *kevala-kumbhaka* (exclusive retention) there is the abandonment of the letters *sa* and *ha*;
thus, the single-syllabled mantra *oṃ*, which is eternal and constant, arises. If it is asked, "What follows from that?", it is said:

since the letter *sa* is the seed-syllable of the moon, it is of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*); and since the letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of the sun, it is of the nature of the act of knowing (*vedana*).

Thus, through the abandonment of the letters *sa* and *ha*, only the syllable *oṃ* remains, which has the nature of illuminating pure consciousness devoid of mental modification (*vṛtti*). Therefore, it is said that the *praṇava* is the indicator of the non-dual Brahman (*niṣprapañca-brahma*).
By means of that [syllable], the Śruti and Āgama—characterized by the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the Liṅga (Śiva) and the Aṅga (the individual soul)—[are established].
It should be understood that this is the well-known supreme liberation. || 20 ||

This being the case, he establishes through two sūtras that by means of the *praṇava* alone there is the knowledge of the partless (*niṣkala*), by the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) there is the knowledge of the with-parts (*sakala*), and by the five-syllabled mantra together with the *praṇava* there is the knowledge of the both-with-and-partless (*sakalaniṣkala*):
"By the mantra consisting of the *praṇava* alone, Śiva in his partless aspect is awakened."
Likewise, by means of the five-syllabled mantra, one becomes the body of the five Brahmas.
The partless Śiva is the form of pure consciousness, while the manifest one exists as the universal form;
Śiva, possessing both natures, is established within the six-syllabled mantra.

In this context, by the word *niṣkala* (partless), the nature of pure consciousness (*śuddhacidrūpatva*) is expressed; by the word *sakala* (with parts), the state of being characterized by the phenomenal world (*prapañcaviśiṣṭatva*) is expressed. Thus, by the *praṇava* mantra alone, Śiva as *niṣkala*—the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*) whose essence is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandātmaka*)—is made known and revealed. By means of the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*) mantra...
Śiva, whose body consists of the five Brahmas and who is composed of the five Brahmas, is thus awakened;
for it is revealed by the Vedic scripture: "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).

This is the meaning. Śiva, who is of a dual nature, consisting of both the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), abides and shines forth within the six-syllabled mantra—that is, within the five-syllabled mantra joined with the *praṇava*. In this regard, although it is said:
"The letter *A* is Brahmā at the navel, the letter *U* is Viṣṇu at the heart, and the letter *M* is Rudra..."

According to the *Tāpanīya-śruti*, "The syllable Oṃ, the Lord of All, is at the center of the eyebrows; [it is] at the end of the twelve [fingers]" (*Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad* 3.4), the *praṇava* (Oṃ) likewise consists of Brahman together with the phenomenal world (*saprapañca*); nevertheless, it is composed of the *bindu*, which is of the nature of the refinement of the object of knowledge (*vedya*).

Because it consists of subtle manifestation (*sūkṣma-prapañca*), it is designated as being partless (*niṣkala*). A brief summary: the *praṇava* is the seed of the tree of the five-syllable mantra, which consists of gross manifestation (*sthūla-prapañca*); this is because it is endowed with five constituent parts characterized by the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the bindu, and the nāda.
Now he states the synonymous names of this five-syllabled mantra:
"The Root, the Vidyā, Śiva, the Śaivasūtra, and likewise the Pañcākṣara—these are proclaimed as the names of the Great Mantra. (23)
The meaning is that these names— *Mahāmanu*, *Pañcākṣaramahāmantra*, *Mūlavidyā*, *Śiva*, *Śaivasūtra*, and *Pañcākṣara*— are proclaimed according to the number of syllables [they contain].
Now, he says that one should recite this five-syllabled mantra together with the *praṇava* as the six-syllabled *vidyā*:
"One should, becoming composed and devoted to the worship of Śiva, recite this five-syllabled *vidyā* along with the *praṇava* as the six-syllabled [mantra]. (24)
"Being composed" means having a one-pointed mind; the rest is clear. || 24 ||
Regarding the question of how one should recite [the mantra], he says:
having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), facing either east or north.
Meditating in the lotus of his heart upon the God of gods, the three-eyed one.
Adorned with all ornaments, accompanied by Ambā, and having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel—one should, with undistracted mind, recite this Great Vidyā which is the very form of Śiva. (26)

Having sat down on a pure spot covered with a deer-skin, a variegated woolen blanket, or similar materials, upon a seat such as the Siddha-padma, facing either east or north, adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads,
and having become a worshiper of the Śiva-liṅga;

Without first worshipping Śiva, it is impossible to describe the fruit [of the rite]. With an unwearied mind, one should perform the recitation (japa) a thousand times, or half of that, or half of that again, or one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eight times.
Praise is equal to ten million acts of worship; recitation is equal to ten million praises;
meditation is equal to ten million recitations; and absorption is equal to ten million meditations.

According to this statement from the Śivāgama, after the worship of Śiva, one should again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), apply the hand-gestures and the six-limbed ritual (kara-ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa), and [meditate upon] the God of gods within the heart-lotus— He who is the three-eyed Lord and the causal source of the threefold entities consisting of the three mandalas, the three qualities (guṇas), and the three deities.

The meaning is that, with a mind focused on no other, one should meditate upon Śiva— the Lord of Bhavānī, adorned with all ornaments and bearing the crescent moon as his crest-jewel— and perform the *sagarbha-japa* (meditative recitation) of the single Great Vidyā in the manner described, according to the method imparted by the Guru. (25–26)
Now, he demonstrates the divisions of recitation (japa):
Recitation is said to be threefold—vocal (vācika), whispered (upāṃśu), and mental (mānasa).
That which is heard by those standing nearby as a sequence of phonemes is the vocal [recitation]. (27)
That [recitation] which is uttered softly with the lower lip slightly touched is to be known as vocal; it shatters all sins. (28)

This is declared to be *upāṃśu* (whispered) when it is not heard by those standing nearby. That which is performed within the inner self, without touching the lower lip and without moving the tip of the tongue— p. 142) [is called *mānasa*]. 10.37–38ab. That which is cultivated in the form of color is known as the mental [image]. || 29 ||

Japa, which is the utterance of a mantra, is threefold: vocal (*vācika*), whispered (*upāṃśu*), and mental (*mānasa*). Among these, that utterance of a mantra which follows the sequence of the phonemes without deviating from the succession of letters and is heard by those standing nearby is called vocal japa; it wards off all sins produced by the mind, speech, and body.

The meaning is "capable of being understood. Whatever recitation of a mantra is uttered softly—touching the lower lip slightly and remaining unheard by those standing nearby—that is proclaimed as *upāṃśu-japa* (whispered recitation).
Whatever recitation of a mantra is performed without touching the lower lip, with the tip of the tongue motionless...

The meaning is that when the tip of the tongue is rendered motionless, one meditates with the internal self—that is, with a mind possessing the nature of the syllables of the mantra in the form of sound; that utterance of the mantra is known as "mental" (mānasa), which is to say, "mental recitation" (mānasajapa). || 27–29 ||
Now, he reveals the greatness of this sacrifice of recitation (japayajña):
"Whatever sacrifices of ritual action there are, as well as vows, gifts, and austerities—all of these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation. (30)

Whatever ritual sacrifices there may be, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, and whatever vows, gifts, and austerities exist—all these together do not equal even a sixteenth part, that is, not even a single portion among sixteen parts, of the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña); this is the meaning. || 30 ||
Now, regarding the question of what the singular nature of the majesty of these three aforementioned types of recitation is, he says:
"The majesty of this sacrifice of vocal recitation has thus been proclaimed.
Therefore, the whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold more effective than that, and the mental recitation a thousandfold. || 31 ||

The meaning is that since this greatness of vocal recitation (*vācikajapa*) has been proclaimed, whispered recitation (*upāṃśujapa*) is a hundred times more effective than that vocal recitation, and mental recitation (*mānasajapa*) is remembered as being a thousand times more effective than that whispered recitation.
In this regard, as to which recitation (*japa*) should be performed among these, he states that those seeking liberation should perform only the mental recitation:
"Compared to vocal and whispered recitation, the greatness of this mantra..."
For mental recitation is the best, as it destroys the terrible cycle of worldly existence. || 32 ||

The meaning is that for this Mahāmanu, mental recitation (mānasa-japa) is superior because, while being a destroyer of the cruel cycle of existence (saṃsāra), it excels both vocal recitation (vācika-japa) and whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa). || 32 ||
To the question "In that case, what is the procedure for those two?", he says:
"Among these, according to this method, in accordance with their nature and in due order, one should mutter this five-syllabled vidyā for the sake of liberation from the bonds. (33)

In these subjects— that is, in the context of recitation (*japa*) performed verbally and so forth— by this method, in the manner described, according to sequence (without transgressing the order), according to state (according to what is possible),
one should [recite] this five-syllabled lore (*pañcākṣarī-vidyā*) for the sake of liberation from the fetters, that is, for the purpose of liberation from the five fetters such as *mala* and *māyā*.
"Should recite" means "should utter. || 33 ||
Then, he states that the worship of the Śivaliṅga should also be performed with this very mantra:
"With this root mantra, one who is endowed with constant discipline, self-restrained, and whose nature is Śiva, should worship the Śivaliṅga daily. (34)

Being perfected in the observances (*niyama*), that is, being perfected in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) and so forth; being one whose self is disciplined, meaning possessing a pure internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and being of the nature of Śiva—since there is a scriptural injunction stating, "One who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra"—being thus endowed with the state of Śiva, [one should worship] by means of this root mantra, namely this *praṇava*-pañcākṣara mantra.
One should always and constantly worship the Śivaliṅga according to one's means; "should worship" is the meaning [of the verse]. || 34 ||
Now, as to the question "What is the fruit of this worship of Śiva accompanied by mantras?", he says:
"Even he who worships Śiva but once with devotion using the five-syllabled mantra alone shall go to the abode of Śiva, solely due to the majesty of this very mantra. (35)
This is clear. || 35 ||
Now, one might ask: since true devotion can arise through vows, observances, and the like, for what purpose is worship enjoined? To this he replies:
"Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others who are emaciated by vows—even with these vows, they do not attain union with the world of Śiva. (36)

The meaning is that for those who subsist on water, those who drink only air, those who feed on wind and leaves, and others who are emaciated by vows— those who have become lean through such observances as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*— there is no attainment of the world of Śiva by means of these vows. || 36 ||
Therefore, he says that all [practices] such as the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Liṅga:
"Therefore, ascetic practices, sacrifices, vows, and likewise observances—these are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of the five-syllabled [mantra]. (37)
This is clear. || 37 ||

Now, since it has been stated that one who is endowed with pure knowledge and so forth is the qualified person for the worship of Śiva, what is the fate of those whose intellects are impure? To this, he says:
"Whether impure or pure, whoever [recites] even once the five-syllabled mantra..."
Even one who has fallen [from his status] should worship; he is liberated—of this there is no doubt. || 38 ||
"Fallen" means one who has failed in his vows; "is liberated" means he is completely freed from all sins. || 38 ||
Now, he says that by the mere single recitation of the five-syllable mantra, there shall be the destruction of all sins for everyone:
"By the mere single recitation of the great five-syllable mantra..."
For all living beings as well, there shall be the destruction of all sins. || 39 ||
This is clear. || 39 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since there are many mantras well-known in the Śiva Āgamas, why is this one superior? To this, he says:
"Many other mantras also exist in all the Āgamas."
Through repeated practice again and again, it bestows the goals of human existence. || 40 ||
This mantra possesses great power and establishes the Lord;
by its mere single recitation, it bestows all spiritual accomplishments. || 41 ||

In all the Āgamas—that is, in the entirety of the Śiva-Āgamas—there are many mantras other than this five-syllabled one; because they require an abundance of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), they bestow the goals of human endeavor. This five-syllabled mantra, however, possesses great power and great efficacy, belonging to the Lord.
It is the elucidator of the majesty characterized by the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between that which consists of the universe and that which transcends the universe.
Therefore, its distinction lies in the fact that it bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*) from the mere single utterance [of it]. || 40-41 ||
Now, he reveals the fruit of worship accompanied by mantras:
"Whoever, having uttered the five-syllabled mantra, casts a flower upon the *liṅga*, for him the fruit of a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices is desired. (42)
"Should deposit" means "should hand over. The remainder is clear. || 42 ||
Now, he reveals the fruit of the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra:
"The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees—these are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra. (43)
The *agnihotra*— the fire sacrifice performed morning and evening— the three Vedas— the study of the Ṛg,

Yajur, and Sāma Vedas— the sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma which involve abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the form of the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*)— none of these are equal even to a ten-millionth part of the recitation of the five-syllable mantra.
The meaning is that they come into being. || 43 ||
Now, by way of demonstrating the greatness of those great souls who have attained perfection through mantras, he describes its superiority:
"In ancient times, there was a lord of yogis filled with bliss, devoted solely to the knowledge of Śiva..."
Having uttered the five-syllabled mantra, he caused the denizens of hell to be delivered.

In ancient times, Sānandagaṇeśa, who was firmly established in the yoga of the knowledge of Śiva, uttered the five-syllabled mantra in the form of a recitation and thereby uplifted— that is, he rescued— the sinners dwelling in the hells, specifically those presided over by twenty-eight crores of hell-wardens. || 44 ||
In ancient times, through the perfection of this five-syllabled mantra, the sage Śatānanda turned even the hell of a sinful person into heaven.
In ancient times, Śatānanda, through the perfection of the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, turned even the hell of the sinful Saṅgiras into heaven; such is the meaning. || 45 ||
In ancient times, the yogi Upamanyu, having attained perfection through this mantra,
received from the Supreme Lord the authority to expound the Śaiva scriptures.
The meaning is that he attained the status of a teacher of the Śiva scriptures. || 46 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and other sages, freed from all taints,
became possessed of great splendor through perfection in this mantra. (47)

The meaning is that the sages Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and others— having been freed from blemish and liberated from sinful deeds— became possessed of supernatural powers through this five-syllabled mantra, becoming highly effulgent and capable of both cursing and bestowing grace. || 47 ||
Then he says that even Brahmā and the other gods became authorized for the tasks of creation and so forth solely through the power of this mantra:
"And for the gods, beginning with Brahmā, in the work of creating the world and so forth..."
It is precisely through the majesty of this mantra that its efficacy arises. || 48 ||

The meaning is that the capacity of the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, for the acts of creating, maintaining, and dissolving the universe, arises solely from the power of this mantra. || 48 ||
Having stated that by the recitation (*japa*) of this six-syllabled mantra accompanied by the *praṇava*,
and by the worship of the Śiva-liṅga performed thereby, one attains nothing but liberation (*mokṣa*), he concludes the section on the place for the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra:

What is the use of many words spoken here? That high-souled one who, at the outset, recites with supreme devotion the five-syllabled mantra accompanied by the *praṇava*, while worshipping the God of gods—
Having cast off the bonds of sin, he attains the fortune of liberation. || 49 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Context of the Recitation of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Śivayogin, a Māheśvara and Brahmin of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*). 8.

Here, having performed the placement on the body (*śarīranyāsa*) with the six-syllabled mantra of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the five-syllabled mantra of dissolution beginning with *nāda* and ending with the *praṇava*, and the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the five-syllabled mantra of maintenance as "Śivāya namaḥ oṃ," according to the path taught by the Guru;
One should mutter the five-syllabled mantra *pravaṇa*. For those born of the classes of women, Śūdras, and so forth, the rule for muttering is "Śivāya namaḥ.
Thus ends the section on the place for muttering the five-syllabled mantra.
Thus [written] by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Occasion of the Recitation of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," in the section on Devotion within the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*.
The Ninth Chapter:
Now, regarding the section on the practice of the path of devotion (*bhaktimārgakriyāsthala*).
In order to define the stage of devotion (*bhaktasthala*), which was previously mentioned, [the following is stated]:
The venerable Reṇuka specifically reminds us:
"One who is endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, who bears the *liṅga*, and who is diligent in the recitation (*japa*) of the five-syllabled mantra, is known as a true devotee of Śiva. (1)
This is clear. || 1 ||
He describes the varieties of devotion: hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the feet of Śambhu, worshiping, bowing down, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender. (2)
Thus, ninefold devotion has been proclaimed by the Lord Śambhu;
it is difficult for sinners to attain in this world, but easy for those of meritorious deeds. (3)

Hearing of Śambhu is the hearing of the stories of Śiva; chanting is hymn-singing; remembrance is meditation; service of the feet is massaging the feet; worship is adoration; salutation is bowing down; servitude is the state of being a servant; friendship is the state of being a friend; and self-surrender is the offering of one’s own self. Thus...

Devotion is of nine kinds, as declared by the Lord whose nature is play; the meaning is that it is difficult for sinners to attain in this world, but easy for those of meritorious deeds who are endowed with righteousness. || 2-3 ||
150) Now, he states that only one who possesses such devotion is a true devotee:
"Whether toward an inferior or a superior, wherever it may be, [if] intense..."
In whom devotion to Śaṅkara exists, he is celebrated as a devotee. || 4 ||
This is clear. || 4 ||

Then he says that one who possesses devotion alone is dear to Śiva: "In whomsoever—whether a barbarian or the best of the twice-born—devotion has been made firm, he is dear to Śambhu; and even a Brahmin devoid of devotion is not dear. (5)
This is clear. || 5 ||
By this, the previously mentioned superior and inferior [types of devotion] have also been clarified. Now, he states that such devotion is of two kinds:
"That devotion is to be known as twofold, through the distinction of external and internal;
the external is gross, while the internal is subtle, as upheld by the Vīramāheśvaras. (6)
The meaning is that devotion directed toward the pleasure of Vīramāheśvara is of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle, with external and internal characteristics respectively. || 6 ||
Now, as to what is meant by "external," he says:
on a lion throne in a pure place, most beautiful and adorned with jewels.
That which is the worship of the Śivaliṅga is called external devotion.

The meaning is that the worship of the Śiva-liṅga performed upon a throne— a lion-seat— situated in a most beautiful and exceedingly charming pure place, a location purified by sixfold sweeping, adorned with jewels, and variegated with the nine gems, is called external devotion (bāhyā bhakti). || 7 ||
Having thus explained the external devotion performed by the devotees of Śiva, he now establishes the internal devotion performed by the yogis of Śiva:
"Having fixed the vital breath (prāṇa) in the liṅga, and the Śambhu-liṅga in the vital breath..."
Having thus made the mind established in its own nature, if one should not think of anything at all; || 8 ||
This is called "internal devotion" by the Śiva-yogins;
for one in whom it exists, life is like a rotten seed.

Having established and fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *śivaliṅga*, and having established and fixed the *śāmbhava-liṅga*— which is the *liṅga* in the form of the digit of Śiva (*śivakalā*)— within the vital breath that consists of the digit of the individual soul (*jīvakalā*),
and having made the mind steady so that one thinks of nothing at all, that is the contemplation whose nature is the state of equilibrium between the *liṅga* and the vital breath.

This is called "internal devotion" by the Śiva-yogins. The meaning is that for one in whom that internal devotion exists, their life—like a fallen seed or a parched seed—is no longer a cause for rebirth.
(8–9) Thus, he states that only one who possesses the aforementioned internal devotion, established through *nirbīja-dīkṣā*, is liberated:
What is the use of saying more here? Devotion to Śiva is supreme, more secret than the secret; there is no doubt that one endowed with it is liberated. 10.
This is clear. || 10 ||
(152) To the question "From what does such devotion arise?", he says:
"That devotion arises solely from grace; grace is born of devotion."
Just as the seed is from the sprout, or as the sprout is from the seed. || 11 ||
This is clear. || 11 ||
Now, he says that such devotion as this is difficult to attain in a single lifetime alone:
"This devotion, preceded by grace, which bestows liberation, cannot indeed be attained by men in a single lifetime. (12)
This is clear. || 12 ||
To the question of how many births it takes to attain this, he says:

"For those purified through many births, who follow the teachings of the Śruti and Smṛti... [cf. Bhagavad Gītā 6.45: "Having attained perfection through many births, one then reaches the supreme goal"].
Maheśvara is pleased with those who are dispassionate and awakened.

The meaning is that Śiva becomes gracious toward those whose minds are purified by meditation on and worship of Śiva performed over many lifetimes, who perform the obligatory and occasional rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, who are free from desire for acts for specific rewards, and who possess excellent knowledge; through His grace, such devotion is obtained.

The intended meaning is that even though Mlecchas and others lack devotion to the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, devotion to Śiva may manifest in them due to the favor they have received from devotees of Śiva in a previous birth. || 13 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since liberation is attained through devotion to Śiva that is earned over many births, what would that liberation be like? To this, he says:
153) "When [Śiva] is pleased, one becomes liberated; once liberated, one becomes equal to Śiva."
Even for that mortal who [performs this] with little devotion, after three births, [the result is attained]. || 14 ||
When Śiva is pleased, one becomes liberated; being liberated, such a mortal becomes equal to Śiva.

The sense is that for one with slight devotion, liberation occurs after three births, whereas for one possessing full devotion, liberation occurs in a single birth alone. In this context, "equality with Śiva" does not mean identity with Śiva.

Because of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad scripture stating, "He is seen as equal to that and even superior," there is an absence of equality with Śiva; for it is impossible for one who is inferior to Śiva to be equal to Him. The meaning is that the state of being beyond comparison—expressed in such sayings as "the sky is like the sky"—is non-difference; thus, one becomes the very nature of Śiva.
And from the Vṛddha-Jābāla Śruti: "He becomes of the very nature of Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, for the Vīras, liberation occurs in a single birth;
but for other Śaivas, liberation occurs after three births.

Thus, according to the statement of the Vīrāgama, the meaning is that for the Vīraśaivas, liberation occurs in a single birth alone, whereas for other Śaivas, liberation occurs after three births. || 14 ||
Now, what indeed is "slight devotion"? Regarding whether or not there is rebirth for one who is liberated, he says:
"There is certainly no more suffering from the pressure of the womb; of this there is no doubt.
That service which is performed with its constituent parts (aṅgas) but is deficient is called 'devotion' (bhakti). (15)

"Once gone there, he does not return; once gone there, he does not return" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1). According to this scripture, there is no rebirth—that is, no further production from the pressure of the womb-machine. "Full devotion" refers to service endowed with the nine previously mentioned limbs;
"slight devotion" means that which is somewhat deficient. || 15 ||
According to the Vedic scripture, "What one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs through action," that devotion is said to be threefold;
it is further divided into three types by means of the mind, speech, and body.
That contemplation upon the form and other attributes of Śiva is known as mental service (mānasī sevā);
vocal service (vācikī sevā) consists of recitation and the like, while physical service (kāyikī sevā) is ritual worship (karmapūjā). (16)
That devotion, together with its ancillaries, is divided into three types according to the instruments characterized by mind, speech, and body.

Among these, the mental [devotion] consists of contemplation on the true nature of the Śiva-liṅga and so forth; the vocal [devotion] takes the form of the recitation of Śiva-mantras and hymns of praise; and the bodily [devotion] refers to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga performed with the body—this is the meaning of "service" (sevā). || 16 ||
Now, he states that such service is threefold according to the divisions of external and so forth:
"The wise know that worship of Him is threefold: as external, internal, and both external and internal; and it is further divided into three by way of mind, speech, and body. (17)
The wise know that the previously mentioned worship—distinguished by the divisions of mind, speech, and body, and joined with the three initiations—is threefold:
external, internal, and both external and internal; the meaning is that those possessing higher knowledge (abhijñā) understand it thus. || 17 ||
Now, as to what their essential nature is, he speaks, preceded by a description of the nature of the mind and so forth:
"The mind is enriched by meditation on Maheśa; the mind is not intent on meditating on anything else.
Speech that delights in the name of Śiva is considered true speech, and no other. (18)
Marked with the signs of Śiva as prescribed, such as the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra) and others, and devoted to the worship of Śiva—that alone is the true body; any other is not.

Marked and sealed with the signs and emblems of Śiva— namely the *tripuṇḍra* and so forth as prescribed in the scriptures, consisting of the forms of the ash-mark, the *rudrākṣa* beads, and ornaments—
one who is devoted to the service of Śiva and intent solely on the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is truly embodied; no other is embodied.
This is the meaning. The remainder is clear. || 18-19 ||
(p. 155) Now, he defines the external and so forth:
"The external consists of the worship of Śambhu and other such acts, which are known by another self."
That very [consciousness], when self-perceived, is declared to be internal;
when the mind is inclined toward Maheśvara, it is called both external and internal. (20)

The worship of Śambhu, such as the ritual of Śiva-pūjā and so forth, which is known by others and falls within the range of another's vision, is external; however, that very same worship and so forth, when self-perceived and not within the range of another's sight or hearing, being accessible only to oneself, is internal— the mind being thus inclined toward Maheśvara.

The meaning is that those who know the scriptures state that the mind, when attached to the Śiva-liṅga, pervades both the external and the internal simultaneously, according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (kākākṣinyāya). || 20 ||
Now, he states that this very threefold worship—consisting of mental, verbal, and physical acts—is further divided into five types:
"That same worship is again described by the virtuous as being fivefold, in the following sequence:
austerity (tapas), ritual action (karman), recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), and knowledge (jñāna). (21)
This is clear. || 21 ||
Now, as to what their essential nature is, he says:
"Austerity (tapas) is not considered by us to be the emaciation of the body for the sake of Śiva, such as the Kṛcchra penance and so forth;
ritual action (karman) is to be understood as the external worship of Śiva, and is not said to consist of sacrifices and the like. (22)
Japa is the practice of the five-syllabled mantra or indeed the practice of the *praṇava*;
it is the practice of the *Rudrādhyāya* and so forth, not the study of the Vedas and the like. (23)
Meditation (dhyāna) is the contemplation of the form and other attributes of Śiva, not the contemplation of the self (ātman) and so forth;
knowledge (jñāna) is the realization of the meaning of the Śiva-āgamas, not the cognition of other matters.
Thus, this fivefold Śivayajña has been proclaimed. || 24 ||

The emaciation of the body itself is considered *tapas* (asceticism) in the procurement of materials for the worship of Śiva; it is not accepted that the mere emaciation of the body through *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances constitutes *tapas*. It should be understood that the act (*karman*) is indeed the worship of Śiva, specifically the adoration of the Śiva-liṅga, because its fruit is eternal. External [acts] such as sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like [are not the primary focus].

It is not called an action such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which is accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and effort, because its fruit is perishable; nor is the study of the Vedas and so forth considered *japa*, because the Blessed One himself has restricted that by stating, "The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their object; be free from the three *guṇas*, O Arjuna" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.45). Rather, it is...

The practice of the five syllables, or indeed the practice of the *praṇava*, or the practice of the *Rudrādhyāya* and so forth— by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Śikhā*, and others are included— the meaning is that *japa* is the practice characterized by the repetition of these. *Dhyāna* is not the contemplation of the Self and such.
The meaning is that contemplation (*dhyāna*) is not the reflection on the self as "I" conjoined with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the finite body, senses, and so forth;

rather, the meaning is that contemplation is the reflection on the form and attributes of Śiva, the reflection on the *liṅga* of Śiva, and the reflection on the physical form characterized by such qualities as having the moon as his crest-jewel (*candraśekhara*). It is not the cognition of anything else.
Knowledge refers to the knowledge of the meaning of other treatises such as Sāṃkhya; it is not [true] knowledge, but rather the specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*) of the meaning of the Śiva-āgamas.
Such fivefold [practices], characterized by body, speech, and mind, consisting of worship, austerity, recitation, meditation, and knowledge—
This type is proclaimed as the Śivayajña (the sacrifice to Śiva). || 22–24 ||
(p. 157) Now, he says that he who worships Śaṅkara with this fivefold sacrifice and with supreme devotion is a devotee:
He who worships Śaṅkara with these five sacrifices,
endowed with supreme devotion, is indeed declared to be a true devotee.
This is clear. || 25 ||
Now, he says that for one who honors such a devotee of Śiva there is a happy destiny, whereas for one who insults him there is a terrible hell:
"From honoring a devotee of Śiva, a meritorious destiny is attained;
from insulting him, a most terrible hell [is reached]—of this there is no doubt. (26)
This is clear. || 26 ||
Now, he states what should and should not be done by a devotee of Śiva:
"A devotee of Śiva, possessed of great luster, should not touch those who are averse to devotion to Śiva, nor should he even look at them, nor should he dwell anywhere with them. (27)

One becomes a devotee of Śiva and possesses great splendor. Therefore, one should not engage in seeing, touching, or dwelling together with those who are not devotees of Śiva even once; the implication is that if one were to do so, there would be a diminution of one's splendor. || 27 ||

Now he states the duty to be performed: "When the entry into initiation occurs, preceded by the wearing of the *liṅga*, from that time forward this devotee should worship those established in his own scripture. (28)
The meaning is that after the *liṅga-dīkṣā*, the devotee should worship daily those established in his own *āgama* as well as those established in the *Vīraśaiva-āgama*. || 28 ||
One should eat in the houses of those twice-born who are devoted to the practice of their own path and are of the same caste, but never in the houses of others.
"By virtue of such authoritative statements as, 'He who exists on earth transgressing the caste-boundaries declared by Śiva is to be known as a Caṇḍāla,' [it follows that] for the twice-born,
[the status of being a Brahmin is established] because they have attained the *mantra-piṇḍa* preceded by the burning of the three impurities (*mala-traya*) by the fire of Śiva-initiation."

The essential meaning is that one should eat in the dwellings and in the company of those who are born of one's own caste, who are devoted to Maheśvara, and who are steadfast in conduct appropriate to the Vīraśaiva doctrine, but not elsewhere. || 29 ||
One should abandon all wealth sent by worldly beings who are ignorant of the conduct of their own path and whose natures are vulgar—even that which has entered into one's own possession. (30)
The meaning is that one should abandon even that which is absorbed within oneself and even that which is under one's own control. || 30 ||
A devotee of Śiva who is firm in his vows should not worship other gods, nor remember them, nor praise them; he should not eat what has been offered to them. 31.

One who is firm in his vows, one whose vow to Śiva is even firmer, and a devotee of Śiva should not worship other gods—such as Viṣṇu and others—with his two hands; he should not honor them, nor praise them, nor offer hymns of praise to them, nor even remember them in his mind, nor meditate upon them; furthermore, he should not eat or consume food and other substances offered to them. This is the meaning.
One should abandon those houses where another deity resides;
one should not look upon mortals who worship other deities at the time of one's own worship. (32)
159) "At the time of worship" means at the time of worshipping the Śiva-liṅga; the rest is clear. || 32 ||
For those who are solely devoted to Śiva and who follow the path of Vīraśaivism, the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and other such items from stationary liṅgas are not to be used. || 33 ||

Indeed, it is well known that for those who are always and continuously devoted solely to the Śivaliṅga and who follow the path of Vīraśaivism, the offerings (nirmālya) and the consecrated remnants (prasāda) from stationary liṅgas established by gods, sages, or humans are unfit [for consumption]. 33.

Now, if it is argued that for Vīraśaivas it is improper to treat a stationary liṅga as a prasāda (consecrated gift), and that one should remain indifferent when the loss of that liṅga occurs, the author says in response: "Where the loss of stationary liṅgas occurs... [and so forth].
Or else, [it is for] those who are devotees of Śiva and who bear the marks of Śiva. || 34 ||
In that situation, one should perform the rite of renunciation even at the cost of one's life;
if one gives up their life for the sake of Śiva, they shall attain union with Śiva.

In whatever place obstacles arise against stationary lingas, or against those who bear the emblems of Śiva—such as an elephant hide, a skull, ashes resembling the cremated remains of Kāma, a staff, a Wherever any harm may befall those mobile deities—the devotees of Śiva who possess the ninefold devotion already described—one should, following the conduct of Pārvatī, seek to prevent it even at the cost of one's own life. (34–35)
To the objection, "Would this not result in an untimely death (durmaraṇa) by abandoning one's life? he replies:
"If one has surrendered their life for the sake of Śiva, they shall attain union with Śiva.
Now, indicating the conduct of Vīrabhadra and Basaveśvara, he establishes the different types of conduct for devotees:
"Upon seeing one who reviles Śiva, one should either strike him down or curse him."
Or, if he is unable [to endure it], he should abandon that place and depart. || 36 ||
The meaning is that if one is unable to kill or curse [the offender], one should cover one's ears and depart from that place. || 36 ||
One should never go to a place where there is censure of right conduct;
one should abandon those houses where there is censure of Śiva. (37)
"Censure of conduct" means censure of the conduct of Śiva. The rest is clear. || 37 ||

Now, as to whether or not there is an expiation for one who reviles Śiva, he says: "For him who reviles the Lord of All Beings, the Sovereign of the Universe, no atonement can be made even in hundreds of years. (38)

The meaning is that, according to the scriptural statement, "The Lord of all beings" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.61), one who reviles the Sovereign of All, the Lord of all living creatures, cannot achieve atonement even in hundreds of years. || 38 ||
Now, if it is argued that for a devotee of Śiva, the remembrance of other deities is likewise improper,
then what is the status of prior rites such as the *saṃdhyā-vandana*? Since those consist of the worship of the Sun and other deities, the author says in response:
By becoming intent on the worship of Śiva, one may cast off past karma;
otherwise, if there remains past karma, that worship shall be fruitless. (39)
"Devoted to the worship of Śiva" means being one who is engaged in the worship of Śiva while being endowed with initiation into the Śivaliṅga; the rest is clear. || 39 ||
161) Now, he says that the downfall would not be merely this much: "Having resorted to the highest goal, yet having adopted a base way of life..."
One who has fallen after having ascended [to a high status] should be known as excluded from all ritual acts. || 40 ||
This is clear. || 40 ||
Now, because he is habituated to the recitation of the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra, the praise of men is censurable; thus [the text] says:
"If one who imparts the instruction of the five-syllabled mantra should offer praise to men, he is unmarked (*aliṅgī*), he is of evil conduct, and he is renowned as a bad poet. (41)

If a man who teaches the five-syllabled mantra, who teaches the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra, and who is a devotee of Śiva, should be one who offers praise [only for gain], he is "without a *liṅga*"—meaning devoid of the Śiva-liṅga; he is a man of evil conduct, a bad poet, a contemptible poet, and "renowned" in the sense of being devoid of the scriptures. || 41 ||
Those devoted to devotion should not accept water or oil from a leather vessel;
if it is accepted by a devotee, he shall go to the Raurava hell.
"Devoted to devotion" means devoted to devotion toward Śiva; the rest is clear. || 42 ||

Now, since it has been stated that those who bear the marks (liṅgin) must abandon their prior karma, one might ask whether the performance of rites such as impurity on birth (jātāśauca) and so forth should be observed for them or not; to this he says:
"There is no impurity whatsoever for him who is attached to the body of the Prāṇaliṅga."
That which arises from birth and that which arises from death exist in the ultimate sense.

The meaning is that for a devotee of Śiva whose limbs are joined with the *liṅga* of the vital breath (*prāṇaliṅga*), there exists in the ultimate sense not even the slightest impurity arising from birth or death, nor any impurity resulting from the remnants of a funeral feast (*kulocchiṣṭasūtaka*). || 43 ||
To the question, "In that case, do women have menstrual impurity (rajas) and birth impurity (sūtaka)?", he says here:
"For a woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, there is no impurity during her menses;
likewise, for one who has given birth, no impurity exists at all. (44)

For a woman devoted to the worship of the Śivaliṅga, there is no *sūtaka*—meaning neither the impurity caused by the monthly appearance of menstrual blood (*ṛtu-sūtaka*) nor the impurity pertaining to a woman who has recently given birth (*prasūtikā-sūtaka*) resulting from the delivery of a child. This is the meaning. || 44 ||
In response to the question, "What then is the status regarding impurity (sūtaka) within the house? he says:
"In whichever house a woman has given birth, there is no impurity here;
by contact with the water from Śiva’s feet, all sin is destroyed. (45)

In her house, at the time of performing the worship of Śiva, all sins—including the sin arising from any period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*)—are destroyed by the falling of the water from Śiva’s feet; thus, the meaning is that there is no domestic impurity (*gṛhasūtaka*).
A woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga remains pure even when she is in a state of postpartum or menstrual impurity (*sūtakī* or *rajasvalā*).
Just as the sun, fire, and wind, so too shall one become pure as ten million [fires].
Thus, according to the statement of the Śiva-āgama, the sense is that for the devotees of Śiva there is no impurity (sūtaka) whatsoever. || 45 ||
Now, one might ask: "Should not the previously prescribed pilgrimages to Śiva’s sacred sites (kṣetra) and holy waters (tīrtha), and so forth, be abandoned?
To this, he says:
"The worshipper of Śiva [should visit] the sacred sites and distinguished holy waters of Śiva."
One should constantly attend the festival of Śiva’s procession with supreme joy. || 46 ||

A worshiper of Śiva, a devotee of Śiva who honors the chosen *liṅga*, [should visit] the distinguished and excellent abodes of Śiva such as Śrīparvata and other sites, the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as Trimaṇḍuka and others, and the festivals and processions of Śiva constantly.
The meaning is that one should practice [this]. || 46 ||
And people devoted to Maheśvara should provide food and drink along the way for those who desire to witness the great pilgrimage festival of the Śiva-field. (47)

The meaning is that all people devoted to Maheśvara, as well as devotees of Śiva who desire to witness the procession arising from the festival in a sacred field of Śiva, should provide gifts of food and water on the road. || 47 ||
Now, one might ask: why is it that, setting aside the giving of clothing and other such things, only the gift of food and water is mentioned? To this he says:
"There is no gift equal to food and water, and no austerity superior to non-violence.
Therefore, a devotee of Maheśvara should constantly provide food and water. (48)
This is clear. || 48 ||
Now, one might ask: why is it appropriate to give a daughter in marriage even to someone [who is not a fellow initiate]? To this he replies:

One who observes the virtuous vow should give a daughter born of a noble family to those of his own caste who abide by the conduct of their own path; from them, he should receive her in marriage. (49)

One who is ever-vowed, constantly observant of the conduct and vows of Śiva, and a devotee of Śiva, should give a maiden born of his own family— one arisen from his own lineage— to those fellow Śiva-devotees of his own caste who abide by the path of Vīraśaiva conduct; "he should take her from them" means he should bring her [to them].

(164) Thus, having been endowed with various kinds of Śiva-conduct, the observer of the hero-vow (vīravratī), a devotee of Śiva, should worship both the venerable Guru and the Liṅga; indicating these two stations, he concludes the section on the station of the devotee (bhaktasthala).
