Thus, one who is endowed with such conduct, a Vīraśaiva observer of the Great Vow, should constantly worship both the Guru and the Liṅga with supreme devotion. (50)
This is clear. || 50 ||
Thus concludes the section on the practice of the path of devotion;
now follows the section on both [devotion and knowledge], according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.23): "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, as he has for the Lord, so too for the Guru."
In accordance with the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, he explains the non-difference between Śiva and the Guru through two sūtras: "By the worship of the Guru as well, Śiva is directly worshipped.
There is no difference whatsoever between the two, because they are identical in their essential nature. (51)

By worshipping the Guru, Śiva is worshipped directly and perceptibly; because those two—the Śiva and the Guru—are identical in their essential nature (tattva) and in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), the meaning is that there is not even the slightest difference or distinction between them. || 51 ||
Therefore,
just as one would act toward the Lord of the World, the benefactor of all,
so should one perform services day by day toward the excellent guru.
"Upacārān" means services such as devotion and so forth; the rest is clear. || 52 ||
(165) Now, one might object: "If there is non-difference between Śiva and the Guru, then the Guru, like Śiva, would be entirely imperceptible. To this he says:
"Mahādeva is imperceptible to all because of his own *māyā*."
He exists visibly in the form of the Guru for the sake of accomplishing devotion.

The meaning is that Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord, although invisible to all by virtue of his own power of *māyā*, remains manifest in the form of a Guru for the sake of accomplishing devotion, having concealed the moon-digit on his forehead and his two arms. || 53 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since a guru is not seen to bestow desired objects in the same way as Śiva, for what purpose should he be worshipped? To this, he says:
"He who possesses the knowledge of Śiva—which enables one to cross the most terrible ocean of saṃsāra—who would not become a person worthy of salutation? (54)"

By which Guru the auspicious knowledge that carries one across the great and terrifying ocean of saṃsāra is bestowed and taught—that Guru, by whom, is not to be saluted? The meaning is: he is to be saluted by everyone, even those tormented by birth and death. || 54 ||

Now, he reveals what that knowledge of Śiva is like, preceded by its respective greatness: "By the mere fraction of whose glance the state of Śiva, characterized by supreme bliss, is attained—who would not worship that Guru? (55)

"By the mere grace of whose sidelong glance," etc. The meaning is as follows: here, since the substratum (*dharmin*)—the "I"—is well-established even in the states of bondage and liberation, even those who are blind from birth, congenitally blind, deaf, mute, and so forth, possess no doubt or error regarding their own self. Therefore, all cognition is non-erroneous with respect to the substratum, though it may be erroneous regarding its specific mode (*prakāra*).

"Reversal" (*viparyaya*) refers to the state of being divided from the Person who has attained identity with one's own Self—according to the universally accepted analogy of the "essence of the egg"—by virtue of the power of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Just as sparks are separated from a fire, [the individual] appears distinct due to the influence of delusion, which is fashioned by the power of *māyā*—a synonym for absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). Thus...

The state of one's own self as Śiva, characterized by the supreme bliss of realized consciousness, is attained and revealed through the tenth illustration; therefore, by whom would such a Guru not be worshipped? The meaning is that he must indeed be worshipped by every seeker of liberation.
(166) Having stated that one must practice only what is beneficial for such a venerable guru (śrīguru) and that his command must not be transgressed, he concludes both sections with two sūtras:
One should always act for the benefit of the peaceful teacher, who is a great treasure-house of the knowledge of Śiva, by means of both one's body and one's wealth. (56)
"Of one who is tranquil" means of one who is free from passion and hatred; the rest is clear. || 56 ||
A wise person desiring spiritual accomplishment must not transgress the command of the Guru;
by transgressing his command, one becomes a violator of the command of Śiva. (57)
The wise one, being discerning, desirous of perfection, and seeking liberation, must not transgress the command of the Guru;
for if he were to transgress it, he would be a violator of the command of Śiva—this is the meaning. || 57 ||
Thus, the section on both [aspects];
now, the section on the threefold perfection.
Just as one who possesses devotion conducts himself toward the Guru and the Linga, so should the wise man always practice devotion toward the mobile [form]. (58)
"Vicakṣaṇaḥ" means one who is proficient and a devotee of Śiva; the rest is clear. || 58 ||

Now, since it has been stated that Śiva alone has descended in the form of the Guru for the sake of accomplishing devotion, and that devotion toward the Guru is as appropriate as devotion toward Śiva himself, one might ask: why should devotion also be practiced toward the living being (the disciple)? To this, he says:
"Śiva alone is directly the bestower of grace upon all."
The Guru exists as the soul of the mobile liṅga, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 59 ||
Because of the Lord’s own statement, "Therefore, He is celebrated in this world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.18),
the Supreme Lord— who is well-known in both the world and the Veda, who bestows grace upon all devotees, and who is the one independent Master—
is alone, while existing as the Guru, the Jaṅgama, and the Liṅga, or as the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama.

The meaning is that since he exists as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the ground of both worldly experience and release, devotion must be practiced toward the living being (jaṅgama) just as it is toward Śiva. || 59 ||
Now, in order to state that the mobile form is superior with respect to the *liṅga*, he first establishes the nature of the *liṅga*:
"The *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds, consisting of the mobile and the immobile."
Just as devotion toward the immobile is prescribed, so too is it prescribed toward the mobile.

The *liṅga*, the emblem of Śiva, is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the division between the moving (*cara*) and the stationary (*sthira*), that is, according to whether its nature is animate or inanimate.
The meaning is that just as devotion is prescribed toward the stationary *liṅga* (the inanimate), so too must devotion be practiced toward the moving *liṅga* (the animate). || 60 ||
(168) Now, as to what the nature of these two is, he says:
"But that linga which is immobile, fashioned from clay, stone, and so forth..."
Therefore, that moving liṅga, renowned as a Śiva-yogin, is superior. || 61 ||
That liṅga which is fashioned from clay, stone, or other materials is "ajaṅgama," meaning it is a fixed or stationary liṅga. || 61 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Śaṅkara dwells in the immobile linga through the consecration of mantra;
Maheśvara always dwells indeed in the mobile linga. (62)
This is clear. || 62 ||
Therefore, he specifies the fruit of giving and worship performed toward a Śiva-yogin with two sūtras:
"Whatever is given to a Śiva-yogin shall yield inexhaustible fruit;
therefore, with every effort, one should give to that Great Soul. (63)
The fruit that a living being obtains through the worship of a Śiva-yogin is declared to be inexhaustible by those who have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas. (64)
In this matter, it has been indicated that scripture (*āgama*) is the authority (*pramāṇa*). Regarding this:
"By seeing and worshipping him, people together with twenty-one generations of their kin go to the state that grants liberation; how much more so those who are devoted to him?"
Thus, the statement from the Yogajāgama should be reflected upon. || 63-64 ||
169) Having thus described the fruit of worshipping him, he reveals the fruit of insulting him:
One should never, under any circumstances, insult a Śiva-yogin who has arrived.
From such contempt, he will undoubtedly fall into a miserable state of existence. || 65 ||
The meaning is that it has come together somewhere, both internally and externally. || 65 ||
Thus, stating that the Śivayogin is to be worshipped, he concludes the section on the locus of the threefold prosperity:
"One should worship the Śivayogin with reverence through the devotion of service (kaiṅkarya), for he is Śiva himself in person—just as one worships a Liṅga and just as one worships a Guru. (66)
The meaning is that *kaiṅkaryabhakti* (the devotion of service) is devotion in the form of the conduct of a servant. The rest is clear. || 66 ||
Thus, having described the locus of the threefold perfection,
[the text now describes] the locus of the fourfold essence: how one receives with devotion the water from the feet of the Great Lord (Maheśituḥ).
Likewise, [this applies] eternally to Śiva and the Self, as well as to the Guru and the Jaṅgama.
Here, "of the Great Lord" means of the Śiva-liṅga; the rest is clear. || 67 ||

Now, after first describing the nature of holding the water from the washing of the feet, he states its fruit: "Holding the water from the feet of Śambhu bestows all auspiciousness, purifies all that purifies, and grants all perfections to men. (68)

The meaning is that wearing the sacred water from the feet of the Śiva-liṅga is the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the purifier of all purifiers, and it brings about all spiritual perfections for men.
Now, he describes the fruit of wearing the remains of offerings (nirmālya) consisting of leaves and flowers:
"Whoever wears upon his head a leaf or flower offered to Śiva, for him there shall arise at every moment the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice. (69)
This is clear. || 69 ||
Now, it is heard in the Purāṇas and other texts that the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Śiva is not to be accepted; how then can it be accepted? To this he says:
"One should eat the food eaten by Rudra and drink the water drunk by Rudra."
"One should always smell that which has been smelled by Rudra"—such is the Jābāli Śruti.

The meaning is that the Jābāli Śruti declares: "One should eat the food of Rudra's devotees and the food of the prasāda offered to Rudra; one should drink the water of Rudra's prasāda which has been drunk by Rudra; and one should smell the flowers struck by Rudra and offered to Rudra. [It further says: "They eat what has been eaten by Rudra, they drink what has been drunk by Rudra, and they smell what has been smelled by Rudra."

The Jābāla Śruti states, "They smell [it]. Therefore, the prohibition of that [smelling] heard in the Purāṇas and other texts refers specifically to stationary liṅgas associated with the office of a Caṇḍāla, and not to Bāṇa-liṅgas and the like;
for when a self-manifested (svayaṃbhūta) Bāṇa-liṅga or a moonstone (candrakānta) is situated in the heart—
The consumption of the food offering (naivedya) of Śambhu originating from a Śālagrāma stone.

Because of this statement; otherwise, the Purāṇic statement—which contradicts the Śruti—would itself become authoritative and thus not universal. This is the summary. Thus, because it is established by the Śruti. || 70 ||
Having offered leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, and all kinds of edible things into his own *liṅga*, the devoted man should partake of them himself.
This is clear. || 71 ||

Now, since it is universally agreed that there is no liberation for those who are averse to the grace of the Guru, and because Śiva—possessing immeasurable splendor—is the sovereign of all sciences according to the Vedic revelation, "He is the Lord of all sciences" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 8.7), and thus the master of all knowledge, let Sadāśiva alone be my refuge. Thus: *sadāśivom*.

And because he is heard of as non-different from the Praṇava, which is the form of the Tāraka-Brahman, and because he is the teacher of all the worlds, his grace must necessarily be accepted; thus he says:
"Because of the greatness of Śambhu, who possesses immeasurable splendor and is the teacher of all beings..."
Everything reported to him should be accepted by those who are devoted to him as their supreme goal.
This is clear. || 72 ||
To the question of who is entitled to this grace of the Śiva-liṅga, he says:
"Those in the world who wear the liṅga and those who are solely devoted to Śiva—for them alone is the *nirmālya* of Śiva appropriate, not for other beings. (73)
This is clear. || 73 ||

To the question, "What then is the fruit of eating food through the grace of Śiva?", he says: "When food of whatever kind is eaten by a devotee offered to Śiva, the fruit of a horse-sacrifice is obtained for every single grain of rice. (74)
The manifestation of fully ripened rice grains is expressed by the word *siktha*. The remainder is clear. || 74 ||
172) Now, he indicates those who are not qualified for this: "The remains of the offering (nirmālya) are stainless and pure, because they have been accepted by Śiva."
It should be maintained by those who are stainless and devoted to it, and not by other ordinary beings.
The meaning is that those who are devoid of initiation into the Śiva-liṅga are ordinary people and lack the qualification; therefore, it should not be worn by them.
The meaning is that it should be worn by those who are purified through Śiva-initiation, who are devoted to it, and who are established in the Śiva-liṅga. || 75 ||
He clarifies that very point:
"For living beings devoid of devotion to Śiva who are engaged in sinful deeds, there is no eligibility whatsoever for the pure remains (nirmālya) of Śiva. (76)

The meaning is as follows: because Śiva, who is the pervasive reality, is conceived as having eight bodies, he becomes common [to all]; thus, in the worship of other deities who share this commonality, [the deity] is nourished by the moon and the Gaṅgā, which have become flowers and water belonging to Śiva.
Because grain is ripened by the tongue of Rudra in the form of fire,

all living beings have the right to both [the cultivation and consumption of grain]; nevertheless, regarding the uncommon worship of the Śiva-liṅga and the acceptance of the Śiva-liṅga’s prasāda, only one who has received Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) possesses the qualification.
This is well-known in all the treatises. || 76 ||
Now, having indicated the greatness of *prasāda*, he concludes this section with two verses:
"Whatever fruit may arise from accepting the *prasāda* of the Śiva-liṅga, such [fruit] likewise arises from accepting the *prasāda* of the Guru and the Jaṅgama. (77)
Therefore, one should worship the Guru, who is Mahādeva and a Śiva-yogin himself; by his grace, one should eat food every day. (78)
One should worship with body, mind, and wealth; this is the meaning of "one should worship. Through his grace alone, one should eat food every single day. (77-78)
Thus,
[this is] the stage of the fourfold essence, consisting of the stages of conditioned, unconditioned, and innate giving.
Now, from the gift of the body comes the accomplishment of truth; from the gift of wealth comes liberation;
from the gift of life comes the accomplishment of knowledge—thus, everything becomes stable.
According to the statement in the *Yogajāgama*, one should give gifts according to one's capacity for the sake of the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*; thus it says:
"One who possesses devotion toward the Śiva-liṅga, the Śiva-ācārya, and the Śiva-yogin..."
One should always practice giving according to one's ability, endowed with a spirit of serene faith.
The word "having that as its object" is to be supplied [to the verse]. The remainder is clear. || 79 ||
Now, he clarifies the essential nature of that gift:
"And gift is declared to be threefold—conditioned, unconditioned, and innate—by all those who are experts in every tantra. (80)

The meaning is that those proficient in all the scriptures have declared that for all devotees of Śiva, *dāna* (giving) consists of three forms— the giving of life, body, and wealth— which are respectively qualified (*sopādhika*), unqualified (*nirupādhika*), and innate (*sahaja*). || 80 ||

In that regard, he defines the occasion of conditioned giving: "That prescribed gift which is joined with the expectation of a fruit is declared to be 'with conditions' (sopādhika), and it is disregarded by those seeking liberation. (81)

The meaning is that whatever gift might be prescribed which is joined with a desire for a hollow fruit, and is therefore disregarded by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), is said to be "with conditions" (sopādhika). || 81 ||
174) Now, he defines the occasion of unconditioned giving: "That which is free from expectation of fruit, offered to the Lord, and performed without desire."
Giving that is free from conditions has been proclaimed by those expert in the art of giving.

The meaning is that the gift which is performed free from the desire for hollow fruits, with the aspiration of offering it to the Lord, is designated as "unconditioned giving" (nirupādhika-dāna) by those who know the true nature of the essence of giving. || 82 ||

He describes the locus of spontaneous giving (sahajadāna): "Contemplating the state of Śiva in the non-giver, the giver, and the gift, as well as one's own state of non-agency—that which is given becomes spontaneous. (83)

The meaning is that the gift which is given while contemplating the auspicious nature (*śivatva*) of the recipient, the giver, and the object given, and while meditating upon one's own lack of agency (*akartṛtva*), is "spontaneous giving" (*sahajadāna*). As it is said: "Having realized the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller—all this is declared to be the one threefold Brahman" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.12).

This should also be understood in the context of the "Natural Gift" (sahajadāna), which serves as the conclusion here, corresponding to the "Secret of the Body" (piṇḍastharahasya) found at the beginning of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. || 83 ||
Regarding which among these is the most excellent, he says:
"Innate generosity is superior, the highest of all gifts;
it bestows the knowledge of Śiva upon men and brings an end to birth and disease. (84)
"Spontaneous giving (*sahaja-dāna*) is the most excellent among all supreme gifts"—this means it is the most distinguished and the best.

To the question "How so?", the answer is: because it bestows the knowledge of identity with Śiva, which serves as the remedy for the great disease characterized by birth and death for human beings. || 84 ||
To this objection—that what is given with such contemplation directed toward the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama is indeed the innate offering—he says:
"If anything whatsoever is given to Śiva or to a devotee of Śiva... (p. 175).
Even that, when performed with devotion, is renowned as the supreme, innate gift. || 85 ||

The meaning is that "gifts such as land given to Śiva" refers to what is given to Śiva in the form of stationary liṅgas other than the installed (iṣṭa) liṅga; and "natural gifts" refers to what is given even to devotees of Śiva other than those who have renounced worldly attachments. || 85 ||
Now, he states the fruit of that gift:
"Whatever fruit may arise from giving a thousand pieces of gold to a worthy recipient, that same fruit is desired for the offering of a single flower to Śiva. (86)
This is clear. || 86 ||

To the question "How so?", he says— with the intention that, because of the Vedic scripture "The Lord of all sciences" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 40.7), Śiva is the supreme vessel, being the storehouse of all knowledge and the most excellent recipient due to his status as the Teacher of the World:
"Śiva alone is the supreme vessel, the Guru who is the storehouse of all knowledge."
Whatever is given to him, however small, shall yield infinite fruit. || 87 ||

This is another point: Śiva alone is the supreme recipient, and likewise the Guru, who is a treasury of all knowledge, is the supreme recipient; what is given to that Śiva and to the Guru yields infinite fruit. || 87 ||
Likewise, it is said that even for a Śiva-yogin [a gift] is given:
"The Śiva-yogin is Śiva himself, the great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva;
whatever is given to him is a gift of ultimate reality. (88)
The meaning is that the ultimate gift is the co-emergent (sahaja) gift that bestows immeasurable fruit. || 88 ||
(p. 176) Now, he specifically describes the greatness of the Lord of Śiva-yogins:
"The Śiva-yogin is a great vessel for all acts of giving."
Therefore, according to the investigation of the scriptures, there is no recipient superior to this one. || 89 ||

Regarding the act of giving, concerning the matter of charity, among all worthy recipients (*satpātra*), the Śiva-yogin is the great recipient; the meaning is that, according to the investigation of the scriptures, there is nothing whatsoever superior or more excellent than him as a recipient. || 89 ||
Now, he describes the fruit of that gift:
"The fruit which is obtained by giving even a mere alms-meal to a peaceful Śiva-yogin cannot be attained even by hundreds of millions of sacrifices. (90)
"Bhikṣāmātra" means merely a mouthful; the rest is clear. || 90 ||
To the question "How so? he says:
When the Śivayoginī is fully satisfied, Śaṅkara becomes satisfied;
through her satisfaction, the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, which is identical with him, attains satisfaction. (91)

According to the Vedic scripture, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9), because the Śiva-yogin is the direct embodiment of Śiva, by his satisfaction Śiva becomes satisfied. By his satisfaction, the entire universe attains satisfaction, for according to the scripture, "All this is indeed Rudra"; thus is the meaning. || 91 ||
Therefore, it is said that one should satisfy the Śiva-yogins with every effort:
"Therefore, by all possible means and by whatever action, one should always satisfy the Śiva-yogins with food and other offerings. (92)
The meaning is that with every effort, by whatever action possible, one should at all times bring satisfaction to the Śiva-yogin through food, drink, and so forth. || 92 ||
Furthermore, he states that one who is endowed with spontaneous generosity toward such worthy recipients (satpātra) is indeed Śiva himself:
"In the reality of the supreme bliss, which is the nature of consciousness free from all limiting adjuncts, everything is complete for him; such a giver is Śaṅkara himself. (93)

The meaning is that for that devotee of Śiva in whom every object— consisting of body, wealth, and life-force— is fully completed and offered unto the Supreme Śiva, who is the very self of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama (the embodied soul) characterized by perfect Being-Consciousness-Bliss, he is himself Śiva, being a natural giver. || 93 ||

Now, with the following verse, he explains that one who is endowed with all the aforementioned conduct, who is naturally generous, and who is a devotee of Śiva alone, attains the state of a Māheśvara:
"He who is devoted to all the aforementioned conduct..."
Constantly bestowing spontaneous gifts,
with a mind detached from the prosperities of Brahmā and the other gods,
the devotee indeed attains the state of Maheśvara.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Stages of the Māheśvara," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, the knower of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). 9.

Since the literal meaning is clear, the underlying significance (*bhāvārtha*) is written here: having surrendered one's body, wealth, and field to the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*, and having taken up a physical form by the grace of the holy *tīrtha* of the *jaṅgama* deity through the lotus-hands of the venerable Guru, one becomes intent upon union with the Great *Liṅga*.
Being a devotee of Śiva and possessing the virtuous conduct of a Māheśvara, he shall become renowned as a Māheśvara. || 94 ||

Thus ends the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences (*padavākyapramāṇa*).
The ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Stages of Practice on the Path of Devotion."
The Tenth Chapter: Now, the Section on Māheśvara.
Following the description of the Section on Devotees, Agastya asks the venerable Reṇuka:
Agastya said:
O Leader of the Gaṇas, you have described the state of devotion;
by what specific dharma does one become a devotee of Maheśvara? (1)
The meaning of the question is: "By what distinction of dharma, that is to say, by what distinction of conduct, would a devotee become a devotee of Śiva (māheśvara)? || 1 ||
Reṇuka said:
One who is proficient in pure, innate generosity, intent upon Śiva,
and turned away from the realms of Brahmā and the other gods, is known as a devotee of Maheśvara.

The meaning is that one who is skilled and proficient in the gift of pure spontaneity, who is free from desire for states such as that of Brahmā, who is a devotee of Śiva, intent upon Śiva, and solely devoted to Śiva, is known as a Māheśvara. || 2 ||
He clarifies that very point:
"When there is an excellence of devotion due to the weight of dispassion, then the devotee is declared to be a Māheśvara, possessing steady discernment. (3)

When, at that time, there arises through the weight of dispassion— that is, the greatness of dispassion— the appropriate excellence of devotion, namely, devotion to Śiva, then at that time one possesses stable discernment.
The meaning is that one who possesses a firm discernment of eternal and non-eternal entities and is a devotee of Śiva is called a Māheśvara.
Now, since there are indeed various divisions of this [Māheśvara] state, he teaches those divisions here:
"I shall describe the stage of the Māheśvara as it was previously taught by Śambhu."
After the praise of Maheśvara and so forth, there follows thereafter the dedication to the Liṅga.
Then follows the rejection of the previous basis, as well as the refutation of non-duality;
subsequently, the abandonment of invocation and the refutation of the eightfold form.
The exclusion of all states of being and the state of Śiva-hood for both Śiva and his devotees—thus has the ninefold great site of Māheśvara been described. (6)

I shall describe the various divisions of the Māheśvara sites exactly as they were spoken by Śiva in former times; "listen," is the implied sense. First is the stage of the praise of the Māheśvara, followed immediately thereafter by the stage of steadfastness in the Liṅga, and after that, the stage of the rejection of prior dependencies, and likewise following that—

The section on the refutation of non-duality (*advaita*), followed by the section on the refutation of invocation; next, the section on the refutation of the eight-formed one (*aṣṭamūrti*); next, the section on the refutation of omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*);
next, the section on Śiva as the essence of the world; and then the section on the physical *liṅga* of the devotee. Thus.
The great site of Māheśvara is said to be ninefold, meaning it is described as having nine varieties.

By stating, "I shall speak here exactly as it was previously told by Śambhu," it is indicated that everything— both what has been said and what is yet to be said— is not a mere fabrication of one's own imagination.

The view of some— that after the refutation of [Śiva’s] having eight forms (aṣṭamūrtitva), it is appropriate to state the refutation of invocation— is set aside because it contradicts the sequence stated by Śiva; nevertheless,
it was not said that invocation is impossible because Śiva is all-pervasive, but rather [that it is impossible] in one's own chosen liṅga.
Since it has already been stated that a further invocation is not possible because it would contradict the practice, there is no room for doubt.

Now, he says: "Listen, I shall describe the definitions of its intermediate stages according to their order of enumeration," beginning from the start, I shall explain the characteristics of each distinct stage in sequence.
O Sage, listen with a concentrated mind. (7)
This is clear. || 7 ||

In this regard, according to the Śvetāśvatara and other Upaniṣadic scriptures— such as "Rudra, the great seer, who transcends the universe, brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning; may he endow us with auspicious understanding" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.4)—
the true nature of Maheśvara is presented through seven aphorisms preceded by a praise of the Great Lord.
He elucidates this through further elaboration: "Rudra is superior to the universe and is the bestower of grace upon the universe;
he whose intellect is firm in this regard is indeed remembered as a true devotee of Maheśvara. (8)

Rudra alone is the benefactor of the entire universe, including the gods, dānavas, and others; he is the Rudra well-known from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3.2): "For there is only one Rudra, no second existed" (or "they did not stand for a second").
He is that Nārāyaṇa, Hari, who is greater than the universe.
The meaning is that he whose firm conviction is that [the Lord] is superior even to Nārāyaṇa, whose universal form is renowned in the Vedas, is indeed remembered as a Māheśvara. || 8 ||
Then, following the meaning of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.8), "Nor is anyone seen equal to Him or superior," he describes the nature of Maheśvara:
"In the stainless Supreme Lord, [there is no one like Him] among those such as Brahmā, who are mostly impure."
He who cannot tolerate the expression of equality is indeed called a Māheśvara.

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all brought forth," Brahmā and the others are stained by the affliction of birth and death; therefore, they are not the Cause.
However, because Śiva, who is the cause of this [universe], is unborn according to the scripture, he is stainless and is thus the one to be meditated upon as the Cause.

The meaning is that one who cannot tolerate the statement of equality with those [deities]—because it is heard further on that Śambhu is endowed with all sovereignty and is the Lord of All in the midst of space—is called a Māheśvara.

Now, regarding the meaning of the Īśāna-mantra: "May the Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Veda, the Brahmā who is Śiva, be ever propitious to me— Sadāśivom" (Nārāyaṇopaniṣad 4.21).

The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine. Seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bhārata. (Bhagavad Gītā 18.61)
Thus, recollecting the meaning of the Bhagavad Gītā, he reveals the true nature of the devotee of Maheśvara:
"The Lord is the Great One among all beings, beginning with Brahmā;
one who, through the yoga of intellect, is attached to Him is remembered as a devotee of Maheśvara. (10)

Through the application of the intellect that [recognizes] the Great One— the Supreme Lord who is the sole sovereign and impeller of all beings, from the four-faced Brahmā onwards to all creatures and animals—
as the most excellent, the devotee who is attached to Him is one attached to Maheśvara, a devotee of Śiva.
The meaning is that he is remembered as Māheśvara. || 10 ||
Then, by means of two aphorisms, he explains that Śiva alone is the bestower of liberation, and one who knows this is a Māheśvara:
"The host of deities beginning with Brahmā is always deluded by Māyā;
they are incapable of granting liberation, being subject to decrease and increase. (11)
The Blessed One, the sole Maheśvara, is liberated from beginningless time and is the bestower of liberation; he who knows this is indeed remembered as a true Māheśvara. || 12 ||
The host of deities beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, which is subject to the excellence of birth and death,
is endless and deluded— rendered blind— by Māyā, which is a synonym for the sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of the Supreme Lord.

But in the matter of granting liberation— that is, bestowing supreme liberation— he is incapable and powerless. The Blessed One Maheśvara, who is liberated from beginningless time, eternally liberated, endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers, that Supreme Brahman (who is the Supreme Brahman),
he alone (who is the one)— he alone is Rudra, he is Īśāna, he is the Blessed One, he is Maheśvara, he...

The meaning is that he who knows— that is, understands— that Mahādeva (Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad 2.3), the Supreme Lord well-known from the Atharvaśiras, is indeed the one who bestows liberation and thus grants both the higher and lower forms of liberation, is remembered as a true Māheśvara. || 11-12 ||
183) Now, having regarded the sovereignty of Brahmā and the other gods as mere straw, one who is intent solely on the bliss of Śiva is called a *vīramāheśvara*; this he states in two sūtras:
The Vīramāheśvara always regards, through reasoning, the riches of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others— though joined with decay and excellence— as being like a blade of grass.
One who is free from desire for even a slight trace of pleasure consisting of sound, touch, and so forth, and who yearns for the bliss of Śiva, shall become a Vīramāheśvara. || 14 ||

The heroic devotee of Maheśvara, who is a devotee of Śiva, by means of reasoning and with the understanding that they are impermanent, always regards— as if they were mere blades of grass— the prosperities of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, which are joined with excellence yet subject to destruction. Therefore, he does not value even a fragment of pleasure associated with limiting conditions, such as the pleasures of sound, touch, and so forth, which are ultimately trivial.
Being free from desire and longing for the eternal bliss of the bliss of Śiva, one should become a Vīramāheśvara full of devotion; such is the meaning. || 13-14 ||

Now, he establishes the stability of those various modes of conduct with six aphorisms: "Free from attachment to the wives of others, averse to the wealth of others, accomplished in the tasks for the sake of Śiva, and devoted to the Śiva-āgamas. (15)
With a mind rejoicing in the tasting of the aesthetic flavor of Śiva’s praise, pure, and intent upon establishing the authoritative proofs for Śiva’s preeminence; || 16 ||
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, with the cage of afflictions cast away; untouched by the bonds of pride, and devoid of the onset of envy. || 17 ||
With the emergence of passion cast away and the turbulence of anger shaken off, his heart is ever contented and he is devoted to the welfare of all living beings. (18)
He is always engaged in the effort to ward off those who oppose the work of Śiva, and he is a constant companion to those who proclaim the preeminence of Śiva. (19)
Upon attaining the extraction of Śiva, even when facing the loss of life, one who is undaunted,
solely devoted to Śiva, and the self of all, shall become a Vīramāheśvara. (20)
One who has cast off the cage of afflictions; one who has warded off the multitude of ignorance and other defilements; one whose turbulence of anger has been shaken away;

one who has prevented the torment of wrath; one who is solely devoted to Śiva; one who is solely devoted to the Śiva-liṅga; one who is the self of all, possessing the full sense of "I-am-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva); one who is free from egoism, being devoid of the limited sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth.

The remainder is clear. The meaning is that one who is distinguished by such attributes as these becomes a venerable Vīraśaiva Māheśvara. Here, there is an alternative reading: *nirastakleśapañcaka* (one from whom the five afflictions have been cast out). || 15–20 ||
Thus ends the section on the praise of the Māheśvara; now follows the section on devotion to the *liṅga*,
wherein devotion to the *liṅga* as enjoined by this Māheśvara is treated in nine aphorisms.
He explains:
For this follower of Maheśvara, the great site of ultimate devotion to the *liṅga* is declared to be that which is ordained as never to be abandoned, even when the loss of life has occurred. (21)

Whatever state of devotion to the *liṅga* is prescribed as not to be abandoned—even when a life-threatening crisis has arisen and even when one has encountered a peril to one's life—that is the great state of devotion to the *liṅga*; this is what has been declared for this devotee of Maheśvara, that is, for the devotee of Śiva who is solely intent upon the *Śivaliṅga*. This is the meaning. || 21 ||
Regarding what kind of life-threatening peril this is:
"There may come a time of renouncing one's life, or even the cutting off of one's head;
yet one should never eat without having first worshipped the Blessed Tryambaka."
In accordance with the statement of the *Śivadharmottara*, it says:
"Let all my possessions depart, or let there be the severing of my head."
A devotee of Maheśvara should not abandon the great vow of worshipping the Liṅga. || 22 ||
This is clear. || 22 ||
Now, he says that for those who do not eat except after performing the worship of Śiva, the Goddess of Liberation shines forth in their hands like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand:
"But those men who do not eat without having performed the worship of the Liṅga..."
The Goddess of Liberation has come into the hands of those great-souled ones.
The meaning is that the fortune of liberation has arrived and remains present; this is stated to be the fruit of devotion to the *liṅga*. || 23 ||
Then, he specifies this very point with two verses:
"What is the use of other doctrines, which are turbid and yield only trivial results?
The dharma of Śambhu, consisting of the worship of the Liṅga, directly bestows liberation. (24)

The dharma consisting of the worship of the *liṅga* of Śambhu, the Auspicious One, directly bestows liberation. Therefore, what is the use of other trivial dharmas—those which are mere semblances of dharma, which yield only worthless or contemptible results, and which are distinct from the worship of the Śiva-liṅga? The meaning is: "What purpose do they serve? || 24 ||
Now he speaks of the greatness of consuming the food and drink offered to the *liṅga*:
"Those who sustain their bodies with the food and drink offered to the *liṅga* worshipped according to the rules are indeed great devotees of Maheśvara. (25)
For this is well known. The remainder is clear. || 25 ||

(p. 186) Now, in accordance with the Vedic scripture which states, "Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs through action," [the author] declares that those who are devoted to the Śiva-liṅga are indeed Śivas themselves, preceded by the three instruments (of body, speech, and mind).
Those whose minds are always steadfastly fixed upon the Śiva-liṅga, which consists of pure consciousness, having abandoned all other objects, are Śivas themselves; of this there is no doubt. (26)

Those whose minds are liberated from all other objects, having abandoned the desire for trivial fruits such as heaven, and who are always firmly established in the Śiva-liṅga which is of the nature of pure consciousness—they are Rudras on this earth; in this matter, there is no doubt—this is the meaning. || 26 ||

Now, having raised the objection that rest in the mind alone has been taught regarding this "liṅga" which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), he shows the rest in all three instruments by means of another aphorism:
"He whose mind is dissolved in the liṅga, and whose speech is intent upon the praise of the liṅga..."
Those hands devoted to the worship of the Liṅga are Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. || 27 ||
Thus it is clear. || 27 ||

Thus, he states that for one established in the *liṅga*, there is no purpose for rituals such as the *agnihotra*: "What need has he who is established in the *liṅga* for ritual action, which is a cause for [attaining] heaven, when his attainment of Śiva, who is eternal bliss, is certain according to the scriptures? (28)

For one who is established in the *liṅga* and for whom the attainment of the state of Śiva, which is eternal bliss, is certain according to the scriptures—the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas—what is the use of rites such as the *agnihotra*, which have heaven as their motive? What purpose do they serve? The meaning is that they serve no purpose at all. || 28 ||
Now he demonstrates its greatness:
"The gods, beginning with Brahmā, always joyfully praise that which is supreme in its devotion to the *liṅga*, peaceful, and endowed with sacred ashes and rudrākṣa beads. (29)
This is clear. || 29 ||
Thus ends the section on abiding in the marks;
now follows the section on the relinquishing of the former substratum.
Possessing a disposition refined by the guru and endowed with a body fashioned by the guru,
one should forget former evil tendencies and act under his guidance.

In accordance with this statement from the *Yogajāgama*, he explains through seven sūtras the place where one who is devoted to the *liṅga* discards their previous abode due to its opposition [to liberation]:
"The person who is a devotee of Maheśvara, whose heart is always fixed solely on the *liṅga*..."
One should abandon those qualities belonging to one's former state of existence that obstruct one's proper conduct. || 30 ||

The meaning is that the Vīramāheśvara, whose mind is continuously fixed on the Śivaliṅga alone, should abandon those duties rooted in former attachments, those ordinary practices, and those worldly behaviors that obstruct his own conduct and contradict the observances of his own tradition. || 30 ||
To the question "What then is he like?", he says:

"One who abandons the duties born of his own caste and family that are inconsistent with the observance of the [Śaiva] insignia, and who has discarded his former refuge, is to be known as a Māheśvara. (31)

The meaning is that a Vīramāheśvara— who abandons those dharmas such as impurity upon birth or death that are opposed to and contrary to the state of being established in the *liṅga*, and which belong to his own caste and family, having been acquired through his Brahminhood and so forth— is fit to be known as one who has rejected his former refuge. || 31 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it is heard that there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) from abandoning the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties acquired in a previous life, how can those dharmas be abandoned? To this he says:
"For those great-souled ones who have been purified through union with the consecration of Śiva..."
Are they considered by you to be composed of the dharmas belonging to the previous period? For they are indeed regarded as belonging to the ordinary [world]. (32)

By virtue of their connection with the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of Śiva— consisting of the previously mentioned initiation (*dīkṣā*) characterized by the destruction of [karmic] bonds through giving— and by their steadfastness in the *liṅga*, they are stainless, having shaken off all impurities both past and yet to come.
What is the purpose of the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and other such rites performed by those who have taken refuge in Śiva, based on their previous state of existence?
The meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever. If it is argued that the purpose is indeed the cessation of sin (pratyavāya), we say no.
"For in this there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a little of this dharma protects one from great fear" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.40).
Since this was spoken by the Blessed Lord himself, its meaning is as follows: it is the supreme purifier for those beyond the stages of life (atyāśramins).

Thus, in this system of castes and stages of life established by the Vedas (*śruti-siddhāntita-varṇāśrama*), the sequence of conduct— consisting of the progressive approach (*abhikrama*) and the practice of *dhāraṇā* (meditative concentration) and so forth obtained through the compassion of a Guru skilled in turning one’s self toward the Self— is subject to no destruction; for, being devoid of forgetfulness due to constant performance with single-minded devotion, there is no interruption.

The meaning is that it does not exist. Now, one might object: "If this were so, there would be sin (pratyavāya) due to the omission of obligatory and occasional rites (nitya-naimittika-karma). To this he says: "No sin exists. Why? To this he says: because even a very small portion of this dharma—namely, the dharma consisting of the wearing of ashes and so forth, which is an ancillary part of the contemplation of Śiva—is [sufficient].
Because it protects even slightly from great fear— that is, from the fear of great sins (mahāpātaka) and the like—
it is as follows: just as there is no transgression for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) when they abandon the duties of their previous stage of life (*āśrama*),
so too there is no transgression for those devoted to taking refuge in Śiva when they abandon the duties of their previous stage of life.

This is the state of being. For it is well known that those qualities of the previous substratum are considered and declared to belong only to ordinary beings who are connected with illusion (māyā). || 32 ||
Therefore,
for those who are connected with the Śiva-dharma through the application of the purificatory rites of Śiva,
engagement in the duties of the unrefined (Prākṛtas) is not appropriate. || 33 ||
It is not produced; the meaning is that it is not born. || 33 ||
(189) Now, as to how there is a twofold division among mortals, he says:
"Human beings are traditionally held to be of two kinds: the pure and the natural."
Those who undergo the Śiva-consecration are considered pure, while others are regarded as belonging to Prakṛti.
This is clear. || 34 ||
Now, to the objection that no twofold division is seen within the duties of the castes and stages of life, he says:
"Indeed, the regulation of the duties of the castes, stages of life, and so forth, is considered to be twofold:
one is ordained by Śiva, and the other is declared by Brahmā. (35)
This is clear. || 35 ||
To the question "Then, what is the dharma for whom?", he says:
"The dharma consisting of devotion to the teachings spoken by Śiva belongs to those who observe the Śiva-āśrama;
the dharma of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is prescribed for those who are devoid of the Śiva-saṃskāras. (36)
This is clear. || 36 ||
Thus ends the section on the refutation of the prior refuge.
Now begins the section on the refutation of universal non-duality (*sarvādvaita*).
Just as the Māheśvara is a refuter of the prior refuge because he opposes devotion to the *liṅga*, so too—

Because it would contradict the state of being established in the *liṅga*, it would also result in the rejection of universal non-duality (*sarvādvaita*); therefore, he demonstrates the context in which that [non-duality] is negated by the following injunction:
"In the absence of the distinction between the *liṅga* and the individual soul (*jīva*), namely between the object of worship and the worshipper..."
Because of the non-attainment of rites such as worship, and because of the contradiction with steadfastness in the *liṅga*. || 37 ||
Due to the absence of knowledge regarding the investigation of universal non-duality, one who rejects universal non-duality becomes a follower of ritual action devoted to Maheśvara. || 38 ||

(190) Since there is no distinction between the worshiper and the object of worship when both are devoted to the Śiva-liṅga, and because any contradiction regarding abiding in the liṅga would result in the impossibility of accomplishing acts of worship and so forth, the practice of the investigation into universal non-duality (*sarvādvaita*) remains firmly established.

In the absence of knowledge, such a state being untenable, the *karmī*—the *Vīra-Māheśvara* devoted to rituals such as the worship of the Śiva-liṅga—would become a proponent of the non-duality of all things (*sarvādvaita-nirāsaka*), because of the Vedāntic statement:
"As long as one lives, three are to be revered: the Vedānta, the Guru, and the Lord"; thus [he would be reduced to] ritualistic dualism (*kriyādvaita*).

Furthermore, from the statement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "it should not be done," the meaning is that a devotee of Maheśvara who is intent upon the [Śaiva] marks (*liṅga*) should not practice universal non-duality (*sarvādvaita*). || 37–38 ||

Now, as to how the method of worship performed with a sense of distinction is to be carried out, he says: "Having understood Śaṅkara as the impeller and the Self alone as the impelled, one should always worship Him through that distinction, and one should not become intent upon non-duality. (39)

Having understood that the Supreme Lord is the impeller of the mental modifications of living beings which have dharma and adharma as their objects, and that the individual souls are impelled by Him, one should constantly worship that Supreme Lord according to such distinctions; one should not become intent on non-duality, for that would contradict the act of worship. || 39 ||
Now, he establishes the distinction by means of another method:
"The Lord is Mahādeva himself, while this bound soul (paśu) is dependent upon him;
how can the relationship of master and servant between these two be maintained if they are non-different? (40)

Mahādeva is the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), for according to the Smṛti he is "the Lord of the universe"; thus he is the Lord (pati), the Lord of the world. This individual soul (jīva) is the dependent (paśu) resting upon him. If there is non-difference—meaning the absence of distinction—between these two, the Lord and the soul in the form of Śiva and the Paśu, how can the relationship of master and servant be intended or made an object of desire? It cannot be so in any way whatsoever.
The meaning is that he is to be worshipped precisely by means of the distinction characterized by the relationship of master and servant. || 40 ||
To the question, "Until what limit does this state of duality persist? he says:
191) When the supreme reality is directly realized through awakening...
Then, for one devoid of knowledge, there is no attainment of non-duality anywhere. || 41 ||
When, through the awakening of hearing the Guru’s instructions and one's own direct experience, the supreme reality—
the great *liṅga* reality known as Paraśiva or Parabrahman— is directly realized and perceived as non-different from one's own self, as in the analogy of the tenth man, then...

The meaning is that for one devoid of knowledge—lacking the hearing of scripture, the instruction of a guru, and personal experience—the attainment of non-duality and the manifestation of non-duality do not exist at any time, in any place, or in any degree whatsoever. || 41 ||
Now, as to why non-duality is not established for one who performs ritual actions, he says:
"Because difference is the cause of ritual action, worldly activity proceeds;
one who is engaged in rituals such as the worship of symbols cannot practice non-duality. (42)

The conventional practice of duality (*bhedavyavahāra*)—specifically the practice of the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśvarabheda*)—proceeds from the cause of karma, as it is motivated by ritual actions such as the worship of Śiva. Therefore, one who is devoted to rituals such as the worship of the Śiva-linga and the recitation of mantras (*japa*) should not practice non-duality (*advaita*). Consequently, for one devoted to rituals such as the worship of the linga...
The meaning is that there is no manifestation of the realization of non-duality. || 42 ||
Now he concludes the point already stated:
"The practice of worship and so forth always exists by relying on duality;
therefore, one intent on the worship of the *liṅga* would not be devoted to non-duality. (43)
One devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* who is a *vīra-māheśvara* should not be, nor should he become, attached to non-duality (*advaita*); this is the meaning. || 43 ||
Thus ends the section on the refutation of non-duality (advaita).
Now begins the section on the refutation of invocation.
Next, having refuted non-duality for the purpose of worshipping the Śiva-liṅga, there is the Māheśvara who accepts duality (dvaita).
Just as a Śaiva would not invoke Śiva into a Śivaliṅga for the sake of worship, [the author] states the point regarding the rejection of invocation (p.
One who is devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*, who is pure, and who rejects all [notions of] non-duality, should not invoke Śiva into his own chosen *liṅga* in the form of Śiva. (44)

The meaning is that one who is devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*— being intent on the adoration of the Śiva-liṅga, free from all dualism, and pure as a perpetually pure Vīra-Māheśvara— should not invoke that well-known Śiva into his own chosen *liṅga*, which already possesses the form of Śiva and is of the very nature of Śiva. || 44 ||
Now, he states the reason for this:
"When the Great Guru bestows the Liṅga conjoined with the Śiva-kalā, from that moment onwards Śiva resides therein; what need is there for invocation here? (45)
In this context, what is the purpose of invocation regarding the Śiva-liṅga? The meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever.
The remainder is clear. || 45 ||
Furthermore, he states another reason:

"Śiva is eternally present within the lingas that possess the creative impressions (saṃskāras). Therefore, no invocation should be performed there, as it would contradict the true nature of reality. (46)
The meaning is that a subsequent invocation contradicts the previous invocation, because it occurs immediately after the dismissal [of the former].
Now, he states that because invocation itself is impossible, dismissal is likewise non-existent:
"One should not perform invocation nor dismissal in one's own chosen *liṅga*;
for the firm conviction of the scripture is that one must always be devoted to the *liṅga*. (47)
This is clear. || 47 ||
Thus ends the section on the refutation of invocation (p.
Now begins the section on the refutation of the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti).
Now, having rejected the invocation based on the notion that the Śivaliṅga itself is Śiva,

and [having shown] that the state of possessing the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtitva) consisting of earth and the rest is impossible due to their difference, he demonstrates the point where the eight forms prescribed by that Māheśvara are refuted:
Just as the oneness of the self and Śiva is not accepted by those attached to ritual action, so too non-duality between Śiva and the elements, beginning with earth, is not desired [by them]. (48)

Just as the oneness— the identity— of the individual self and Śiva, that is, the embodied soul and the *liṅga*, is not accepted or approved by the Māheśvara who is attached to ritual action and devoted to practices such as the worship of Śiva (because the distinction between the object of worship and the worshipper is impossible),
so too is the non-duality or non-distinction of the earth and other elements from Śiva.
The intention is that [the self] is not accepted [as being distinct] among the eight forms beginning with earth, because the self has entered into them as well. || 48 ||

Now, to the objection that even non-difference between Śiva and the earth and other elements is not possible, he says: "The Lord's state of having the eight forms, beginning with the earth, is proclaimed;
this is by virtue of being their presiding deity, and not through direct identity. (49)

The state of possessing eight forms (aṣṭamūrtitva), as proclaimed in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad beginning with "He whose body is the earth" (BṛU 3.7.3) and ending with "He whose body is the self" (BṛU 3.7.23),
consists in being the eightfold form of earth and the rest by virtue of being their presiding deity.

As it is stated by the learned: "Since the scriptures declare that you, O Maheśvara, preside over the universe as the presiding deity of the eightfold forms beginning with Earth, they metaphorically attribute the nature of the universe to you.
Just as there is the conventional usage "she drinks from the breast" despite the difference between the breast and the milk, so too is this usage of non-difference.
May the eight forms of Hara protect you: the metaphorical, the direct,
the single nature, the two-fold heat, the two-fold cold, the two-fold that is neither hot nor cold,
and the two-fold intangible.
Thus, because they are distinct from one another, and because the relationship between the body and the embodied requires difference [as its constituent]. || 49 ||
194) Now, he states that their identity is impossible because of the relationship between cause and effect: "All this, beginning with earth, is the effect; the Great Lord is the agent."
This Maheśa is not directly [the creator] in this way, just as a potter [is not the direct cause of the form] in the case of clay. || 50 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the sense organs along with the elements are produced from Him; He is not a [mere] cause.

For the Śruti declares: "Śambhu, who is to be meditated upon, is the Cause in the midst of space. This is because the earth and other elements fall within the category of effects, whereas Śiva is of the nature of the Cause. And thus:

The meaning is that just as identity is impossible between a pot and the like—which are indicated by the word "clay"—and the potter, so too identity is impossible between the earth and other effects in their causal form and Śiva.
Now, one might ask: why is there not an absolute difference between the Lord and the earth and so forth, as there is between a pot and its maker? To this, he says:
For this manifold universe, beginning with the earth and ending with the Self, exists in eightfold form;
it is the body of the Lord, and this Self is the regulator of all principles (tattvas). || 51 ||

The entire phenomenal world, existing in eight forms—earth, water, fire, air, ether, moon, sun, and fire—is the body of the Lord, extending up to the Self (Ātman). This Lord is the meaning of "the Embodied One" (Śarīrī), being the controller of all principles (tattvas) and the Self who impels the body composed of all those principles. And thus:
The meaning is that there is a distinction [between the two] because the relationship of body and embodied being is absent between a jar and a potter. || 51 ||

To the question "In that case, what is non-difference?", he says: "There is neither non-difference nor a separate existence of the God who is the Self from this phenomenal world which constitutes His body. (52)

The meaning is that there is no difference, but rather non-difference, between this phenomenal world— which is perceived as being pointed out by the finger as "this"— and Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who constitutes its very body. Nevertheless,
for the God who is the self of all and whose body is the universe, there is no separate existence, because there is no mutual externality as there is between a jar and a cloth.
The meaning is that there is no fixed abode for Śiva because of his all-pervasiveness. || 52 ||
To the question, "In that case, how is there difference? he says:
"Because earth and the other elements are insentient, and because the self is ignorant."
It is not maintained that the omniscient Maheśvara possesses a manifold nature. || 53 ||

Because the earth and other elements are insentient (*jaḍatva*), and because the self—the sacrificer who maintains the *agnihotra*—is ignorant, meaning he possesses only limited knowledge; whereas because Maheśvara, Śiva, whose body is the universe characterized by the moving and the immobile, is omniscient. Thus, the identity of form—that is, the oneness of the form, the body, and the embodied—is not accepted.
It is not made the object of desire; therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed difference. || 53 ||

Now, to the question "Who is this person who possesses such knowledge of difference?", he says: "He who constantly contemplates Mahādeva as distinct from the eightfold form consisting of earth and the rest—he is the one who has dispelled the notion of the eightfold form. (54)
This is clear. || 54 ||
Thus, having established the section on the refutation of the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti),
now he elucidates the section on the refutation of the omnipresent [Lord],
and then the section on the refutation of the omnipresence that contradicts the Maheśvara’s abiding in the *liṅga*.
If Maheśa were omnipresent, his worship would occur everywhere; it would not be restricted to the linga alone. One who is devoted to that [linga] would not remember Śiva as being all-pervading. (55)

If Maheśvara were omnipresent, his worship would have to take place everywhere, not merely at the *liṅga*; therefore, the meaning is that one who is devoted solely to the *liṅga* should not meditate upon Śiva as being omnipresent. || 55 ||

(196) Now, if Śiva were not omnipresent, he would be limited; and since there is an abundance of devotees in the world, as well as a multiplicity of *iṣṭaliṅgas* associated with their respective bodies, [the question arises] regarding one particular location...

Since it is impossible for Śambhu to remain elsewhere once the entire burden of his body has come to rest, how can his presence be established in various locations? To this, he says: "Although all-pervading, Śambhu is especially established in his own support."
Therefore, turning away from anything else, one should worship Śiva in one's own chosen liṅga. || 56 ||

Although Śambhu is omnipresent and all-pervading, he resides especially—meaning with preeminence—in his own support, the liṅga which has become his own substratum. Therefore, the meaning is that being averse to other places, one should worship Śiva in one's own chosen liṅga. || 56 ||
[Objection: But how is it that Śiva, who is omnipresent, dwells specifically within this or that *liṅga*? To this he says:
"Although Śiva is omnipresent, he is manifested intensely in his own support (*svādhāra*), just as fire is perceived specifically within the interior of a *śamī* tree. (57)

Just as fire residing in a tree shines forth especially in a *śamī* tree, so too Śiva, although omnipresent, is manifested and revealed most intensely—that is, with great preeminence—in his own support, the *liṅga*. || 57 ||
Now, as to the question of why the Liṅga remains specifically here, he says:
"The omnipresence of Maheśvara is established by all the scriptures;
nevertheless, its presence here is superior for the purpose of worship by means of the *āśraya-liṅga*. (58)
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the forms of the Guru and the Carama are indicated. The remainder is clear. || 58 ||
Regarding this point, he introduces the very meaning of the Vedic scripture— *yā te rudra [yā te rudra śivā tanūraghorā'pāpakāśinī]* (Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā 16.2)— by way of a verse:
"O Rudra, you who are that auspicious form of yours which shines eternally."
The eternal Śruti declares: "She is non-terrible and does not cause sin. (59)

O Rudra, that body of yours which is the form of the Śiva-liṅga is auspicious (śivā), blessed (maṅgalā), non-terrible (aghorā), bestower of fearlessness (abhayaṅkarā), free from sin (apāpakāśī), and devoid of defects; you, being eternally connected to that liṅga, shine forever—thus says the eternal Veda, meaning it declares this. || 59 ||
Therefore, he says that one should worship only one’s chosen *liṅga*:
"Therefore, with every effort, the best of worshippers, turning away from all other places, should worship Mahādeva in his own chosen *liṅga*. (60)

Therefore, because it is established by the Śruti, Maheśvara is the supreme worshipper; the meaning is that, with every effort and turning away from all other places, one should worship Mahādeva in one's own chosen liṅga, or in a liṅga chosen as being connected to oneself. || 60 ||
Having understood this, he says that one who worships while [focusing] on their own chosen *liṅga* is indeed a remover of [the misconception of] omnipresence:
"Even though Śiva is omnipresent, one who is devoid of attachment everywhere, worshipping the Lord in his own chosen *liṅga*, is a remover of [the misconception of] omnipresence. (61)
This is clear. || 61 ||
Thus ends the section on the refutation of omnipresence;
now follows the section on Śiva being identical with the universe.
Furthermore, even though omnipresence has been rejected for the sake of Maheśvara’s worship, omnipresence [is asserted] by the force of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).

Just as it is accepted [as the locus], so too must its being composed of everything be accepted by the force of valid cognition; thus, he describes the state in which Śiva and the world are identical: "In the ritual of worship, because He is the object to be constrained, Śiva resides in the *liṅga* alone."
Even while worshipping, one should contemplate the omnipresence of the Divine.
Although Śiva is the controller of all, at the time of worship, because He is governed by His devotees (p.
198) and is dependent upon His devotees, the devotee, while worshipping Śiva who is present in the *liṅga* alone, [attains] the grace of the Lord...

One should contemplate the omnipresence of Śiva, who, abiding in the *liṅga*, is of the nature of light; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of his being limited, like a potter. || 62 ||
Thus, when the omnipresence of Śiva, the Self, is established, it follows from the scriptural passage, "From [the Self] ether was produced; from ether, air;
from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), that He is heard to be the non-different instrumental and material cause, as demonstrated through numerous analogies.

He establishes that Śiva is the essence of the universe: "Since this entire world of moving and non-moving things has arisen from Mahādeva, therefore it is not distinct from him, just as a jar and other such objects are not distinct from clay. (63)
The connection is "from Mahādeva"; the remainder is clear. || 63 ||
The world, which has arisen from the Śiva-principle, is not distinct from it; just as foam, waves, and bubbles do not differ from the ocean.
This is clear. || 64 ||
Just as cloth produced from threads is considered to be composed of threads, so too the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, having arisen from Śiva, is indeed Śiva himself. 65.
This is clear. || 65 ||
Now, one might object that the aforementioned analogy is flawed because clay and the like are subject to modification, whereas Śiva is changeless; to this he says:
"By the unfolding of his own power, Śiva exists as the soul of the universe."
Just as a cloth appears [small] due to its being folded, but [large] from its own unfolding. (66)

Just as a cloth appears through its contraction from a state of expansion—having attained identity with its own power of spreading—so too Śiva, existing as the self of the universe through the unfolding of his own power, appears; this is the meaning. || 66 ||
Now, one might object: "Just as even a cloth undergoes modification by means of its power of expansion, so too Śiva might be subject to modification by means of his own inherent power.
Anticipating this, the author presents another illustration and concludes the stated point:
Therefore, this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is composed of Śiva;
it appears as non-different from him, just as the state of being a snake [appears] in relation to a rope.

Just as a rope, by virtue of its inherent power of being long, circular, and wheat-colored, appears as a snake due to the absence of any actual transformation, so too Śiva, through his own inherent power of Māyā and in the absence of any modification,
appears as non-different from the universe; therefore, this entire universe of moving and unmoving things is composed of Śiva.
The meaning is that it is distinct from that. || 67 ||
Now, for the sake of strengthening [the argument], he provides many examples preceded by the cited illustration:
It appears as a snake in a rope, and as silver in mother-of-pearl; it appears as a thief in a post, and as water in a mirage. (68)
In Śiva, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss, who is devoid of the reality of duality, and who is like a city of Gandharvas in the sky, the universe shines forth. (69)

Just as the state of being a serpent exists in a rope through the potentiality of the color of wheat, just as the state of being silver exists in mother-of-pearl through the potentiality of whiteness,
just as the state of being a person exists in a post through the potentiality of height, just as the state of being water exists in a mirage through the potentiality of an excess of clarity,
and just as a city of Gandharvas appears in the sky through the power of time— so it is in that which is devoid of all mundane distinctions.

The meaning is that within Paraśiva-Brahman, whose nature is changeless and consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), the universe appears as non-different from it, due to the power of Māyā which manifests as the radiance of the power of self-reflection (vimarśaśakti) inherent therein. || 68-69 ||
to the objection that by these examples the universe might be merely apparent, he states another example:
"Just as a tree exists in the form of leaves, branches, and so forth..."
In the same way, the one Śiva shines forth in the form of the earth and other elements.

Just as a tree, by virtue of its temporal power and its freedom from modification, appears as characterized by the internal differentiation of its own leaves, flowers, and so forth— which are of a different nature [from the tree itself]— so too does Śiva alone, through the process of self-reflection, appear in the form of the earth and other elements, which are embraced through identity with the powers inherent within him.

The meaning is that it shines. In this regard, the distinction is as follows: through steadfastness (*dhṛti*) it is the earth; through compassion (*karuṇā*) it is water; through brilliance (*ujjvalatā*) it is fire;

through the vibration of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-spandana*) it is air; through the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*) it is space; and that which is characterized by the mind (*citta*) resulting from the contraction of consciousness (*citisaṅkoca*) is the individual soul (*jīva*).
Now, one might object: since a tree possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), whereas Śiva—who is ever-united with the light of existence (*sadābhāsa*)—is partless (*niravayavatva*).

One should not raise the objection: "Since the power inherent in that [Śiva] is non-different from Him, it too must be of that same nature; how then is its manifestation as the manifold world of parts possible? For, while the power is non-different from Śiva, it possesses the capacity to accomplish the seemingly impossible, according to the analogy of the serpent and its coils.

For it has been stated that this is possible because the power of Māyā, which constitutes its effects, possesses parts—just as in the case of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), which is an effect produced from atoms where distinctions are presented through the conceptualization of one's own autonomy; and also because of the Lord’s own declaration: "Pervading all this, I stand with one part, supporting the world" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.42).
Even in the form of empirical manifestation (*prātītika-prapañca*), it is Śiva alone who appears due to the diminution of His own power;

for one who asserts that there is no element of conjunction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver because they do not exist in relation to each other, even that [conjunction] must be admitted as a counter-correlate of negation and as being on an equal footing, since it is sublated in the subsequent moment.
The power [of manifestation] is based on its own diminution; thus, in brief, the entire universe is indeed composed of Śiva.
In reality, however, there is no sublation at all, because even the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell possesses the same ontological status as the cognition of a jar or a cloth.
Nor is there a sublation of the cognition of silver by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, as is the case with the cognitions of a jar and a cloth.

Because they differ in time and differ in object. Now, since it is impossible for two contradictory appearances— namely, "this is silver" and "this is not silver"— to both be valid with respect to a single substratum (*dharmin*),
the subsequent cognition of the absence of silver must [invalidate] the previously arisen cognition of silver.

If it is argued that sublation (*bādha*) is accepted [as a fact], we say no; for since cognitions are necessarily restricted to a duration of three moments, at the time when the cognition of the absence of silver exists, the cognition of silver is already non-existent. Furthermore, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator depends upon a mutual connection, according to the maxim of the staff and the vessel (*daṇḍabhāṇḍanyāya*).

Because cognitions, being qualities, lack mutual connection; therefore, since the opening and closing [of the eyes] must be accepted as being like the cognitions of a jar and a cloth, there is no sublation—this is the direction [of the argument]. || 70 ||
Thus [ends] the stage consisting of Śiva and the universe;
now follows the stage of the bodily liṅga of the devotee.

Now, even though Śiva is thus identical with the universe— He whose conduct transcends the synthesis of the meanings of the Vedic and Vedāntic scriptures, whose supreme bliss consists in the state of being a devotee, and who is accessible solely through the state of devotion.

In accordance with the statement from the *Yogajāgama*, "He manifests within the heart of the devotee," he establishes the section on the bodily signs (*liṅga*) of the devotee through seven aphorisms:
"Although Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, is the self of the entire universe..."
He shines forth especially within the lotus-heart of his devotees. || 71 ||

Śaṅkara, the creator of happiness, the Supreme Lord, though he is the self of the entire universe and consists of the phenomenal world in the form of existence and non-existence, shines forth preeminently— that is, he manifests with excellence— within the lotus of the heart, the heart-lotus, of his devotees. || 71 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
"He is especially established on Kailāsa, Mandara, the Himālaya, and the Golden Mountain (Kanakācala), as well as within the hearts of his devotees. (72)
Just as Śiva manifests specifically in these places, so too does he manifest in the hearts of his own devotees.
This is the meaning. || 72 ||
To the question, "How can the Supreme Lord, who is indeed unlimited, appear as if limited within the hearts of devotees?
he says:
"Just as the Universal Self, though all-pervading, exists as if limited within bodies."
In that same way, Śaṅkara always manifests among his own devotees.

The meaning is that although the Supreme Lord is the self of all, He manifests eternally among His own devotees in the same manner as He appears through the process of reflection within all bodies— characterized by gods, animals, and humans— which are distinguished by their respective diverse internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa). || 73 ||

Regarding this matter, he states a word containing authoritative evidence: "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which shines eternally among your [other forms], the eternal Śruti declares it to be 'non-terrible' (aghorā) and 'not appearing as evil' (apāpakāśī). (74)

O Rudra, that body of yours which is the form of the Śiva-liṅga—being non-terrible (aghorā), gentle (saumyā), free from sin (apāpakāśī), and devoid of defects—that very form of the liṅga shines eternally among your own devotees;
thus the eternal Veda declares it to be constant (sanātanī). This is the meaning. || 74 ||

Now, as to why [Śiva] does not appear to those other than the devotees of Śiva, he says: "In those who are pure, dispassionate, discerning, and great-souled—who bear the marks of Śiva—the All-Self Śiva abides. (75)

The meaning is that Śiva, the soul of all, dwells eternally among those who are pure and dispassionate, those who possess knowledge of the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*), and those who are the final embodiments; that is, among the discerning great souls such as the yogis Śuka and others, and among those who bear the insignia of Śiva— that is, those who wear only sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
The meaning is that it shines forth. || 75 ||
If this is so, one might ask: since they are common to all, what is the distinction among those who are devotees of Śiva? To this he says:
[It belongs] to those who are constantly endowed with contentment and whose karma has been shaken off by knowledge.
The Supreme Lord shines forth as the inner dweller within the devotees of Maheśvara. || 76 ||

The meaning is that, because their impurities have been shaken off by the knowledge of Śiva, He— residing within those Supreme Lords who experience the bliss of Śiva— shines with extreme clarity, just as a face or other object appears clearly upon a stainless mirror. || 76 ||

Now, he indicates the stage of the *prasādin* (one who has attained grace) which is about to be described: "Elsewhere than Śambhu, devoid of even mere attachment, with his inner self fixed upon his own chosen *liṅga*, and perceiving this entire universe as being of the nature of Śiva—he is a *māheśvara* who becomes a *prasādin*. (77)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Stages of the Māheśvara," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). 10.

Being devoid of even a mere trace of delight in any other deity besides Śambhu, the auspicious one, and being free from even a fraction of affection for them, this devotee of Maheśvara—possessing a restrained inner self, that is, one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is disciplined—regards this universe as "this," appearing as something to be pointed out by the finger. This universe... [is thus perceived].
The meaning is that by realizing, through examples such as those of the liberated soul whose nature is Śiva, that "all is composed of Śiva," one becomes gracious (śivaprasādī).
Regarding this, there is a Vedic scripture: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon; He is the maker of auspiciousness; abandon everything else. (77)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Stages of the Māheśvara," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 10.
The Eleventh Chapter. Now, having arrived at the place of Prasādi, Agastya said:
