O Leader of the Gaṇas, you have described the devotee of Maheśvara as one who possesses the dharma of being established in the liṅga and so forth; how then is he called "prasādī" (one who has received grace)? Tell me.
This is clear. || 1 ||
Reṇuka said:

One whose bonds of sin have been destroyed through the state of being established in the *liṅga* and so forth, and who possesses the yoga of mental serenity, is called "Prasādī" (the Serene One). || 2 ||

The meaning is that this devotee of Maheśvara, whose mass of sins has been destroyed through the thorough knowledge of and the practice of the stages beginning with the culmination of the aforementioned signs, is called "gracious" (prasādī) by virtue of his connection with the purity of mind. || 2 ||
Now, regarding what kind of place this is and of what nature it is, he says:
"The 'Place of Grace' (prasādisthala)—this indicates its majesty;
it is proclaimed to be sevenfold according to the internal divisions of the place. (3)

The meaning is that these seven types of "places of grace" (*prasādasthala*)—which correspond to the collection of right conducts (*sadācāra*) mentioned in the section on the devotees of Maheśvara—are proclaimed to be of seven kinds according to their internal subdivisions, serving to demonstrate the greatness of this [tradition]. || 3 ||
p. 205) Now, as to the question "How is that so?", he indicates it here:
first, the stage of the one who has been graced, and then the majesty of the Guru.
Then follows the praise of the linga, and then the respect for the mobile [form]. || 4 ||
Then the majesty of devotion, then the glorification of taking refuge,
and the majesty of Śiva’s grace— thus it consists of seven types.
The proclamation of refuge means the proclamation of its greatness; thus, the answer is that it is of seven kinds.
Now, regarding the statement "the characteristics of the aforementioned places are described in order," he says here:
"O Great Sage, I shall describe their characteristics in sequence.
This is clear.
Now, for by the serenity of the mind one destroys both good and evil karma;
with a serene self, established in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. (Maitreyī Upaniṣad 1.6)
Thus, following the *Maitreya-śruti*, he establishes the clarity of the mind arising from the grace of Śiva through twelve aphorisms:
"Purity of the mind is the mark; it is called clarity (*prasāda*)."
It is accomplished solely through the grace of Śiva in the form of the Liṅga.

The meaning is that the purity of the mind (*manas*)—the sign or mark of stainlessness—is called *prasāda* (serenity). This serenity, which consists of the mind’s stainlessness, is accomplished through the grace (*prasāda*) of Śiva, who is of the nature of the *liṅga*. || 6 ||

(206) Now, one might ask: what is this grace of Śiva (*śivaprasāda*) which serves as the cause for the clarity characterized by the purity of the mind? To this he says: "The substance that constitutes the grace of Śiva is that which has been offered to Śiva."
That offering of remains (nirmālya), however, is the cause of mental purity for the devotees of Śiva.

The substance that has been offered and dedicated to Śiva is "Śivaprasāda" (the grace of Śiva); the meaning is that its *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) becomes the cause for the purification of the mind of the specialized Śaivas, namely the Vīraśaivas. || 7 ||
Now, he describes the "one who possesses grace" (prasādī), who accepts such grace from Śiva:
"One who accepts the grace of Śiva, which is the cause of stainless knowledge for the sake of achieving serenity of mind, is called a 'prasādī'. (8)

Accepting the cause of knowledge— the cause of the knowledge of Śiva— which is the grace of Śiva, namely the *nirmālya* (the remains of offerings) in the form of the grace of the Śiva-liṅga, for the sake of attaining serenity of mind and for the sake of achieving purity of consciousness, this Vīramāheśvara is called a *prasādī*.
This is the meaning. || 8 ||

Therefore, based on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad scripture, "Through purity of food, there is purity of the principles" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2), he states that by consuming the pure nirmālya of Śiva, the devotee attains the clarity of mind through the purification of all the constituent principles (tattvas).
For it is taught that through the purification of food, the purification of all things occurs;
indeed, the mass of food that is thoroughly purified is offered to Śiva. (9)
Thus, eating at all times while being devoted to the *liṅga*, one attains incomparable serenity of mind, which is the cause of knowledge. || 10 ||

The knowers of the scriptures have declared that through the purification of food, there occurs the purification of the reality (tattva) for all living beings, as well as the purification of the body, the senses, and the manifold world (prapañca). Therefore, one who is intent upon the Liṅga should regard that very collection of food which has been offered to Śiva as pure.
The meaning is that one who eats at all times with a serene disposition attains incomparable mental clarity—the cause of auspicious knowledge—and the purity of mind. || 9-10 ||
Therefore, whatever substance is obtained that has been set aside for the sake of one's own enjoyment— all those things that are beneficial to oneself— [should be considered] as "offered to Śiva."
In accordance with the words of the *Śivarahasya*, it is said that one should eat after offering everything to Śiva:
"Whatever substance has been set aside for one's own enjoyment, having offered each of those to the Lord, one should eat for the sake of self-purification. (11)

The meaning is that one should consume those various things—restricted for one's own enjoyment, prepared, and properly acquired—after offering them to the Lord in the form of the Śivaliṅga, for the sake of self-purification, that is, for the purpose of purifying the mind. || 11 ||
Now, he demonstrates its greatness:
"Whatever has been graciously bestowed by the eternally perfected Lord, the Physician, for those afflicted by the disease of birth—by consuming that, each thing becomes an elixir against birth. (12)

That substance which has been enjoyed and graciously bestowed by the Supreme Lord, the eternal physician and perfected doctor for those diseased by birth and diseased by worldly existence—who is ever-present as the perfected one within the Śiva-liṅga—is a *rasāyana* (elixir) for birth; that is to say, it is an elixir for the disease of saṃsāra. || 12 ||
Then he states that it is also the cause of health and other benefits in this world:
"It is the cause of health for men, bestowing purity upon the internal organ;
it is the medicine that eradicates the great disease of the three-fold suffering. (13)
It brings clarity to knowledge, destroys calamities, is the gateway for the descent of wisdom, and is the cause for the eradication of delusion. (14)
The root of the perfection of dispassion, which increases great bliss, is difficult for those with sinful minds to attain, but easy for those of pure karma. (p. 208) 15.
Food accepted by Śiva, which is honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, as well as by ascetics such as Vasiṣṭha, should be accepted by those who desire spiritual perfection.
In this context, the word "that" (tat) is understood from the preceding verse. That substance of grace, being the cause of health for men,
bestows purity upon the internal organ and serves as the medicine for uprooting the great disease characterized by the threefold afflictions, such as those pertaining to the self.
It is the cause for the attainment of specific knowledge, the destroyer of calamities and artificial defects,

the gateway for the descent of the knowledge of Śiva, the cause for the eradication of ignorance, the fundamental cause of the wealth of dispassion, the illuminator of eternal bliss, and difficult to obtain even for the most sinful.

Such food and other offerings accepted by Śiva— the prasāda substances consisting of food and the like accepted by the Śivaliṅga— are easily obtained by those of meritorious soul, and have been made an object of affection by gods such as Brahmā and sages such as Vasiṣṭha.

They are to be sought by those who desire spiritual perfection (siddhi)— that is, those seeking the perfections characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation— here and in the hereafter, and by those who possess a spirit of grace (prasādins).
The meaning is that it must be accepted. || 13–16 ||
Furthermore, he states that by accepting this [offering], there is the destruction of all sins:
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water... (To be compared with: *patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ toyaṃ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati*).

"Therefore, I eat what is offered with devotion by one whose self is disciplined" (Bhagavad Gītā 9.26). Whatever is offered to Śiva, through the act of its acceptance, there shall be the destruction of all sins. (17)
The meaning is "whatever substance. The remainder is clear. || 17 ||
209) Then, having stated that the *prasāda* of the venerable Guru and Śiva-yogin is likewise to be accepted just like the *prasāda* of the Śiva-liṅga, he concludes the section on *prasāda*:
Just as food from Śiva’s grace is to be accepted by those devoted to the Liṅga, so too is the food from the grace of the Guru, and likewise that of the Śiva-yogins. 18.

The meaning is that just as food offered through grace (prasādānna) is to be accepted by those devoted to the *liṅga* who have attained serenity (*prasādin*), so too the food-grace (*annaprasāda*) of the venerable Guru and Śiva-yogins is to be accepted. || 18 ||
Thus concludes the section on Grace;
now follows the section on the Greatness of the Guru.
Next, he describes the section on the Greatness of the Guru, which is to be understood by one established in grace:
In this matter, the Guru alone is the cause of all accomplishments;
for Mahādeva is present in person in the form of the Guru.
In this world, the Guru alone is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*) characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*);

for there is nothing superior to the Guru, nothing superior to the Guru—according to the statement in the *Śivarahasya*. This means that the Supreme Lord himself stands present, manifest in the form of the Guru. (19)
Now, one might ask: for what purpose does Śiva, who is partless (*niṣkala*), manifest in the form of a teacher with parts (*sakala*)? To this he says:
"For Mahādeva, though partless and an ocean of eternal knowledge, becomes the benefactor of all by appearing in the form of a teacher with parts. (20)
The Supreme Lord, who is an eternal ocean of knowledge, though partless and without limbs, becomes possessed of parts by assuming the form of a Guru;
being thus characterized by hands, feet, and other features, he becomes the benefactor of all. The meaning is that he manifests for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world. || 20 ||
Therefore, he says that there is no difference between the Guru and Śiva:
"He who is Śiva is to be known as the Guru; he who is the Guru is remembered as Śiva."
A person of great intelligence should not make a distinction between these two when seeking the attainment of knowledge. || 21 ||
Since the guru is not distinct from Śiva by virtue of bestowing the knowledge that serves as the cause of liberation— otherwise,
the arising of such knowledge would be impossible— the meaning is that one with subtle vision should not, for that reason, make a distinction or difference between the two. || 21 ||

As it is stated in the Āgama: "Just as I am the teacher of all worlds together with Ambikā," one should worship the venerable Guru, who is equal to Śiva, without describing him as being like ordinary people; thus he says: "One should not say he is equal to others on account of the similarity of his hands, feet, and so forth."
The teacher, pure and abiding as the very form of Śiva, is the giver of knowledge. || 22 ||

One should not speak of the venerable Guru—who is pure, whose inner organ is stainless, who illumines the knowledge of Śiva, and who exists in the form of Umā and Maheśvara—as being similar to ordinary people by virtue of the equality of his hands, feet, and other limbs.
To the question, "What happens because of that? he says:
Through disrespect toward the teacher, the attainment of the highest good is obstructed;
therefore, for the sake of attaining the supreme goal, one should honor him with a concentrated mind.

By insulting the teacher or addressing him with the same speech used for common folk, the attainment of the highest good—characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation—is obstructed. Therefore, for the sake of attaining the supreme good and for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation, one should worship that venerable Guru while being composed and single-minded; this is the meaning.

Now, making manifest the meaning of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.23), "He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine, so for the Guru," he concludes the section on the greatness of the Guru:
For one devoid of devotion to the guru, devotion to Śiva does not arise;
therefore, as there is devotion to Śiva, so too should there be devotion to the guru. (24)
This is clear. || 24 ||
Thus concludes the section on the greatness of the Guru;
now, he describes the section on the greatness of the Liṅga,
and then the section on the greatness of the Liṅga as revealed by the grace of the Guru:
Through the power of the greatness of the Guru and by virtue of his own superior knowledge, the greatness of the Linga is also perceived as being the most excellent of all. || 25 ||

By means of the yoga of knowledge regarding the greatness of the Guru, and due to the excellence of one's own knowledge, even the greatness of the *liṅga*—that is, the Śiva-liṅga—is perceived as being supremely exalted; that is to say, it is understood [as such]. || 25 ||
(Description of the section on the majesty of the Liṅga)—
Now, since it is impossible to know the majesty of the Liṅga without knowing the Liṅga itself, by what has the nature of the Liṅga been made known? To this, he says:
That which is the consciousness-liṅga (bodhaliṅga) of Śiva, perceived by a mind awakened by the Guru—that alone is to be known as the Liṅga of Śaṅkara, the cause of all. (26)

That which is Śiva’s *bodhaliṅga*, the *liṅga* consisting of consciousness—that is the *liṅga* of Śaṅkara, the cause of all, the cause of the entire universe including Viṣṇu and the others; it is to be known, that is, fit to be known, only by one whose mind has been awakened by the Guru.
The meaning is that it is made known by the Guru alone. || 26 ||
Now, as to what that is like, he says:
"The supreme, pure, stainless Liṅga is the eternal Brahman;
it is designated as Śiva, consisting of pure consciousness, ever-blissful, and unrestrained. (27)
The cause of all worlds and even the cause of the Vedas;
the fulfillment of every reality and the deliverance from the ocean of birth. (28)
How can that which consists of light, which is indefinable, and which resides within the self of yogis, be understood in this world without the compassion of a great teacher? (29)
Here, by the phrase "the filling of all reality," it is stated that through the single flavor of one's own self— according to the analogy of the essence of the *śikhaṇḍi*-egg—

the state of consisting of the entirely full universe is expressed. For yogis, that which is indescribable by the practitioners of Śiva-yoga, which abides within the self in its own essential nature, is the light-filled, invisible *liṅga* that blazes like a pillar.

According to the *Yājñavalkya-śruti*, the Great Liṅga known as Paraśiva—the Supreme Brahman—is self-luminous, being inaccessible through any means of knowledge other than itself. Furthermore, there is the statement in the *Śivarahasya*: "The knowledge of That must be learned from a true Guru; it cannot be attained otherwise, even by millions of scriptures. Thus, in this world, [this realization] is not possible without the compassion of a great Guru.
How, in what manner, is it known? The meaning is that it cannot be known by any manner whatsoever.
The remainder is clear. || 27-29 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if it is impossible for people like us to understand [the truth] without the compassion of a guru, since Brahmā and others are omniscient, they have no need for such assistance; how then is the stated point established?
To this, it is said: "Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, plunged into the earth; Brahmā flew up to heaven, and the vulture quickly [ascended]."
He establishes the stated meaning according to the intention expressed in the *Liṅgasūtra*:
"The Liṅga consisting of light, which was previously [manifested] by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, was beyond limitation; by whom could it be limited? (30)

The great Śiva-liṅga, which is of the nature of light and composed of light, was previously unascertainable and unfit to be known even by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; by whom, then, can it be fully defined? The meaning is: by whom is it truly understood? || 30 ||
Now, as to the question "What is the nature of this Liṅga that is inaccessible even to Brahmā and others?", he says:
"What is the use of saying much more here? The Liṅga is the eternal Brahman, wherein yogins, freed from the bonds of fetters, are absorbed. (31)
What is the use of speaking much on this matter? The eternal Brahman alone is the *liṅga* that serves as the cause for the dissolution of the universe;
within that *śivaliṅga*, which is the Self of the Supreme Brahman, yogins such as Sanaka and others have their bonds of bondage released.
The meaning is that, having been released from the bonds of the five afflictions beginning with ignorance, they dissolve, which is to say, they attain identity [with Him]. || 31 ||
Now, if Brahman alone is the *liṅga*, what is its pedestal? To this he says:
"The supreme Śakti is the pedestal; the *liṅga* is Paraśiva himself.
The union of Śiva and Śakti—that is called the universal *liṅga*. (32)

Based on the statement in the Śivāgama, "The seat (pīṭha) consists of the power of action (kriyāśakti) belonging to the Lord whose nature is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti)," the supreme power, the most excellent power of action, is the seat; and the Supreme Śiva, the Supreme Lord whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa), is the linga itself. This is the union of Śiva and Śakti.
The universe is like that linga which possesses the union of Śiva and Śakti;
do not see the world as marked with the thunderbolt, the wheel, or the lotus, nor as marked by the phallus—rather, see it as marked by the yoni (bhaga).
The universe, through its organs of knowledge and action, has the form of the linga consisting of consciousness and activity.
Thus, according to the statement in the Purāṇa, the meaning is that it is called the form of the entire universe. || 32 ||
Now, he states that Brahmā and the others, having worshipped such a *liṅga*, attained great sovereignty:
"All the gods beginning with Brahmā, and the sages beginning with Śaunaka..."
By the mere worship of the Śiva-liṅga, they shall each attain their respective station.

Regarding this, the Ṛgveda Śruti states: "O Rudra, for your glory the Maruts have cleansed that which is your beautiful and wondrous birth, even that supreme station of Viṣṇu which has been established" (Ṛgveda 5.3.3). This is the meaning:
O Rudra, the Maruts—the gods such as Brahmā and others—for the sake of the glory of Viṣṇu’s station, the abode such as Vaikuṇṭha and so forth...

Having placed in their minds a beautiful, captivating, and wonderful simile as an illustration, they worshipped— that is, they honored— the *liṅga*, which is the source of manifestation for all beings.
Through the greatness of worshipping the *liṅga* of Śiva, Viṣṇu attained abodes such as Vaikuṇṭha and great sovereign power.
Taking "he obtained" as the illustrative example, it means that all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, worshipped the Śivaliṅga for the sake of prosperity. || 33 ||
(214) Now, one might ask: "Since Śiva also possesses great sovereignty, such as being superior to the universe, did he acquire this through the worship of someone else? To this, [the author] says:
The eternal Śruti declares that the sovereignty over the universe belongs to the Lord in his Liṅga form, arising from his own nature, and that he has no likeness among other gods. 34.
"Rudra, the lord of all, the great seer, generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.4),

and "Neither his equal nor his superior is seen" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8). According to these Śvetāśvatara scriptural passages, there is no similarity between the Supreme Lord— who is the Īśa in the form of the *liṅga*— and any other deity.

The meaning is that the eternal Śruti declares that His status as the Lord of the universe—the quality of being the regulator of the manifold world of moving and non-moving beings—is innate and established by itself. || 34 ||
Thus ends the section on the greatness of the *liṅga*;
now follows the section on the greatness of the *jaṅgama* (the embodied manifestation).
Next, he elucidates the section on the *jaṅgama*, which is to be realized through the greatness of the Guru-liṅga:

Due to the attainment of the majesty and perfection of the *liṅga* mounted by the Guru and the disciple, everything is said to possess the superiority of the mobile [form] through the realization of the nature of consciousness. (35)

Based on the Vedic scripture, "The teacher is the prior form, the disciple is the subsequent form, and knowledge is the junction" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1), the excellence of the Śiva-liṅga situated between the guru and the disciple is such that the entire phenomenal universe is known through the realization of its nature as consciousness, and through the realization of it as the activity of consciousness; thus, the superiority of the mobile [the living being] is declared.

The meaning is that when the teacher and the disciple, through the cultivation of identity (*tādātmya-bhāvanā*) regarding their desired objects, vital breaths, and states of being, attain the perfection of the greatness of the installed *liṅga*, the very realization that the entire universe consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti constitutes the superiority of the "mobile" [liṅga]. || 35 ||
Now, as to who those "mobile" ones are, he says:
"But those who, through their excellence, know Śiva, the illuminator of the universe...
But by virtue of their own essential nature, they are proclaimed as "mobile" (jaṅgama). || 36 ||
According to the Śruti text, "By His light all this shines" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14), Śiva— who is the illuminator of the universe through His own powers of consciousness and action—
is pre-eminently so, because He is eternal, whereas the objects denoted by the words "all" and "not-all" have entered the sphere of Māyā’s effects.

Because this [nature] consists of the eternal qualities of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*), otherwise—due to the absence of knowledge regarding its own object—the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatva*) would follow, like the luminosity of a crystal and such;
for these two are the innate nature (*nijasvabhāva*) of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is common to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Thus, by itself...
The meaning is that those mobile beings know [the object] as their own essential nature through a firm conviction that it is not distinct from themselves.
Now, he establishes the greatness of the *jaṅgama* (the living devotee) who is renowned as a Śiva-yogin through five aphorisms:

"Those who, by means of Śiva-yoga, perceive the web of the universe as being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), and whose contact with impurity has been shaken off—they are remembered as Śiva-yogins. (37)

As for those who are moving deities, because everything [becomes] subject to conceptualization as being external to consciousness in the absence of a relation with Śiva— due to the yoga of Śiva with the universe— a relation with Śiva must indeed be accepted. Furthermore,
that [relation] is not of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since conjunction presupposes action and is only possible between two things situated in different locations.

Because it has been established that, due to the absence of any region external to Brahman, [the Self] consists of identity alone, those who see and know it as "of the nature of consciousness" (cidrūpa) and "having the nature of conscious activity" (citkriyāsvarūpa) are called Śiva-yogins— meaning they are those whose contact with impurity has been shaken off, having emerged from the connection with the impurities such as āṇava-mala. || 37 ||
Those who possess the knowledge of Śiva, which is the cause for utterly destroying the darkness of terrible saṃsāra, are considered Śiva-yogins. || 38 ||
The meaning is that those who possess the supreme knowledge of Śiva, which dispels the terrifying darkness of saṃsāra, are considered and remembered as Śivayogins. || 38 ||
Now, as to what they are like and how they abide, he says:
216) "They have conquered desire, they have conquered anger, and they have severed the knot of delusion."
The virtuous Śiva-yogins regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal. || 39 ||
Equal toward enemy and friend, having directly realized the Self as Śiva, free from desire and devoid of ego, the Śiva-yogins abide thus. (40)
This is clear. || 39-40 ||
Those who are endowed with the knowledge characterized as described above are indeed Śiva himself; thus he says:
"Knowledge of Śiva is indeed difficult to attain, and meditation on Śiva is difficult to attain.
Those who possess both of these are truly of the nature of Śiva himself. (41)

Knowledge of Śiva, knowledge of the preeminence of Śiva, contemplation of Śiva, and the realization through the aforementioned reasonings that one is oneself Śiva—these are difficult to attain. The meaning is that those who possess these two are the very embodiment of Śiva.
Furthermore, he describes their greatness with two verses:
"Wherever the dust from the tips of the feet of the Śiva-yogins falls, that very place becomes a meritorious abode, purifying even for householders. (42)
The sight of Śiva-yogins brings about all accomplishments for men;
their touch pacifies sin, and worshiping them is the means to liberation. (43)

The meaning is "of the Śiva-yogins," that is, of the wandering deities (*jaṅgamadeva*). The meaning is "of householders," that is, of those living as family-men (*gṛhamedhin*). "Puṇya" means a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); "pāvana" means purifying (*pavitra*).
The remainder is clear. (42–43)
Now, he states that through such contact with yogins of Śiva who are like this, all desired aims are accomplished:
"For the great ones who know the intent of Śiva and who rejoice [in it]...
Or rather, what fruit could not be accomplished through association with the yogins of Śiva? (44)

Through association with great and virtuous persons—Śiva-yogins who are mobile deities (jaṅgamadevas), who understand the intent of the Śivarahasya, and who rejoice in the bliss of Śiva—what fruit would not be accomplished? The meaning is that everything is accomplished. || 44 ||
Thus ends the section on the greatness of the *jaṅgama* (the moving [deity]);
now follows the section on the greatness of the devotee (*bhakta*).
Next, the greatness of the devotee who is devoted to the greatness of the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama* is presented in twelve aphorisms (*sūtras*).
He explains:
"By describing the greatness of the Guru’s insignia (liṅga) and of the Śiva-yogins, the greatness of the devotee is established; nevertheless, this [Guru] is also praised. (45)

Since devotion is practiced toward the Guru, the Liṅga, and the mobile [deities] preceded by such knowledge of their majesty, the majesty of the devotee is established. In the same way, he is praised in the scripture;
that is to say, he is described as being preeminent. || 45 ||

Now, regarding the question "Who are the devotees?", he describes the nature of a devotee in accordance with the meaning of the Vedic scripture: "Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs through action": those who worship Mahādeva, the supreme self, the imperishable.
Those who [serve] through action, mind, and speech are proclaimed as devotees. || 46 ||

The meaning is that those who worship Mahādeva, the Supreme Self in the form of the *liṅga*, through physical action consisting of worship with both hands, through mental action consisting of meditation on the form of Śiva, and through vocal action consisting of hymns of praise— they are called devotees (*bhakta*). || 46 ||
To the question of whether there is any distinction of caste regarding devotion to Śiva, he says here (p.
"For devotion to Śiva, which carries one across the fear of saṃsāra, is indeed difficult to attain."
Wherever she is present in person, he is proclaimed as a true devotee. || 47 ||
This is clear. || 47 ||
Therefore, he says that for people tormented by birth and death, there is no need for any virtuous deed other than devotion to Śiva:
"What is the use of the Vedas? What is the use of those scriptures? What is the use of sacrifices? What is the use of austerities and vows?"
If embodied beings who are afflicted by the disease of birth lack devotion to Śaṅkara, [there is no remedy]. (48)
The meaning is: by means of the scriptures that follow the sense of the Vedas, such as the Śiva-Āgamas, the Sūtras, the Purāṇas, and so forth. The remainder is clear. || 48 ||
Now, he states with the aid of an illustration that virtuous action performed apart from devotion to Śiva is fruitless or even yields contrary results:
"Even the well-performed deed of one devoid of devotion to Śiva is fruitless."
And even for a skillful person, there may be a contrary result in a great sacrifice.
It would mean "it was not. || 49 ||
(p. 219) Now, [the author] states, by means of an illustration, that even an evil deed becomes a virtuous deed through devotion to Śiva:
"Even one who has committed extremely sinful deeds is purified through devotion to Śiva;
just as in ancient times Caṇḍa, though a slayer of his father, became Śiva himself through devotion. (50)
Śiva is the lord of the hosts of Śiva; this is the meaning. The rest is clear. || 50 ||
If this is so, one might ask whether devotees of Śiva have a connection with merit and demerit or not; to this he says:
"Indeed, for the devotee of Śiva there is neither good nor evil action;
for those devoid of devotion to Śiva, there is the binding of the fetters of karma. (51)
This is clear. || 51 ||

To explain how this is so, he states it by means of two sūtras preceded by an illustration: "For living beings who have taken refuge in Śiva, there is no connection with karma. How could horses [fear] the darkness of the Lord of Day? (52)

Just as the Sun, the Lord of Day, has no fear caused by darkness, so too for the devotees of Śiva there is no connection—that is, no association—with action consisting of merit and demerit; this is the meaning. || 52 ||
It is not possible to restrain those devoted to Śiva who are free from all fetters;
how could a chain made of lotus fibers bind intoxicated elephants? (53)

Since the three impurities, beginning with *āṇava*, have been removed by the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śiva, it is neither capable nor able to restrain the actions of those devotees of Śiva who are thus unshackled. The illustration for this is as follows: just as a chain made of lotus fibers cannot restrain an intoxicated elephant, so it is here. || 53 ||
Therefore, he states that only a devotee of Śiva is worthy of worship: "Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra."
Or even an outcaste who is a devotee of Śiva—he indeed is to be honored like Śiva himself. (54)
This is clear. || 54 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since Śūdras and others are inferior in comparison to Brāhmaṇas and the like, how can they possess equality with them? To this, he says:
"In the immersion of devotion to Śiva, where is the conceptualization of caste?"
When the fuel has been consumed by the fire, what distinction can possibly be proclaimed? || 55 ||
This is clear. || 55 ||
Therefore, having stated that only those devoted to Śiva are the lords of the Gaṇas, he concludes the majesty of devotion:
"Those in this world who are pure, joined with self-restraint, and whose acquisition of fruits is offered to Śiva, and who worship Śiva—they are to be known as the lords of the Gaṇas. (56)
Those who are pure, purified by initiation, perfected in their observances, observers of the Śiva-vow,

who have dedicated the fruits of their actions to Śiva and the arrival of the fruits of their merit and demerit to Him— being such, they worship the Śiva-liṅga in this world; for one who is not Śiva, the practice of Śiva-worship is not possible even in ten million aeons, nor is one who is not Rudra [fit for it].
The meaning is that by such statements as "one should worship Rudra," they are to be understood as the lords of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvaras) and as the Rudras. || 56 ||
Thus ends the section on the majesty of devotion;
now follows the section on the greatness of seeking refuge.
This concerns one who, having understood that the Guru, the *liṅga*, and so forth exist, takes refuge in Śiva alone as the sole protector.
221) He establishes the greatness of refuge: "One who is joined with the search for and the awakening to the majesty of the Guru, the Liṅga, and so forth..."
The attainment of Śiva as the universal self is said to be the place of refuge. || 57 ||

The meaning is that, through the connection of seeking knowledge regarding the greatness of the Guru, the Liṅga, Śiva, the Yogins, and the devotees of Śiva, one attains Śiva in every way and by various means; this state of total surrender, based on the conviction that Śiva alone is the protector, is called the "place of refuge. || 57 ||
Now, he clarifies that very point:
"Having considered all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as possessing only natural power, one seeks refuge in Śiva; that is declared [to be the true refuge]. (58)

Based on the Vedic scripture, "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the bringer of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else," that which one attains— meaning one takes refuge in Śiva by way of surrender— after setting aside (muktvā) the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu who possess natural majesty and the prosperity born of Prakṛti, is declared to be "Śaraṇa," the place of refuge.
The meaning is that it has been explained. || 58 ||
Now, he clarifies the true nature of one who has come for refuge:
"He who is the refuge of all beings, the benefactor Śaṅkara, the moon-crested Lord—having surrendered to him with one's whole being, one is called 'one who has come for refuge' (śaraṇāgataḥ). (59)

Śaṅkara, whose crest is the moon, is the Supreme Lord; he is the refuge for all beings, meaning he is capable of protecting all living creatures. Having approached him with one’s whole being and in every way, thinking "He will protect me," one is said to be a *prapanna*, that is, one who has come for refuge. This is the meaning. || 59 ||

Now, he describes the nature of one who seeks refuge: "One who has abandoned attachment to enjoyments, who is free from longing for other deities, and who prays to Śiva for liberation, is proclaimed as a seeker of refuge. (60)

One who has abandoned attachment to enjoyments and is dispassionate toward the positions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, seeking liberation from Śiva, is "sung"— that is, described— as one who "seeks refuge. || 60 ||
Thus, he says that for those who have taken refuge in Śiva, there may not even be any need for virtuous action:
"For those who have taken refuge in Mahādeva through the actions of mind, speech, and body—what need have they for the multitude of ritual acts or for offerings to other deities? (61)

For those who have taken refuge in Mahādeva Śiva through the actions of mind, speech, and body— by means of meditation, praise, and acts of worship— with what purpose would there be for them in the collection of ritual acts such as sacrifices, or in the propitiation of the gods and other deities? Indeed, there would be no purpose whatsoever.
The meaning is that it does not exist. || 61 ||
To the question "Why?", he explains that point with two sūtras:
"The fruit of all sacrifices results in the perishable heaven;
however, one who has taken refuge in the Supreme Lord attains an imperishable fruit. (62)
The "imperishable fruit" means liberation; the rest is clear. || 62 ||

To the question "How so for sinners?", he says: "What might not be attained even by embodied beings who are sinners through surrender (prapatti) to Bhava, the Supreme Self, who is the wish-granting tree (pārijāta) for those who have sought refuge? (63)

By taking refuge in Śiva, the Supreme Self who is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who have come for shelter, through such surrender as his protector—what could not be achieved even by sinful living beings? The meaning is that everything would indeed be attained. || 63 ||
Therefore, he says that only those who have surrendered to Śiva are the most excellent: "For those who have surrendered to Mahādeva and whose inner selves are fully ripened..."
Birth alone is true birth for them, and not so for others who are attached to futile existence.
For those men whose inner faculties are fully ripened, having taken refuge in Mahādeva, birth itself is the fruit of birth;
for those who do not take refuge and merely endure the process of being born, birth is not truly birth at all—it is not even "birth" in the meaningful sense. This is the meaning. || 64 ||
Now he clarifies that very point:
"Having obtained a human birth, which is difficult to attain and the means for attaining knowledge, those who do not know the Lord of Gods—their own self is rendered useless. (65)

Having obtained a human birth—a rare attainment that serves as a means for knowledge and bestows self-knowledge—those who do not know Paraśiva, the Lord of Gods, their very soul, their individual life-force (*jīva*), is useless; the meaning is that it is purposeless. || 65 ||
Then, having elucidated the greatness of seeking refuge according to the *Sūta-saṃhitā*— that "the family is purified" and "the mother has fulfilled her purpose"— he concludes that section:
"For that family is ever pure, and his life is fruitful."
And whose mind is directly dissolved in Śiva, not turned toward external objects. || 66 ||

The family of one whose mind is always directly upon the Śivaliṅga—dissolved in such a way that it does not turn outward, having reached a state of special absorption—is pure; the meaning is that his life and very existence are fruitful. || 66 ||
Thus ends the section on the greatness of refuge;
now follows the section on the greatness of grace (prasāda),
since the abiding experience of the greatness of the previously mentioned Guru, the Liṅga, and so forth, is obtainable through the grace of Śiva.
It describes the greatness of that grace:
"The state of abiding in the experience of the specific majesty of the Guru, the *liṅga*, and so forth. (p. 224)
Since it occurs through the grace of Śiva, its greatness is now described.

Because, through the grace of Śiva, there arises from this cause a state of abiding in the specific experience of the greatness of taking refuge in Śiva— the devotees of Śiva who are the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Embodied (jaṅgama)— for that reason, the majesty, that is, the greatness, of this grace of Śiva is said, meaning it is described. || 67 ||
Now, one might ask: how is it that the grace of Śiva becomes the cause for the persistence of the experience of the specific greatness of the Guru, the Liṅga, and so forth? To this, he says:
"For those who are always devoted solely to the Liṅga and who are intent upon the worship of the Guru..."
Maheśvara is pleased with those who have sought refuge and are purified.
This is clear. || 68 ||
Regarding what that grace of Śiva is like and what happens by means of it, he says:
"Even the grace of Maheśa is proclaimed to be difficult to attain, by which the cessation of the torment of terrible saṃsāra is produced. (69)

For others who do not bear the [Śiva] insignia, this is difficult to obtain. By that grace of Śiva, the cessation of the threefold worldly afflictions (tāpa) which cause fear arises; such is the meaning. || 69 ||

Now, an objection is raised: since the scripture states, "The Brahmins seek to know that very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22], it is heard that sacrifices and the like are means for attaining realization; therefore, since the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra occurs by that alone, what [is the need for further effort]?

Regarding the phrase "by the grace of Maheśvara," it is said: Sacrifices, austerities, the recitation of mantras, meditation, and awakening are proclaimed as means for the grace of Maheśvara; of this there is no doubt. (70)
In this context, *cintā* is meditation (*dhyāna*), and *prabodhana* is the knowledge of the preeminence of Śiva. The remainder is clear. || 70 ||
(225) Now, one might object: "Since liberation is rooted in devotion, what is the need for divine grace? To this he replies:
"For all [beings], devotion is invariably rooted in grace."
For one who is devoid of Śiva’s grace, even devotion does not attain perfection. || 71 ||

The devotion of all people, which is unfailing and directed toward no other, has its root in grace; the meaning is that for one devoid of Śiva’s grace, devotion itself cannot be accomplished. || 71 ||
Therefore—
whether situated in the womb, being born, or already born, whether a Brāhmaṇa or even an outcaste—
one may be liberated provided there is the grace of Śaṅkara.
This is clear. || 72 ||
Then, he states that even Brahmā and the others are eternally perfected solely through the grace of Śiva:
"All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, who dwell in their respective abodes, indeed become eternally perfected through the grace of the Supreme Lord. (73)
This is clear. || 73 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the cessation of the sufferings of saṃsāra occurs through the very knowledge that everything has Śiva as its essence, what is the use of his grace?
To this, [the author replies]: "The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, the impeller, and the instruments of enjoyment..."
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, everything shines as consisting of Śiva.
According to this statement from the Sūta-saṃhitā, he says:
"When the grace of Śambhu has been attained—the cause of supreme bliss—then the entire universe is seen as consisting of Śiva; there is no doubt in this matter. (74)
This is clear. || 74 ||
226) Now, he explains the greatness of Śiva’s grace once more with two aphorisms: "Karma alone is the cause for being driven around the wheel of saṃsāra."
Without the grace of Śambhu, no one at all can turn back [from saṃsāra]. || 75 ||

Karma alone is the cause that sustains the wheel of saṃsāra; it is not destroyed by sacrifices and the like, because since those too are of the nature of karma, they only further nourish it. Therefore, the sense is that for no one is karma destroyed without the grace of Śiva. || 75 ||
What is the use of saying more here? In the three worlds, there is nothing equal to or even superior to the grace of the Great Lord.
This is clear. || 76 ||
When grace from Śiva has been attained by one who possesses yoga,
everything shines as being of one essence with Śiva;
liberated from his own karma, his self is permeated by Śiva.
He is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*. || 77 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Sevenfold Stages of the Gracious One," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brahmin of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). 11.

When Śiva’s grace— which partakes in yoga, which is devoid of the loss or increase of its own nature, and which consists in a state of equilibrium with the Śiva of the same genus— is attained, the entire universe, the whole world, shines forth as having Śiva alone as its self, through non-difference from Śiva. Therefore, one whose self is permeated by Śiva [perceives] through non-difference from Śiva.

Possessing the nature of that which has been cultivated, he is gracious and liberated from his own karma; because even karma, by virtue of being identical with Śiva, does not act as an obstacle due to its being one's own true nature, he—being completely freed from the bonds of his own karma—is called, or designated, a "Prāṇaliṅgin. This is the meaning. || 77 ||

Thus ends [the section] in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences (*padavākyapramāṇa*).
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Sevenfold Application of the Serene," is concluded. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter:
Now, regarding the site of Prāṇaliṅgin;
Agastya said:
He is known as a devotee, a follower of Maheśvara, and one who has attained grace;
how is it that he alone is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*? (1)

The meaning of the question is as follows: it has been taught that there is only one devotee of Maheśvara, known as the Prasādin; and how, or by what manner, is this person called a Prāṇaliṅgin? || 1 ||
Śrī Renuka said:
"He is celebrated as a devotee of Maheśvara and as one who has attained grace; through the application of the primacy of action, the yoga of knowledge is taught to him. (2)

This very person, having attained initiation into the Śiva-liṅga through the yoga of the predominance of ritual action— that is, through the yoga characterized by the performance of rites prescribed in the Karma-kāṇḍa— is celebrated as a *bhakta*, a *māheśvara*, and a *prasādī*. For one who is thus endowed with these three forms, there is the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*).

The yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) as taught in the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) is now being described. The meaning is that by means of this yoga of knowledge, one becomes purified and is thus called a "prāṇaliṅgin" (one whose liṅga is the vital breath). || 2 ||
Now, as for the question "Who is this Prāṇaliṅgin?", [it is said]:
The vital breath (prāṇa) consists of all the principles (tattvas); Śiva consists of all knowledge.
This very union of these two is here called the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Thus, one who possesses the *prāṇaliṅga* in the form described in the *Vīrāgama* is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*. He states:
"The *liṅga* is Brahman, whose nature is consciousness; its power (*śakti*) has the form of *prāṇa*.
One who possesses the realization of the *liṅga* in that form is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*. (3)
Brahman itself, whose nature is consciousness, is the Śivaliṅga; its Power (Śakti) is the Power of the Śivaliṅga-pīṭha,

which consists of vital breath (prāṇa), possessing the nature of the vital breath that is the Self of the Praṇava, because the Praṇava is composed of the Bindu characterized by the latent impressions of the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, because it is constituted by the power of *unmeṣa* (expansion), characterized by the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between consciousness (*cit*) and activity (*kriyā*), it is said to consist of all the *tattvas*.
The meaning is that one who possesses the knowledge of the *liṅga* of that nature—one who has the cognition of the *liṅga* in its specific form—is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*. || 3 ||
Now, [the author] asks: "Are there also different stages for this? To this he says:
"And this stage of the Prāṇaliṅgin is endowed with five stages:
first the stage of the Prāṇaliṅgin, and after that the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga. (4)

Then there is the stage of the absorption of Śiva-yoga, followed by the stage of the inherent nature of the Liṅga, and then the stage of the Liṅgin who possesses the limbs; thus the distinction among these is stated in sequence.
This is clear. || 4-5 ||

Now, they say that the mark of the mind is within the vital breaths (prāṇas), according to the scriptural testimony of the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Kaṭhavallī*: "It raises the prāṇa upward and casts down the apāna; the Viśvedevas worship the dwarf seated in the middle. [Kaṭhopaniṣad 2.6.3]

He explains the *prāṇaliṅgisthala* with five aphorisms: "Arising from the center of the *kanda* due to the union of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, that is declared as the *prāṇaliṅga* by those who restrain *prāṇa* and *apāna*. (6)
Through the union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* according to the instruction of the teacher, when the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds come into contact,
that light which arises— that is, becomes manifest— from the center of the *kanda*, from the center of the *nābhi-kanda*, is [the one described].
That light is called the "liṅga of the vital breath" (prāṇaliṅga) by the Śiva-yogins who possess the restraint of the prāṇa and apāna winds; this is the meaning of what has been stated. || 6 ||
To the question "By whom has this been known?", he says:
"Where the vital breath (prāṇa) goes to its dissolution, like frost in the sun—that is designated as the 'liṅga of the vital breath' (prāṇaliṅga); one who bears it shall have that very form. (7)

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), dissolves into that Śiva-liṅga composed of the Supreme Brahman—just as frost dissolves into the sun; therefore, it is designated and taught as the "vital-breath liṅga" (*prāṇaliṅga*).

The meaning is that one who bears it, who contemplates it, who takes its form, and whose very nature becomes identical with it, shall become such [a Śiva]. This is because it is untouched by space, time, and other limiting conditions.
The meaning is that consciousness itself, appearing as a generic form (sāmānyākāra) and as the "I-sense" (ahantā), is the vital-organ (prāṇaliṅga). || 7 ||
Now, regarding the question of for whom that sign (liṅga) manifests, he says:
For the wise who are disciplined in yoga, it flashes within like a lamp;
the sign of the Supreme Brahman, whose form is consciousness, is not perceived by the ignorant. (8)
The vibration in the form of consciousness, the *liṅga* of the Supreme Brahman— the *prāṇaliṅga* consisting of the Supreme Brahman—

shines forth like a lamp within the heart-lotus of those who are disciplined in yoga, specifically the knowers of Śiva who are engaged in the yoga of Śiva; it is not perceived by the ignorant, the common folk who lack the instruction of a guru.

It is cultivated, meaning it is made to enter the heart. For it is well-known from the Upaniṣads that Brahman resides in the heart within the circles of the moon, sun, and fire—as the light within the heart, the Person who stands like a lamp in a windless place (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7). || 8 ||
231) Now, he says that those who, having abandoned such a *prāṇaliṅga*, are devoted to external *liṅgas* are fools:
"The supreme *liṅga*, which is of the nature of Śiva and consists of light, resides within."
Having abandoned those established in external signs, they are proclaimed as the deluded. || 9 ||

Here, "external linga" refers to the ordinary linga other than the chosen linga (iṣṭaliṅga); the sense is that the chosen linga is internal because it consists of the mass of consciousness and bliss. || 9 ||

Therefore, being turned away from external signs (*bāhyaliṅga*), one who reflects upon the sign of consciousness (*cilliṅga*) alone is a "possessor of the breath-sign" (*prāṇaliṅgin*); thus it is said:
"The yogin who always abides reflecting upon the sign of consciousness, with his back turned toward external objects—he is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*. (10)

By the term "external object" (bāhyavastu), the external *liṅga* and the substances used as means for its worship are denoted. In that regard, the Śiva-yogin who, being turned away from those [external objects], is always and continuously engaged in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the *liṅga* of consciousness, and who internally possesses an inquiry into the *liṅga* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose nature is consciousness— he is the Śiva-yogin known as a *prāṇaliṅgin*.
The meaning is that it is being told. || 10 ||
Now, as to the question "What is the basis for aversion toward external lingas and the like?", he says:

"Constantly reflecting that the universe is born of the conceptualization of Māyā and is therefore to be abandoned, one who possesses the *prāṇaliṅga* becomes dissolved in the *liṅga* consisting of consciousness and bliss. (11)

Having reflected that the universe is born of the conceptualization of *māyā* and arises from the differentiation of the qualities of *māyā*, and thus considering it as something to be abandoned and renounced, and having thoroughly contemplated this constantly and always, the practitioner of the *prāṇaliṅga*— whose mind has dissolved— becomes merged in the *liṅga* consisting of consciousness and bliss, which is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
The meaning is that he is said to be "one who possesses the liṅga of the vital breath. || 19 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the *cilliṅga* transcends *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, whereas the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, how can it be possible for that [breath] to have the nature of a sacred seat (*pīṭha*)?
Dispelling this doubt, he concludes the section on the practitioner of the *prāṇaliṅga*:
Existence is the power consisting of breath; its true form is the sign of breath (prāṇaliṅga).
Through the realization of the state of equilibrium with that, one is called a "bearer of the breath-sign" (prāṇaliṅgin). || 12 ||

The state of being existent is "existence" (*sattā*). This very manifestation included within the first-person singular pronoun "I" (*asmīti*) is the vitalizing power (*prāṇamayī śaktiḥ*) of the subtle body (*cilliṅga*), which constitutes its life; for in the absence of such a manifestation, the consequence would be insentience.

The meaning is that the *prāṇaliṅga* consists of the Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*), possessing a true form and such a manifestation. By means of the realization of their essential identity—that is, by the realization of the mutual identity of Śiva and Śakti—one is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*. || 12 ||
Thus [ends] the section on the Prāṇaliṅgin;
now follows the section on the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga.
Now, by the Prāṇaliṅgin, the vital breath—renowned in all the Yoga scriptures—is being prescribed...

He explains the method of worshipping the *liṅga* through seven aphorisms: "The supreme *liṅga*, which is of the nature of Śiva and consists of consciousness, exists within; that which is worshipped with the flowers of one's inner disposition is indeed the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*. (13)
That which resides in the heart-lotus, whose form is consciousness— like the nature of a jar consisting of its long neck and so forth— is the manifestation of consciousness; such is the supreme,
most excellent *liṅga* composed of Śiva, the *liṅga* that is the life-force of the universe whose very nature is Śiva.
The meaning is that it is well known that this worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* is performed with "mental flowers," which are specific modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). || 13 ||

Now, as to where it is to be worshipped, having described the upper heart-lotus which serves as the locus for the *prāṇaliṅga*, he says that it is to be worshipped with flowers of contemplation (*bhāvapuṣpa*):
"Touched by the internal breath and adorned by the extremely subtle ether..."
Exceedingly cool from the sprinkling of nectar dripping from the moon upon its crown.

Having meditated at all times upon the linga of consciousness, which is the form of Śiva, seated upon a lotus throne in the heart-abode— the lamp of awakening where the nine gates of the senses are bound— one should worship it with offerings of contemplation. || 15 ||
Touched by the internal wind, pervaded by the vital breath, beautified by the most subtle ether, shimmering in the exceedingly subtle space,
and rendered intensely cool by the sprinkling of nectar flowing from the orb of the full moon situated in the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*).
In the lamp of the knowledge of Śiva, which has the nine gates consisting of the five sense organs such as hearing bound [within it],

there exists the auspicious form of Śiva seated upon the lotus-throne in the center of the twelve-petaled lotus at the abode of the heart above; this is the *cilliṅga* (flame-liṅga), the *prāṇaliṅga* (life-force-liṅga).

The meaning is that, having cultivated [the deity] and meditated according to the method taught by the guru, one should always worship with "objects of existence," that is, with mental entities. || 14–15 ||
Now, as to what those things are, he says:
"Patience is said to be the water for consecration; discernment is called the garment;
truth is declared to be the ornament; and detachment is the flower garland. (16)
Fragrance is the perfection of meditative concentration, and freedom from egoism is its preservation;
faith is the incense, and great wisdom is the lamp that illuminates the world. (17)
The offering for the proliferation rooted in delusion is that very offering; silence is the ringing of the bell, and the presentation of sense-objects is the betel.
The absence of delusion regarding objects is the conceptualization of circumambulation; the power of the intellect that consists of that [circumambulation] is considered the act of salutation. (19)
With such offerings, pure in intention and free from defect, one should,
with a mind turned toward it, worship the internal liṅga.
[1. tulanīya]—
A seat fashioned with jewels, a bath with snowy waters, divine garments adorned with various gems, and sandalwood marked with the fragrance of musk;

O God, O Paśupati, O ocean of compassion, please accept this flower fashioned from *jātī*, *campaka*, and *bilva* leaves, as well as incense and a lamp prepared by me. [Śi0 Mā0 Pū0] Forgiveness itself is the water for consecration; the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things is the garment.

Truthfulness and avoidance of falsehood are the ornaments; detachment from the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next is the flower-garland; one-pointedness of mind alone is the fragrance; freedom from egoism is the unbroken grains of rice; trust is the incense;
and the great wisdom that illuminates the universe is the lamp. In this regard—

By the word "delusion" (bhrānti), ignorance is indicated. That which is the offering of the fundamental phenomenal world— consisting of the group of ego-identifications such as the body, rooted in the ignorance that "I am not the Lord"— is the *naivedya* (offering).

Silence is the resonance of the bell, because it is the cause for the contemplation of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*). Just as objects—consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—are merged into the one ocean through the medium of the waves, such as foam, so too is the contemplation of the dissolution of the object into the means of knowledge, the means of knowledge into the knower, and that knower into the Supreme Knower, who is the Light-Linga (*jyotirliṅga*). This is indeed [the true meaning of silence].

The meaning is the offering of tāmbūla consisting of betel nut and leaf powder. "Circumambulation" (pradakṣiṇa) is the absence of the delusion of duality regarding objects such as sound and so forth in relation to Śiva. "Power" (śakti) is the capacity of the intellect to take the form of the Liṅga; it is the dissolution of the modification of the intellect into the Liṅga.
This is the meaning, and that is the salutation.

With such offerings, purified in their inner disposition and beyond reproach, one who has turned the mind away from the external should worship the internal *cilliṅga* (the flame-liṅga) and the *prāṇaliṅga* (the vital-force-liṅga); this is the meaning. || 16–20 ||
Thus concludes the section on the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*;
now follows the section on the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Śiva-yoga, according to the *Yoga Sūtras*: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.2).
He describes the stage of the meditative absorption (samādhi) of Śiva-yoga, which is attainable through the worship of the prāṇaliṅga:
"For one who is devoted to internal practice, the perfection of meditation on the Self as Śiva, achieved through the sequences of worshipping the prāṇaliṅga, is called samādhi. (21)

Through the methods of worshipping the *prāṇaliṅga*— that is, by means of the previously mentioned modes of worshipping the *prāṇaliṅga*— this *prāṇaliṅgin*, who is intent upon internal ritual action, attains the perfection of meditating on Śiva as the Self;
this indeed is the perfection of realizing the state of *samarasa* (equilibrium) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva, who are of the same form as the *liṅga* and the body.
The meaning is "concentration" (samādhi). || 21 ||

To the question "How is that so?", he explains *samādhi* through the yoga of Śiva in the form of the *ajapā-gāyatrī*, in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "That which is the Puruṣa, that am I" (p.
Transcending all principles, radiant with being, consciousness, and bliss, self-luminous, indefinable, and beyond the reach of speech and mind. || 22 ||

One should contemplate the Supreme Self in the form of a *haṃsa*, illuminated by the Great Power known as Umā, whose nature is consciousness; through the realization of "I am That," the attainment of one-pointedness is considered the supreme *samādhi*. (23)
It transcends all principles (*tattva*), existing as that which has passed beyond the thirty-six principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva;

it shines forth in the form of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). For it is said in the *Śruti*: "From whence words return, together with the mind, not having attained it" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.4.1); thus, it is beyond the path of speech and mind, and for this very reason, it cannot be described as "this" or "such."

One should contemplate the Supreme Self in the form of the *Haṃsa*, which is impossible to perceive, not accessible through other means of knowledge such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and illuminated by the great power known as *sphuraṇarūpā* inherent within itself— according to the analogy of a white cloth— by means of the realization "I am He" (*so'haṃbhāva*), thinking "I am indeed that."

The accomplishment of their oneness—the establishment of the identity of those two, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—is considered the supreme samādhi, that is, the most excellent state of meditative absorption; this is the accepted view. This is because it is stated in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* that the referent of the word "That" transcends the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).

For the individual self (jīvātman), who is bound by the noose of the path of phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, the letter *a* is established by the force of such scriptural authorities as: "I am the first-born" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.10.6), "I am indeed the first of the gods" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 10.2), and "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 10.8). Thus, the letter *a*.

The letter *ha* is called Śiva, and *śakti* is said to be [the letter *sa*] (Si0 Śi0 20.39); thus, one should contemplate identity with that which consists of the supreme power (*parāvāk*), characterized by the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) that is the cause of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*), because it is non-different from our own nature, being permeated by it.
The meaning is "meditative concentration" (samādhi). || 22-23 ||
Now,
that which is of the nature of vital breath (prāṇa) is here called the individual soul (jīva), while that which is of the nature of the subtle body (liṅga) is remembered as Śaṅkara;
he who knows their identity is a knower of both the vital breath and the subtle body, a yogi of Śiva.
In accordance with this statement from the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā (p. 236), he describes the characteristics of one established in samādhi:
"The supreme Brahman is proclaimed as the Great Liṅga; the vital breath is proclaimed as the individual soul (jīva)."
Because of the contemplation of that single state of being, one is proclaimed as established in samādhi. || 24 ||
The Great Liṅga itself is declared to be the Supreme Brahman, the reality of Paraśiva known as the Supreme Brahman;

and because of the scriptural statement, "The individual soul (jīva) becomes mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa)," the vital breath is said to be the very life-force of the soul. Through the contemplation of their identity, with reference to the vital breath of the Liṅga, there exist the Liṅga and its possessor (the embodied soul).

The meaning is that one who possesses the contemplation of the equal and essential oneness (*samarasaikya*) of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*), being established in *samādhi*, is proclaimed as "one steadfast in the *samādhi* of Śiva-yoga. || 24 ||

Then, having pressed the anus and raised the vital air from below, having circumambulated the *svādhiṣṭhāna* three times to the right, having gone to the *maṇipūraka*, having passed beyond the *anāhata*,
having restrained the *prāṇa-liṅga* at the *viśuddha*, and meditating upon the *ājñā* while contemplating the *brahmarandhra*.
In accordance with the statement of the *Haṃsa Upaniṣad*, "One should always meditate: 'I am of three measures' (*trimātraḥ aham*)," he elucidates the complete samādhi:
"One should visualize the lotuses established within the six internal cakras."
From the base up to the midpoint between the eyebrows, these constitute the abodes beginning with Brahmā. || 25 ||
Above the midpoint of the eyebrows, one should visualize a thousand-petaled lotus;
within that, one should contemplate a stainless lunar orb.
One should recognize the subtle aperture; the wise know that to be the station of Kailāsa.
One should meditate upon Śambhu, the cause of all causes, as residing there.
Within the subtle body that serves as the locus for both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara),

one should contemplate the six lotuses— six lotuses established in and arising from the six chakras— which extend from the root foundation (mūlādhāra) up to the midpoint of the eyebrows, reaching as far as the Ājñā-cakra, and which constitute the abodes of Brahmā and the other deities.
One should contemplate according to the method taught by the guru. "Above the midpoint of the eyebrows" means at the *brahmarandhra*;

one should visualize a thousand-petaled lotus, a flower adorned with a thousand petals of energy (*śakti*). Therein, in the center of that lotus, one should visualize a stainless, pure lunar orb, the mandala of Soma.
In the interval within that lunar orb, one should know there is a subtle aperture— an aperture exceedingly subtle, equal to the tip of a hair— knowing it through instruction.
The learned who know the scriptures recognize that subtle aperture as the station of Kailāsa, the abode of Kailāsa.

They should know: one should contemplate Śambhu, Śiva, who is present there—the cause of all causes, existing as the very cause even of Brahmā and the other lords of the causes—meditating upon him as non-different from one's own self; this is the meaning. (25–27)
Then, by the friction of earth and water located in the *ādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*, having caused the bulb of the navel (*nābhikanda*), known as the *maṇipūraka*, to arise—
Following that, within the twelve-petaled heart-lotus known as the Unstruck (anāhata),

the solar mandala shines, endowed with the twelve digits beginning with Tapinī. Above that, in the sixteen-petaled Viśuddhi lotus, is the lunar mandala, endowed with the sixteen digits beginning with Amṛtā.

It shines forth. Above that, in the *ājñācakra* consisting of two petals, the fire-maṇḍala composed of the ten *kalās* beginning with Jvalinī is radiant. Above that, in the *brahmacakra* adorned with a thousand petals, it is situated above the *kuṇḍalī*-maṇḍala endowed with thirty-eight *kalās*.

With two aphorisms, he states that for the *prāṇaliṅgin*— one who has attained the *samādhi* of Śiva-yoga characterized by the complete integration of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*— there is no experience of worldly (*māyika*) pleasure apart from the bliss of Śiva:
"By external latent impressions, the universe appears as an object of conceptual construction."
For those whose minds have been inwardly perfumed, the bliss of the Self is revealed. || 28 ||

The meaning is this: by means of an outward-turned mental formation (*saṃskāra*), the entire world appears as the object of conceptualization and discursive thought (*saṅkalpa-vikalpa*). By contrast, when the mind is dissolved within through an inward-turned state expressed as "I," the bliss of the Self—which is indeed the bliss of Śiva—shines forth. || 28 ||

Now, as to how external latent impressions (vāsanā) are removed, he says in this regard: "The wise man should burn the entire web of bonds consisting of the world with the fire of knowledge, produced from the churning-stick of the Self through the friction of supreme joy. (29)
The wise one who bears the *prāṇaliṅga*, through the churning of delight by reflecting upon the bliss of Śiva,
[consumes] everything with the fire of knowledge arising from the fire-drill of the Self— that is, with the fire of the knowledge of non-difference from Śiva.
The meaning is that one should burn—that is, reduce to ashes—the entire collection of bonds consisting of impurity (mala), illusion (māyā), and so forth, which pervades the world. || 29 ||
Now, explaining the greatness of the meditation on Śiva through two aphorisms, he concludes the section on the stage of *samādhi* in Śiva-yoga:
Of the poisonous tree of transmigratory existence, which has the five afflictions for its leaves...
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.3).
Contemplation on Śiva is the axe for cutting the root of karma. (30)

The meaning is that meditation on Śiva alone is the axe for cutting down the poisonous tree of saṃsāra— characterized by birth and death— which has karma rooted in the nature of dharma and adharma and possesses leaves characterized by the five afflictions beginning with ignorance. || 30 ||
Meditation on Śiva, however, is the fierce sun for the darkness of saṃsāra belonging to those whose selves have been withdrawn by the demon of ignorance that causes its manifestation. 31.

Meditation on Śiva is the fierce sun—the meaning is, the scorching orb—acting as the fierce sun that opens the eyes of the rākṣasa characterized by ignorance within the dense darkness of saṃsāra. || 31 ||
Thus [ends] the section on the meditative absorption of Śiva-yoga;
now follows the section on the innate state of the Liṅga.
Now, he describes the innate state (*nijasthala*) of the *liṅga* which becomes manifest for one who is thus endowed with the yoga of Śiva:
"The state of direct experiential realization of the Śiva-liṅga residing within one's own heart—that very Supreme Liṅga is called 'innate' (*nija*) by the wise. (32)

That very state of direct experience which exists as "I" in a general sense— without the contraction caused by space, time, or form— belonging to the Śivaliṅga that abides within one's own self through identity,
is itself the "own" [nature] of the supreme liṅga, the Great Liṅga.
The meaning is that "one's own true nature" (*nijasvarūpa*) is spoken of—that is, described—by the wise, those who possess knowledge of the reality of the self (*ātmatattvajñānin*). || 32 ||
Now, he reveals its true nature through two verses:
"Wherein all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as all the Vedas and so forth, dissolve and from whence they proceed—that is the Liṅga, the absolute Brahman. (33)

That into which Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, as well as the entire collection of words such as the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, go to dissolution and from which they manifest again—that is the Liṅga; it is designated by the word "Liṅga," meaning the absolute Brahman, that is, Brahman alone. || 33 ||
Now, if it is argued that Brahman alone— designated by the term *liṅga* and being the locus of the origin, dissolution, and maintenance of the universe—
is indeed Śiva’s own nature or something distinct from it, [the author] says in response: "The stainless one, consisting of consciousness and bliss, is directly Śiva himself."
It is called the *liṅga* and nothing else, from which the manifestation of the universe arises. || 34 ||
Since the origin of the universe— the birth of the cosmos— proceeds from the sign (liṅga) that is the nature of Brahman,
that sign which is the nature of Brahman, consisting of consciousness and bliss, whose essence is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda),
stainless and free from defects, is said to be Śiva himself directly manifest; it is nothing else, for no other entity is so described.
This is the meaning. || 34 ||
240) Now, he states the essential point: "What is the use of saying much here? It is called 'liṅga' by the wise."
The supreme Brahman, named Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, is the locus of the universe.
In this matter, what is the use of much talk?

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman itself—the very nature of which is the vibration that serves as the support of the universe—is called by the names Śiva and Paraśiva; it is the Liṅga, which is described as one's own Liṅga (nijaliṅga) by the wise who know the scriptures.
With two sūtras, he demonstrates that the *liṅga* established by the Māyika Vedānta school is not his own *liṅga*:
"Others say that the knowledge born from the Vedāntic statements is the *liṅga*."
Therefore, because the mark (liṅga) which has the form of Brahman is of the nature of the non-existent knowable. || 36 ||
The wise ones say that "Brahman" is the wisdom born from the Vedānta statements— such as "I am Brahman," "That thou art," and "This Self is Brahman"—
as well as the True Self (sad) which is their own *liṅga* and the illuminator of that [wisdom]. That is what they call it.

That [state] is characterized by the knowledge revealed by the Vedānta texts; because the *liṅga*—which is of the nature of Brahman, being the very essence of the Supreme Brahman—is of the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and because it is to be known through the light of the "I-consciousness" (*aham-prakāśa*) which is one's own *liṅga*-form of consciousness, it is "unreal," meaning it is not praiseworthy. This is because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*) are necessarily grounded in the substrate of the knower (*pramātṛ-bhitti*).

Because there is a rule that [the means of knowledge] must illuminate the object of knowledge; otherwise, one would fall into the Buddhist position. This is because Brahman, being devoid of marks (aliṅga), enters the category of the "object of knowledge" (prameya) and thus would depend upon another knower (pramātṛ). || 36 ||
Now, he refutes another view:
"They say that the unmanifest (avyakta) is the subtle mark (liṅga), the root cause of the worlds, and that Maheśvara is the possessor of the mark (liṅgin); this doctrine is inconsistent. (37)
p.

241) They say that the unmanifest *māyā*-principle, the root cause of the worlds, is the *liṅga*, and that Maheśvara is the *liṅgin* (the possessor of the *liṅga*). This view [is expressed in the verse]: "But *māyā* is *prakṛti*..."

The view of the Śvetāśvataras, namely that "one should know Maheśvara as the wielder of māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10), is inconsistent, as it is not accepted by those who take the vital breath (prāṇa) as their defining characteristic; for Prakṛti, being insentient, falls within the category of things to be abandoned.
Now—
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
Everything shines only after Him, as He alone shines.
By its light all this shines.
Thus, in accordance with the *Kaṭhavallī* scripture, he establishes through two sūtras the nature of the "own-liṅga" (nija-liṅga) as accepted by those who bear the liṅga of Prāṇa:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon, nor lightning, nor fire."
When the supreme Self shines forth as the Great Liṅga, there are no stars.

When the Supreme Self, the Great Liṅga, shines forth as the supreme self, then in that great light, the sun does not shine, the moon does not shine, fire does not shine, lightning does not shine, and the stars do not shine. || 38 ||
To the question, "In that case, how is their manifestation? he says:
"The Śruti declares that the supreme Liṅga consists of light and is of the nature of Śiva; by its radiance all this shines forth, without a doubt. (39)
The supreme *liṅga*, whose nature is Śiva, is indeed the Great *Liṅga* (*mahāliṅga*),
consisting of light and having a form of illumination that is independent of anything else. Therefore, by its radiance...

The meaning is that the *Kaṭhavallī* Śruti declares: "By the light of the Jyotirliṅga alone, all this—the sun, the moon, and so forth—is made manifest; there is no doubt in this matter. The underlying idea is as follows:
because fire, the sun, and the moon consist of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in the form of the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge (*mātṛ-māna-meya*).
Since it is established that the manifestation of these [entities] depends upon the manifestation of the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga),
if one were to further accept that this Mahāliṅga is manifestable by the light of knowledge produced by the Vedāntas,

it would follow that it is absolutely insentient (*jaḍa*) because its manifestation would be dependent on something else. [Therefore,] the reality is unobjectifiable (*aprameya*) and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

This is the meaning of the term "one's own liṅga. In our view, there is no fault because the means of valid knowledge, such as the Nigamas and Āgamas, consist of one's own power (svaśakti) and are thus self-evident. || 39 ||
Then, having described the greatness of the *liṅga* by means of two verses, he concludes the section on the location of his own *liṅga*:
"There is no reality higher than the *liṅga*, from which the universe is born;
that which assumes this very form, and in which it meets its dissolution. (40)

From this *liṅga*, as the cause from which this world is born— that is, produced— and by which this world maintains its form— that is, its state of persistence— and into which this world undergoes dissolution— that is, experiences its withdrawal—
from that cause, from this *liṅga*.
There is no reality higher than that which consists of self-luminosity appearing independently of anything else, based on its own intrinsic mark (liṅga). || 40 ||
Therefore, the *liṅga* is the Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; through meditation on it as one's own true form, that very state is produced. (41)
