Therefore, through meditation—that is, through contemplation—upon the fact that one's own form is the *liṅga*, which is none other than the Supreme Brahman whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), that very state arises; the meaning is that the state [of the self] manifests as the *liṅga* itself. || 41 ||
Thus [ends] the section on the innate linga;
now follows the section on the bodily linga.
Now, he defines the possessor of the body as the limb (aṅgin) and the limb as the possessor of the body (aṅgaliṅgin) by means of two verses:
"They say that knowledge is the limb and the eternal object of knowledge is the sign (liṅga);
he in whom both of these exist is proclaimed as the possessor of the limb and the sign (aṅgaliṅgin). (42)
The meaning is that they say the living being (*jīva*) who possesses the knowledge of Śiva is the "limb" (*aṅga*) for every limb.

They say that the object to be known (*jñeya*)—the eternal and constant reality (*liṅga*) which must be directly realized by this possessor of the knowledge of Śiva—is the "sign. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Two birds, companions and friends... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
The meaning is that he in whom these two—the two types of bodily liṅgas—exist is proclaimed as an "aṅgaliṅgin," one who possesses the liṅga on his body. || 42 ||
Now, to the objection that "in this way, one would enter the doctrine of the dualists," he replies:
"The mark is mounted upon the member, and the member is present within the mark;
he who possesses this pair is one who possesses both the member and the mark. (43)
The *liṅga*, the Śiva-liṅga, is mounted upon the *aṅga*, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*);

likewise, the *aṅga*, the individual soul, is present within the *liṅga*, the Śiva-liṅga, in a state of aesthetic equilibrium. He who possesses this pair—this twofold knowledge according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout—is a possessor of the *prāṇaliṅga*.
The meaning is that he possesses the limbs and the *liṅga*. || 43 ||
Now, one might ask: why is it that mere knowledge alone is intended here? To this he says:

"He who, having known the Linga residing within his own heart as consisting of light, should constantly worship and meditate upon it—him one should know as an 'Angalingin' (one whose limb is the Linga). (44)

He who is a bearer of the vital-force-linga (prāṇaliṅgī), having known his own linga— the eternal, constant linga consisting of light, composed of light, situated within himself in the lotus of his own heart—
and having realized it as the nature of equanimity through scripture, the guru, and his own direct experience;
One should worship and meditate upon that *prāṇaliṅgin*; "one should know" means one should understand him. || 44 ||

Now, having stated the synonyms for his own *liṅga*, he explains with three verses that one who possesses a firm mind therein is a *jīvanmukta*: "The *liṅga* alone is known by all the eternal scriptures."
"Brahman," "the abode of the universe," and also "that which is beyond liberation. || 45 ||
He whose mental state is that "this linga is the very form of liberation," is liberated even while joined to a body; he is a man of knowledge, he is a great guru. (46)

By means of all the eternal and constant scriptures, [it is established] through the expression of the intention regarding the commencement [of the teaching], namely that one’s own *liṅga* alone is the Supreme Brahman, the support of the world, and the locus of supreme liberation—according to the Vedic revelation: "With speech that is multiform and eternal. This is because it consists of both Śiva and Śakti.
Through the authorities of the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*, it is known that this innate *liṅga* is the form of liberation and the very nature of supreme liberation.
He in whom this resides as the mental state of a living *liṅgin* is liberated even while joined with a body;
because there is no further rebirth, he is a *jīvanmukta*. He is the man of knowledge (*jñānī*), and he alone possesses the knowledge of Śiva.
The "Great Guru" (mahāguru) means the venerable teacher (śrīguru). || 45-46 ||
Now, he states that there is no liberation for those who are devoid of knowledge regarding the *liṅga* as follows:
"The *liṅga* is without beginning or end; it is the cause of the worlds.
Those who do not know this are deluded and excluded from the path to liberation. (47)
"Without beginning or end" means being devoid of origination and destruction; the rest is clear. || 47 ||
Then, having stated that one who possesses the dharma of worshipping the *prāṇaliṅga* and so forth— being indeed a *prāṇaliṅgin*—
is called "the refuge" (*śaraṇa*) by virtue of the ripening of knowledge, he concludes the section on the *prāṇaliṅgin*:
He who is endowed with those dharmas preceded by the disposition of worshipping the *prāṇaliṅga*, and whose self is permeated by Śiva—
That very state is proclaimed as the Fourth (turya); through the ripening of consciousness, it is designated as "Refuge" (śaraṇa). || 48 ||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Five Stages for the Prāṇaliṅgin," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Śivayogin named Reṇukācārya, a Brāhmaṇa of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). 12.

He who is a *prāṇaliṅgin*— endowed with the *śivācāra* dharmas headed by the practice of worshiping the *prāṇaliṅga*, whose very bodily form is meditated upon as being of the nature of the *liṅga*, and who is the fourth (*turya*) in relation to the devotees— he, that very *prāṇaliṅgin*, becomes a refuge through the maturation of his knowledge.
The meaning is that he possesses such a designation. || 48 ||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Occasion of the Five Stages of the Prāṇaliṅgin," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 12.
The Thirteenth Chapter: Now, the Place of Refuge;
then, the Question of Agastya. Agastya said:
He has been taught that he is a devotee of Maheśvara, one who is gracious, and a bearer of the *prāṇaliṅga*;
how then has he been further designated as one named Śaraṇa? || 1 ||

Having been awakened by the thought, "He is the gracious Lord Maheśvara," how and in what manner does he, being one whose very life-breath is the *liṅga*, come to possess the designation of "one who has sought refuge"? This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Reṇuka provides the answer to this question, saying:
"The possessor of the limb (aṅgin) is the nature of knowledge; the knowable Śiva is the Lord (pati).
The bliss that exists in that immersion (samāveśa)—he who possesses that [bliss] is the one named Śaraṇa. (2)

"Consisting of knowledge" (*jñānarūpaḥ*) means one whose very nature is the knowledge of Śiva; thus, the meaning is "one possessed of the knowledge of Śiva. "One who possesses the bodily *liṅga*" (*aṅgaliṅgī*) should be understood as one who has attained the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) with the bodily *liṅga*, that is, one who possesses the *prāṇaliṅga*. "Śiva" should be understood as the Lord (*pati*) who is the *śivaliṅga* itself. In the immersion (*samāveśa*) into that...
Regarding those two, the woman and the man, who take the form of the *aṅga* and the *liṅga*, there is a bliss arising from their union in a state of equalized passion;

that bliss is such as is well-known from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "As one embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without or within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21). He possesses that, being endowed with such bliss.
The meaning is that he possesses the name "Refuge. || 2 ||
p.
247) Now, to the question "Does this [ground] also have a division of stages?", he says: "This stage is declared to be fourfold according to the distinction of its qualities (dharma)."
First, taking refuge was taught; then, the abandonment of the qualities of darkness (tamas).
Then, having indicated the instruction, there follows the accomplishment of ethical discipline;
I shall now describe their characteristics in sequence—let it be heard. (4)
This stage of refuge is declared to be fourfold according to the distinction of the Dharma and the distinction of conduct: first, the stage of refuge;
immediately following that, the stage of dispelling darkness; then, the stage of instruction; and finally, the stage of accomplishing ethical discipline.
It has been pointed out and explained. The meaning is: "I shall state the characteristics of these four in their proper order; listen. || 3-4 ||
I am Satī, and my husband, the Lord himself, is united with the *liṅga* within his heart;
there is no worldly pleasure there, for it is the supreme place of refuge.

In accordance with this statement from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, he defines the state of taking refuge: "He who, like Satī toward her lover, perceives Śakti within Śiva and turns away from everything else—he is known as one who possesses the name 'Refuge' (śaraṇa). (5)
He who, like a virtuous wife devoted to her husband, remains intent upon Śiva— the beloved object of his life—
and contemplates his own self as the Śakti (the consort) in relation to the Śivaliṅga; and who, being averse to everything else,
turns his face away from other deities besides the Śivaliṅga— he alone is one who has found refuge.
"Known as one who possesses a place of refuge" means he is worthy to be known. || 5 ||
Then, by means of many illustrations, he establishes that devotion to the Śiva-liṅga alone is the true refuge: "When Śiva is directly realized, who would desire anything else?
When a great treasure has been obtained, who would beg for glass from elsewhere? (6)
(248) When Śiva, Paramaśiva, is directly known through well-established means of valid cognition such as scripture,
and is recognized as being greater than Brahmā and the other [deities], who else would one desire? The meaning is that no one desires anything else.

Just as when a great treasure has been obtained, who would beg for glass from anywhere else? The meaning is that no one would; likewise, [the devotee] is averse to any other deity besides Śiva, meaning he finds refuge in Him alone. || 6 ||
Having attained the bliss of Śiva, who else would resort to another?
Having abandoned the nectar of the Gaṅgā, who would long for a mirage?

Having attained and reached the bliss of Śiva’s Liṅga, who would resort to another deity? The meaning is that no one would take refuge in another. Just as who, having abandoned the water of the Gaṅgā, would desire or long for a mirage—the water of a sunbeam?—so too, one should turn away from anything other than Śiva.
The meaning is "refuge. || 7 ||
Without the sun that is Śaṅkara, how could the gods be capable of dispelling the darkness of saṃsāra for embodied beings? They would be like fireflies.

Just as fireflies are creatures that emit little light and are incapable of dispelling darkness, whereas the sun is capable of doing so, likewise, apart from Śaṅkara, who is like the sun, the gods beginning with Brahmā are not capable of cutting through the darkness of saṃsāra.
The meaning is that he is averse to anything other than Śiva and has him as his refuge. || 8 ||
One afflicted by saṃsāra should go to Śiva; what fruit is there in [worshiping] the gods beginning with Brahmā?
When a cakora bird is thirsty, does it look at the stars instead of the moon?

Just as a thirsty cakora bird, tormented by thirst, might look toward the moon and not toward the stars, so too one exhausted by saṃsāra should take refuge in Śiva alone, wondering what fruit could be gained from Brahmā and the other gods; the meaning is that, like such a cakora, one should turn away from everything else and seek refuge in Śiva. || 9 ||
Śiva alone is the refuge for all who seek refuge;
he is the omniscient remover of all defects for those bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra. (10)
When the knowledge of Śiva has arisen, supreme bliss shines forth;
the wise yogi whose mind is attached to that does not delight in anything else. (11)
When the knowledge of Śiva’s majesty arises— that Śiva alone is the protector, the omniscient one who destroys all defects, for all those bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra and seeking refuge—
then the manifestation of supreme bliss occurs. With his mind thus attached to Him, the Śiva-yogin does not [find delight] in any other deity.
The meaning is "he delights. || 10-11 ||
Now, concluding the aforementioned subject, he completes the section on taking refuge:
"Therefore, having gone for refuge to Śaṅkara with every effort, one attains His infinite bliss and rejoices, no longer occupied with other thoughts. (12)

Therefore, with every effort through the actions of mind, speech, and body, having gone for refuge to Śiva and knowing him to be skilled in protection, one has surrendered; having attained that infinite bliss and having obtained infinite bliss from that Śiva, one rejoices, and not with any other thought— that is, not with thoughts of another deity.
The meaning is "he rejoices. || 12 ||
Thus, having described the place of refuge, he now describes the place of the dispelling of darkness, and then the place of the effectuation of the dispelling of darkness by means of that refuge:
Since the darknesses of being are dispelled by the Guru— who rejoices in the supreme bliss attached to Śiva— he is the dispeller of the tamasic state.

Being devoted to Śiva and rejoicing in supreme bliss, because the states of darkness and the transformations of darkness are cast out and warded off by that most excellent refuge, the Guru, for that reason, he—
The meaning is that one should become a dispeller of darkness (tamas). || 13 ||
To the question, "Why indeed should states of darkness (tamas) be rejected? he says:
"For one whose knowledge is mixed with darkness, no progress is desired;
for the wise know that purity is the very essence of the yoga of knowledge. (14)

"Purity" means that which is eternally the means for attaining stainlessness. The remainder is clear. Therefore, the meaning is that the transformations of darkness (tamas) must be dispelled. || 14 ||
Now,
from the quality of *sattva* arise happiness, knowledge, dispassion, and indeed bliss;
whereas from *rajas* arise the onset of suffering, passion, and redness.
Delusion, error, as well as laziness and blackness, arise from tamas.
In accordance with this statement from the Sūta-saṃhitā, he reveals those endowed with the three qualities:
tranquility, self-restraint, discrimination, dispassion, full realization, patience, the perfection of compassion, and faith arising from truth. (15)
Devotion to Śiva is the supreme dharma; those who possess the knowledge of Śiva are his kinsmen.
Endowed with these qualities, the great yogi is proclaimed as one of pure sattva.

Tranquility (*śama*) is patience (*kṣānti*), or the restraint of the mind; self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the external senses; seclusion (*viveka*) is the investigation into the nature of eternal and non-eternal things; dispassion (*vairāgya*) is detachment from sense objects; perfect contemplation (*pūrṇabhāvanā*) is uninterrupted meditation (*akhaṇḍadhyāna*); forbearance (*kṣānti*)—also known as endurance (*titikṣā*)—is the perfection of compassion and mercy toward all beings (*bhūtadayā*).
Faith arising from truth, which arises from things as they truly are; confidence; devotion to Śiva;

supreme dharma, which is the most excellent conduct of Śiva—these are the kinsmen of the knowledge of Śiva, meaning they are related to the knowledge of Śiva. A great yogin endowed with these ten qualities is *sāttvika*, meaning one who is possessed of the quality of *sattva*.
Thus it has been proclaimed. || 15-16 ||
(251) Now, one might ask: "Do desire, anger, and so forth ever arise even for a great yogin endowed with these qualities? To this, he says:
How can the elephants of desire, anger, great delusion, pride, and envy remain in the presence of the lion of the knowledge of Śiva? (17)

The meaning is that because the knowledge of Śiva takes the form of a lion insofar as it acts to subdue the intoxicated elephant of the mind, there is no room for the elephants of desire, anger, and so forth to remain in its presence. || 17 ||
Now, he demonstrates one who is possessed of the quality of *rajas*:
"He who hates anything whatsoever within this phenomenal world, which is in essence Śiva, should be known as a hater of Śiva, his mind overcome by *rajas*. (18)

He whose mind is possessed by *rajas*—meaning one whose consciousness is veiled by desire, anger, and other effects of the *rajas* quality—who hates this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) anywhere within its form as Śiva, is to be known as a hater of Śiva who is *rājasa*; the meaning is that he is fit to be recognized as such. || 18 ||
Now, he defines one endowed with the quality of *tamas*:
"He who hates all people, or who always acts with egoism, and who is possessed of untruthful inclinations—he is known as *tāmasa*. (19)
This is clear. || 19 ||
Now, having stated in two verses that this quality of darkness (tamas) does not exist for those who have taken refuge in Śiva, he concludes the section on the removal of darkness:
"For the trees of passion, hatred, and so forth, have indeed grown with darkness as their root."
For they are incessantly cut down by the axe of the knowledge of Śiva. (20)
Having the root-nature of the quality of *tamas*, the trees of passion and hatred have grown;

these Rajasic trees of desire, anger, and so forth are indeed famously and constantly cut down by the axe of the knowledge of Śiva—that is, by the hatchet consisting of the Sattvic knowledge of Śiva. || 20 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that the trees of passion, hatred, and so forth, which have arisen from the root of *tamas*, may be cut down by the axe of the knowledge of Śiva; but by what means can the cessation of the quality of *tamas*—which is the cause of these—be achieved?
Without that, the cessation of their sprouts is impossible. To this, he says:
When the knowledge of Śiva, which resembles a thousand suns, has arisen, how could there be any transformations of darkness for the great Śiva-yogins? (21)

When the knowledge of Śiva, which resembles a thousand suns, has arisen, how could there be modifications of darkness—the sprouts of ignorance—for the great ones, the supreme beings, the Śiva-yogins who have taken refuge in Śiva? From what cause could they arise? [The answer is: because of the destruction of the very root of the darkness that serves as their cause.
The state of being. || 21 ||
Thus concludes the section on the removal of darkness;
now follows the section on the instruction.
Thereafter, by means of the removal of darkness, he describes the section on the instruction as it appears:
Having dispelled the portion of darkness that sets saṃsāra in motion, that knowledge which is pointed out is known as "nirdeśa" (instruction). || 22 ||

Having dispelled the portion of darkness (*tamas*) which is the root cause of the progression of *saṃsāra*, that knowledge which is pointed out and taught—that knowledge is called "the pointing out" (*nirdeśa*), and it is known as "the place of pointing out" (*nirdeśasthala*);
this is the meaning of "it is remembered" (*smṛtam*). || 22 ||
Now, as to the question of by whom that knowledge is taught, [the author] clarifies its greatness in many ways, stating:
"The Guru alone reveals the supreme reality to embodied beings."
Or who else in the world, apart from the sun, is the dispeller of darkness? (23)

The meaning is that just as in the world there is no one else who can illuminate objects by dispelling darkness without the sun, so too there is no one who can illuminate the supreme reality by dispelling darkness without the Guru. || 23 ||
He states another illustration:
"Without a realized Guru, how can there be liberation from saṃsāra?
Or, without a physician who knows the cause [of the disease], is a malady ever cured? (24)

The meaning is: how could there be liberation from saṃsāra—that is, the cessation of the disease of existence—without a Siddha Guru, that is, without a Guru who has attained the perfection of knowledge? Regarding this, there is an illustration: one who is skilled in medical treatment based on the prior diagnosis of a disease, knowing that "this is the cause of this disease" and "this is the medicine for it."
Does a disease subside without a physician? The meaning is that it does not subside.

Just as a disease cannot be cured without a physician who possesses knowledge of its cause, so too the cessation of saṃsāra is impossible without a Guru who has attained realization through knowledge; this is the intended meaning. || 24 ||

To the question, "How indeed is this guru to be known? he says: "He who purifies the mirror of the mind, which is stained by ignorance, through the application of the power of wisdom—him they call the best of gurus. (25)

The meaning is that they call him the best of teachers, the most excellent of gurus, who, by means of the application of the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), purifies—that is, renders stainless—the mirror of the mind which is soiled by ignorance, through connection with the glory of the knowledge of Śiva as established in the scripture: "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*, *Aitareya Upaniṣad* 3.5.3). || 25 ||
Now, he states that all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise from such a glance of the Guru:
"For one who has directly realized reality and whose nature is that of one liberated while living...
When the guru’s glance has attained perfection, what indeed is difficult to obtain in the worlds? (26)
For one who has directly realized the reality of Śiva through his own essential nature— that is, for one whose nature is that of a *jīvanmukta* who has perceived the truth of Śiva—
there is knowledge free from conceptual construction and action free from prohibition.
A form that delights the world is the characteristic of one liberated while living.

According to this statement of Vasiṣṭha, when the glance—the side-long look filled with the essence of compassion—of the true Guru, who possesses the nature of one liberated while living, is attained, what indeed is difficult to obtain in the worlds? The meaning is that nothing is unobtainable; the sense is that all perfections characterized by worldly enjoyment and liberation come to pass. || 26 ||
If it is asked, "Why are there such gurus?
[the answer is: There are many gurus who plunder the wealth of their disciples;
but even a single guru who plunders the very heart of the disciple is rare to find.
In accordance with the statement from the *Śivarahasya*, he says:
"The gurus, who are abodes of compassion and kalpa-trees for the sake of liberation, are indeed difficult to find in this world—those who are devoted solely to the non-duality of Śiva. (27)
This is clear. || 27 ||
Therefore, stating that the venerable Guru, who is devoted to the Śiva-liṅga, is superior to ordinary gurus, he concludes the section on the locus of instruction:
"Like the milk-ocean among oceans, like Mount Sumeru among mountains..."
Like the sun among the planets, like the Kaustubha among jewels. || 28 ||
He is like Bhadraśrī among trees, like Śaṅkara among the gods;
he is the supreme, auspicious Guru, more praiseworthy than even the gurus of those with ordinary natures. (29)
"Bhadraśrī" means "born of Malaya. The rest is clear. || 28-29 ||
255) Thus ends the section on the exposition;
now follows the section on the accomplishment of ethical discipline.

Now, having stated that the nature of one who possesses the discipline (*śīla*) is the desire to know the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*) through the yoga of knowledge as instructed by the venerable Guru, he explains the essential character of such a disciplined person with seven aphorisms:
"The desire to know the reality of Śiva is called the discipline (*śīla*) by the wise."
Through the application of what is to be demonstrated, one who possesses that [virtue] is called "one of moral conduct" by the noble ones. || 30 ||
Because he possesses the yoga of knowledge to be taught by teachers who themselves possess the previously mentioned characteristics,

and because it is his nature (*śīla*) to desire to know— that is, to have the wish to understand— the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*), he is called "one who possesses that nature" (*śīlī*) by the wise, that is, by the knowers; one who possesses such a nature characterized by the desire to know is thus designated as *śīlī*.
This is the meaning. || 30 ||

Now he states the essential conclusion: "The wise declare that the union with the stability of devotion toward the Lord Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self who removes the distress of those who have sought refuge, is called *śīla* (virtue). (31)

"Protect [us]," [this is the meaning]: for those who have come for refuge, O Śiva, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman and who removes afflictions, "the stabilization of the mind is called *śīla* (virtue/conduct) by the wise who know the Śiva scriptures. This is the sense. || 31 ||
Now, he states its definition by another method:
"Virtue is the singular knowledge of Śiva, one-pointed concentration on the meditation of Śiva, and an intense longing for the attainment of Śiva; such a practitioner is remembered as virtuous. (32)
In Śiva, consciousness is Śiva himself; specific knowledge is the state of being one-pointedly absorbed in the meditation on Śiva;

and within that very meditation on Śiva, the absence of any other mental activity is called *śīla* (virtue). The meaning is that the yogi who possesses such virtue, through his longing for the knowledge of Śiva and his eagerness to approach Śiva, is remembered as "one possessed of virtue" (*śīlavān*).
Having clarified this very point, he says:
"He whose aversion toward consciousness other than Śiva is firmly established..."
They say that one whose mental activity is attached to that is a vessel of virtuous conduct. || 33 ||

He whose refuge is steadfast and firm in its aversion toward anything other than Śiva— the Śivaliṅga— namely, toward the specialized knowledge of other deities; he whose mental activity and mental operations are attached solely to the Śivaliṅga, being devoted to it alone— he is a vessel of virtuous conduct.
They say that one who possesses virtue is truly peaceful. || 33 ||
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"The virtue of a devoted wife is praised because of her husband;
likewise, one who lacks devotion is said to be ill-behaved because of his lack of affection for Śiva. (34)

Just as the virtuous conduct (*śīla*) of a devoted wife—her *pātivratya*—is praised because it arises from love for her husband and is under the influence of affection for him; likewise, through devotion to Śiva and love toward Śiva, one who is "unseparated" (*abhakta*) is a "refuge" (*śaraṇa*), meaning one possessed of excellent character (*suśīla*). This is because the relationship between the refuge and the *liṅga* has been described as being like that of a chaste wife and her husband.
The illustration of a devoted wife has been told. || 34 ||
Now he clarifies this very point:
"Just as for women, service to anyone other than their husband is censurable, so too for those of purified self, service to anyone other than Śiva is blameworthy. (35)

Just as for women, service to another man— that is, any other person besides their husband, who is the beloved of their very life— is censurable and condemned, so too for those of perfected self, who have accomplished their purpose and have taken refuge in Śiva,
service to others— such as Viṣṇu and other deities— besides Śiva, that is, the Śivaliṅga, is to be condemned.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 35 ||
257) Now, summarizing the meaning already stated, he says: "What is the use of saying more here? [It is simply] being solely devoted to the knowledge of Śiva."
This is called "virtue" by the virtuous; one who possesses it is considered devoted to that supreme goal. || 36 ||
In this matter of ethical conduct (*śīla*), what is the use of much talk?
Devotion solely to the knowledge of Śiva—that is, steadfastness in the knowledge of Śiva as instructed by the venerable Guru—is what is called "ethical conduct" (*śīla*) by the virtuous.
One who is intent upon that and attached to that conduct is considered, that is, recognized, as being "possessed of ethical conduct" (*śīlavat*). This is the meaning. || 36 ||
Then, concluding the section on Śaraṇa— where one who possesses such conduct attains identity with the Śivaliṅga through refuge alone— it says:
"One who delights solely in the awakening to the Self as Śiva is firm in resolve."
Having taken refuge in Śiva, the sovereign lord of the worlds,
and being adorned with a character dedicated solely to Śiva,
he is indeed called by the wise "one who has attained identity with Śiva" (śivaikyavān). || 37 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Four Stages of Seeking Refuge," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Śivayogin named Reṇukācārya, a knower of the Brahman in the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). || 13 ||

Delighting solely in the realization of the self as Śiva, being firmly established in the knowledge that the Liṅga and the body are one, he has taken refuge in Śiva, the Lord of the worlds, saying "Protect me"; having gone for shelter with a steady disposition,
his mind is endowed with a firm state of devotion toward the husband of Satī, who is the refuge of Śiva.

The meaning is that he is indeed well-known as being described by the wise who are proficient in the Śiva scriptures as "one whose ornament is conduct dedicated solely to Śiva," "one whose form, conduct, and ornaments consist of devotion solely to the Śivaliṅga," and "one who possesses oneness with Śiva. This is the established sense. || 37 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Occasion of the Four Abodes of Śaraṇa," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the Padas, Vākyas, and Pramāṇas. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter: Now, the Section on Unity.
Then the Question of Agastya—Agastya said:

Since there is a connection with the abandonment of falsehood, and likewise because of the instruction regarding conduct, how can the unity of this [path] known as "Refuge" be further established? (1)

Because it dispels the portion of darkness, because it is designated as knowledge, and likewise because it accomplishes ethical discipline— how can this [refuge] be defined as a unity merely on that basis, given that the sign (liṅga) and the limb (aṅga) are constituted by difference? || 1 ||

He provides the answer, saying: "The venerable Reṇuka said"—"One who has attained supreme bliss through the yoga of the vital-force-liṅga (*prāṇaliṅga*) and so forth, known as 'the refuge' (*śaraṇa*), shall become one with Śiva through the cultivation of the realization of identity. (2)
Through the yoga of the *prāṇaliṅga* and other internal forms,

by turning away from the worship of external *liṅgas*, and through the yoga of meditation on the worship of the internal *liṅga*, one named Śaraṇa attained— meaning he obtained— the supreme bliss, the supreme bliss of Śiva, by means of Śiva in the form of the *śivaliṅga*.

The meaning is that through the contemplation of oneness (*aikyabhāvanā*), that is, through the reflection upon unity, one becomes possessed of oneness—that is, possessed of oneness with the Śiva-liṅga.

This is the underlying idea: a difference between the Liṅga and the Self is not possible, because both are of the single nature of consciousness (*cidekarūpatva*). If it is objected that even if they are of the nature of consciousness, there is still a difference in their individual manifestations (*vyaktibheda*), it is replied: that individual soul (*jīva*) is either of the nature of a limited manifestation of consciousness, or...

Or is it of the nature of an undivided luminosity of consciousness (*citprakāśa*)? Not the first [option], because, like the limited luminosity of objects such as a jar, it would be restricted solely to its own object; consequently, with respect to other objects and the essential natures of others, it would be as if blind and deaf, such that one could not perceive:
"Caitra is distinct from Maitra," "Maitra is distinct from Caitra," or "I know Caitra," "I know Maitra."
I know—thus, because the connection between the external and the internal is not possible, for the manifestation "I am Caitra" is grounded solely in that [subjectivity] alone. (p. 260)

Because both the essential nature of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and its object are, for all practical purposes, like those who are blind and deaf [to each other], there would be no manifestation such as "I am loving-kindness.

Now, if it were an undifferentiated manifestation, the acceptance of two such distinct manifestations would be impossible, because the relationship of the served and the server (*sevyasevakabhāva*) and so forth could not exist when there is unity of manifestation; therefore, one must resort to an imagined distinction (*kalpitabheda*) within that unity.
Because that [consciousness] arises from it, the identity of light must be accepted;

for since both the words "all" and "not-all" fall within the range of effects of Māyā and are thus intermediate, knowledge and agency alone are innate. Therefore, by contemplating their oneness, one becomes possessed of unity. || 2 ||
Now, to the question of whether there are also different stages for this [practice], he says:
"O bull among sages, this stage of unity is said to be fourfold:
unity, the perfection of conduct, and the single vessel."
The characteristics of these, beginning with "eating together," are stated in order. || 3 ||
This is clear. || 3 ||
That becomes one alone; it is non-conceptual, yet not even non-conceptual. There is no division whatsoever here; there is truly no division here at all.
One who perceives a division here becomes split a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and goes from death to death. This very reality is self-luminous. (Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad 8.7)
Thus, in accordance with the *Uttaratāpanīya* scripture, he establishes the definition of the unity of the subtle body (*liṅgaikya*) through five aphorisms:
"One who is free from desire for even a drop of the pleasure derived from sense objects, and whose inner disposition is pure..."
Through immersion in the great ocean of Śivānanda, oneness is declared. || 4 ||

Being free from desire for even a drop of the pleasure derived from sense objects, and being detached from the mere sprays of pleasure found in objects such as sound, one whose disposition is stainless— that is, one whose mind is pure— attains oneness through immersion in the great ocean of Śiva-bliss, by entering into identity with that great ocean of Śiva-bliss.
The meaning is that it is called the "place of the unity of the *liṅga*. || 4 ||

To the question, "Of what kind of person is such oneness possible?", he says: "One whose connection with impurity has been shaken off, whose mind is stainless, and who is firmly established in the realization 'I am Śiva'—such a one indeed attains oneness with Śiva. (5)

It is well known that one who has warded off contact with the impurities of the individual soul (āṇavamala) and possesses mental activity free from blemish, having established identity with the Śivaliṅga through the reflective awareness "I am Śiva," indeed attains [liberation]. || 5 ||
Now, regarding what one sees when [one realizes] "it does not exist," he says:
Having attained oneness with Śiva, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, one no longer perceives the web of the world, which is a manifestation fashioned by Māyā. (6)
The meaning is that he remains beholding the universe as it is conceptualized by the power of illusion (māyā-śakti). || 6 ||
To the question "Why does he not see that?", it is said:

"The ocean of Māyā—which expands with the bursting of the bubble of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and possesses the waves of the [twenty-five] principles—goes to dissolution in the submarine fire of its unity with Śiva. (7)

The ocean of Māyā— which expands through the bursting of the bubble of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which grows by the manifestation of bubbles in the form of the cosmic egg, and which possesses the waves of the principles (tattva) characterized by the thirty-six categories— goes to dissolution in the submarine fire of the unity with Śiva, that is, in the submarine fire whose nature is the oneness with the Śivaliṅga. For this reason:
There is no perception of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), because the destruction of the effect must necessarily be admitted upon the destruction of its material cause. || 7 ||
(p. 262) Now, he clarifies that very point:
"Due to the concealment by the power of *māyā*, the conceptualization of duality arises with respect to Śiva."
But upon the destruction of that [duality], nothing at all remains for the self other than non-duality.

O Śivā, due to the concealment of the power of *māyā* and the expansion of the self—the individual soul (*jīva*)—there may arise the conceptualization of duality. Upon its destruction—that is, upon the cessation of the expansion of *māyā*—not even the slightest difference from non-duality (*advaita*) is admitted or made an object of desire. (8)

Now, as for the objection: "Since scripture declares a distinction between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) characterized as Lord (pati) and bound soul (paśu), how can it be said that not even the slightest difference is admitted?"—to this [the author replies]:
"I am one; there is no one belonging to me, nor do I belong to anyone else."
I do not see him whom I do not see, nor him who belongs to me.
According to the statement of the *Devikālottara*, he establishes the well-known non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvaita*)— the identity with the *liṅga* of Śiva— through five aphorisms:
"The state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) and the state of being a Lord (*patitva*) are both conceptualized through the delusion of *māyā*."
When that has reached dissolution, who indeed is the bound soul (paśu) and who is the Lord (pati)?
This is clear. || 9 ||
Now, since this saṃsāra has the nature of a serpent dwelling in the anthill of duality, [the author] states what the remedy for it is:
"For the terrible serpent of saṃsāra, which lies within the anthill of duality, the supreme medicine that acts as its antidote is the contemplation of supreme non-duality. (10)

Of the serpent of terrible saṃsāra dwelling within the anthill of duality— characterized by the fivefold distinctions consisting of the distinction between the insentient and the sentient, the distinction between the individual soul and the non-soul, the distinction between the individual soul and the insentient, the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, and the distinction between the insentient and the Lord.

The supreme contemplation of non-duality (*paramādvaitabhāvanā*)—meaning the contemplation of the identity of the insentient and the sentient—is the remedial medicine that counteracts the serpent of *saṃsāra*, which causes fear through birth, death, and so forth. || 10 ||
(263) Now, since this saṃsāra is like a great ocean produced by the cognition of duality, [the author] says in response to the question: "By what means does who cross over it?"—
The teacher crosses the great ocean of saṃsāra, which has arisen from the cognition of duality, by means of the boat of non-dual cognition. || 11 ||
The meaning is that the guide is the oneness with the Śivaliṅga; the remainder is clear. || 11 ||
Now, one might ask: by what is this cycle of existence (saṃsṛti)—which acts as the demon of desire and is the Night of Time (kālarātri)—destroyed? To this he says:
[It is destroyed] when it is intensified by the darkness of ignorance and acts as the demon of desire.
But the night of saṃsāra shall perish by means of the sun of non-duality.
Therefore, for yogis, there is no means equal to the state of non-duality for the cessation of the great torments of terrible saṃsāra. (13)

The night of saṃsāra—which has arisen from the thick darkness characterized by ignorance and is intensified by the gloom of nescience, performing the deeds of the rākṣasa of desire (kāma) and acting as the rākṣasa-characterized passion—is destroyed by the sun of Śiva’s non-duality, the sun of advaita. This is the meaning. || 12–13 ||
Now, having described the excellence of non-dual Śiva with two verses, he concludes the section on unity:
"The bliss that arises from the contemplation of non-duality, even for a single moment—that bliss cannot be attained by those who indulge in sense-objects, even in ten million years. (14)
For the Śiva-yogin, in whom the world is completely dissolved within the fluctuations of the mind, the full manifestation of the bliss of Śiva is designated as liberation. || 15 ||
"By the *bhogins*," meaning by royal *bhogins*; the rest is clear. || 14-15 ||
p.
264) Thus ends the section on Unity;
now follows the section on the Perfection of Conduct.
Now, according to the statement in the *Śivarahasya*: "Just as the sun consumes all flavors and the fire indeed consumes everything,
even so the yogi enjoys sense objects and is not tainted by auspicious or inauspicious karmas"—
[this illustrates] the attainment of right conduct through the identity of the *liṅga*.
He establishes this through twelve aphorisms:

"The teacher who has attained the state of Śiva through the contemplation of the oneness of Śiva is indeed not tainted, even while possessing a body, by his own conduct such as birth-impurity (sūtaka) and the like. (16)

The meaning is that the Guru, having attained the state of Śiva through the singular contemplation of Śiva, and being one with the Śivaliṅga even while possessing a body, is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and is not tainted by birth-impurities (sūtaka) and the like, nor by his own customary behaviors or his own spontaneous conduct. || 16 ||
To the question "Why?", he says:

"When the thorough realization of the non-duality of Śiva is established for the wise, what indeed could remain to be accomplished by ritual actions—whether by what is done or by what is left undone? (17)

For those of noble mind whose mental fluctuations are established in the unity of the Liṅga, once the non-dual knowledge of Śiva has become firm, what indeed could be affected by unperformed action—whether it be evil karma—or by performed good karma?
The meaning is that nothing at all would remain [to affect them]. || 17 ||
To the question "Why is that?", he says:
"By virtue of the realization of the oneness of Śambhu, one who perceives equality everywhere—even while performing great deeds—does not obtain their fruit. (18)

Seeing with equanimity everywhere, regarding clods of earth, stones, gold, and so forth as equal; seeing with equanimity everywhere, unified with the Śiva-liṅga; through the state of oneness with Śambhu, by means of that state of unity, even while performing great karma in the form of merit and demerit.

One would not obtain that fruit; for since everything is seen as being composed of Śiva, there is no staining by it—this is the sense. Whether one be a doer of good or evil, a Brāhmaṇa or even an outcaste (antyaja).
For those who are endowed with the singular state of being Śiva, he certainly becomes like them.

For those who are endowed with the singular state of Śiva, who possess the knowledge of non-difference from Śiva everywhere, and who have attained oneness with the Śivaliṅga— whether they be doers of good or meritorious souls, or doers of evil or sinful souls, whether they be Brāhmaṇas or outcasts, or even dog-cookers— they certainly and decisively become equal and identical. 19.
Now, one might ask: "How can even those who possess the knowledge of Śiva abandon the duties pertaining to their caste and stage of life?
To this, he says:
"What purpose does the knowledge of a knower serve through the constant conduct prescribed for castes and stages of life?"
But worldly right conduct is practiced even in the absence of [visible] results. || 20 ||

For those who have attained the castes and stages of life—meaning those who have entered the castes such as the Brāhmaṇa and the stages of life such as celibacy (brahmacarya)—and for the wise ones who possess knowledge of Śiva, what purpose do the practices of good conduct serve? The meaning is: they serve no purpose at all. Why is this so? To this he says: "But the worldly practice of good conduct..."
The meaning is that the constant and occasional right conduct pertaining to the castes and stages of life is cultivated—that is, it is enjoined—even in the absence of [worldly] results. || 20 ||
Now, one might object: "Since even the wise possess a connection with a body, how can they be abandoned?
For it is heard that there is sin (pratyavāya) in failing to perform [one's duties]. To this, he says:
"For one whose seeds of karma have been burnt away by the fire of stainless knowledge..."
For one who appears as if possessing a body, the worldly maintenance of the body indeed continues.

For the knower of Śiva, whose seeds of karma characterized by merit and demerit have been utterly and completely burnt away by the fire of stainless Śiva-consciousness— being thus devoid of any apprehension of rebirth— there can be no connection with adverse consequences (pratyavāya).

It does not exist at all. By the analogy of a burnt cloth, for one who is like ashes, the maintenance of the body—namely, the worldly activity of moving the hands, feet, and so forth—continues until the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*); thus, it is "unstable" in meaning. || 21 ||
"Then, for him, there is delay only as long as he is not released; then he shall be united [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2].
His sons inherit his property, his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3]
In accordance with the Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage, "He is the Supreme Person; he moves about there" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3), it is said:
"Characterized by stable dispassion attained through the knowledge of Śiva..."
One shall not be stained by one's own karma, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

One who possesses the mark of firm dispassion attained through the knowledge of Śiva and has become one with the Śivaliṅga is not stained by his own actions or by actions performed according to his will, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water; such is the meaning. || 22 ||
Just as even the very swift wind does not travel without the ether (ākāśa),
according to the *Niḥśvāsakārika*, he demonstrates through five aphorisms (*sūtras*) that every action of one established in the Śiva-liṅga is of the nature of worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or even waking, the one of great intelligence is always intent upon the worship of Śiva through union with the knowledge of Śiva.
Mahāmati, being one with the Śiva-liṅga, while walking at the time of walking, standing at the time of standing,

sleeping at the time of sleep, waking at the time of waking, and perceiving objects at the time of perception, is always and continuously intent upon the worship of Śiva through his union with the knowledge of Śiva and his connection with the contemplation of Śiva.
The meaning is that he is established in the *liṅga*. || 23 ||
(267) Now, one might ask: "At the time of perceiving an object, how can there be contemplation of Śiva? To this he says:
Whatever object the Teacher perceives in the worlds with joy...
In various places, there was the attainment of the vision of Śiva for that Great-Souled One.

The Guide, who is one with the Śiva-liṅga, perceives whatever object exists in the worlds— be it a pot, a cloth, or anything else— as being full of fragrance and endowed with joy; in each and every such object, there arises for that Great Soul,
who is one with the Śiva-liṅga, the perfection of the vision of Śiva, the perfection of beholding Śiva, as nothing other than Śiva.
The meaning is that, because there is no other entity [apart from consciousness], the cognition of being composed of consciousness arises. || 24 ||

Now, you are the Self; Girijā is your intellect; the senses are your attendants; the body is your home; the arrangement for the enjoyment of sense objects is your worship; and sleep is your state of meditative absorption.
The movement of my feet is the rite of circumambulation; all songs are hymns of praise;
whatever action I perform, O Śambhu, that entire deed is your worship.

In accordance with the words of the learned, he concludes the section on the perfection of conduct by demonstrating, through three aphorisms, the ritual service (*upacāra*) of the Śiva-liṅga purified in the three instruments (*karaṇa*):
"Whatever a yogin, possessing pure contemplation, contemplates with his mind..."
Meditation on Śiva is declared to consist in perceiving each and every thing as being composed of Śiva. || 25 ||
"Possessing pure cultivation" means being endowed with stainless cultivation. The remainder is clear. || 25 ||
Whatever has been spoken in the world by the Śiva-yogin according to his own will—
all this is a hymn to Śiva, because Śiva is the self of all. (26)
This is clear. || 26 ||
Whatever movement arises for the yogins of Śiva, each and every one of those is always an act of worship for Maheśa, as their very selves are absorbed in Him.

Whatever movement or physical action arises for those Śiva-yogins who have attained oneness with the Śiva-liṅga—those whose very nature has entered into the Śiva-liṅga through identification—that very action is at all times the worship of Maheśa, the Śiva-liṅga; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
Thus, there is the ground of the perfection of conduct;
then, "In the one Imperishable, all become unified" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7); this is the ground of the single vessel.

In accordance with the statement of the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, he establishes through five aphorisms the state of being in a single vessel with the *liṅga* of Śiva for one who possesses all proper conduct:
"For one who always contemplates with their intellect that the universe is composed of Śiva..."
Because its nature consists solely in being the singular vessel for Śiva, it is called the "single vessel. || 28 ||

The meaning is that because the unity of the *liṅga* constitutes the state of being a vessel for the unity with Śiva, and because it has Śiva as its sole support, it is called the "place of the single vessel. || 28 ||
To the question, "What does this accomplish? he says:
Through the vision of the non-duality of Śiva, one's own self and the entire world, by virtue of being joined as a single vessel, there arises the realization of the oneness of grace. (29)

Through the vision of non-duality— meaning the vision of the oneness of consciousness as "I" regarding oneself, one's own self, and all people in the world— there arises, by virtue of being contained within a single vessel, the realization of the oneness of grace; that is, grace from Śiva alone.
One's own grace is indeed one's own grace, which is the grace of Śiva; this very [grace] should be understood as the oneness of grace for the devotee of Śiva who appears as if separate from himself.
The sense is that even the water from the feet of the moving form (caramūrti) is suitable for Śiva as well as for oneself. || 29 ||
Now, if Śiva and the universe are of one and the same nature, how can there be a distinction between them? To this he says:
"In Śiva, this entire universe exists; Śiva shines everywhere.
The existence of the world within Śiva is by way of the relationship between the container and the contained. (30)

The meaning is that the existence of Śiva and the world is through their state of equilibrium (sāmarasya), by way of the relationship of support and supported according to the logic of the seed and the sprout, expressed as "the universe is in Śiva" and "Śiva is in the universe. || 30 ||
Thus, he says that for one who has attained the state of being the sole vessel of consciousness, there is no purpose in illusory differentiation:
"For him whose mental state is the sole vessel of consciousness and consists of the nature of Śiva, what need has he for this other reality rooted in māyā? (31)

For that unity of the *liṅga*—the mental activity of the mind—for which consciousness itself, in the form of the operation of the mind, is the single vessel whose nature is Śiva, the single vessel of the very essence of Śiva;
for him, what purpose is there in this duality rooted in *māyā*, and what utility does it serve? None at all.
The meaning is: "some purpose. || 31 ||
Now, as to how this universe is of the nature of Śiva, he says:
"The intellect illumines the universe; indeed, without it, no object exists. For those whose minds are fixed solely upon the Intellect, what is the use of things imagined by Māyā? (32)

The entire universe—the totality of the phenomenal world characterized by jars and so forth—is illumined by consciousness (*cit*). Without that illumination of consciousness, no object, such as a jar or the like, exists. Even the Prābhākaras maintain that when the existence of an object is admitted, the blessed Consciousness alone is the ultimate refuge. Therefore, whatever appears as dependent upon something else [is that very thing].
(p. 270) "Consisting of this and that, like waves and so forth in water"— thus [it is said] for those whose minds are fixed solely upon Consciousness, regarding [the world] as imagined by Māyā.
The meaning is: what purpose is there in objects of experience belonging to the realm of phenomenal diversity? || 32 ||
Now he concludes the section on the single vessel:
"The yogi who always abides in his own heart, which is devoid of mental activity, merged in Śiva, and undisturbed—he is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (33)

That Śiva-yogin who always abides within his own heart—which is devoid of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), devoid of activity (*vyāpāra*), undisturbed, free from agitation, merged in Śiva, and become one with the Śiva-liṅga—is liberated; the meaning is that he is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*). The sense is that there is no doubt in this matter. || 33 ||
Thus, there is the place of the single vessel,
then the place of eating together; then he swallows that which is not to be swallowed by means of the wind-element with the wind-element, and Soma with the lunar element, by his own [nature].
"Salutations again and again to the one who withdraws [the world] by his splendor, the Great Devourer"—
according to this Atharva Veda scripture, he establishes the state of communal dining for those established in the single vessel through ten sūtras:
The remembrance of the Guru Śiva as one's own true nature is declared to be "eating together," by virtue of the state of being the self that swallows all. (34)

The remembrance of the Śrī Guru, the Śiva-liṅga, and the disciple as being one's own essential nature— through non-difference from one's own self and as not exceeding the notion of "I"— arises from the state of being the Self that swallows all objects, such as: "A pot was known by me," "A cloth was known by me," "Caitra was known by me," and "Maitra was known by me."

The meaning is that "eating together" is precisely the devouring of all differentiation, because it is one's own essential nature; it is the act of re-experiencing an object already perceived by way of its resting within one's own self, characterized as a reflective awareness. || 34 ||
271) Now he states the essential conclusion:
One should constantly unite the auspicious universe and the Guru directly within one's own self.
In the form of consciousness, through oneness, this indeed is the communal meal.

One should eternally unite Śiva, the Guru, and the universe as one—that is, as having a single form—within the Self, which is the direct manifestation of consciousness (*cidākāra*). This "union" consists in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) that they are not distinct from our own nature; this is what is meant by "eating together. In this regard, because the Guru and Śiva are not distinct from our own nature, [they are to be united with us].
The unification with one's own self is possible. One should not raise the objection: "How can a connection with the self be possible for that which is inert and appears as 'this'?
For even that [the inert], according to the aforementioned method, finds its rest in the Self; otherwise, there would be no memory, nor even the cycle of transmigratory existence.
Because it is inherent in the self precisely by virtue of having an object. || 35 ||

Furthermore, he states the essential point: "He who has no such notion as 'this is Śiva,' 'this is the Guru,' 'this is the world of moving and unmoving beings,' and 'I am [this]'—he is the enjoyer of the universe. (36)

He whose intellect is free from the notion of duality—thinking "this is Śiva," "this is the Guru," "this is the Lord," "this is the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving," and "I am [that]"—is one who is unified with the Śivaliṅga;
the meaning is that he is the devourer of the universe, the consumer of the distinctions of the world. || 36 ||
Now, he states the essential conclusion even from this [perspective]:
"I am the servant, Śiva is the master; I am the disciple, and He is indeed the guru"—he whose mind is not thus [dualistic] is established in the state of non-duality (advaita). || 37 ||
He whose mind possesses no sense of duality—such as "Śiva is the master, I am the servant," or "this is the guru, I am the disciple"—is one who has attained oneness with the Śivaliṅga;
the meaning is that he remains established in the state of non-duality (advaitapada), which consists of Śiva's non-duality that swallows up all worldly distinctions. || 37 ||
272) Now, he says that one who is indeed perfected in such a communal meal (*sahabhojana*) is called a "performer of the universal oblation" (*viśvahomī*):
"In the fire of one's own self, which consists of supreme subjectivity (*parāhaṃtā*), shines the light of the universe."
By means of the oblation of "this-ness" (idantā), one is called a performer of the universal sacrifice (viśvahomī). || 38 ||

In the *Viśvaprakāśa*, the meaning is that one is called a "sacrificer of the universe" (*viśvahomī*) by means of the oblation of the sacrificial substance consisting of the form of objectivity (*idantā*) into the fire of one's own self, which is composed of the supreme root-egoity (*ahaṅkāra*). || 38 ||
Now, as to the question "What is this supreme I-consciousness?", he says:
"I am Śiva, I am the Guru, and I am the universe of moving and non-moving beings;
that by which this is correctly realized is known as the Full I-consciousness. (39)

"I am Śiva, I am the Guru, and I am the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings"—it is by means of this consciousness (*citi*) that this is correctly realized. Herein: "That consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which flows by its own inherent savor, is the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*). Having withdrawn the multitude of phonemes from beginning to end, it is the True I-consciousness (*satyahantā*). (Compare with *Citiḥ*).

"Supreme Speech (parāvāk), whose nature is reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) and which arises by its own inherent force (svarasa)— this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self. According to this principle established in the *Pañcāśikā-śāstra*,
[the Lord is characterized] by the absence of any contraction caused by the forms of space, time, and so forth.

Because, prior to the emergence of the gross universe, it exists as the cause thereof— by way of the analogy of the essence within an egg— in its nature as Śiva and Paraśakti, which is manifested by the vibration of the *bindu* characterized by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the objects of knowledge contained therein, resulting from the union of the letters *A* and *Ha* (which are themselves the contraction characterized by the encompassing of all the phonemes of the Mātṛkā that denote those objects).

The meaning is as follows: first there is the "I" in its general sense; subsequently, that which is mixed with other things, not independent, and incapable of appearing as differentiated is called a "reflection. Because it possesses the same characteristics [as a reflection], it is remembered as the "Full I-consciousness" (pūrṇāhaṃtā), which, by way of being a reflection, manifests through its own sovereignty as consisting of the entire universe. || 39 ||

273) Now, he states that one who is initiated into the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*) is indeed one for whom the entire universe, as defined by the aforementioned characteristics, is the sacrificial oblation:
"In the fire of the substratum, which is the nature of consciousness, the world—consisting of the multitude of differentiated entities—is the oblation."
He who performs the sacrifice of knowledge by offering oblations is to be known as the consumer of all sacrificial offerings.

He who offers as an oblation the entire world— the sacrificial butter fashioned by Māyā consisting of all differentiated phenomena— into the fire of consciousness, which is the nature of knowledge and resides in the *ājñācakra*, is to be known as the consumer of the universal oblation (*viśvahavyabhuk*),

the enjoyer of the universal sacrificial butter, the sacrificer of knowledge (*jñānayajvan*), and one initiated into the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajñadīkṣita*). This is how he is to be understood.
This is the meaning. || 40 ||
Now, one might object: "When wood and other such things distinct from fire are cast into perceptible fire, their destruction is not seen;
how then can there be the destruction of the universe when it is cast into the fire of consciousness? To this, he says:
"In the form of consciousness, the supreme ether, shining with supreme bliss..."
For those whose mental fluctuations have dissolved, what indeed remains of the state of universal manifestation? || 41 ||
In the supreme space of the form of consciousness, within the hollow of the pericarp of the upward-pointing heart-lotus,
shining with supreme bliss— that sun known as the Great Liṅga consisting of eternal bliss—
for those whose mental fluctuations have dissolved, whose mental operations have become absorbed, and who possess the unity of the Liṅga;
The meaning is that there is no such thing as "abiding in universal strides" or "the operation of universal activity. || 41 ||
Now, he describes the nature of liberation for that state of oneness with the shared meal by means of two aphorisms:
"In the stainless sky of consciousness, where all worldly congestion has been dispelled..."
One should meditate upon the self as absorbed, by virtue of its nature of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya). || 42 ||
This very knowledge is to be known as supreme; it reveals existence and bliss.
It is called liberation by the wise, for it turns back the delusion of the world.

One should contemplate oneself—the self denoted by the word *aṅga*—as merged within the Great Liṅga, which is the nature of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), free from defects, and devoid of the afflictions such as birth and death; one should contemplate it as being absorbed through a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with that which is of the same genus, without any loss or increase of its own essential nature, and as possessing stable perfection. This indeed is...

The meaning is that she is called "Supreme Knowledge" (parā vidyā) by the virtuous because she illumines the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), is worthy of being known, dispels the delusion of the world, and removes the error of universal duality; thus she is termed "Supreme Liberation" (parā mukti). || 42-43 ||

(p. 274) Now, having stated that this very oneness with the Śiva-liṅga is the dwelling place for the residence of the Goddess of Liberation (mokṣalakṣmī), he concludes the section on the occasion of communal dining:
Through the application of dharma offered to the abode of the Lord and other such acts, one attains a state of singular oneness with Śiva— the most wonderful,
whose nature is the sky of consciousness— and thus becomes directly a recipient of the glory of liberation.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Fourfold Stages of the Unity of Śiva and the Liṅga," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). 14.

He has attained oneness with Śiva— the Śivaliṅga— who consists of the sky of consciousness, who abides in the center of the upward-facing heart-lotus as the very nature of the space of consciousness, who is supremely wonderful and of a most marvelous form, and who, being equal through a state of perfect equilibrium, is free from any loss or increase in his essential nature.

The meaning is that through the application of dharma offered to the abodes of devotees and others by means of union with the Śivaliṅga, and through connection with the virtuous conduct existing in the places of devotees and others, one attains— that is, reaches— the state of being a recipient of the manifest glory of liberation. || 44 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Occasion of the Fourfold Stages of the Unity of Śiva and the Liṅga," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇḍadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 14.
The Fifteenth Chapter:
Now, the Stages of the Liṅga. First, the stage of the initiating guru;

then, from the stage of the devotee and so forth, up to the final stage of oneness with the Śiva-liṅga—consisting of the six stages mentioned, beginning with the *piṇḍa* and ending with communal dining (*sahabhojana*).

The stages for the practice of the *liṅga*—characterized by the unity of the *liṅga* endowed with the conduct of the virtuous as defined across forty-four intermediate sites, which, through being free from the conceptual constructions of caste, stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth, results in the cessation of worldly conduct and the perfection of communal dining—are as follows:

1. **The Stage of the Practice of the Liṅga** (*liṅgācārasthala*): Because it possesses the nature of the *liṅga* due to the perfection of communal dining arising from the cessation of natural worldly conduct through the state of being devoid of the conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpavikalpa*) regarding caste, stage of life, and the like, this constitutes the stage for the practice of the *liṅga*. [The text continues with the enumeration of these forty-four intermediate sites.]
The venerable Rēṇuka explains:

For one who is endowed with the virtuous conduct described in the *Ṣaṭsthala*, the stages of the Liṅga (liṅgasthala), which culminate in liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), are now declared in their proper sequence. || 1 ||

The meaning is that, for one who is endowed with the right conduct (*sadācāra*) described in the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣaṭsthala*), the six stages of the Liṅga (*liṅga-ṣaṭsthala*)—which lead sequentially to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) through identity with the Śiva-liṅga—are now being expounded. || 1 ||
Now follows the inquiry of Agastya. Agastya said:
"The six stages, beginning with devotion and ending with oneness, have been mentioned.
Which are the stages of the Liṅga here, and how many are they?"
This is clear. || 2 ||
Śrī Renuka said: Now, the fifty-seven distinct stages (sthalas) are proclaimed, beginning with the Guru and ending with Jñānaśūnya, and including those such as Bhakta and the rest. (3)

(276) There are fifty-seven distinct categories of *liṅga*-stations, beginning with devotion (*bhakti*) and ending with oneness (*aikya*), which rest upon the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*); these range from initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the conduct of the guru (*guruvṛtti*) and so forth, down to the end of knowledge devoid of emptiness (*jñānaśūnya*).
The meaning is that they are now being described. || 3 ||
Now, he describes the distinctions between the stages of the devotee (*bhakta-sthala*) and the stages of the *liṅga* by means of three verses:
"First, nine stages here are presented based on the stages of the devotee; they are told according to the essence of their qualities. Listen to their names individually. (4)

Here, within the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*) of the *liṅga*, because they take their support from the location of the devotee (*bhakta-sthala*), nine locations are first established as superior by virtue of their essential qualities (*guṇasāra*). The names of these nine locations are stated individually;
the meaning is "listen. (4)

Now he enumerates them: first the station of the initiation teacher (dīkṣā-guru), then the station of the instruction teacher (śikṣā-guru), then the station of the wisdom teacher (prajñā-guru), and thereafter the station of the ritual emblem (kriyā-liṅga). || 5 ||
Next is the stage of the Bhava-liṅga, and after that the stage of the Jñāna-liṅga;
their characteristics are stated as being "self-existent," "supreme," and "mobile."
This is clear. || 5-6 ||
Now,
that in which knowledge is bestowed and the threefold impurity is destroyed is designated as *dīkṣā*; in that [rite], the teacher is considered the *dīkṣā-guru*.
In accordance with this statement from the *Vātulottara*, he explains that the initiation-guru (*dīkṣāguru*) is indeed one with the Śiva-liṅga:

"By which [process] supreme knowledge is bestowed (*dīyate*) and the bondage of the fetters (*pāśabandhana*) is destroyed (*kṣīyate*), that is called initiation (*dīkṣā*); the teacher in that [initiation] is known as the initiation-guru. (7)

By means of which supreme knowledge— the exalted knowledge of Śiva— is given (*dīyate*) according to the root *dā* meaning "to give," [thereby severing] the bondage of fetters, namely the bondage of the fetters such as *mala* and *māyā*, according to the root *kṣi* meaning "to destroy."

That initiation is considered and agreed upon to be "wasted" (kṣīyate) [if performed otherwise]. In that initiation, which is characterized by the activity of consciousness (cit-kriyā), the teacher (guru)—according to the etymology of the root *gṛ* meaning "to swallow"—is traditionally known as the "initiation-teacher" (*dīkṣā-guru*) because he effects the unification with the Śiva-liṅga. This is the meaning.

Now, he clarifies the true nature of the Guru: "He who bestows that which transcends the qualities (guṇātīta), signified by the syllable 'gu', and that which transcends form (rūpātīta), signified by the syllable 'ru'—that which is beyond qualities and form—is known as the Guru. (8)
The letter *gu* transcends the qualities of Prakṛti; the letter *ru* transcends the form of impure Māyā.

He who bestows and instructs that which is beyond qualities and form—the three qualities consisting of the three maṇḍalas, the reality consisting of consciousness, the void, and the luminous lunar digit (*bindu*)—is known as the Guru.
The meaning is that he is traditionally known as the "Guru. || 8 ||
Now, in this context, he clarifies the true nature of the teacher (ācārya):
"Because he gathers together the meanings of the scriptures, firmly establishes them in right conduct, and practices them himself, he is therefore called an ācārya. (9)

Having revealed the meaning of the scriptures—the secret meanings of the Vīraśaiva scriptures—he explains them; he firmly establishes and disciplines his disciples in the conduct (*ācāra*), namely the Vīraśaiva conduct;
and he himself practices the Vīraśaiva conducts. For that very reason—[the word *ācārya* is used in place of *ācārya*].

The reading "āścaryaḥ" (wonderful) is found in the Kaṭhopaniṣad. According to the Śruti of the Kaṭhavallī, "A skilled speaker of this has been found" (Kaṭhopa. 1.2.7), the meaning is that he is called the Ācārya (Teacher). || 9 ||

Then, having provided the etymological derivation of the word *deśika*, he concludes the section on the initiation-guru— stated in two sūtras as being the "Teacher of the World" precisely because of his identity with the Śiva-liṅga— with the following:
The Guru who strives through the yoga that transcends the six paths is Śiva, the Teacher of the Universe, the cause and means for crossing the ocean of Māyā. || 10 ||
"He who bestows liberation through knowledge is known as the *deśika* (guide)," according to this statement from the *Kāmika-āgama*.

The *deśika* thus established strives through the yoga that transcends the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*), by means of the yoga that transcends the six paths—consisting of phonemes, words, and so forth—as proclaimed in the Veda: "O Lord of the Paths, [lead us] to the further shore of the path, the most excellent of paths."
The meaning is that Śiva remains diligent, being one with the Śivaliṅga, the teacher of the world, and the cause of the means for crossing the ocean of Māyā. || 10 ||
Now, as to how he is the teacher of the world, it is said:
"He by whom undivided consciousness is manifested in all things through the power of his own yoga—that teacher is the illuminator of the universe. (11)

In all things— namely, in every object such as blue, yellow, and so forth— that consciousness which is partless and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*) is manifested by him through the power of its own conjunction with the Self and by the force of his own experience;
even at the time when specific objects such as blue or yellow appear, [it manifests] as the partless "I."

Consciousness indeed persists; otherwise, there would be no perception of that which is to be known. Thus it is made clear that the Guru is the illuminator of the universe, meaning he is the light that reveals all things. || 11 ||
Thus ends the section on the initiating preceptor;
now follows the section on the instructing preceptor.
He by whom a disciple is instructed through the means of knowledge, in the relationship of the object to be known and the knower,
is called a *śikṣāguru*.
In accordance with the statement of the *Vātulottara*, [the author] defines the station of the teacher of instruction (*śikṣāguru*):
"This teacher of initiation (*dīkṣāguru*) is the cause for the disciple's training;
he who explains through questions and answers is called the teacher of instruction. (12)
This initiation preceptor, being the awakener of the disciple, is the expounder of questions and answers;
having provided the answer to the question posed by the disciple, he is also the cause of instruction, acting as the one who imparts that instruction.
The meaning is that he is called a "teacher of training" (śikṣāguru). || 12 ||
Now he clarifies this very point:
"This one is declared to be the teacher (bodhaka), and this is clearly the subject to be understood (bodhya);
he by whom the disciple is thus engaged is called the preceptor of instruction (śikṣāguru). (13)

The meaning is that this [work] is the expounder of the Śiva-siddhānta and the illuminator of the supreme reality (*paratattva*). This is clear from the statement of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas): "There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words; all knowledge appears as if permeated by speech" (Vākyapadīya 1.123, second half).

The meaning is that the teacher by whom the disciple— who has been fully instructed— is enjoined and directed so that he may understand this knowledge of Śiva-yoga, which has become manifest through the instructions of the *deśika*, is called the *śikṣāguru*. || 13 ||

Now, in accordance with the Śruti passages, "The teacher is the prior form, the pupil is the subsequent form, and knowledge is the junction" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2–3) and "The teacher instructs the pupil" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1), he describes its nature through these two aspects:
They declare him to be a Teacher whose words proceed forth like the rays of the autumn moon, which dispel the darkness of saṃsāra.
They declare him to be a true teacher (ācārya) whose words and instructions proceed like the rays of the autumnal moon for the destruction of the darkness of saṃsāra. || 14 ||
They know him to be the best of teachers who bestows the knowledge of the Self that removes the world-illusion and provides the means for the cultivation of non-duality. (15)

To him who bestows— that is, reveals— the knowledge of Śiva as non-different from one’s own self, as proclaimed in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad: "The Lord of the universe, the Self of the Lord, the eternal, auspicious, and infallible" (NārU 13.1)— a knowledge which removes the illusion of the world and dispels the delusion of dualistic distinctions in phenomenal existence.
They know him as the best of teachers, the most excellent of teachers; the meaning is that they understand him as such. || 15 ||
Then, with two aphorisms, he states that a teacher who is endowed with the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva and who removes the doubts of his disciples is indeed the most excellent:
"Having adopted the prima facie view consisting of the conceptualization of the duality of the world..."
This Guru, who has established the doctrine of non-duality, is preeminent in his virtues. || 16 ||

Having taken up—that is, having accepted—the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) characterized by the dual variety of worldly distinctions consisting in the conceptualization of the world's diversity, this teacher, who maintains the final doctrine (siddhānta) of non-duality, is indeed the Teacher of Instruction;
the meaning is that he is superior and most excellent because of his excellence [in wisdom]. || 16 ||
He whose stream of pure eloquent speech is an axe for utterly cutting down the thicket of the forest of doubt—he is the crest-jewel among gurus. (17)

The stream of whose well-spoken words is stainless and pure—that stream of the teacher’s instructional speech which serves as an axe for utterly cutting down the thicket of the forest of doubt, an axe for completely clearing away the wilderness of uncertainty—he is the crest-jewel among teachers; this is the meaning of "the most excellent. || 17 ||
Now, he further elucidates this very point with two verses:
"He in whose expansive mirror of eloquent speech the splendor of liberation is always seen in the form of a reflection—he is the Guru who delivers one across [the ocean of existence]. (18)

He in whose stainless mirror-disk of the spoken word of instruction the Fortune of Liberation is seen— that is, manifests in the form of a reflection— is the Guru who delivers one across [the ocean of existence].
The meaning is: "the one who carries [beings] across the ocean of saṃsāra. || 18 ||
Then he speaks by way of another method: "Who could be equal to that Guru who himself illuminates the inner heart of his disciples with this lamp of knowledge? (19)

That glorious Guru who, by means of the lamp of knowledge—the light of wisdom—illuminates and reveals the painting of his own form residing within the lotus of the heart, which is the inner canvas of his disciples: with whom could this Guru, the teacher of instruction, be equal? The meaning is that no one is his equal. || 19 ||
