Now, regarding whether such a guru exists or not, having stated that he is difficult to find, the author concludes the section on the teacher of instruction: "By virtue of bestowing the supreme medicine of the realization of non-dual supreme reality..."
By whom can that Teacher, the destroyer of the disease of saṃsāra, be obtained? || 20 ||
The meaning is that it cannot be obtained by anyone who is devoid of Śiva’s compassion. || 20 ||
Thus ends the section on the Preceptor of Training;
now follows the section on the Preceptor of Knowledge.
He by whom knowledge that investigates the nature of Śiva is taught for the sake of attaining liberation to one desiring liberation is called a *jñānaguru*.
In accordance with the statement from the *Vātulottara* (p. 282), he describes the station of the Knowledge-Guru (*jñānaguru-sthala*) as follows:
"He who effects the severance of doubt regarding the instructions of the teacher."
He is remembered as the direct bestower of right knowledge, this very teacher of wisdom.

The teacher of the secret meanings of the instructions, the one who provides instruction, the one who cuts through doubt, and the remover of the student's uncertainty— this very preceptor of training (śikṣāguru) is rightly the bestower of knowledge directly; being Śiva manifested in person as the giver of knowledge, he is remembered as the "Knowledge-Guru" (jñānaguru).
This is the meaning. || 21 ||
Now, as to what the knowledge of Śiva is like and how one realizes it directly, he says:
"He who, through reasoning, directly realizes the sky of consciousness—which is free from the distinctions of the universe and devoid of modification—is called a Guru of Knowledge. (22)

By means of reasoning, through the investigation of the subject— the blue, the white, and so forth— which appear with extreme clarity, one arrives at the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) which is free from modification and has dispelled all worldly distinctions by the force of the realization of emptiness, thinking, "I was not aware of anything; all diversity has been negated."

The meaning is this: since the attainment of the ultimate subject (pāramārthikapramātṛ) is taught here, he who makes it directly manifest through the reasoning of his own experience as set forth in the Śivādvaita scriptures is the "Guru of Knowledge" (jñānaguru). || 22 ||
Now, he introduces the knowledge of Śiva with two aphorisms:
"That moon possesses a spot and is overwhelmed by waning and waxing;
but the moon of knowledge, being free from change, remains stainless. (23)
This moon, possessed of a spot, is overwhelmed by waning and waxing and is afflicted by waning and waxing;
however, the moon of consciousness—the moon of gnosis—remains free from modification, devoid of change, and established in stainlessness, meaning it abides without any blemish. || 23 ||
A lamp fashioned from jewels dispels the darkness situated nearby;
the unrestrained lamp of awakening dispels all-pervading darkness. (24)
Just as a lamp fashioned from jewels or gems dispels the darkness situated nearby,
so too the lamp of awakening, the lamp of consciousness— unrestrained and unimpeded— dispels all-encompassing darkness everywhere.
The meaning is that it dispels the darkness that is already present. || 24 ||
Now, with two verses, he introduces the venerable Guru, who is intent upon the instruction of the knowledge of Śiva:
"The Jñānācārya is intent upon imparting the specific knowledge that accomplishes all goals; he is Śiva himself, bestowing grace upon all. (25)

The meaning is that the Knowledge-Guru alone— who is intent upon the instruction of the specific knowledge of Śiva that accomplishes all purposes characterized by both worldly enjoyment and liberation— is the direct Śiva who bestows grace upon all those seeking liberation. || 25 ||
He whose sidelong glance is a moon that increases the ocean of knowledge and cuts through the darkness of saṃsāra— that guru has reached the further shore of wisdom.

The glance of that teacher is a moon that increases the ocean of the knowledge of Śiva and cuts through the darkness of saṃsāra; he is the Guru, the Śrīguru, who has reached the further shore of knowledge—the meaning being that he has attained the farthest limit of both supreme (para) and non-supreme (apara) knowledge. || 26 ||
Now, describing that very Guru as the sun and establishing his superiority even over it, he says:
"This sun is proclaimed as the dispeller of external darkness;
but the all-pervading sun that is the Teacher is the destroyer of both external and internal darkness. (27)

This Sun is the dispeller of external darkness, the remover of outer obscurity; he is the all-pervasive Lord, the Sun who is the Teacher, the Sun who is the Preceptor of Wisdom, cutting through both outer and inner gloom. He shatters the ignorance residing in objects, which thinks "this is not Śiva," as well as the internal ignorance which thinks "I am not Śiva."
Thus it has been proclaimed. || 27 ||
284) Now, having indicated the knowledge of Śiva which makes Śiva known, he concludes the section on the Guru of Knowledge with two sūtras:
That in which one realizes the state of Śiva through a mere glance, without the conceptualization of meditation and the like, is considered the Śāmbhava Veda.

Without the conceptualization of meditative absorption (dhyāna), retention (dhāraṇā), and so forth, by the mere glance of the compassionate side-long look of the venerable Guru, one should contemplate the state of Śiva; that which becomes manifest is known as the Śāmbhava Veda—this is the meaning of "it is considered" (sammata). || 28 ||
He who bestows the pure knowledge that makes one a knower of Śiva, by which the disciple becomes liberated while living—he is a guru who is an ocean of wisdom. (29)

The meaning is that when the illustrious Guru has bestowed the stainless knowledge of Śiva—which is skilled in making manifest the state of one's own self as Śiva within the hand of the Veda of Śiva—the disciple becomes liberated even while living; such a Guru is the "Ocean of the Knowledge of Śiva. || 29 ||
Thus ends the stage of the Guru of Knowledge (jñānaguru-sthala).
Now follows the stage of the Symbol of Action (kriyāliṅga-sthala). Regarding this, the Ārṣeṇī Śruti states: "One bestows desired vigor through austerity. This [text] serves as a commentary upon that.
The entire great site of the chosen *liṅga* is perceivable by the faculty of sight;
it directly bestows the attainment of desired goals and wards off the undesired.
The Atharvaṇa Śruti declares that it is called the "desired liṅga" because it always bestows the desired vigor upon its devotees.

By this statement from the *Vātula-tantra*, he establishes through seven aphorisms that the "station of the mark of action" (*kriyā-liṅga-sthala*) is where the ritual action taught by the Guru of Knowledge reaches its dissolution:
"Where ritual action dissolves through the yoga of the Guru’s realized knowledge..."
That which has action as its characteristic mark is called the verb (ākhyāta) by all those who have reached the further shore of the Āgamas.
In that locus where the ritual action of the Guru— the Teacher of Knowledge— dissolves through the yoga of higher knowledge (*vijñāna-yoga*), that is the *kriyā-liṅga*.

The meaning is that this has been declared and proclaimed by all the Vīraśaiva Ācāryas who have reached the further shore of the Śiva-siddhānta and have mastered the scriptures, according to the traditional teaching: "The optative suffix (liṅga) is used when there is a desire for an action. || 30 ||
Now, as to what its essential nature is, he says:
"The Supreme Brahman alone, whose form is supreme bliss and consciousness, appears as the Linga, having assumed the nature of existence, for the sake of the manifestation of the universe. (31)

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman alone— which is eternal bliss by nature, which is reality, which is inward-turned knowledge by nature, and which is pure existence— having become the "liṅga" (the sign) for the sake of the manifestation of the universe and for the accomplishment of all virtuous activities, is characterized as the "iṣṭaliṅga" (the chosen sign). || 31 ||
Now, as to how that perfection (siddhi) comes about, he says:
"The linga alone is the supreme light, it is the absolute Brahman.
Therefore, from its worship alone arises the fruit of all actions. (32)
The supreme light, whose nature is the absolute, is the Supreme Brahman alone, which is the indicative mark (liṅga) for the purpose of ritual action.
Therefore, from the worship of that alone arises the fruit of all actions; the meaning is that there occurs the manifestation of the fruits of all virtuous deeds. || 32 ||
Therefore, he says that the *liṅga* alone is supreme:
"Having abandoned all ritual actions, all yogins abide solely intent upon the worship of the *liṅga*; therefore, the *liṅga* is distinguished [as superior]. (33)

All yogins—all yogins beginning with Sanaka and the rest—having abandoned all activities, including the entire range of practices such as yoga, remain solely intent upon the worship of the *iṣṭaliṅga*; therefore, the meaning is that the *kriyāliṅga* is superior. || 33 ||
(286) Now, one might ask: on what basis did Sanaka and the others renounce ritual acts such as sacrifice? To this he says:
"All ritual acts, such as sacrifice and the like, are commensurate with a portion of the worship of the *liṅga*."
Thus, that which is worshipped by the Siddhas is called the *kriyā-liṅga*.

The meaning is that all rituals such as sacrifices and the like partake only of a fraction of the worship of the *liṅga*; therefore, because the *liṅga* is worshipped by the perfected ones (siddhas) such as Sanaka and others, it is called the "action-liṅga" (*kriyāliṅga*), the *liṅga* which is the goal of all ritual actions. || 34 ||
Therefore, he says that for one who is perfected in the worship of the *liṅga*, no other ritual action whatsoever is required:
"What is the use of sacrifices such as the *agnihotra* and the like? What is the use of austerities difficult to perform?
He whose devotion is fixed on the worship of the *liṅga* is successful in all undertakings. (35)
"In all rites" means in the domain of every ritual action; "accomplished" (siddha) means possessing success (siddhimān). The remainder is clear. || 35 ||

Now, having stated that even Brahmā and the others, being endowed with the accomplishment of activities such as the creation of the universe solely through the greatness of the worship of their chosen *liṅga*, shine resplendent in their respective abodes,
he concludes the section on the *kriyā-liṅga*:
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, have taken refuge in the Liṅga;
as perfected beings (siddhas) presiding over the governance of the universe, they shine in their respective stations.
"Siddhāḥ" means those who are well-known; "jagattantrādhikāriṇaḥ" means those who possess the authority for activities such as the creation of the world. The rest is clear. || 36 ||
Thus ends the section on the signs of action;
now follows the section on the signs of state (bhāva).

According to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (5.14), which states: "Those who know the Lord— who is graspable through existence, called the 'nestless,' the supreme cause of both existence and non-existence, and the creator of the emission of the *kalās*— they have abandoned the body," the *niṣkala-liṅga* would be graspable through existence (*bhāvagrāhya*).

In accordance with the statement from the Vātula Tantra, "the highest of the high," he defines the locus of the *bhāvaliṅga*—the *prāṇaliṅga* which serves as the cause for the dissolution of *bhāva*—wherein even *bhāva*, like *kriyā*, attains dissolution: [The text continues: ...and according to the statement of the Vātula Tantra, "the highest of the high," he defines the locus of the *bhāvaliṅga*—the *prāṇaliṅga* which serves as the cause for the dissolution of *bhāva*—wherein even *bhāva*, like *kriyā*, attains dissolution.
Just as action reaches dissolution, so too does existence (bhāva) dissolve;
that state wherein this occurs is clearly called the "liṅga of existence" by the teachers.
Just as the place where action dissolves is the linga of action, so too the place where existence dissolves is the linga of existence;
and that which serves as the cause for the dissolution of existence is the prāṇaliṅga—this is the meaning clearly stated by the teachers. || 37 ||

Now, as to what the distinction between these two is, he specifies the characteristic of *bhāva* (the state of being) with two verses: "The Supreme Lord Śiva, the Divine, is perceived through *bhāva*.
What can be done for Him? For He is remembered as eternally perfect. (38)

The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers, is grasped through *bhāva*—that is, he is revealed by the activity of the stainless internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Therefore, what purpose is there in external ritual action? The meaning is: none at all. Why is this so? To this he says: "For that Supreme Lord..."
Because He is remembered as eternally full and eternally satisfied for that reason, the meaning is that there is no purpose in the worship of ritual actions. || 38 ||
The Supreme Śiva, whose nature is unbroken supreme bliss and consciousness, becomes gracious toward devotees through ritual service and the yoga of inner disposition. (39)

The Supreme Lord Śiva, whose nature is consciousness of unbounded supreme bliss, becomes pleased—that is, he becomes gracious—through the yoga of bhāva (devotional disposition), which consists of the mental placement [of the deity] by means of mental offerings preceded by devotion on the part of the devotees of Śiva; this is the sense in which the bhāvaliṅga is praised. || 39 ||
Therefore, he states explicitly that the *bhāvaliṅga* alone is superior: "The *bhāvaliṅga* excels the *liṅga* fashioned from clay or stone."
Because all defects have been cast out and because of the entry into the path of knowledge. || 40 ||

The *bhāvaliṅga* (the liṅga of being) is superior—that is, distinguished—from a *liṅga* fashioned from clay, stone, or other materials; it is superior because it is free from all defects, being devoid of such flaws as cutting or splitting. To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
"Because it is free from all defects. This means it is devoid of defects such as being cut or split.
"Because of entering the path of knowledge. || 40 ||
Now he describes the one who possesses the internal sign (bhāvaliṅgin):
"Having abandoned external signs and remembering the sign of consciousness (cilliṅga) in the mind, he who worships with the flowers of internal disposition (bhāva) is called a bhāvaliṅgin. (41)

He who, having abandoned external lingas fashioned from clay, stone, and so forth, remembers within his mind the heart-lotus that linga consisting of consciousness— famous in the Atharva Veda as the "linga of the vital breath within"—
and worships it with the flowers of devotion, namely the eight flowers of non-violence and the rest conceived through contemplation; he [is such].
"Bearing the liṅga of being" (bhāvaliṅgī) means that he is said to possess the vital-force-liṅga (prāṇaliṅga) which has become the object of his being. || 41 ||
Now, it is said that he alone who worships that *prāṇaliṅga* is a Śiva-yogin:

"Worshipping the extremely pure liṅga, which is shaped like a lamp, either in the *mūlādhāra*, in the mind (*citta*), or between the eyebrows with the substances of meditative visualization (*bhāva*), he is a possessor of yoga. (42)

In the *mūlādhāra*, in the root-lotus, or else in the mind at the center of the heart, between the eyebrows, or in the upper heart— within the center of the heart-lotus— one should meditate upon that which is shaped like a lamp, the essence of the Vedas, consisting of the *praṇava*, inconceivable, and accessible to yogis through meditation.

He who worships with the substances of inner disposition—that is, with the previously mentioned flowers of disposition—the *liṅga* known as the *prāṇaliṅga*, which is like the lamp celebrated in the Yoga scriptures and is utterly stainless, is a practitioner of yoga;
the meaning is that he is a practitioner of the yoga of Śiva. || 42 ||
289) Now, having specifically distinguished the worship of being (bhāvapūjā), the Śiva-yogin declares that he is not one who is devoted solely to the external liṅga of ritual action (kriyāliṅga):
Endowed with the light-linga (jyotir-liṅga) as the means of valid knowledge through his own direct experience,
he does not worship a linga made of stone, clay, or wood.

This Śiva-yogin, being united with the *jyotir-liṅga*— the *cinmaya-prāṇa-liṅga* (the life-force-linga consisting of consciousness)— by means of the authority of his own experience, namely the authoritative experience of "I am" which is free from action (*akarmaka*), should not worship a linga fashioned from stone, clay, or wood.
The meaning is that he does not honor [them]. || 43 ||
Then, having distinguished the worship of the Jyotirliṅga established through *bhāva*, he concludes the section on the *bhāvaliṅga* site:
"But that worship which consists of ritual action (*kriyā*) should be known as intended for those of limited consciousness."
But internal worship of Śiva is considered by the wise to be the highest form of devotion. || 44 ||
The worship of Śiva, which consists of ritual action—

that worship whose nature is the performance of rites well-known in the *Karmakāṇḍa*— should be understood as being intended only for those of limited consciousness, namely the ignorant. However, internal worship through devotion (*bhāvapūjā*)...
The worship established in the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa) is considered and approved by the knowers of wisdom—those who possess the complete knowledge of Śiva. || 44 ||
Thus ends the section on the signs of spiritual disposition (*bhāvaliṅga*).
Now begins the section on the signs of knowledge (*jñānaliṅga*):
That which is inconceivable and immeasurable, manifest and unmanifest, and supreme—

"May that knowledge which is subtler than the subtle be my mind, intent on auspicious resolve. In accordance with this Vedic scripture, that which is declared to be higher than the highest is called the Liṅga of Contentment; it is the unmanifest Supreme Brahman, named Śiva, which transcends all mental conception.

And following the words of the *Vātulottara* that have been set forth, he describes the locus of the dissolution of knowledge (*jñāna*), which reveals the *bhāvaliṅga* and is synonymous with the *tṛptiliṅga*, namely the station of the *jñānaliṅga*:
"Wherein the knowledge that makes that state known attains dissolution."
This has been declared as the sign of that knowledge by those proficient in the meaning of the Śiva-tattva. || 45 ||
The knowledge that makes known the existence of that [object]—that is, the knowledge that illuminates the mark (liṅga) of its existence—is that in which [the object] reaches dissolution.

The meaning is that this has been declared by the Vīraśaivas, who know the secret significance of the Śiva-tattva, as the "mark of knowledge" (jñānaliṅga), which is the mark of contentment that serves as the substratum for knowledge. || 45 ||
Now, he clarifies that very point:

"That Brahman which is realized as being free from the distinctions of the three forms (trimūrti) and possessing a majesty that transcends the three qualities (triguṇa) is declared to be the *jñānaliṅga*. (46)

Brahman— devoid of the distinctions of the three forms characterized as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and transcending the triad of qualities consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas— is realized as the plenitude of the fourth (turya) that is beyond the fourth (turyātīta);
it is made known through the Vedas, the Guru, and direct experience, and is the sign of that knowledge.
The meaning is that [contentment] is called the sign (liṅga) of the satisfaction that serves as the substratum for knowledge. || 46 ||
Now, he characterizes that mark of knowledge with two aphorisms:
"The attainment of action occurs in the gross; the manifestation of being occurs in the subtle;
but in the Supreme Self, which transcends the gross and the subtle, there is only knowledge. (47)

In the gross, which is the desired liṅga in its gross form, there is the perfection of worship in the form of ritual action; in the subtle, the liṅga of the vital breath (prāṇa), there is the arising of internal disposition, the meaning of which is purity; and in the Supreme Self, which transcends both the gross and the subtle—the Supreme Self in the form of the liṅga of contentment—there is knowledge alone. || 47 ||
Now, as to the objection that the gross and subtle forms of Śiva must necessarily be resorted to for the purpose of meditation, he says:
"For the gross forms of the Supreme Self are indeed conceptual constructs."
Moreover, how could they possibly effect the awakening of another, even if it were something subtle? || 48 ||

Since the gross and subtle forms of the Supreme Self are merely imagined by *māyā*, those seeking only liberation have no need for them; therefore, the meaning is that one should practice only that which is the sign of satisfaction consisting of the Supreme Brahman—the realization of the Supreme—and should recognize that alone as being superior. || 48 ||

291) Now, he explains that only one who possesses the supreme, transcendent awakening is truly characterized by knowledge: "But that Brahman which is higher than the high is characterized by supreme bliss."
That by which that which is called Śiva is known is termed a "Jñānaliṅgin. || 49 ||

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman, known as Śiva, which is higher than the high (*parātpara*)—meaning more excellent than the *Śakti-tattva* in relation to the entire universe because it is its substratum—and which is characterized by supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), is that by which one is known; such a person is called a "knower of the *liṅga*" (*jñānaliṅgin*). || 49 ||

Then, having stated that one who possesses the mark of knowledge alone is the supremely liberated, he concludes the section on the mark of knowledge: "Having abandoned external action as well as mental thought, he who abides in the nature of undivided knowledge is indeed liberated. (50)

The meaning is that he who, having abandoned external ritual action associated with the *iṣṭaliṅga*— namely, external ritual worship— as well as mental contemplation associated with the *prāṇaliṅga*— namely, internal meditative worship— and instead worships the *liṅga* of perfect contentment which is the nature of undivided knowledge, is indeed liberated. || 50 ||
Thus ends the section on the marks of knowledge;
now follows the section on the Self: "Having attained the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form; he is the Supreme Person there."
According to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.12.3), which states "he moves about," he who possesses the bliss arising from the thorough knowledge of the *liṅga* of Prāṇa is marked with the sign of Śiva;
having abandoned external ritual action, he himself is called the *liṅga*.

And because of the statement from the *Vātulottara*, "Thus," he establishes that one who possesses the signs of knowledge (*jñānaliṅgin*) alone is truly endowed with the state of self-mastery (*svayaṃsthala*): "Wherein the knowledge that makes known that state [of self-mastery] should dissolve into [higher] knowledge."
This [mantra] possessing that [quality] is declared by the wise to be named after itself. || 51 ||

The meaning is that this one, who possesses the state of abiding in the knowledge that makes known that [reality] and who bears the marks of knowledge, is designated by the wise— those who possess the knowledge of Śiva— as "one whose own name is the mark" (*svābhidhāna-liṅgin*) and "one whose own name is the mark" (*svayaṃ-liṅgābhidhāna*).
Now, he elucidates his conduct through four aphorisms:
Content with his own spontaneous conduct, devoted to the Jyotirliṅga,
with all forms established within himself, he was the best of sages, known by his own name.

The meaning is that one who is devoted to the *jyotirliṅga*, who is established in the *cilliṅga* (the consciousness-liṅga) through aversion to external liṅgas, who is content with his own conduct, and who possesses all forms within the self of Śiva— he alone, the best of sages, is truly designated as a *svayamliṅga*. || 52 ||
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, having cast off the five afflictions, subsisting on alms, and possessing equanimity of mind, the sage becomes one who is almost liberated. (53)

Free from the sense of "mine" regarding sense objects, free from the egoistic conceit of "I" regarding the body and so forth, devoid of the five afflictions such as ignorance, subsisting on alms-food, possessing an equal mind toward clods of earth, stones, and gold, the sage who bears his own characteristic marks is a *yati*, one who is almost liberated.
He would be similar to one who has attained final liberation because he possesses his last body. || 53 ||
Content with whatever is obtained by chance, devoted to the sacred ash, and having conquered his senses, the yogi should maintain an even disposition toward both a mendicant and a king. (54)
This is clear. || 54 ||
Beholding all beings situated in the cycle of existence in every respect,
the wise one, smiling, abides with his self merged in supreme bliss. (55)

The wise one, possessing excellent intellect, himself observing all beings everywhere throughout the entire cycle of worldly existence, smiling with wonder and filled with amazement, has his self dissolved— having attained absorption— in the Great Liṅga consisting of supreme bliss.
The meaning is that it exists. || 55 ||
Then, having described the daily duties of that lord of ascetics, he concludes the section on his own station:
"Meditation on Śiva, as well as knowledge, alms-gathering, and the practice of solitude—these are the four duties of an ascetic; a fifth is not desired here. (56)

Knowledge of Śiva, knowledge of the superiority of Śiva, meditation on Śiva, subsisting on alms, and the practice of solitude—these four are the duties of the ascetic who is a *svayamliṅga* Śiva-yogin. A fifth duty is not made an object of his desire. || 56 ||
Thus [is] the state of being self-established; now, the state of movement:
he who finds delight in the Self, who plays with the Self, who has the Self as his companion, and who finds bliss in the Self—he becomes a self-ruler.

"His movement is at will in all worlds," according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.25.2). One whose self is devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine," who perceives with the singular form of innate awakening, moves having become himself by himself; thus he is known as a *cara*.

And because of the statement in the *Vātulottara*, "Having himself become one who is perfected in the *liṅga*, he wanders about," it is said that [the teacher] is of the nature of the *caraliṅga-sthala*.
Endowed with the knowledge of his own true nature, with the forms of "I" and "mine" destroyed, he moves having become himself by himself; thus he is designated as "the Moving One" (cara).

The word "svayaṃliṅgī" (one who is his own liṅga) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. One who has cast off the notions of "I" and "mine," and is endowed with the knowledge of his own true nature, is a *svayaṃliṅgī*; the meaning is that he moves about having himself become his own [liṅga], and thus he is designated as a *caraliṅgin* (one whose liṅga is his conduct). || 57 ||
Now, he explains the conduct of that mobile liṅga through five sūtras:
"Free from desire, anger, and the like, endowed with tranquility and self-restraint, the yogi should move about everywhere with equanimity, perceiving Śiva in all things. (58)
This is clear. || 58 ||
Forming no such thoughts as "this is superior" or "this is inferior," the yogin should move everywhere while contemplating that "everything is Brahman. (59)
The term *yogī* means a *śivayogī*. The remainder is clear. || 51 ||
Established in his own immutable self, the yogi should move about without feeling delight in honors nor distress in insults. (60)
Established in his own immutable self— the innate form characterized as the inner Self witnessed by the fourth state—
the Śiva-yogī should move about, neither feeling delight in honors nor suffering pain in insults, remaining indeed without performing [such reactions]. 60.
Amazed by his own extraordinary qualities, causing everyone to wonder,
he should move about like an ordinary embodied being, rejoicing in the supreme bliss of non-duality. (61)

The Śivayogin, satisfied by the supreme bliss arising from the non-duality of Śiva, moves about like an embodied being— meaning he wanders— while causing all people to be filled with wonder by his own extraordinary, supermundane qualities. || 61 ||
The wise ascetic, whose mind has transcended all partiality toward his own body, its worldly diversions, religious duties, or misdeeds, moves about like an ordinary embodied being.

One whose intellect is free from partiality—meaning one whose mind is devoid of biased judgment regarding injunctions, prohibitions, and the like—who is steadfast (dhīra) with a stable mind, such a Śiva-yogi, even while possessing his own body, does not "act like a body" within the phenomenal world (prapañca);
that is to say, he does not engage in meritorious deeds (dharma) nor does he engage in sinful deeds (pāpa). || 62 ||
Now he concludes the section on the Caraliṅga:
With his mind turned away from the attainment of worldly sovereignty, established in his own self which is the bliss of consciousness, the best of sages rejoices. (63)

The meaning is that the best of ascetics, whose mental fluctuations have turned away from the abundance of power belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others arising from the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva), and who is established in the true nature of consciousness and bliss, rejoices, remaining while experiencing happiness. || 63 ||
Thus, having known that "I am that Brahman" through the moving state, the stationary state, and the transcendent state, one attains the supreme Brahman; thus is immortality. (Brahmabindu Upaniṣad)
From the *Brahmabinduśruti*:
"Having attained its own selfhood by itself, it moves; no other [agent] is recorded.
Therefore, because he has transcended the [distinctions of] castes and stages of life, he is remembered as the Supreme.

And because of this statement from the *Vātulottara*, he establishes through seven sūtras that for that sovereign Śiva-yogin who moves about as one whose own nature is self-established, there is no "higher" [state], thus demonstrating the locus of the supreme sign (*paraliṅga*):
"Having himself become himself, he moves about by virtue of his own essential nature."
The "supremacy" of awakening is designated as such because there is nothing beyond it.

The meaning is that for that Śiva-yogin who, having himself become the Self, moves about, the state of "supreme liṅga" is predicated of his knowledge that there is nothing higher than his own true nature. || 64 ||

Now he describes the manner of his conduct: "Independent in all his actions, having cultivated the notion that his own self is another, the sovereign of Śiva-yogins conducts himself while treating the entire web of the world as if it were a blade of grass. (65)

The meaning is that the sovereign of Śiva-yogins, the lord of Śiva-yogins— who has contemplated and grasped himself as "the other" (paratvena) and as being superior to the universe— exists while treating the entire web of the world, the multitude of worlds, as if it were a blade of grass, remaining independent in all his actions. || 65 ||
Now, as to how he rejoices, the author says:
"Turning his back on devotion to the path of conduct prescribed for the castes and stages of life, the yogi rejoices while beholding his own Self as the most exalted. (66)
The "yogi" means a Śiva-yogin; the rest is clear. || 66 ||
Now, as to what this "supremacy over all" is, he says:
"The Supreme Brahman, called Śiva, who transcends the universe and whose nature is consciousness—that very one am I. The knower who possesses such knowledge is said to be supreme over all. (67)
This is clear. || 67 ||
(297) Now, it might be objected that if [the self] has the nature of Brahman, it would be liberated just like Brahman; to this he says:
"Constantly perceiving the Self as immovable and eternal..."
With all delusions dispelled, the sage becomes one liberated while living. || 68 ||
Constantly perceiving the Self as his own nature— unmoving, unwavering, fixed, eternal,
and as an uninterrupted, indivisible whole— and seeing it as non-dual, the sage, the yogi of Śiva,
having cast off all worldly delusion and eliminated the confusion of the phenomenal world, is one liberated while living.
The meaning is that although he continues to live through the processes of eating, speaking, and so forth, he is liberated because there is no further existence in another birth. || 68 ||

Now, one might object: "If the deities of action become angry due to the abandonment of the customary practices pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), how can one be liberated while living? To this, he says:
"What indeed can the deities, beginning with Brahmā—who themselves follow the path of action—do [to one who has transcended it]?"
Of one who stands in the state beyond karma and is himself of the nature of Brahman.

For the Śiva-yogin— who is himself of the very nature of Brahman, who possesses the nature of Brahman, and who stands in the state beyond karma, having transcended the sphere of ritual action consisting of merit, demerit, and the like— what indeed can the deities such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who follow the path of karma, do? Nothing at all.
The meaning is that they are skilled in performing whatever task may arise. || 69 ||
Furthermore, he says that this very Śivayogin liberates ignorance:
"The yogin may move about according to his own will, abandoning the conceit of being a body;
through [his] sights and touches, he may liberate all ignorant beings. (70)

The Śiva-yogin, casting off the conceit of the body and the identification with the body, even while wandering at his own will and being endowed with independent conduct, shall liberate all ignorant worldly people through [their] sight and touch; that is to say, he shall make them liberated. || 70 ||
p.

298) Then, having stated that according to the Śruti, "the stainless one attains supreme divine equality," the Lord of Yogins who possesses the form of the Supreme Liṅga-Śiva is indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta), because he is perfected in the state of Śiva.
He concludes the section on the supreme state:

"The practitioner of self-restraint has attained identity with the Supreme Śiva, who is eternal, whose nature is stainless, incomparable, from whom all worldly delusion is washed away, and whose essence consists of existence, bliss, and consciousness."

Having shattered the shackles of the stages of life (āśrama) and the duties of caste (varṇa-dharma), moving about according to his own will, possessing wondrous majesty like a liberated being, the wise one who is liberated while living reigns supreme. || 71 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Liṅgas within the Stage of Devotion," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the Six Stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). 15.

In the Supreme Śiva— who is eternal, whose nature is stainless, who transcends all comparison, from whom all defects have been cast out, and whose essence is Being-Consciousness-Bliss— one has attained equality through the union with the states of knowing and acting;
having shattered the shackles of the duties of the four castes and four stages of life, he is one whose conduct is free and spontaneous.
Acting according to his own will, liberated while living, a wise yogi of Śiva in the form of another’s body—
who, though possessing a body like others, possesses wondrous majesty and a wealth of greatness that is a source of wonder— he triumphs, meaning he exists with supreme excellence. || 71 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Marks of Devotion," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 15.
The sixteenth chapter: Now, the section on the scripture of ritual action;
then, the inquiry of Agastya. Agastya said:
The nine sacred sites (sthalas) based on the Bhakta-sthala have been proclaimed;
tell me now the classification of the sites within the Māheśvara-sthala. || 1 ||
This is clear. || 1 ||
The illustrious Renuka speaks in reply: Renuka said— "O ascetic, there are nine sites in the region of Maheśvara:
first is the site of the Kriyāgama, and after that is the site of the Bhāvāgama. || 2 ||
Then the stage of the arrival of knowledge (jñānāgamasthala) is described, followed by the stage of the body (sakāyasthala);
thereafter the stage of the bodiless (akāyasthala) is proclaimed, and after that the stage of another's body (parakāyasthala). || 3 ||
Next is the stage of the practice of dharma, then the stage of the practice of bhāva, and finally the stage of the practice of jñāna; thus is their distinction stated in order.
This is clear. 2-4 ||
p.

300) Now, because of the Vedic revelation: "Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, and not others" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1), and because of the statement in the Vātula Tantra: "O Maheśvarī, in Vīraśaiva there is little effort but great fruit."
The Lord of Śiva-yogins, who is endowed with the aforementioned supreme state, is indeed Śiva; his worship alone is "action" (kriyā), and the scripture devoted to that is the Kriyāgama.
Thus, he describes the section on Kriyāgama:
"Śiva is indeed the supreme, manifest reality; his worship is called 'action'."
Since the scriptures are devoted to that, this scripture of ritual action (kriyāgama) has been taught by him. || 5 ||

The supreme one is indeed Śiva himself—the Lord of Yogins who possesses the aforementioned supreme *liṅga*—who has become manifest as Śiva; his worship is called "action" (*kriyā*), meaning it is designated as action. For this reason, the scriptures (*āgamas*) are devoted to that [supreme state], having action as their primary focus; therefore, for that very reason, this...
The meaning is that it is called the Kriyāgama. || 5 ||

Now, he distinguishes that very act of worship with five verses: Just as fire does not manifest in the fire-drill without friction, so too Śiva, who resides within, would not manifest without ritual action (kriyā). (6)

Just as fire in a forest does not manifest without the friction of wood, so too Śiva—who dwells within and resides in the center of the *liṅga*—will not become manifest without the performance of worship; this is the meaning. || 6 ||

Now, regarding how that worship should be performed, he says: "One should perform the ritual action in such a way that there is no lapse in the prescribed rule, so that the Lord may be pleased, and so that the scripture may remain authoritative. (7)

"Omission of the rule" (vidhilopa) means the omission of the restriction characterized by the manner of performance. If there were an omission of the rule, Śiva would not be pleased, and likewise, the scripture would incur invalidity. Therefore, the meaning is that worship must be performed in such a way that no omission of the rule occurs. || 7 ||
(301) Now, as to the question "For what purpose should the worship of Śiva be performed?", he says:
This is an injunction from Śiva; therefore, regarding the prescribed action...
The wise person should remain devoted solely with the intention of worshipping Śiva. || 8 ||

Regarding the prescribed action—that is, the action declared in the scriptures—this injunction (*vidhi*) means that the worship of Śiva must be performed; it is the command of Śiva, taking the form of Śiva’s decree. Therefore, the wise person, being proficient and devotedly attached to the thought of propitiating Śiva, should act accordingly; otherwise, there would be a transgression of Śiva’s command.
The meaning is that he would go to hell. || 8 ||
Now, as to how the method of worshipping Śiva is to be known, he says: "Having received the instruction of the Guru, one should worship the Supreme Lord;
when the Supreme Lord is worshipped, all the deities are worshipped. (9)

One should worship the Śivaliṅga according to the method instructed by the Guru. When that is worshipped, all the gods become worshipped; the meaning is that because the Śivaliṅga embodies all the gods, all the gods become pleased. || 9 ||
Now, to the question "What is the fruit of the worship of Śiva?", he says:
"The yogi whose mind is constantly intent on the collection of means for the worship of Śiva and who is devoted to the yoga of Śiva is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. (10)

The Śivayogin, who is steadfast in Śiva-yoga through the constant procurement of the materials required for the worship of the Śivaliṅga, becomes liberated from the bonds of impurity (mala), illusion (māyā), and so forth; there is no doubt regarding this matter—this is the meaning. || 10 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "From statements such as 'Liberation arises from knowledge alone,' it is understood that knowledge itself is the means to liberation, not action. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "Knowledge is not devoid of action, nor is action devoid of knowledge."
The blind man, not seeing, was burnt; the lame man, though going, was also burnt.
In accordance with the statement from the *Śivarahasya*: "Knowledge and action are mutually dependent, like the blind man and the lame man," he provides the following resolution: [p. 302]...
Therefore, one who is detached regarding the arising of fruits should practice those two. || 11 ||
Knowledge and action, as well as the powers of cognition and activity, are mutually dependent like the blind man and the lame man;

thus, there is this pair, the dyad of knowledge and action. Therefore, the meaning is that one who is dispassionate toward the arising of results—that is, the arising of the fruits consisting of liberation in its higher and lower forms—should practice [these two]. || 11 ||
Now, to the objection that those who have attained perfected knowledge have no need for ritual action, he says:
"Even when knowledge is established, action is also enjoined for the wise;
therefore, one should not abandon action that is free from attachment to its fruits. (12)

Because the scriptural statement "not by action" refers specifically to optional (kāmya) actions, even though knowledge is established for the wise through the Vedānta, action free from expectation of fruit is indeed enjoined— just like the Agnihotra— for one would incur a fall (pātitya) by abandoning the duties prescribed for their respective stages of life (āśrama).
Knowledge is primary, but not devoid of action;
action is primary, but not devoid of consciousness.
Therefore, both together must exist.
For a bird does not fly with only one wing.
And because of the statement by the learned, the meaning is that one should not abandon the performance of desireless action (niṣkāma-karma). || 12 ||
Now, he demonstrates the preeminence of conduct:
"Conduct alone is ordained as the ornament for all;
a person devoid of conduct is censured in the world. (13)
This is clear. || 13 ||
Therefore, having stated that one should be a practitioner of virtuous deeds, he concludes the section on ritual action (*kriyāgama*):
"Through knowledge conjoined with right conduct, Maheśvara is pleased."
Therefore, one should remain possessed of right conduct and knowledge until the fall of the body.
This is clear. || 14 ||
Thus ends the section on the scripture of action;
now follows the section on the scripture of disposition:
"Whatever one worships, that indeed one becomes; according to one's disposition, so one becomes, just as according to one's conduct."

In accordance with the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* statement, "As one acts, so one becomes," and based on the established position of the *Yogaja Āgama* that "Śiva shines forth in the state of being through the contemplation of the state of Śiva," [the author] now defines that for one who is detached and performs actions without desire, the very sign of that state (*bhāvacihna*) constitutes the locus of the *Bhāvāgama*: [The text continues: ...Thus, he explains that for the dispassionate practitioner of selfless action, the indicator of that internal state itself is the ground of the *Bhāvāgama*.
Those signs of the state that belong to the wise man who is free from passion, those very same things exist for all embodied beings as the arrival of the state. (15)

The meaning is that those signs of disposition belonging to the dispassionate, learned, and wise Śiva-yogin— who is detached from the fruits of improper actions— exist for all embodied beings as the source of their worldly dispositions. || 15 ||
Now, with two sūtras, he explains that, in comparison with the previously mentioned conduct of knowledge (*jñānācāra*), it is indeed *bhāva* (inner disposition) that is preeminent:
"The disposition 'I am Śiva' is the cause for attaining the state of Śiva;
neither mere knowledge nor conduct, even when joined with *bhāva*, makes one Śiva. (16)

The sense of "I am Śiva" is the cause for attaining Śiva-hood; the meaning is that mere knowledge alone is not the cause for the attainment of Śiva-hood. Nor is conduct—meaning conduct consisting merely of virtuous actions—the cause for attaining Śiva-hood; rather, it is only when joined with the internal state, namely, the realization "I am Śiva," that it becomes so.
The meaning is that Śiva becomes one whose very nature is auspiciousness (śiva). || 16 ||

(304) Now, as to the question "What is the difference between knowledge (*jñāna*) and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?", he says: Knowledge is the discernment of an object; meditation is the cause for its cultivation.
Therefore, once Mahādeva is known, the wise man should become absorbed in meditation.
The discernment of objects (*vastupariccheda*) is the knowledge that determines the essential nature of an object, thinking "this is such-and-such.

The cause of its existence (*tadbhāvakāraṇa*) is meditation (*dhyāna*), which is the cause for the attainment of the qualities (*dharmalābha*) of the determined object; it is precisely this that is the contemplation "I am that. Therefore, when Śiva is known, one becomes a wise person of excellent knowledge (*sudhīḥ sujñānī*).
The meaning is that he should become one who is joined with meditation and endowed with the [proper] disposition. || 17 ||

Now, as to how one should meditate, he says here: "The most excellent of the wise should meditate upon the Great Lord as completely full within and without, everywhere, for the sake of attaining supreme bliss. (18)
"Internally and externally" means within and without the body; the rest is clear. || 18 ||
Now, he states with two verses and an illustration that such ritual worship is in vain if it is devoid of devotion:
"Just as speech is meaningless, just as a virtuous wife is [worthless] without a husband, and just as intelligence is useless without learning—so too is ritual action without devotion. (19)
"Devoid of sacred learning" (śrutihīnā) means lacking the approval of the Vedic revelation; "intellect" (buddhiḥ) here signifies knowledge (jñāna). || 19 ||
Just as one devoid of sight is unable to perceive any form, so too a yogin devoid of bhāva is not capable of beholding Śiva. (20)
The meaning is that Īśvara is capable. The rest is clear. || 20 ||
One should worship the Supreme Lord with a mind purified by devotion;
He does not accept an offering, however great it may be, if it is devoid of devotion.
"Purified in being" means purified through meditation; "he" refers to that Supreme Lord.
The remainder is clear. || 21 ||
Just as even a worm becomes a bee when occupied with thoughts of wandering bees,
so too one who is pervaded by the thought of Śiva will certainly become Śiva himself.
Thus, in accordance with the words of the *Vīrāgama*, he reveals the greatness of spiritual disposition (*bhāva*):

"When a disposition toward Śiva is cultivated through uninterrupted continuity, that very state of being arises [within one], just as it does for a worm or an insect from the constant contemplation [of its own nature]. (22)
Just as the state of being a bee-worm arises from contemplating a worm, an insect, or a bee, so too, when the mind— characterized by its own mental content—
is perfected through uninterrupted meditation on Śiva, that very state of being arises as the nature of Śiva itself, and one perceives Śiva.
This is the meaning. || 22 ||
Then, having stated that if one is unable to contemplate the partless Śiva (niṣkala-śiva), one should instead contemplate his manifestation (vibhūti),
he concludes the section on the scripture of contemplation (bhāvāgama):
"The supreme Brahman, named Śiva, is stainless and formless."
Even if one is unable to meditate upon it directly, one should contemplate its glory.
"His majesty" (tadvibhūtim) means his great sovereignty consisting of omniscience and so forth; the rest is clear.
Thus ends the section on the attainment of existence (bhāvāgama).
Now begins the section on the attainment of knowledge (jñānāgama).
Now, because of the *Amṛtabinduśruti* stating, "The knower is intent upon higher knowledge (*vijñāna*)," and because of the statement in the *Patiparatantra*,

"This knowledge is established in Śiva," the ground of the tradition of knowledge (*jñānāgama*) is indeed the sign of knowledge for the supreme yogin who is perfected in the realization of that state.
He explains: Whatever signs of knowledge belong to embodied beings, those function as the means for the attainment of knowledge for the sake of liberation. (24)

The meaning is that for ordinary worldly beings (*paśu*), the very signs of knowledge belonging to another— a supreme Śiva-yogin endowed with the realization of existence— function as the source of knowledge for their liberation and for attaining that same state. || 24 ||

Now, according to the Vedic revelation: "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6), and "Having known the God, one cuts the bonds of death" (comparable with Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11: "Having known the God, there is the casting off of all bonds"), [one should proceed].
Having stated that there is no fruit from the previously mentioned pure states of being (*bhāva*) and actions (*karman*), he qualifies knowledge itself with five aphorisms:
"What fruit is desired for men from their state of being (*bhāva*), or what is desired from their actions (*karman*)?"
Knowledge alone, when conjoined with the agent and the object, bestows liberation. || 25 ||
"I am Brahman"—this immediate knowledge (aparokṣajñāna) is what is meant by "knowledge. The remainder is clear. || 25 ||
Even through hundreds of millions of births, liberation for the selves does not arise by means of action alone; for knowledge is indeed the cause of liberation. (26)

For this matter is well-established by numerous scriptural passages such as "Not by action" (Kai. U. 3) and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chā. U. 7.1.3). The remainder is clear. || 26 ||
307) Now, it is not only that there is no liberation through action; rather, he states that if action is devoid of knowledge, it is once again a cause of saṃsāra:
Action devoid of knowledge is always the cause of transmigratory existence for men;
that very same action, through the yoga of knowledge, becomes the means of turning back from transmigratory existence.
This is clear. || 27 ||
Now, as to how action devoid of knowledge can again be a cause of saṃsāra, he says here:
"Since the fruit for men engaged in ritual action is perishable, such as heaven and the like, therefore one should practice knowledge alone in order to attain an enduring fruit. (28)

"Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals" (Bhagavad Gītā 9.21). By the force of such statements, the fruit of heaven and the like for men devoted solely to ritual action is perishable and subject to destruction; therefore, for the attainment of the permanent fruit of liberation, knowledge alone [is required].
The meaning is that one should practice correctly. || 28 ||
To the question, "How indeed should that knowledge be practiced?", he says:
"Through the effort of practicing the scriptures and so forth, and by the instruction of a true guru, one should practice knowledge itself; what need is there for anything else? (29)
Through the effort of studying the scriptures and so forth—
specifically through the diligent study of the Nigamas, Āgamas, and the Siddha-Vīraśaiva scriptures—
and by means of the grace and instruction of a true guru, one should practice *jñāna* alone, that is, the knowledge of Śiva alone.
One should practice correctly.

What is the purpose of any other scripture, such as the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, which was previously employed for the consumption of animal sacrifices? The meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever. || 29 ||
Now, he elucidates the greatness of that knowledge through two aphorisms:
308) Knowledge is the definitive certainty regarding the maturation of the non-duality of Paraśiva.
By which there may be the cessation of connection with saṃsāra for the virtuous. || 30 ||
Knowledge is precisely that mature conviction that there exists nothing other than the mark of the Supreme Brahman;
by means of which knowledge, for the virtuous, the cessation of the affliction of saṃsāra occurs. || 30 ||
Now he clarifies that very point:
"All this is of the nature of Śiva; nothing exists apart from Śiva.
The cognition 'I am Śiva'—that alone is the supreme knowledge. (31)
This is clear. || 31 ||
Now, he illuminates the greatness of that knowledge with two verses:
"Just as a blind man does not see the objects situated before him, so the embodied soul devoid of knowledge does not perceive Śiva abiding within itself. (32)
This is clear. || 32 ||
Now, to the question "What is gained by the vision of Śiva?", he says:
"From the vision of Śiva, there is the cessation of birth and disease for men;
they say that the vision of Śiva is easily attained by those who possess the eye of knowledge. (33)
In this context, the word "syāt" (would be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The connection is that there would be the removal of birth and disease. The remainder is clear. || 33 ||
Therefore, having stated that there is no cessation of ignorance without knowledge, he concludes the section on the attainment of knowledge:
Just as darkness does not cease in a house without a lamp, so too delusion does not cease in the mind without knowledge. (34)
"Without knowledge" means without the knowledge of Śiva; "delusion" means ignorance. The rest is clear.
Thus ends the section on the acquisition of knowledge;
now follows the section on the body—indeed, the body is the primary means for accomplishing dharma. [Kuṇḍalasaṃhitā]

In accordance with the statement, by means of six aphorisms, he establishes the section on "Possessing a Body" (*sakāya*), defining the body of the yogi— who is endowed with that knowledge of Śiva— as the self because it is the cause of action, existence, and knowledge; thus, this world is said to be "possessing a body."
The body of another should be understood as belonging to one who lacks the conceit of bodily action;
by means of that [body], this world possesses a body, because it is defined as having that as its essence. (35)
For the supreme yogin— who, unlike worldly people, is devoid of the conceit of body and action such as "I am fat" or "I am acting," and who is endowed with the aforementioned knowledge—
the body that exists as an object of cognition for others is defined as his very self; thus, it is [the body] of that [yogin].
Because its nature as a self has been defined, this world is "with body" (sakāya), meaning it is accompanied by a body. || 35 ||
Now, one might ask: for what purpose does the supreme yogin, who is devoid of identification with the body, require a body? To this he says:
"Without a body, there is no ritual action nor meditation for anyone; there is no knowledge [without it]. Therefore, the yogin should move about possessing a body. (36)

For this reason, because all [actions] would be devoid of activity and meditative absorption without a body, the Śiva-yogin, endowed with the knowledge of Śiva, should indeed move about possessing a body. || 36 ||
310) Now, one might ask: since this yogin is fully endowed with the knowledge of Śiva, why does he have a need for a body? To this, he says:
"Even for the great-souled yogin who is joined with the singular knowledge of Śiva..."
Through the yoga of the body, worldly enjoyments, liberation, and so forth are always accomplished. || 37 ||
The meaning is that liberation has knowledge as its root, and knowledge has the body as its root. || 37 ||
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"Just as fire does not arise without wood and is not luminous, so too a yogin, without the [divine] form (mūrti), is not possessed of the illumination of the reality of the Self. (38)
This is clear. || 38 ||

Furthermore, he states another illustration: "Just as the worshipability of a deity is conceived by means of its embodied form, so too the worshipability of this supreme yogin is [conceived] by means of his physical body. (39)
This is clear. || 39 ||
Furthermore, he states that Śiva also performs the creation and other acts through his embodied self alone:
"For Mahādeva is partless; Sadāśiva is eternally perfect.
Yet, for the sake of accomplishing the creation and so forth of the world, he appears as if possessing a form. (40)
This is clear. || 40 ||
Now, he states that even those possessing divine knowledge, such as Brahmā and others, are indeed embodied: (p.
311) "All deities beginning with Brahmā, as well as the sages seeking liberation..."
For those who possess a body perform austerity, which accomplishes all goals. || 41 ||
This is clear. || 41 ||

Then, following the statement in the *Devikālottara*, "The wise should never abandon the body through dispassion," he concludes the section on the state of being with the body (*sakāyasthalam*), stating that since the body is the root of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*), its abandonment is not appropriate.
For austerity is indeed the root of all accomplishments in the three worlds;
since that austerity has the body as its root, one should therefore not abandon the body. (42)
Austerity is the cause of all accomplishments, and the body is the cause of austerity; therefore, one should not abandon the body out of dispassion. || 42 ||
Thus, there is the state with body, then the state without body, and then the shadowless state, according to the Śruti: "bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.2).

And because the supreme yogin possesses a body only in a figurative sense, he is "without body" (akāya); this is established by five sūtras: "Because he possesses a body only figuratively, because he has cultivated the realization of being the self of the universe, and because he is devoid of connection with illusion, the Supreme is indeed remembered as 'without body'. (43)

On the other hand, the supreme yogin, who possesses a body as previously defined, because his bodily nature is metaphorical, because he is devoid of the conceit of being the body, and because of the cultivation of the realization that the universe is his own self— according to the established principle of the *Śiva Sūtras*, "The entire universe is the expansion of one's own power" (*Śi0 Sū0* 3.30)— [perceives] the whole universe.

It consists of the powers of consciousness and action which have become the very nature of Śiva; because it is the object of that [consciousness], otherwise it would be an external object and thus a non-cognizable effect. Through such contemplation, due to the absence of connection with *māyā*, and for that very reason the absence of the notion of duality characterized by mutual existence, it is traditionally known as "bodiless" (*akāya*). Indeed, this is well-established.
This is the meaning. || 43 ||

(312) Now, one might object: "Even though this [Self] lacks a body due to being devoid of identification with the body (*dehābhimāna*), since its connection with the body still exists, does it not undergo modifications caused by that? To this, he says:
Even when conjoined with another's body, there is no modification based on that body, because he is like Śiva; therefore, he is proclaimed to be bodiless (akāya).

The meaning is that just as there is no transformation such as desire caused by the body even when Śiva possesses a body, so too there is no transformation caused by the body for the supreme yogin, because he is equal to Śiva. || 44 ||
To the question, "By what is this manifestation as a body without a body caused?", he says:

"For one who has dissolved into the supreme Liṅga, which consists of supreme bliss and consciousness, how could there be a connection with a body? To appear as if possessing a body is an illusion. (45)
The meaning is that this is an error on the part of those who perceive [the self as a seer]. The remainder is clear. || 45 ||
Now, he says that even though there is a connection with a body, there is no obstacle [to liberation] because of it:
"For one who is devoid of identification with the body, whose self is established in the state of Śiva, this entire world is his body; what pain can there be from a single body? (46)

For this supreme yogin, whose true nature abides in the state of Śiva due to being devoid of identification with the body, the entire universe becomes his body like that of Śiva; thus, what pain could there be from a single body? The meaning is: none at all.
Now, to the question "Why does [the individual soul] not exist [in that way], since it lacks the sovereignty of Śiva?", he says:
313) For one who is solely devoted to the knowledge of Śiva, there is no delusion of ego or of worldly existence.
And for one who has abandoned the conceit of "I am the body," there is no suffering arising from the sense organs.

The meaning is that for one who is established in the state of identity with Śiva, because he is devoid of the limited ego of the body, there is neither the delusion "I am not the Lord" nor the suffering produced by the senses. || 47 ||
Now, having clarified the very meaning already stated, he concludes the section on the "abode of the body" (akāyasthala):
"I am neither a human nor a god, neither a yakṣa nor a rākṣasa;
I am Śiva"—for one who realizes this through the intellect, what is the use of bodily action? (48)
What purpose does that bodiless [self] have for bodily action? The meaning is: none at all. The remainder is clear. || 48 ||
"This is the place of one's own body,
and then the place of another's body;
that alone is the supreme abode of Brahman," according to the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (3.2.1).

He demonstrates through five aphorisms that the one who practices the yoga of the supreme non-body is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*) because he possesses the body of the Supreme Brahman, and is thus the "supreme body" (*parakāya*):
"Because of having brought *prakṛti* under control, and because of transcending the path of *māyā*."
This is declared to be the supreme body, whose nature consists of truth, knowledge, and bliss. || 49 ||

The meaning is this: this "bodiless one" (akāya), the yogi of Śiva, because he has brought nature under his control, and because by that mastery he has transcended the path of Māyā, consists of truth, knowledge, and bliss; being of the very nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), he is designated as the "supreme body" (parakāya). || 49 ||

(314) Now, one might object: "Even though it has been stated that [the body] belongs to another, since the gross body is still present, how can it be said to belong to another's body at this very moment? To this, he says:
Since his body is that of the Supreme Brahman, radiant with the bliss of awakening, what is gained for him by this material body? (50)
What is the use of this ordinary body for one whose very form is the Supreme Brahman, manifesting through consciousness and bliss?
[This is achieved] by transcending the path of Māyā, which consists of the cognition of mutual difference and non-difference.

Because the *prakṛti-tattva*, which has that [liberation] as its effect, is brought under control by means of subjugating it—according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves—and is thus made subject to one's own will, what obstacle can there be from a body produced by *prakṛti*? The meaning is: "There is no obstacle whatsoever. || 50 ||
Now, even so, [the opponent might argue] that the body itself is the obstacle; to this he says:
"That body whose seed of birth has been completely consumed by the fire of perfect knowledge, which rests upon the principle of Śiva—that is called 'another's body' (parakāya). (51)

One whose physical body (*kalevara*)— meaning the subtle body that serves as the cause for future births— is such that it has been thoroughly burnt by the fire of right knowledge, the fire of the firm realization of the non-duality of Śiva, so that there is no longer any suspicion of rebirth; he is one of such a nature.
The meaning is that he who relies upon the Śiva-principle and possesses the nature of Paraśiva is called "Parakāya.
The sense is that because the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra), which initiates birth and disease, has been destroyed, there is no obstacle even though the gross body (sthūlaśarīra) remains. || 51 ||
Now, one might object that because the body continues to exist, the activity of the sense organs persists, and thus [the state of liberation] is indeed contradicted. To this he says:
"The sense organs, the functions of the mind, and the latent impressions (vāsanās) arise from karma;
when these merge into dissolution within that Supreme Self, then this body [is truly abandoned]. (52)

This [Self] is that Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, by which the mental fluctuations and latent impressions born of karma, the latent impressions of sense-objects, the senses themselves, and the activities of the ten organs— all of which arise from karma and are produced by the snare of karma— attain dissolution. This is He.
The body of another (parakāyaḥ), being accompanied by one's own body (sakāyaḥ), exists together with the body; the sense is that even this [one's own] body consists of Brahman. || 52 ||

Now, as to how the body can consist of Brahman, he says: "Having attained the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*), one should perceive the entire universe as consisting of consciousness; for even while possessing a body, that is merely a great delusion, since his true nature is certainly that of Śiva. (53)
For one who, having attained the realization that the supreme reality— which is synonymous with supreme *ahantā*, the supreme Brahman, supreme Śiva, and the supreme Self— is indeed oneself,

perceives the entire universe, the whole web of worlds, as consisting of consciousness (*cidātmaka*) and as being identical with that [reality] because it is contained within the creative power (*cit-kriyā*) whose very nature is the supreme Brahman; for such a person...

"Being with the body" (sadehaḥ) means existing together with the body; this is a great delusion, the delusion of ordinary observers. For its nature as Śiva is certain; indeed, the nature of that body as Śiva is certain because it consists of Śakti. || 53 ||
In this regard, he says:
"Contemplating directly his own true nature as the light in the form of consciousness, the practitioner, though possessing a body, is indeed bodiless and liberated while living. (54)

The meaning is that it is well known that the practitioner, while contemplating his own true nature as the direct light consisting of consciousness, is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) because, despite possessing a body, he will never again have another body and is thus effectively bodiless. || 54 ||

He establishes this very point: "Whether the body of the yogi who has awakened to his own Self remains or departs, there shall immediately be liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which radiates the light of consciousness and bliss. (55)
On this point, he provides an illustration:
"For the affliction of saṃsāra ends with the knowledge of the Self."
Even at sunrise, is the world still obstructed by darkness? || 56 ||
"It is obstructed" means it is pervaded. The rest is clear. || 56 ||
Now he concludes the section on entering another's body:
"How can the great wise one, who is free from the conceit of 'I' regarding the body and who takes refuge in the state beyond the parts [of limited perception], undergo limitation within bodies? (57)

Being devoid of the conceit of identifying with the body, and because the body is composed of the five elements, the great wise one— having taken refuge in the state of the Supreme Brahman which transcends the kalās that serve as its causes—
is a supreme knower whose body is the Supreme (parakāya). How and by what means could there be limitation or finitude within such bodies?
In what manner does it go? The meaning is that it goes by no manner at all. || 57 ||
Thus ends the section on the bodies of others;
now follows the section on the practice of the Dharma—
namely, the attainment of ignorance [of the self] and the following of the Dharma that has been understood.

According to the Maitreyī Śruti (Maitri Upaniṣad 4.3), "In one's own hermitages alone, the progression of one's own dharma increases; like the branches of a tree, by this one becomes elevated above others, otherwise one falls. Thus, the conduct of that supreme body (*parakāya*) is indeed the dharma-conduct for all people.
He establishes the locus of righteous conduct: "That very practice which is desired for another's body is considered *dharma*; it is intended for the benefit of all the worlds. (58)

The meaning is that whatever conduct is made the object of the will of that Śiva-yogin who possesses the body of the supreme Brahman (parabrahmakāya), that is Dharma; being real, it is intended for the benefit of all people. || 58 ||
Now, he describes that practice of Dharma with three verses:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity, worship, recitation, and meditation—this is the summary of Dharma. (59)

The meaning is as follows: *dāna* is spontaneous giving; *pūjā* is the worship of the Śiva-liṅga; *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the Śiva-liṅga; and *japa* is the practice of the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva (*śivapañcākṣara*). The remainder is clear. || 59 ||
To the question, "For what purpose should this practice of Dharma be performed?", he says:
"Since the compendium of Dharma was ordained by Śiva through the Āgamas, therefore the wise man who practices it is fit for His grace. (60)
Since the entire collection of dharma has been ordained by Śiva through the scriptures, it must indeed be practiced.
Therefore, one who possesses the conduct of dharma becomes capable of attaining Śiva’s grace; otherwise, being devoid of Śiva’s grace, he would go to hell—this is the meaning. || 60 ||
To the question, "How indeed should that dharma be performed?", he says:
One should not touch even the slightest unrighteousness; one should practice the prescribed dharma, and that too free from desire, and furthermore, preceded by knowledge. (61)
The meaning is that it consists of non-violence and other such qualities as prescribed. The remainder is clear. || 61 ||
318) Now, as to what that knowledge is like:
one should regard the wives of others as one's own mother, and the property of others as a clod of earth.
He who sees all beings as himself is a sovereign of righteousness.

Thus, in accordance with the Śruti, he says by means of two sūtras: "The best among those who know Yoga should perceive all beings as being like himself, because of the state of the world having a single Self, and because of the contradiction [otherwise] regarding restraint and so forth. (62)

The supreme knower of yoga, the lord of yogis, because of his realization of the single selfhood of the universe (*jagadekātmatā*), contemplates the world as being of the singular nature of light; thus, due to the contradiction inherent in such acts as suppression,
there is no room for either suppression or favor, and he regards all beings as equal to his own self (*svātmavat*).
"Should behold" means he should look upon [it] without partiality. || 62 ||
To one who sees thus, the sense of "mine" does not exist at all; as it is said:
"For one who clearly perceives that this entire world is manifestly Śiva alone, how could the sense of 'mine'—which is indeed a delusion—not cease to arise? (63)

For one who clearly perceives directly that "this entire world is indeed Śiva alone," what would not arise? Everything would certainly be so. The meaning is that in that world, there is no sense of "mine-ness"—that is, the delusion of the conceit "this is mine" does not exist. || 63 ||
Now, he says that one should not abandon the practice of that dharma even if one is dispassionate:
"Since dharma alone is the cause of the complete accomplishment for all, the great yogi, though free from desire, should not abandon the path of dharma. (64)
The meaning is that it is the cause of perfection and the cause of enjoyment and liberation. The remainder is clear. || 64 ||
(319) Now, to the objection that those who possess knowledge have no need for the practice of dharma, he says:
"Even though the yogi is satiated by the nectar of knowledge, he should not abandon dharma."

Indeed, worldly people proceed by observing the conduct of the great. As it is said: "Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. Even though the great yogi is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge—the nectar of the auspicious knowledge of Śiva—for the sake of the welfare of the world...
The meaning is that one should not abandon the practice of Dharma. || 65 ||
Now he states another reason:
Śambhu is fond of virtuous conduct; He is to be worshipped through virtuous conduct.
Without virtuous conduct, His grace never arises. (66)
The implication is that even for the wise, the practice of the dharma of non-violence (ahiṃsā) is necessary for the sake of attaining the grace of Śiva. || 66 ||
Thus ends the section on the practice of the Dharma;
now follows the section on the practice of the spirit.
Meditating upon Śiva, who is the form of light, complete, the dispeller of all worldly radiance,
and the illuminator of the inner heart, one shall become absorbed in Him.

In accordance with this statement from the *Kāmika*, he establishes that for a Śiva-yogin who is perfected in righteous conduct, his very state of being (*bhāva*) constitutes the conduct of all states of being:
"His very state of being is proclaimed as the conduct of all states of being."
Existence consists of mental activity; it is complete and has Śiva as its refuge.

The very disposition (*bhāva*) of this Śiva-yogin, who is perfected in the practice of Dharma, is proclaimed to be the "disposition and conduct" (*bhāvācāra*) for all ordinary people. To the question of what this "disposition" (*bhāva*) is, he says: "Mental...

The meaning is that "the state of being a qualifier" (viśeṣaṇabhāva) refers to that which, while consisting of mental activity, has as its locus the perfect Śiva—meaning that whose locus is the perfect Śiva both internally and externally. || 67 ||
Now, he distinguishes action conjoined with contemplation by means of two verses:
"Action performed with contemplation is purifying even more than that which is merely purifying;
therefore, one should practice the duty of another [the teacher] while joined with contemplation. (68)
This is clear. || 68 ||
Now, to the question "What is the purpose of inner disposition (bhāva)? he says:
"For by disposition comes purity of mind, and by action comes purity of disposition.
Reflecting thus in his mind, the yogi should not abandon inner disposition. (69)
This is clear. || 69 ||
If it be objected that if the accomplishment of action depends upon *bhāva* (inner disposition), there would be an obstacle [to liberation], he says in response:
"Even while performing all obligatory and occasional rites through the contemplation of Śiva, the great yogin is not afflicted by virtues or defects. (70)
The meaning is that by performing [action] with the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that Śiva alone is the agent, the yogin is not tainted by virtues or defects. The remainder is clear. || 70 ||

(321) Now, one might object: "Since the supreme lord of yogins is free from attachment to obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), how can his performance of them be accepted? To this, he says:
The constant worship of the sun of consciousness, which shines within, through one's own being—that they know as the twilight ritual (saṃdhyāvandana). || 71 ||

The meaning is that the Vīraśaiva teachers understand *sandhyāvandana* (the twilight worship) to be the attendance upon and the continuous following of the nature of the Sun of Consciousness (*cidāditya*), which shines incessantly within the heart-lotus above. || 71 ||
If that is so, then the oblation (homa) is also necessary; as to what kind it is, he says:
"The offering of all objects into the light of the Self by means of an inward-turned disposition is proclaimed as the rite of oblation. (72)

The offering of all sense-objects into the fire of consciousness—the light of the Self—by means of an inward-turned state of being rather than an outward-turned state, contemplating their dissolution according to the analogy of waves subsiding into the ocean;
that which consists of contemplating this state of complete unification is called, or described as, the act of *homa* (sacrificial oblation). This is the meaning. || 72 ||
Thus, he states that by contemplating the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittika-karmāṇi*) in this manner, one shall become free from attachment:
"One should contemplate all obligatory and occasional rites as being solely for the purpose of pleasing Śiva, in order to achieve freedom from attachment. (73)

The meaning is that one should contemplate that all obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karmāṇi*), performed for the purpose of ceasing the bonds of *saṃsāra*, are indeed acts that cause the pleasure of Śiva. || 73 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since action is a cause of attachment, how can there be freedom from attachment? To this he says:
"The fortunate one who, having resolved through discernment all that is to be done and not to be done upon Śiva, proceeds in life—he shall be free from attachment. (74)
(322) Through discernment— that the agent, the instigator, the action, and its fruit are Śiva alone—
the fortunate one who, having discerned what is fit and unfit for performance, places and offers both the obligatory and the non-obligatory duties into Śiva;
