That great person exists; he is free from attachment, meaning he is free from attachment to worldly existence. || 74 ||
To the objection that freedom from the bonds of worldly existence is not possible without the vision of Śiva, he says:
"Only by constantly perceiving the self and all things as Śiva, who consists of bliss and consciousness, with a sense of oneness, does one truly see. (75)
Constantly perceiving oneself, one's own self, every object, and the entire universe as the non-dual, single reality— namely, Paraśiva who consists of bliss and consciousness—

one realizes the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) because of being of the nature of consciousness, and because of being pervaded by the creative activity of consciousness which constitutes the very essence of Śiva.
The meaning is that one who perceives the entire universe as being of the nature of Śiva because it is not external to Him, truly sees Śiva while seeing. || 75 ||
Thus ends the section on the conduct of devotion;
now follows the section on the conduct of knowledge.
Regarding that, according to the Vedic revelation (śruti): "Truth, knowledge, and infinite is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).

For the Śiva-yogin who is perfected in the conduct of being (*bhāvācāra*), his very conduct of knowledge (*jñānācāra*) constitutes the conduct of knowledge for all embodied beings; thus, he describes the section on the conduct of knowledge:
"The conduct of knowledge of this yogin [is the conduct] of all embodied beings."
This practice of knowledge which has been described is called the conduct of knowledge (jñānācāra). || 76 ||

The meaning is this: because the very conduct of knowledge belonging to this yogin who is perfected in the conduct of being is said to be the "conduct of knowledge" for all embodied beings, for that reason he is called the "conduct of knowledge. || 76 ||
323) Now, he explains that very conduct of knowledge (*jñānācāra*) preceded by its defining characteristics through three sūtras:
"Knowledge that is supreme non-duality with Śiva is called 'knowledge' (*jñāna*) by the wise."
Whether it be accomplished or unaccomplished, what is the use of another cognition as a result? (77)

Knowledge in which non-duality with Śiva alone is the supreme and primary principle is called "knowledge" by the wise; what fruit is there from any other kind of knowledge—whether established by scripture or not established—i.e., from a knowledge that is distinct [from this]? The meaning is: none at all. || 77 ||
Now, as to how that is so, he says:
"For the stainless knowledge of Śiva is the supreme cause of ultimate liberation;
[knowledge] defiled by passion, hatred, and the like is, on the contrary, the cause of transmigratory existence. (78)

The knowledge of Śiva is the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva; it is stainless, meaning free from the impurities such as *āṇava* and the rest, and being real, it is the supreme cause of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), meaning it bestows the highest form of emancipation.
Knowledge of duality distinct from that [non-dual Śiva] is defiled by passion, hatred, and so forth, and is mixed with desire, anger, and the like.
The meaning is that it is well known to be the cause of repeated wandering in saṃsāra, the cause of coming and going again and again. || 78 ||
Having thus described the nature of knowledge, he now describes the nature of its practice:
"That which is undertaken by relying upon the perfect Great Knowledge that illuminates the Supreme Reality is called the conduct of knowledge (jñānācāra). (79)

The meaning is that the conduct which proceeds by relying upon— that is, by maintaining— the great knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva, which reveals the supreme reality, is complete and undivided, is called *jñānācāra*. || 79 ||
Now, he elucidates the practitioner of knowledge (jñānācārin):
"One should unite everything with knowledge in the supreme, partless abode named Śiva; such a one is proclaimed a practitioner of knowledge. (80)

In the supreme abode— the support of the Supreme Brahman— which is partless (*niṣkala*), without components (*niravayava*), free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), devoid of differentiation (*bhedarahita*), and named Śiva— that is, possessing the designation "Śiva"— he who, through knowledge— that is, through the knowledge of non-duality— [perceives] the entire web of the world...
He who should thus apply [these] is celebrated as a "knower of conduct" (jñānācārī); this is the meaning. || 80 ||
Now, he explains with two verses that for one who practices through knowledge, there is no wretchedness regarding ritual action:
"Having obtained the knowledge that bestows liberation through the grace of the Guru's gaze, who would harbor a desire for wretchedness in ritual action, which only increases worldly existence? (81)

Having obtained through the grace of the guru’s compassionate glance this knowledge of Śiva—which bestows liberation and grants both the higher and lower emancipation—who would harbor a desire or longing for the increase of worldly existence or for the wretchedness of ritual action? The meaning is: no one at all would do so. || 81 ||
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Karma burnt by the fire of knowledge shall not sprout in any way whatsoever;
for the wise have said that it is the root of transmigratory existence, following along with the stream [of rebirth]. (82)

That karma which the wise declare to be the root of saṃsāra— the primary cause that follows the current according to the analogy of a flow of water, existing as beginningless and in accordance with the Śruti— that bond of karma,
once consumed by the fire of the knowledge of Śiva, shall not sprout again in any way whatsoever.
The meaning is that it should not sprout. || 82 ||
To the question "In that case, to whom does the bondage of karma belong?", he says:
"A person devoid of knowledge is always bound by karma;
indeed, the volitional intentions toward action belonging to the knower become fruitless. (83)
"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this; he is the Supreme Person"— according to this *Chāndogya* Śruti,
all actions of the yogi who is endowed with non-dual devotion [do not cling].
For, according to the analogy of the burnt cloth, mere actions are indeed not true actions.
And because of the statement in the Vīrāgama, "Thus," the meaning is that for the knower (jñānin), there is no bond of karma. || 83 ||
Now, he concludes the section on the conduct of knowledge:
One who is discerning, possessing a pure disposition within the conduct of purity,
perceives the light as one and the same everywhere.
The divine yogi, liberated while living, acts with the phenomenal expansion of the material self destroyed by knowledge.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Nine Liṅgas Residing in the Māheśvara Stage," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the Six Stages (*Ṣaṭsthala*). || 16 ||

One who is pure in conduct, whose conduct is characterized by stainless knowledge, and who possesses a pure disposition— that is, one who is discerning— thus beholds from all sides the Śaiva splendor, which is devoid of any counter-correlate,
with the phenomenal world of the material self destroyed by knowledge.

The meaning is that the divine yogi— whose expansion of a body distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has been destroyed by the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva, who is himself of the nature of self-luminosity, and who is a Śiva-yogi liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)— performs actions and conducts himself like an ordinary worldly person. || 84 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Occasion of the Nine Liṅgas Residing in the Māheśvara Section," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 16.
The seventeenth chapter: Now, the section on the basis of serenity (or the section on the basis of physical well-being).
Now follows the inquiry of Agastya. Agastya said:
"Those places which were mentioned as being in the Maheśvara-sthala have been described;
tell me now the distinctions between the various sthalas that are situated within the Prasāda-sthala."
"Speak"—the meaning is "instruct. The remainder is clear. || 1 ||
Śrīreṇuka said: Nine distinct types of sacred sites (sthalas) have been declared, residing within the Prasādisthala:
first, the favoring of the body (kāya), and thereafter the favoring of the senses (indriya).

Next, the offering of the vital breaths is considered; thereafter, the offering of the body is taught; then the offering of the instruments is proclaimed; and after that, the offering of one's being is considered. (3)

Then the stage of the disciple (śiṣyasthala) is proclaimed, as well as the stage of service (śuśrūṣāsthala); after that, the stage of the one to be served (sevyasthala). Listen now to their characteristics in due order. || 4 ||
Now, regarding the place for supporting the body (p.
according to the *Kaivalya-śruti*, "Then, being pure, with neck, head, and body erect" (*KaiU* 5), he [should remain thus].
He explains with three aphorisms that the Śivayogin, possessing the conduct of knowledge, bestows grace by manifesting his own essential body, thus being the "bestower of grace upon the body":
"Insofar as he bestows grace upon the worlds by manifesting his own body..."
Therefore, this is declared to be named "Benefiting the Body. || 5 ||

Because this Śiva-yogin, endowed with the conduct of knowledge, bestows grace— that is, shows favor— upon ordinary worldly people by manifesting his own body, for that reason he is known by the name "Kāyānugraha," meaning "Grace through the Body"; such is the intended sense.
To explain how this is so, he provides an illustration:
"Just as Śiva bestows grace by entering the bodies of embodied beings, so too the yogi, while remaining within the body, becomes the benefactor of all. (6)

Just as Śiva, having entered the bodies of embodied beings through forms such as Candraśekhara, bestows grace upon them, so too the yogi, while remaining within the body—specifically while residing in a divine body consecrated by the initiation of Śiva—becomes a benefactor to all; this is the meaning. || 6 ||

Now, he says that [the yogi] is unattached like Śiva: "Just as Śiva is devoid of attachment even while joined with a body, so too the yogi, though abiding in a body, always remains free from attachment. (7)
The meaning is that he is free from attachment to pleasure, pain, and so forth. The remainder is clear. || 7 ||

328) Having thus stated that the Śiva-yogin is equal to Śiva, [the author] establishes with five sūtras, preceded by illustrations, that he does not perceive the phenomenal world of *māyā* and is therefore Śiva himself:
Endowed with a firm and non-conceptual contemplation of Śiva,
one becomes Śiva himself, with the turbulent agitation of the penetration of Māyā completely shaken off.

In this context, "the Śiva-yogin" is the understood subject. The meaning is that one who is endowed with the firm contemplation "I am Śiva," which is free from duality, becomes Śiva himself, having had the disturbances caused by the influence of Māyā warded off. || 8 ||
Now, one might ask: how is it that he has no affliction from the intrusion of illusion? To this, he says:
"When the fluctuations of the mind have dissolved into Śiva, the ocean of consciousness and bliss, the practitioner of restraint perceives nothing else but the reality imagined by ignorance. (9)

The meaning is that when the mental fluctuations— the operations of the mind— have dissolved into the Supreme Śiva, who occupies the place of an ocean for knowledge and bliss, the Śiva-yogin no longer perceives any other object imagined by Māyā. || 9 ||
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"Just as when it is said, 'This is not silver,' mother-of-pearl is revealed;
so when it is known, 'This is not the world,' the reality of Śiva is revealed. (10)
When [the word] is spoken, the meaning is "it is known. The remainder is clear. || 10 ||
Furthermore, he states an analogy:
"Just as an object created in a dream ceases upon waking, so too, through the realization of Śiva, one no longer perceives saṃsāra. (11)
This means "this is a Śiva-yogin. The remainder is clear. || 11 ||
329) Now, he states another illustration:
ignorance alone is the cause of the delusion of saṃsāra for all beings.
When that has ceased, how could there again be the perception of the wandering in saṃsāra? || 12 ||
Just as the ignorance of mother-of-pearl is the cause of the delusion of silver,
so too is ignorance regarding Śiva the cause of the delusion of saṃsāra. Upon its cessation—
just as the delusion of silver ceases when the ignorance of mother-of-pearl ceases— so it is here.
The meaning is that when ignorance regarding Śiva ceases, the perception of the delusion of worldly duality no longer exists.
The underlying idea is that just as mother-of-pearl is itself silver, so too is Śiva himself the universe. || 12 ||
Therefore, stating that this Śiva-yogin is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he concludes the section on the favor bestowed upon the body:
"With the knot of egoism dissolved, assuming a body as if for play, the yogin who is liberated while living moves about like an embodied being, yet remains free from all limiting adjuncts. (13)

One who possesses the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) regarding the body and so forth—which have ceased to be perceived as limited—and who assumes a body fashioned by his own will for the sake of sport, is therefore "without limiting adjuncts" (nirupādhika), meaning free from all obstructions. Being liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he may move about like one possessing a body for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the world. || 13 ||
Thus concludes the section on the support of the body;
now follows the section on the support of the faculties.

Then, according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (2.8), "Having established the body evenly with its three parts raised, and having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind," the very discernment of the senses belongs to that Śiva-yogin who has attained mastery over the body.

He defines the locus for the favoring of all the sense organs: "Through the vision of another's body and through the discernment of the instruments [of perception], the favoring of all the sense organs has been proclaimed by the knowers of reality. (14)

The meaning is that through the vision of a Śiva-yogin who has attained the supreme benefit for another’s body, there occurs a withdrawal (*viveka*) of the instruments—the sense organs—resulting in the benefit for all ordinary sense organs; this is what was proclaimed and declared by those who know reality, the knowers of the principles (*tattva*). || 14 ||
Now, as to how that is so, he demonstrates that operation of the senses through five aphorisms:
"When there is contact of all the senses with their respective objects, either passion or aversion arises; the yogi should avoid these two. (15)

In the world, when all the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest, come into contact with their respective objects, either attachment or aversion arises. A yogi—a yogi of Śiva—should completely avoid, that is, renounce, those two, attachment and aversion. || 15 ||
And thus, because the activity of the yogi’s senses is supramundane, it possesses the quality of being beneficial—this is the intended meaning:
"The outward functioning of the senses reveals the manifold world (prapañca); immersion within Śiva internally is the cause of the cessation of the manifold world. (16)
This is clear. || 16 ||
This being the case:
"Beholding Śiva within for a moment with the mind alone,"
Momentarily experiencing external objects through the eyes and other [senses], || 17 ||
Though established in all the senses, the yogi whose mind is dedicated to Śiva is as if devoid of all senses; he perceives Śiva and nothing else.
Being inward-turned, with a mind alone— free from attachment to external senses—
the yogi, for a moment beholding Śiva, and for a moment experiencing external objects such as sound through the eyes and other external organs like sight, has his mind fixed upon Śiva.

The supreme yogin whose mind is fixed on Śiva, even though not established in all his senses, even though attached to all his senses, and even though being devoid of all his senses, perceives Śiva; he perceives Śiva alone both internally and externally, and perceives nothing else—that is, nothing other than Him. The sense is that the discernment of those senses is beneficial. (17–18)

Now, one might object: "Even for a Śiva-yogin who perceives Śiva both within and without, since old age, death, and so forth are still observed just as they are for ordinary people, how can he be a benefactor to the world? To this, he says:
"There is no old age, no death, no thirst, and no hunger."
Of this high-souled one, who has offered his senses to Śiva and is free from pride. || 19 ||

For this great-souled one, this great person, this Śiva-yogin whose senses are dedicated to Śiva, whose sensory activities are directed toward Śiva, and who is free from pride— being devoid of the conceit of identifying with the body and so forth—
there is neither old age nor death, since those two are attributes of the physical body; nor do hunger and thirst exist for him, for they too [belong to the body].
Because it is a property of the vital breath. || 19 ||

In accordance with the Purāṇic statement—"Of all limbs, the head is foremost; of all senses, the eye is foremost; the mind is the lord of the senses, and the vital air (māruta) is the lord of the mind"—[the author] effects the restraint of the mind and the vital air, which are the causes of the functioning of all the senses, by means of three aphorisms.
He explains: Wherever the mind functions, there the abiding of all the sense-faculties occurs.
When the mind has dissolved into Śiva, where is there any consideration of the senses?

Wherever there is the abiding of the mind, there is the abiding of all the senses. When the mind has dissolved into Śiva, where is the investigation of the senses, that is, the activity of the senses? The meaning is: it does not exist. || 20 ||
Whatever the yogi sees with his vision or even contemplates with his mind,
all that shines forth as the form of Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness.

Whatever the yogi, the Śiva-yogin, sees with his vision or thinks of with his mind—all that shines forth as the true reality, the form of Śiva, whose nature is consciousness; this is the meaning. || 21 ||

By this, the method for restraining the internal and external senses has been shown. Now, he shows the method for restraining the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "The self-controlled one, having placed the vital breath together with the organs into the mind..."
He should apply himself there where that Śiva is directly present and where the delusion of the world does not exist. || 22 ||

Having established the vital breath (*prāṇa*), together with the instruments such as the eyes, within the mind—that is, having fixed it there—the self-controlled Śiva-yogi should unite it with Brahman.

For the mind alone is the form of the vital breath for the instruments beginning with the eyes; the mind is of the nature of air because of its speed, just as [the wind] is directed toward some object in the world.

If one joins the flickering eye with the state of equanimity (*sāmarasya*) through the oneness of the three—because the dissolution of the mind is experienced by means of restraining the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*)—he is indeed Śiva himself. For him, there is no delusion of the world nor the error of universal duality; if the fluctuations of the mind are dissolved into Brahman, the activity of the external senses [ceases].
The meaning is that because of the absence of that [duality], the delusion of differentiation ceases; it does not exist. || 22 ||
Now he concludes the section on the support of the senses:
"By worshipping Śiva externally and internally through the activity of all the senses, the self-controlled one moves at will everywhere and becomes happy. (23)

The self-restrained Śivayogin, by means of the activity of all the senses and the engagement of both internal and external faculties, worships and adores Śiva— the *liṅga* of Śiva who is the nature of the desired vital breath— and, becoming one who acts according to his own will in all circumstances, [attains liberation].
"He becomes happy" means that he remains experiencing happiness. || 23 ||
Thus is the stage of favoring the senses;
now follows the stage of favoring the vital breaths.
Then, having suppressed the vital breaths here, being free from exertion, one should breathe through the nostrils once the breath has been exhausted.

In accordance with the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (2.9), this passage defines the contemplation of the intended meaning (*tātparyāvalokana*) by a Śiva-yogin who has attained mastery over the senses as the very locus for bestowing grace upon all living beings:
"The contemplation of the intended meaning of Śiva, whose body is supreme..."
That is declared by all the seers of truth to be the favoring of their life-breaths.

The meaning is this: the observation of the intent (*tātparya-avalokana*) of the body of another— namely, the auspicious body of the Supreme Brahman belonging to the Śiva-yogin who is endowed with the grace of the sense faculties— and that observation of the intent which occurs through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu-nirodha*),
is said by those who perceive reality and possess knowledge of reality to be "the grace upon the vital breaths" (*prāṇānugraha*) for all beings.
Now, he explains what the observation of that purport is like:
"When one's vital breath (prāṇa) dissolves into Śiva, the supreme cause, how can there be the manifestation of the senses for him? How can there be the perception of saṃsāra? (25)

For that Śiva-yogin whose vital breath— the life-force wind— dissolves into the Supreme Cause, Śiva, the Parameśvara who is the cause even of Brahmā and the other lords of the five causes [namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva], for that Śiva-yogin...
From where could there be the manifestation or the functioning of the senses? The meaning is that they do not exist.
Thus, the sense is that the vision of the Śiva-liṅga free from phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca) is the perception of its true purport. || 25 ||
(p. 334) Now, as to how that is so, he says:
"When the instruments have ceased [their activity], through effort arising from attachment to one's own object..."
Having merged the vital breath with them, he himself, with a tranquil mind, [rests] within his own heart.

O Śivā, when the vital breath has dissolved into the *kevalakumbha* [the solitary kumbhaka], and when the sense organs— the eyes and so forth— have ceased their own functions of their own accord through effort due to the cessation of attachment to their respective objects such as sound; then, having placed the vital breath together with those senses into the mind (*svānta*).
Having joined [the mind] thus, Śāntamati shall become free from passion and hatred. || 26 ||
This being the case:
because the functions of the vital breaths have become tranquil, the mind becomes tranquil along with its fluctuations.
When that [mind] is tranquil, nothing other than Śiva is perceived by the yogis. (27)

Because the functions of the vital breath— the breath-movements consisting of exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka)— have been stilled, having ceased through pure retention (kevalakumbhaka), the mind, along with its fluctuations in the form of volitions and doubts,
becomes tranquil. When that [mind] has become still, nothing other than Śiva is seen by the yogis.
This is the meaning. || 27 ||
Now, having raised a doubt here with two sūtras, he refutes it with the third:
"Prāṇa alone is the cause of maintaining the body for human beings;
Śiva is declared to be its support, the cause of all causes. (28)
This is clear. || 28 ||
The reply to this is:
Śiva is directly without support; the vital breath (prāṇa) is established by him.
The body should be known as having that [consciousness] as its support, by which the living being is set in motion. (29)
"Having that as its support" means having the vital breath (prāṇa) as its support. || 29 ||

Since it is universally accepted that the individual soul (*jīva*) moves by means of that very vital breath (*prāṇa*), there arises the doubt: "How can the body remain active when the vital breath has dissolved into Śiva? The answer to this is:
"Even though the vital breath has dissolved into Śiva, [the body remains] for the yogin through the path of yoga."
Through the connection with the latent impressions of its own power, it indeed maintains a physical form.

The meaning is that even though the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the yogin— the Śiva-yogin— has dissolved into Śiva, having reached its absorption through the path of yoga, specifically the path of yoga consisting solely of the *kumbhaka* (retention) form, it nevertheless continues to sustain the body (*vigraha*) by virtue of the connection with its own power’s latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that is, through the force of its own innate potentiality. || 30 ||
To explain how he remains in that state, he speaks by means of two verses:
"And through the power of practice, he [remains] further in that which transcends all principles (tattva), which is stainless, formless, and free from every trace of affliction. (31)

And that vital breath (prāṇavāyu), which serves as the support for the individual soul (jīvātman), through the power of further practice, reaches the stainless state— beyond all principles (tattvas), situated above the principles beginning with earth and ending with Śiva,
devoid of old age, death, and other defects, formless, and therefore free from natural forms such as blue or yellow.
In whom all agitation has been cast out and every obstruction has ceased; || 31 ||
The yogi, whose self is everything, having dissolved into Śiva—which is called the bliss of perfect fullness arising from the play of consciousness—does not move anywhere. 32.

The meaning is that the Śiva-yogin— the yogi whose entire self has dissolved and whose every activity has ceased into the supreme Śiva, who is the void beyond duality, whose nature is perfect bliss, and who is the non-dual fullness of happiness through the abundance of the play of consciousness— never at any time or in any place moves or vibrates. || 32 ||
336) Now, as to why it does not waver at all, he says:
"Because of the destruction of attachment to latent impressions and because of the complete cessation of the activity of the vital breath."
Having become one with Śiva as the self of all, the self-restrained one shines like a pillar.

The self-restrained master of Śiva-yoga, through the destruction of attachment to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the cessation of contact with the impressions of sense-objects, and the dissolution of the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— that is,
the destruction of the activities of the vital breath in both their natural and modified forms— becomes the universal self, unified with Śiva.
The meaning is that, while his activities of all the sense organs have become one with the Śivaliṅga, he appears as motionless like a pillar (sthāṇu) or a piece of wood (kāṣṭha). || 33 ||
Thus ends the stage of favoring the vital breaths;
now follows the stage of offering the body.
O Goddess, when one has surrendered one’s own self to Śiva, who is the soul of the Guru, then one becomes a devotee of Śiva (Śaiva); from that, there is no further rebirth.

Thus, in accordance with the statement of the *Yogajāgama*, he describes the suitable place for offering one's body to Śiva, who possesses the power to grace the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and whose supreme form graces all: "In the worship of Śiva, whose supreme form is the benefactor of all..."
The renunciation of the identification with the body is declared to be the offering of the body. || 34 ||

The meaning is that in the worship of Śiva— the supreme yogin who benefits all, who is the benefactor of all, whose form is the Supreme (para-rūpa), whose body is the Supreme Brahman (parabrahma-kāya), and who is endowed with the grace of the vital breaths— within the context of the adoration of the Śivaliṅga, the abandonment of identification with the body is called "the offering of the body" (kāyārpaṇa). || 34 ||
337) Now, as to what happens by this, he says: When the yogi offers his own body to Śiva...
Then it becomes that very form, the form of Śiva; of this there is no doubt. || 35 ||
The meaning is that such a form becomes the very nature of the yogin, which is the form of Śiva. The remainder is clear.
Now, as to whether only the body is to be offered, or if there is something else as well, he says:
"The yogi of Śiva should offer to the nature of bliss-consciousness those pleasures that arise from attachment to sense objects and those caused by the gratification of the senses. (36)
The meaning is that one should offer to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, the pleasure arising from contact with objects that serve as the cause of sensory delight. || 36 ||
Now, as to how that is so, he says:
"Whatever pleasure arises from the sense objects—whether from seeing, touching, eating, hearing, or even smelling—one should offer that to Śiva. (37)
"From sense-objects" means from objects such as clothing and ornaments distinct from these [previously mentioned]; the remainder is clear. || 37 ||
Now, stating that whatever happiness is obtained through the medium of the body must all be offered to the Śivaliṅga, he concludes the section on the offering of the body:
"Whatever happiness may accrue to the self through the medium of the body..."
By offering each of these to Śambhu, the yogi becomes stainless. || 38 ||
Whatever pleasure may be incidentally attached to oneself through the door of the body— that is, through the ten sense organs connected to the body—

Offering—that is, surrendering—each respective pleasure to Śambhu, the Śivaliṅga, the yogi, being the Śivayogin, moves about while remaining stainless and untainted; this is the meaning. The sense is that the surrender of physical pleasure itself constitutes the surrender of the body. || 38 ||
Thus ends the stage of offering the body; now follows the stage of offering the senses.
But he who possesses discernment and whose mind is always disciplined, his senses are under control, like well-trained horses are under a charioteer. (Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.3.6)
Thus, in accordance with the *Kaṭhavallī* scripture, [the author] describes the locus of the senses for one who has offered his body [to the Lord]:
"The attachment of all the senses is in that which is higher than the highest."
O Śivā, that which has been declared in the Āgama as being offered through the instruments [of the senses]—this very thing [is meant].

In the *vīraśaiva* doctrine as set forth in the *āgama*, it is stated that "the offering of the instruments" (*karaṇārpaṇa*) refers to the state of being the agent who effects the attachment— that is, the conjunction— of all the instruments (faculties), both internal and external, with Śiva, the Śivaliṅga, who is higher than the highest (*parātpare*), meaning superior even in comparison to the supreme power (*paraśakti*). This exists within the entire universe.
"Proktam" means "spoken" or "declared. || 39 ||

Now he explains the "offering of the instruments" (karaṇārpaka): Whatever instrument [of sense] one relies upon to enjoy the pleasure born of objects, offering each of those to Śiva—he is called the "offerer of the instruments. (40)

The meaning is that having offered into the Śivaliṅga that sense-pleasure derived from an object which one experiences by depending upon a particular instrument (organ), and having thus perfected the offering of the body, such a person is called a "surrenderer of the instruments" (karaṇārpaka). || 40 ||
(p. 339) Now, he explains that method by means of five sūtras:
"The elephant of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is inflamed with egoism and pride..."
He who would bind [it] to the sacrificial post of Śiva is a steadfast man possessed of all perfections. || 41 ||

He who binds the elephant of the internal organ— characterized by the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and intoxicated by the pride of upward and downward tendencies in the form of "I-making" and "mine-making"— to the auspicious hitching post, which is the binding pillar in the form of the Śiva-linga,
is a steadfast one who possesses all perfections. || 41 ||
Now, one might ask: since the sense organs are many, how can steadfastness be achieved by binding the mind alone? To this he says:
"The mind is said to be the foremost of all the senses; when that auspicious [mind] is brought under control, what need is there for the others that follow its lead? (42)
The meaning is that it is the primary cause, according to the Vedic scripture which states, "The mind is the lord of the senses.
The remainder is clear. || 42 ||
To the question "What follows from this?", he says:
"The mastery over the senses is proclaimed as their cessation. When Śiva is made their objective, how could there be any further immersion into saṃsāra for them? (43)

The wise declare that the very mastery over the senses is liberation (nivṛtti). When those senses are fixed upon the Śiva-liṅga, how could there be any sinking into the cycle of worldly existence? The meaning is that it does not exist. || 43 ||
Now, one might ask: how can there be a cessation of saṃsāra merely through the mastery of the senses? To this he says:
"The mastery of the senses is the axe that utterly cuts down the poisonous wilderness of saṃsāra; for men, there shall be peace when the senses are brought under control. (44)
"Quiescence" means being without expectation. The rest is clear. || 44 ||

Now, as to the question of how the bondage of karma is brought to an end by mere non-dependence [on the senses], he says: "Sins and merits are produced by the very senses; since they are offered to the Lord, how can there be any bondage of karma? (45)
This is clear. || 45 ||
Now, since it is heard that there is an increase [of merit] through objects offered to Śiva, why does an increase not occur through the surrender of both merit and sin to Śiva? To this he says:
"While the fire of consciousness, consisting of the world both external and internal, is shining forth..."
Having surrendered all sense objects, a person becomes like one who is liberated. || 46 ||

Since the destruction of objects cast into fire is observed, one must necessarily admit the destruction of even those objects offered into the Śiva-liṅga— which is the form of the fire of consciousness— manifesting as the universe both externally and internally; thus, due to the absence of growth, all objects [are dissolved] therein.
The meaning is that a person, a possessor of a body tormented by birth and death, is born as if liberated after having surrendered [the self]. || 46 ||
Now, since the offering of fire is of the nature of a *homa*, one might ask what its instrument is; to this he says:

"Having taken up the substance of the mind, the great oblation consisting of the born universe, for those who offer it within the fire of consciousness—how could there be the calamity of saṃsāra? (47)

For the Śiva-yogins who, having gathered the sacrificial material of the mind—which takes the form of objects such as sound and so forth—by means of the world's nature as the five subtle elements (tanmātras), offer it within the fire of consciousness residing in the heart-lotus, how could there be any affliction from saṃsāra? The meaning is that there is none. || 47 ||

(341) Now, one might ask: what is the nature of a person who is born like one liberated through such an all-encompassing oblation? To this he replies: [He is established] in the light of the Self, whose nature is consciousness, which is awakened by the vital breath (prāṇa).
Offering all sense objects as oblations, he certainly becomes absorbed in that [the Self]. || 48 ||

Offering and surrendering the objects of pleasure and so forth produced by the various sense organs into the fire of Śiva—the light of the Self which is the nature of consciousness, revealed by the vital breath—the Śiva-yogin becomes, indeed arises as, one whose very essence is that [Śiva], whose essence is consciousness; this is the certain conclusion. || 48 ||
Now, one might ask: since the organs are material (prākṛta), how can the pleasure and other experiences produced by them be fit for offering to Śiva? To this he says:
"All the sense organs and the body are the instruments of experience."
Meditating upon it as being an integral part of the worship of Śiva, one shall attain liberation. || 49 ||

The meaning is that since the body and so forth are ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the worship of Śiva, even the pleasure and other experiences arising from them are indeed fit for offering to Śiva. This offering of the instruments (*karaṇārpaṇa*) was mentioned incidentally in the context of the offering of the body (*kāyārpaṇa*), and thus there is no tautology. || 49 ||
Thus [ends] the stage dedicated to the instruments; now, the stage dedicated to the states of being.

Therefore, having abandoned the state of being connected with phenomenal proliferation (prapañca) and having resorted with effort to the reality whose nature is Śiva, one should perform activity within the Lord.

In accordance with this statement from the *Yogajāgama*, he describes the offering of internal states (*bhāvārpaṇa*) prescribed for the Śiva-yogin who has achieved perfection through the instruments [of yoga]:
"The offering of all states of being to Śiva with an unwavering disposition..."
This has been declared by those who know the true nature of Śiva to be offered through meditative realization.

The meaning is that the offering of all things with an unwavering and steady disposition toward Śiva, who is the Śivaliṅga, is what is called "offered through one's state of being" (bhāvārpita) by those who know the true nature of Śiva.
342) Now, as to what is meant by "existence" (bhāva), he says: that which is the mental cogitation of all objects residing within the mind is [existence].
The mental disposition that offers that [offering] directly to Śiva is called *mānasa-bhāva*.

A mental modification (*mānasavikāra*) is called "state" (*bhāva*); according to Amara, "state" refers to a mental modification. Within this state, which is a mental modification, there exists that which is the "thinking"—the contemplation in the form of direct experience—of all objects residing in the mind, that is, all things established in the consciousness.
The meaning is that when Śiva has become directly manifest in the form of the Śivaliṅga, the offering made to it is said to be "offered" (arpitam). || 51 ||
Now, he characterizes the essential nature of that state with five aphorisms:
"Indeed, for living beings, mental disposition alone is the cause of bondage and liberation.
When the disposition is pure, there is liberation; when it is the opposite, there is transmigratory existence. (52)
This is clear. || 52 ||
Now, as to what is meant by the purity of being (*bhāvaśuddhi*), he says:
"The purity of being is declared to be the application [of thought] that 'I am Śiva.
When there is a contrary conjunction, how can there be the cessation of suffering? (53)

The wise have declared that the very yoga of experiencing one's own true nature as "I am Śiva" is the purification of one's being. When there is a contrary conjunction—namely, when the contrary state "I am not Śiva" occurs—how can there be the cessation of suffering, the removal of the sufferings of saṃsāra? The meaning is that it cannot exist. || 53 ||

(On the question of how this universe, appearing as "this," is to be meditated upon: "Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller— this threefold Brahman is said to be all" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad).
In accordance with the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad [1.12], he says:
"The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the one who causes enjoyment—all this, including the moving and the unmoving, becomes Śiva in reality by contemplating it as having the form of Śiva. (54)

The enjoyer is the *jīva*; the object of enjoyment is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) entity suitable for experience; and the provider of enjoyment is Śiva, the bestower of experience. Contemplating this entire web of the world, including all that is moving and unmoving, as being of the nature of Śiva—because it is the effect of the powers of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*) which constitute his own innate nature—the Śiva-yogin perceives it as Śiva.

In reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), he becomes Śiva; the meaning is that he becomes Śiva alone. Here, by the phrase "in reality" (vastutaḥ), his status as the primary position is indicated. || 54 ||
Now, he explains cultivation from another perspective:
"Meditating on the universe as illusory and remembering Śiva, who transcends the universe and whose form is existence, bliss, and consciousness—how could one be bound here? (55)
Contemplating the universe as false because it is an effect of ignorance (avidyā) characterized by the superimposition (adhyāsa) of what is distinct from Himself,

and remembering Śiva— who transcends the universe, who is beyond the universe, whose form consists of existence, bliss, and consciousness, and whose nature is eternal, perfect Being-Consciousness-Bliss— one [is unable] to be bound by the fetters of impurity (mala), māyā, and so forth.
How is it fitting here? The meaning is that it is not fitting in any way whatsoever. || 55 ||
Now he states another mode of contemplation: "All ritual action is the worship of Śambhu; his word is its recitation.
For one who constantly contemplates thus, how could there be bondage through karma? (56)

For one who constantly contemplates that every action being performed is the worship of Śambhu’s Śivaliṅga, and every word being spoken is the glorification and praise of that Śivaliṅga—how could there be any bondage created by karma? The meaning is that it cannot occur in any way whatsoever. || 56 ||
344) Now, describing the contemplation that brings about liberation while living, he concludes the section on the stage of being absorbed in the state:
"Whatever happiness or suffering pertaining to all the senses arises from karma..."
Meditating for the sake of Śiva, the yogi shall become liberated while living. || 57 ||

The meaning is that by contemplating all pleasure arising from the ears and other senses, as well as the suffering born of sinful karma, as objects offered to the Śivaliṅga for the sake of Śiva, the Śivayogin becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 57 ||
Thus, having established the stage of the objective state, now follows the stage of the disciple: just as copper becomes gold through contact with an alchemical elixir, so it is here.
Through hearing what has been taught by the guru, the disciple likewise becomes identical with reality.

In accordance with this statement from the *Yogajagama*, he describes the locus of the disciple who is to be instructed by the supreme yogin who has attained perfection through the dedication of that state:
"He who is to be instructed at all times by means of another's body..."
But through his grace, one who seeks liberation is proclaimed as a disciple. || 58 ||

He who is always to be instructed and taught by the Śiva-yogin— who has attained the state of being offered into the body of another, the body of the Supreme Brahman— by virtue of that [instruction], namely by virtue of the grace of one who has attained the state of being offered into that [Supreme Brahman],
is proclaimed and described as a disciple, one who seeks liberation and looks toward both the higher and lower liberation.
This is the meaning. || 58 ||
345) Now, he states its definition by way of another method:
"He whose disposition is always stable through the actions of mind, speech, and body..."
He is proclaimed as a true disciple when his own guru is noble in virtue. || 59 ||

He whose disposition remains constant and firm—through the actions of mind, speech, and body, in the form of meditation, praise, and worship—toward his own Guru, the venerable Master, who is noble in qualities and exalted by virtues such as knowledge and dispassion;
he is called, that is to say, declared to be a "disciple" (śiṣya). || 59 ||
Now he states the characteristics of the principal disciple:

"One who is tranquil, self-controlled, devoted to austerity, truthful in speech, possessed of equal vision, and established in equanimity toward both the Guru and Śiva—he is the best among disciples in this world. (60)
He who is tranquil, possessing restraint of the internal senses; who is self-controlled, possessing restraint of the external senses;

who is devoted to austerity, established in the yoga of austerity characterized by the eight limbs beginning with *yama* and *niyama*—[namely, *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*...]

Possessing the eight limbs consisting of meditation and concentration (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.29), being truthful in speech— that is, speaking according to reality— and possessing equal vision toward clods of earth, gold, and other such things; being one who maintains equal vision toward the venerable Guru and the Śiva-liṅga— he who abides thus is the most excellent among disciples in this world.
The meaning is "the most excellent. || 60 ||
Now he describes the conduct of a disciple with two verses:
One should see the Guru as Śiva, and likewise Śiva as the Guru;
a wise person should perceive no difference whatsoever between these two. (61)
The meaning is that the disciple is discerning. || 61 ||
(346) Through the conduct of Śiva, the meditation on Śiva, and the stainless knowledge of Śiva,
one shall attain the supreme state by the mere command of the Guru. || 62 ||
The meaning is that one should attain completion and confidence; the remainder is clear. || 62 ||
Now, he describes the greatness of the glance of the illustrious Guru’s grace through two verses:
“The submarine fire of the Guru’s glance swiftly swallows the vast ocean of Māyā, from which the bubble of the universe has arisen. (63)

The meaning is: "the source of the emergence of the bubbles that are the cosmic eggs" (*brahmāṇḍabudbudodbhūta*). The submarine fire of the Guru's sidelong glance instantly devours—that is, swallows—such a vast ocean of *māyā*. This is because the eye is composed of fiery energy (*taijasa*).
Description as the submarine fire (vaḍavānala). || 63 ||
Through the piercing glance of the Guru, a human being becomes Śiva,
just as iron attains the state of gold through the process of alchemical elixirs.
"Human being" means a disciple; "proper penetration" means piercing; the rest is clear.
Now, it is said that one who thus knows the greatness of the Guru should not transgress the Guru’s command:
"One should not transgress the Guru’s command while manifesting knowledge itself;
with a mind devoted to Śiva, one shall attain all perfections. (65)
By means of a mind attached to Śiva and fixed in meditation on Śiva, one attains knowledge—the meaning being the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva. The remainder is clear. || 65 ||
347) Now, he indicates the secret of the Guru’s instruction: "The world other than Śiva is false; Śiva is the very nature of consciousness."
When designated by the Guru as "You are Śiva," he is indeed liberated.
The meaning is that the world is not other than Śiva; it is of the very nature of Śiva. To the question "How so?", he says:
"Śiva is of the nature of consciousness. Since the universe is contained within consciousness, it consists of consciousness, just like waves and the like.
Otherwise, if it were external to consciousness, there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence, and thus it would be non-existent—this is the sense.

"You are Śiva" means that you are of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*); this is the intended meaning, according to the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (6.9.4): "All this has that as its essence; That is Truth; That is the Self; That art thou, O Śvetaketu. Thus, the disciple who is instructed by the venerable Guru is liberated even while living—that is, he is indeed a *jīvanmukta*. || 66 ||
Now he concludes the section on the disciple:
"He who, having received from the Guru the great knowledge which is the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, rejoices as one who is happy and tranquil—he is indeed liberated while living. (67)

That disciple who, having obtained from his guru— the illustrious teacher— the great knowledge that is the medicine for the disease of worldly existence, the remedy for the sickness of saṃsāra, remains happy and experiences the bliss of Śiva,
dwelling in joy while experiencing that happiness— he is indeed renowned as one who is peaceful, free from attachment and aversion, and liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
This is the meaning. || 67 ||
Thus is the stage of the disciple; now, the stage of service.
Therefore, having properly received the innate [nature] from a true guru who has correctly resorted [to that state],
one should constantly remain devoted to the practice of the Self without effort.

In accordance with the statement of the *Yogajāgama*, he [the disciple]— being intent on service to the Guru and desiring to know the secret meaning, being one who wishes to listen— is described by three aphorisms: "He is always instructed by the Guru through the body of another."
A disciple who delights in serving him is celebrated as one who is "eager to serve. || 68 ||
Constantly being awakened by the glorious Guru, who is the body of the supreme Brahman, that disciple—
being devoted to service toward him and being intent on the desire to hear from him— is celebrated, meaning he is called, "one who desires to hear" (śuśrūṣuḥ). || 68 ||
Now, he demonstrates the manner of those questions:
"What is real, or what is not real? Who is the self, and who is the other, Śiva?
A disciple who is thus intent on hearing [these things] from the Guru is distinguished [as superior]. (69)
"What is truth? What is eternal? What is untruth? What is impermanent? Who is the self? Who is the individual soul (jīva)? Who is the other? Who is Śiva?

Who is the Supreme Self?"—the disciple who is intent on hearing from the presence of the Guru, the illustrious Guru, being devoted to listening to the answering words and desirous of service, is distinguished as a true disciple.
The meaning is that he is distinguished in comparison to disciples who are devoted solely to service. || 69 ||
Now, as to how he is "supreme," he says:
"Having heard and repeatedly heard the words of the Guru which bring about the direct realization of Śiva, he who becomes tranquil within his own mind shall attain the state of liberation. (70)

The disciple who is desirous of learning, having heard again and again—from the venerable Guru—the words of instruction consistent with the Vedas which bring about the act of the direct realization of Śiva, becomes pacified—that is, he becomes tranquil—within his own heart; such a one shall attain, that is, obtain, the state of liberation. || 70 ||
To the question, "Could a disciple not become liberated merely by serving the guru? he says:
"The mind of the disciple does not awaken without the word of the guru;
how can the lotus blossom without the light of the thousand-rayed sun? (71)

Without the words of the guru’s instruction, the disciple’s mind—the heart-lotus—neither awakens nor blossoms. Regarding this, there is an illustration: without the light of the thousand-rayed sun, how can a lotus shine and blossom? It does not blossom at all; such is the meaning. || 71 ||
Furthermore, he states another illustration:
"By the mere rising of the sun, the sun-crystal (sūryakānta) shines."
By the mere glance of the guru, the disciple shines with awakening.
The meaning is that [this occurs] through the words of the teacher's instruction, and not by mere sight alone. The remainder is clear. || 72 ||

Now, in accordance with the statement of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, "Then, for the sake of knowing that, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12), he describes the manner of surrendering oneself to a guru for the purpose of hearing that [teaching]:
Having approached a true guru with palms joined in reverence, the disciple should listen to the means that uniquely illuminates the awakening to non-dual supreme bliss. (73)
Having approached the true Guru with offerings in hand and with palms joined in reverence, the disciple— with his two hands folded like a bud—
should listen, preceded by questions, to the means that primarily reveals the awakening of incomparable supreme bliss, namely the means in the form of the secret of the instruction.
The meaning is that one should listen. || 73 ||

Now he explains the manner of the inquiry: "What is the supreme reality to be known? By what are all things established? Through the direct realization of what is there liberation? Tell me this in brief. (74)
"O venerable Guru, what is the supreme reality to be known? By what entity are all things, both moving and unmoving, established?
Through the direct realization of what would liberation—namely, mokṣa—occur? Please explain all of this briefly, in summary; that is, grant us instruction. || 74 ||
Then,
to him who had approached him properly, that wise one—
To him whose mind was tranquil and who was endowed with peace, he fully declared that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the imperishable, true Person. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3)
Thus, in accordance with the *Muṇḍaka* Śruti, he explains the answer to that question in five aphorisms:
"When this question has been posed by the disciple who is previously self-restrained, the Guru should declare the reality to him, by which there may be a dissolution of transmigratory existence. (75)
"With a restrained self" means with a one-pointed mind; the rest is clear. || 75 ||
Now, he provides the answer in sequence to the question posed:
"Śiva alone is the supreme reality, whose form is consciousness, bliss, and existence.
He is the ultimate reality; for the world other than him, there is no permanence. (76)

Śiva alone, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), is the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattva*) worthy of being known; he is the ultimate reality in its true sense, meaning he is eternal. As for the world of Viṣṇu and others, which appears as something different in nature from consciousness, its eternality—that is, its being co-eternal like Śiva—[is not established].
The meaning is that it does not exist. || 76 ||

Now, he provides the answer to the question, "Upon what are all things established?": "This unreal proliferation is established in Śaṅkara, the eternally existent Self, just as the nature of silver is established in mother-of-pearl. (77)

"Non-correspondence with reality" (ayathārtha) means "impermanent" (anitya). An illustration of this is the nature of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell— a common object of worldly existence— which, because it has become an object of cognition through both types of sense organs characterized by knowledge and action, [is perceived as such] within the existent self.

The meaning is that just as the nature of illusory silver— which exists only as an object of the sense organs alone and is sublated in the subsequent moment— is established, so too does the impermanent phenomenal world exist within the eternal Śaṅkara. || 77 ||
351) Now, he provides the answer to the question, "By the realization of what is liberation attained?"—
by the state of "I am Śiva," when Śiva has been firmly realized.
He becomes liberated from cyclic existence through the breaking of the knot of delusion. || 78 ||

When Śiva is directly perceived through the firm conviction "I am Śiva," one becomes liberated from the bondage of delusion—that is, the knot of ignorance—which consists of worldly existence (saṃsāra) and its specific distinctions; this is the meaning. || 78 ||
Then, having thus explained the meaning, he enjoins the disciple:
"Meditate upon yourself as Śiva and do not think of anything other than Śiva.
When the non-duality with Śiva is thus stabilized, you will become liberated while living. (79)
O disciple, contemplate yourself as Śiva;
the sense is that there is no distinction in the nature of the self between Śiva and his devotee. Do not conceive of this manifest universe appearing before you as anything other than Śiva.

The meaning is that you should contemplate [the world] as being nothing other than the very nature of Śiva, because it is included within the activity of consciousness whose inherent nature is Śiva, according to the analogy of waves in water. Thus, when non-duality with Śiva is firmly established, you will become liberated while living (jīvanmukta), even though you are still alive. || 79 ||
Now he concludes the section on service:
"Thus impelled by the virtuous Guru, the disciple, perceiving the entire world as Śiva alone, becomes liberated while living. (80)

In this manner, having been thoroughly enlightened by the venerable Guru— who is endowed with qualities such as knowledge and dispassion— the disciple perceives the web of the world as nothing but Śiva,
not seeing it as consisting of anything other than Śiva, namely, the nature of ignorance.

The meaning is that, by perceiving [all things] as being essentially Śiva because they consist of the powers of consciousness and action which have Śiva as their very nature, one is born as liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 80 ||
Thus ends the section on the place of service; now follows the section on the place of attendance.
Then the knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted, when He is seen, who is both the high and the low (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).

According to the statement of the *Muṇḍakopaniṣad*: "He whose vision is steady without an object of sight, whose breath is steady without effort, and whose mind is steady without a support—he alone is a yogin, he is a guru, he is to be served. And according to the statement of the *Yogajāgama*: [the same].
Only one who is intent on serving [the teacher] and has attained perfection through the guru’s instruction is to be served; thus, he describes that state:

"Because of tasting the nectar of the guru’s words, one attains the great fruit of awakening. Being intent on service, such a person is called 'to be served' because they are worthy of being served by all. (81)

The meaning is that one who has attained the great fruit of the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva by tasting the nectar-like essence of the words of the guru’s instruction is called "the one to be served" (sevya), because such a person, being truly desirous of hearing [the truth], is worthy of being served by all. || 81 ||
Then, with three verses, he states that the one to be served is indeed worthy of worship like a guru:
"When the wisdom taught by the guru has become stable in the mind, the disciple, having realized Śiva directly, is always worshipped like a guru. (82)
"In consciousness" means in the specific knowledge characterized by the non-duality of Śiva; the remainder is clear. || 82 ||
Surely he should be served and worshipped like a guru; why is he to be worshipped? To this he says:

"Since the attainment of superior knowledge has been acquired from the guru, therefore, through the acquisition of that knowledge, the disciple shall attain a state of worshipfulness equal to that of the guru. (83)

Because a greater abundance of wealth has arisen from the knowledge of the venerable guru, therefore, from that acquisition of knowledge, the disciple shall attain—that is, go to—the state of being worthy of worship, just like the venerable guru; this is the meaning. || 83 ||
Now he states another reason:
"Because of the particularity of the continuous state of 'I am Śiva,' once the state of Śiva has arisen, he is indeed worthy of worship just like Śiva himself. (84)

The meaning is that when the state of Śiva— Śivatva— has arisen and become manifest through the specific practice of the uninterrupted and unimpeded state of "I am Śiva," then that seeker of instruction is indeed worthy of worship, just like Śiva himself. || 84 ||
Now, one might ask: since this [deity] possesses attachment while Śiva is free from attachment, how can he be worthy of worship in the same manner as Śiva? To this, he says:
"Even though his mind is attached to sense objects, he is devoid of attachment to those objects."
The yogin endowed with the state of Śiva is to be served like another Śiva himself. || 85 ||

In this context, the phrase "endowed with the state of Śiva" (śivabhāvayuta) is a qualifier containing a reason. The meaning is that a yogi who desires to hear [the teachings], a Śiva-yogin—even if his mind is fixed upon sense objects—is one who is entirely free from attachment to those objects; because of the firmness of his state as Śiva, he is to be served and worshipped like a second Śiva. || 85 ||
Freed from the noose of doubt, with a mind steady in that awakening which bestows liberation,

and shattering the delusion of embodied beings— the very root of the great cycle of existence— with his vision, [he abides] in the supreme state of Śiva, which is incomparable and consists of the essence of existence, bliss, and consciousness.
The yogi whose self is absorbed and whose worldly power has perished is served by people. || 86 ||

Thus ends [the section] in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a determination of the Vīraśaiva Dharma, composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a knower of Brahman through the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*).
The seventeenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Nine Liṅgas Situated on the Ground of Prasāda. || 17 ||

Freed from the noose of doubt— the uncertainty as to whether "I am Śiva" or not— and liberated, O bestower of liberation, with a steady mind and a firm heart fixed upon the realization of the non-duality of Śiva and the consciousness that grants both supreme and relative liberation,
[he perceives] the delusion of embodied beings, which is the root, the fundamental cause of great transmigratory existence.
Dissolving the ignorance of embodied beings with his vision— the gaze of compassion— and restraining it,

the yogi whose self is merged in the supreme state of Śiva, which is beyond analogy and whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss; possessing a personal identity that has become one with That, he is a Śiva-yogi whose worldly power and expansion have been extinguished.
The meaning is that he, having caused the majesty of the entire cosmic manifestation to dissolve into his own power, is served and worshipped by people.
According to the tradition, these three signs (liṅgas) are to be joined respectively with these three limbs of the gracious one (prasādin). || 86 ||

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Nine Marks Residing in the Prasādi Site," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Maritoṇṭadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 17.
The Eighteenth Chapter:
(Now, the Section on the Self) Next, the divisions of the section on the Liṅgin of Vital Breath are described. Now follows the question of Agastya:
The various divisions of sacred sites connected to Prasāda have been proclaimed;
now tell me of the divisions of sacred sites situated upon the Prāṇaliṅgi site.
"Distinctions of place" means intermediate subdivisions. "Tell" means "instruct. The remainder is clear. || 1 ||
Now, Śrī Renuka explains that division in three verses: "Nine stages (*sthala*) are proclaimed, resting upon the stage of the *prāṇaliṅgin*.
First, the stage of the Self (*ātma-sthala*) is proclaimed, and after that, the stage of the Inner Self (*antarātma-sthala*). (2)
After that is the station of the Supreme Self (Paramātma-sthala), then the one known as Nirdeha-āgama,
then the one known as Nirbhāva-āgama, and after that the station of Naṣṭa-āgama.
Now, listen to the characteristics of these: first, the "initial clarification," then the "final clarification," and then the "clarification of the object to be served. (4)
This is clear. 2-4 ||

356) Now, according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (ChāU 8.1.4), this Self is "free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true. It is thus, in accordance with this scriptural authority, that this [Self is described].
The Self alone is to be served; thus he describes the section concerning the Self:
"When reality is contemplated by abandoning the state of being a living soul (jīva), through the awakening of the Guru, then this is proclaimed as the Self. (5)

This very one is to be served; by means of the connection with the auspicious Guru’s knowledge of Śiva, when the state of being a living being—that is, the condition of individual existence—is abandoned and the supreme reality is realized, then he is proclaimed as the "Self" (ātman); this is the meaning. || 5 ||

Now, as to the question "What is this living being (jīva)?"— the self (ātman) should be known as a part [of the intellect] divided a hundredfold, like a hundredth part of the tip of a hair; and that [self] is fit for infinity.

Thus, in accordance with the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, he establishes the nature of the individual soul (jīva) through five aphorisms: "Residing in the heart, it is like a hundredth part of the tip of a hair."
Not consuming any fruit of action, the Self shines forth like a lamp.
The meaning is that, being like a hundredth part of the tip of a hair (*vālāgra*), while experiencing the fruit of his own accumulated karma,

he remains situated within the heart— that is, in the heart-lotus. Now, if this is so, then because [the self] is restricted to one part of the body, how can there be such experiences as "pain in my foot" or "pleasure in my head"?

Anticipating the question of how consciousness is perceived throughout all parts of the body, he says: "Like a lamp. Just as a lamp, although situated in only one part of a house, pervades the entire house with its own light and illuminates every object contained within it, so too [is it] for the individual soul (*jīva*) in relation to one part of the body.

Even though [the self] is situated within, according to the scriptural statement, "having mounted the body by means of intelligence," the individual self (jīvātman) manifests— that is, shines forth— by pervading the entire body through the omnipresence of its intellect and experiencing consciousness throughout all its limbs. || 6 ||
(357) Now, one might ask: why is such a form the natural state of the individual soul (jīva)? To this he says:
"The Self, too, resides within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of all beings."
Bound by primordial karma, it has experienced [suffering] due to attachment to impurity.
The Self of all beings— that is, of the five elements— is, from the perspective of ultimate reality,

both all-pervasive and the substratum [of all]; yet, due to the attachment of impurities and the permeation by the *āṇava* and other stains, it becomes atomic (*aṇu*), exceedingly subtle like a supreme atom, and remains constrained by its initial karma, bound by the fetters of past actions.
The meaning is that he resorted to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), that is, he took recourse to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). || 7 ||

Now, since the connection with the body would likewise follow from the connection with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), he says in this regard: "Just as redness may arise in a crystal gem through association with a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), so too does the self's identification with the body arise through association with the ego-sense. (8)
The meaning is that through connection with limited egoity, connection with the body is attained. The remainder is clear. || 8 ||
Now, one might ask: "How can there be a connection with a body for the Self, which is free from all defects, in the manner described? To this he says:
"Though bodiless, though all-pervading, and though stainless, the Self, residing within a body produced by *māyā*, wanders through the cycle of transmigration. (9)
Although bodiless by virtue of possessing a body of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) which is the cause of liberation for both higher and lower beings,
he is all-pervasive because of his lack of spatial limitation; and although untainted (*nirañjana*) due to being free from defects,
he possesses his own downward-facing power of *māyā*, which is the cause of the thirty principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth.
The meaning is that, possessing a body distinguished by the imagined digit of the moon, he wanders about in saṃsāra. || 9 ||
358) Now, he explains the manner in which such a living being attains the state of the Self:
"The realization of the nature of the Self [is attained] through the distinction between the body and the senses."
The attainment of that Self is said to be by way of its nature as the indivisible Brahman. || 10 ||

Self-knowledge consists in realizing the Self as the undivided Brahman, as the unlimited Brahman, by way of its being distinct from the body and the senses— which are of the nature of effects of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, which are *māyika* and *prākṛta*, and which possess the characteristics previously described.
When the knowledge of one's own true nature arises, that is called the attainment of the Self (ātmaprāpti), the acquisition of selfhood (ātmatva).
The meaning is that this is based on the Vedic scripture: "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self; there is no gain greater than this" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). || 10 ||
Now, one might ask: for what purpose has the undivided Brahman come into being as characterized by a limited body? To this he says:
"There is no connection with a body for that which is naturally bodiless; through the conjunction of ignorance and karma, it becomes embodied for the sake of experience. (11)

Although, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no connection with a body for the bodiless Supreme Self, nevertheless, for the sake of experience— just as a king, though already expanded by the joy of the power of a universal sovereign, [enjoys his kingdom].
Playing, he performs the duty of a foot-soldier because of his adherence to that duty.

Thus, according to the illustration stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise, even one who is nourished by the savoring of the undivided rasa (akhaṇḍa-rasa) becomes an embodied being (*dehī*) when, through the desire for the savoring of divided rasa (*khaṇḍa-rasa*), there occurs a connection with the impurity of *āṇava* and so forth, as conceived by His sovereignty, by means of the conjunction of ignorance and karma.

By the analogy of the solidity of clarified butter (*ghṛtakāṭhinya*), he becomes embodied in part. Therefore, it should be understood that because the one who has become a partial manifestation is connected with impurities such as ignorance (*jñāna-ādi-mala*), he lacks the knowledge "I am Śiva," just like a mortal king.
On this point: "He indeed did not find delight. Therefore, being alone, he does not find delight. He desired a second. He...
"Of such extent was He" [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.37–38; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.3]; "Having created that, He entered into it;

having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)" [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 6.4]—so says the Śruti. "Pervading this entire world, I stand with one part" [Bhagavad Gītā 10.42]; "A portion of My very self is in the world of living beings."

And there is the statement of the Blessed One: "The eternal one who has become the life-force" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.7). Even though Śiva is partless, because of his absolute sovereignty, he possesses the state of having parts as conceived through his own sovereignty.

This is possible, as illustrated by the analogy of the calf being taken away; for according to the principle that "action indeed rests only upon the object and not upon the agent," there is no bondage of the Self. In reality, however, this is so because of the Śruti: "In the beginning, the Self alone was all this" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1), and because of the scriptural statement: "The seventeenth digit is the Lord, within whom the moving and non-moving worlds are dissolved."

Previously, at the time of universal dissolution within the Supreme Lord, this entire world existed in a state of non-difference from its cause— known as His own Māyā— which was itself non-distinct from Him.
"Or rather, it exists only in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) and not as a state of non-existence"—
from this statement in the *Pārāśaropapurāṇa* as well,

the entire universe [is established] by the analogy of the essence of a mango fruit within the power of the sky of consciousness (*cidambara-śakti*), which is characterized by the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with the activity of consciousness inherent in the Self.

There is no inconsistency whatsoever in the claim that [the Supreme Self] exists through identity (*tādātmya*); for, according to the method to be explained in the section concerning the Supreme Self, it creates, sustains, withdraws, conceals, and bestows grace upon sparks of consciousness that have attained identity with itself—just as fire [creates] sparks—each in accordance with their respective karma. || 11 ||
To the question, "What then is the name of this living being (jīva)? he says:
"It is neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor a yakṣa, nor indeed a rākṣasa;
it is neither a human, nor an animal, nor one with the form of an immobile being. (12)
He shines forth with various names according to his association with various bodies; this is clear. || 12 ||

To the question of what these [individuals] are like, [the answer is]: according to the Vṛddha-Jābāla Śruti, they are transmigrating souls (jīvas) bound by their own respective evil deeds and by the impulsion of the Supreme Lord.

He says that, through the state of equilibrium between duality and non-duality— which is like the simultaneous perception of two eyes— beings, though possessing various forms due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of individual souls imagined by the sovereignty of Śiva, become the objects of Śiva’s play: *Śivasya svātantryaparikalpitajīvopādhinā nānārūpāḥ santaḥ śivasya krīḍābhājanarūpāḥ.*
They possess various ripenings of karma and resort to various wombs;
they have entered into various yogas and exhibit various mental activities. || 13 ||
Embarked upon various paths, forming diverse intentions, lacking independence, possessing limited knowledge, and being the causes of limited agency,
they have become the objects of the divine play of Śiva, the Supreme Self. (14)

Due to the ripening of various kinds of past karma, according to the statement that there are sixteen hundred thousand gods, they have entered into various wombs such as those of gods, animals, and humans;
they contemplate various means for the enjoyment of heavenly realms and are possessed by various types of intellects.

The meaning is that individual souls (jīvas)— who have entered the paths of various philosophical systems such as Vaiṣṇava and others, who form diverse volitions, who possess limited knowledge, who act as the causes for limited agency, and who are devoid of independence— have become vessels for the divine play of the Supreme Self, Śiva; that is, they have become like toys for his sport.
Now, regarding the question "What do these go?", he says:
Impelled by the Supreme Lord according to their respective karma, living beings who are performers of action go either to heaven or even to hell. (15)
This is clear. || 15 ||
Now, as to whether there is stability for them in heaven or hell, he says: "Furthermore, by the remainder of their karma, they are born from the womb;
having been born, they die; being born again, they are subject to death once more."
They wander in the terrible cycle of existence without any talk of rest. (16)
The meaning is: "by means of talk concerning rest," that is, excluding any discourse on not resting in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). The remainder is clear. || 16 ||
If this is so, why does the wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra continue eternally? To this he says:
"The state of being a living soul (jīvatva) is the totality of suffering; this very state is fashioned by impurity (mala).
It is cast off through the awakening of the Guru, and the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) shines forth. (17)

The state of being a *jīva* (an individual soul) is imagined through impurities such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*); that is to say, it is imagined through impurities such as ignorance (*ajñāna*). Therefore, it is of the nature of the totality of suffering. This very state of being a *jīva*, which is of the nature of the totality of suffering, is cast out—that is, removed—through the awakening of the Guru, meaning through the awakening to the non-duality of Śiva taught by the venerable Guru; this is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
The meaning is that the capacity of the power of knowledge regarding one's own true nature is manifested. || 17 ||
Thus [ends] the section on the Self;
now follows the section on the Inner Self.
Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by external ocular defects,
so too the one Inner Self of all beings is not [defiled].
The outsider is stained by the suffering of the world. (Kaṭhopaniṣad 2.5.11)
Thus, in accordance with the *Kaṭhavallī* scripture, he establishes that the Self, having discarded its state as the individual soul (*jīva*), becomes the inner self (*antarātman*):
"When the state of being a soul has been dispelled through the instruction of the Guru..."
Then, for one who has cast it off, even the state of an inner self will certainly cease to exist. || 18 ||
(p. 362) When the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), the condition of being a *jīva*, is cast off through the awakening by the Guru— that is, through the Guru’s instruction—
then for that Self whose state of being a *jīva* has been cast off, the state of being the Inner Self (*antarātmabhāva*) will certainly come to be.
The meaning is "certainty. || 18 ||
Now, he describes the nature of the inner self (antarātman) by means of three verses:
"Although this individual soul (jīva) resides within the body, it is devoid of contact with the body;
because it is realized as the Supreme Self through awakening, it is celebrated as the 'inner self'. (19)

The meaning is this: although this *jīva* resides within the body, because it is free from attachment to the body, and because through awakening—knowledge of its own true nature—it possesses the state of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it is called the "inner self" (*antarātman*).
(19) Now, he explains this by means of another method:
