Because it exists in the interval between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), and because of its union with the attributes of both, it is celebrated as the "inner self" (antarātman). || 20 ||

The Self, which has cast off the state of being a *jīva*, is to be served at the time of instruction for the disciple, because it exists in the interval between the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*); that is to say, because it stands in the middle. At that time, by virtue of its connection with the nature of Śiva through its role as the instructor of the disciple's intellect and as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*), [it is to be served].

Because it possesses the characteristics of a living being through the existence of functions such as eating and speaking, and because it is thus endowed with the qualities of both [the body and the soul], it is celebrated as the "inner self" (antarātman). || 20 ||
Then he speaks by way of another method: "The delusion of being a human and so forth arises from the connection with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
because it is known that this is not one's true nature (svabhāva), it is called the 'inner self' (antarātman). (21)

The meaning is that because of the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva) whose nature is limited, there arises the delusion of being a human being and so forth, but not by its own inherent nature; thus, through the knowledge that this state of having a limited nature is not intrinsic, it is called the "inner self" (antarātman). || 21 ||
363) Now, regarding whether or not he has a connection with the body, [the author] states this by means of three sūtras preceded by an illustration:
"Just as there would be no clinging of water to a lotus leaf,"
Likewise, even though it inhabits a body, it has no contact with that body.
Just as a bird situated in its nest appears distinct from the nest, so too this Self, though residing within the body, is revealed as other than the body. (23)
This is clear. || 22–23 ||

Furthermore, he gives another illustration: "Just as the moon is covered by clouds that are themselves devoid of attachment, so too is the Self enveloped by the aggregate of the body, though it is free from attachment. (24)

Just as the moon is covered by clouds that are free from attachment and entirely detached from it, so too the Self—having ceased its state as a living soul—is served and enveloped by the aggregates of the body, that is, by the collection of bodies beginning with the gross; the meaning is that, while remaining unattached, it is surrounded by them. || 24 ||
To the question "Then, seeing what does he remain?", he says:
"Free from the sense of 'mine,' free from egoism, and with the affliction of limiting adjuncts cast off, the Self, even while residing in the body, always perceives Śiva through yoga. (25)
Viklava means affliction. Yoga refers to the efficacy of yoga. The remainder is clear. || 25 ||
To the objection that "in that case, this [consciousness] appears as such because it perceives Śiva," he says:
"By abandoning the enjoyer and the enjoyed, through the grace of the Impeller."
Freed from the state of being an enjoyer, the Self shines forth by its very nature. || 26 ||

Through the relinquishing of the enjoyer and the enjoyed— that is, through the abandonment of the objects of enjoyment by the living soul that is the enjoyer— and by virtue of the grace of the Impeller, the Lord, one becomes free from the state of being an enjoyer; thus,
being divested of the condition of the living soul characterized as an enjoyer, [one remains] by one's very nature.
The meaning is that it shines forth, i.e., manifests, by virtue of its essential nature as *ātmatva* (selfhood), which is common to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). || 26 ||
Now he concludes the section on the abode of the inner self (antarātma-sthala): "Śambhu always resides within as the impeller of all;
through the yoga of realizing that, the yogi rejoices like one who is liberated. (27)
This is clear. || 27 ||
Thus [ends] the section on the inner self;
now follows the section on the supreme self.
Having thus known the Supreme Self, which dwells in the cave of the heart, partless and non-dual,
the witness of all, devoid of both being and non-being—
It proceeds toward the pure form of the Supreme Self.
Thus, in accordance with the Śruti on Kaivalya, he establishes that this very inner self (antarātman), by virtue of its stainlessness, is the supreme self (paramātman):

When the impurity that is the cause of saṃsāra has been shaken off by the awakening to that [reality], this one is called the Supreme Self (paramātman) because he abides as the Supreme Self through the state of essential identity (sāmarasya). || 28 ||

When this inner self (*antarātmā*), having its impurity—the cause of *saṃsāra*—which is ignorance, has been shaken off and removed by the awakening to that [Self], namely by the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva, it is called the "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) because of its state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), that is, its state of being of one flavor with the Supreme Self (*paramātma-stha*). This is the meaning. || 28 ||
Now, as to the question "Who is this Supreme Self?", it is said here:
Because he is superior to all the various individual selves by virtue of his own splendor, Śiva is called the Supreme Self; though omnipresent, he is luminous. (29)
By his own splendor—that is, by his innate radiance—Śiva, although all-pervading and omnipresent, is luminous;
because he is superior to all distinctions of the self (ātman), he is called the Supreme Self (Paramātman); this is the meaning. || 29 ||
Now, he states its definition by way of another method:
"He in whose great ocean of Māyā the multitude of bubbles that are the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) emerge and submerge is called the Supreme Self (paramātman). (30)
This is clear. || 30 ||
Now, he describes the very nature of that [Self] through three aphorisms preceded by an illustration:
"In which all the hosts of luminaries, like sparks from a fire, arise and then go to their dissolution—that is the form of the Supreme Self. (31)

That object in which all the hosts of luminaries—the entire collection of the vital energy of all living beings—arise and then dissolve like sparks born from fire; that is the form (*rūpa*) of the Supreme Self, meaning its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Then he speaks by way of another method: "That form of the Supreme Self, in which all things, having come together like waves in the ocean, go to their dissolution. (32)
That reality in which all the principles, beginning with the earth, merge together like great waves into the ocean— that is the form of the Supreme Self.
Again, he speaks by way of another method:
"The essential nature of the Supreme Self is declared to be free from any connection with impurity, consisting of the entirety of the universe, and situated above all principles (tattvas). (33)

The nature of the Supreme Self, which is free from connection with the impurities of individuality (āṇava) and so forth, and which constitutes the life-force of the entire universe consisting of name and form, is said to exist above all the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth and ending with Śiva. || 33 ||

Now, as to how the Supreme Self manifests, he says: "Just as the sun shines, pervading the entire world with its own light, so too the Supreme Self manifests, pervading [all] with its own powers. (34)

The meaning is that just as the sun exists pervading the entire world with its own radiance, so too the Supreme Self shines forth, pervading the universe by means of His five powers, such as Dhūmāvatī and the others. For instance, because that which is to be created consists of the five elements, [the power] Dhūmāvatī— whose other synonym is Bhūmi— is present in the earth.

The power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) resides in water; the power of preservation (*pālana-śakti*), characterized by nourishment, resides in fire; the power of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-śakti*), characterized by the illumination of the universe, resides in air; the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-śakti*), characterized by desiccation, resides in ether;
and the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*), which is adept at unifying [the soul] with the all-pervading Śiva, resides in space.
The power of sovereignty (*vibhutāśakti*). Thus, the meaning is that [the Lord] exists pervading the universe through these five [powers]. This same point has been stated in the *Pañcāśikāśāstra*:
Dhūmāvatī is manifest on earth, Hlādā in water, and Bhāsvatī shines in fire;
Spandā is in wind, Vibhvī in space, and by them the entire world is pervaded.
Dhūmāvatī is the power for invisibility, Bhāsvatī for illumination,
Spandā for agitation, Vibhvī for pervasion, and Hlādā shall be for nourishment.

Thus, the meaning is that He exists pervading the universe by means of His own powers (*śakti*). In this regard, just as there is no difference between the sun and its manifestation when it pervades and illumines the universe with its own radiance, so too one should not suspect any difference between Śiva and the universe; for the earth and other elements are of the nature of power (*śakti*), and [there is no difference] among powers.
Because [the universe] has Śiva as its essential nature. It is not the case that the universe consists of the nature of Sāra and Tejas; rather, there is merely a relationship.
Since no example exists for every single aspect, the example applies only to the pervasion (vyāpti). || 34 ||

Now, answering the objection— "In that case, since the Lord appears as all-pervading, why is it not possible for Him to be a transformation of the universe?"— he concludes the section on the Supreme Self:
Though manifesting everywhere, the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the universal illusion and whose nature is self-luminous light, becomes the inner self of all individual souls. (35)

The Supreme Self, although manifest everywhere in the universe, is distinct from the cosmic illusion (*viśvamāyā*); it is the material cause of the universe and, like space, pervades the universe, remaining unaffected by the sixfold modifications of existence (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*)— namely, "it is born," "it exists," "it grows," "it transforms," "it declines," and "it perishes"— as stated in the *Nirukta*.

Being free from defects, He exists as the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss; for those individual souls who have developed the discernment that the world is to be abandoned, He becomes the form of light that illuminates their intellects. || 35 ||
Thus ends the section on the Supreme Self;
now begins the section on the arrival of the bodiless one.
Now, it is said that the "basis" is duality; the supreme self-control consists in the abandonment of duality.
The yogi who is liberated while living is fully liberated upon the casting off of the body.

Thus, in accordance with the words of the *Devīkālottara*, having refuted the attributes of the body, [the author] describes the state of bodiless liberation for the Śiva-yogin who possesses the contemplation of the nature of the Supreme Self:
"For one who possesses a body yet contemplates the state of being the Supreme Self, and is devoid of ego..."
For one whose bodily attributes have been cast off, it is called the arrival of the bodiless state. || 36 ||

The attainment of the bodiless state (nirdehāgama), meaning the reaching of the state beyond the body, is said— that is, described— for the Śiva-yogin who possesses a body yet is one whose nature is that of the Supreme Self, who is devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine," who has cast off the attributes of the body, and who has discarded corporeality and other such bodily characteristics. || 36 ||
Now, he establishes through six aphorisms that for the Śiva-yogin who possesses the state of the Supreme Self, there is no connection with the body:
"When 'mine-ness' and 'I-ness,' which are the causes of the delusion of transmigratory existence, have dissolved..."
For one who has entered into the supreme I-consciousness, whence can there be a body, and whence pleasure?
The meaning is: from what [source] do the body and joy arise? || 37 ||
How can a yogi whose mind is submerged in the profound, great ocean of consciousness—the sole, manifold-free flood—ever contemplate the body? (36)
The Śiva-yogin, whose mind is submerged in the unfathomable ocean of consciousness where the entire manifold of moving and non-moving things has ceased, [abandons] the body.
In what manner should one contemplate? The meaning is: in no manner whatsoever. || 38 ||
Remembering the self as the indivisible sky of consciousness,
one is not tainted by the modifications residing in the body, even while joined with a body.

The meaning is that the Śiva-yogin, remembering his own self as the space of consciousness free from all limitation, is not tainted by the modifications of the body and senses even while the body exists. || 39 ||
Where can one who considers the Self to be the supreme ether—the indivisible form of consciousness, non-dual, and of the nature of bliss—ever be deluded? (40)
Considering one's own self to be the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*) in the form of indivisible, non-dual consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*),

and knowing it according to the *Chāndogya* (and *Taittirīya*) Upaniṣad [1.6.2]: "Brahman has space as its body, is the true self, rejoices in vital breath, delights in the mind, and is enriched by peace."

In what place or upon what substratum does the Śiva-yogin become deluded, thinking "I am embodied"? The meaning is: nowhere at all, because there is no location whatsoever apart from Brahman. || 40 ||

"Surely, even space is seen to be limited by adjuncts such as a jar; to this he replies: 'He whose mind perceives that distinctions are seen in a single reality only as ordained by adjuncts—how could such a person be limited by the body? (41)
This is clear. || 41 ||
Now, to the question "Why is that?", he says:
"The cognition of difference is the cause of the delimitation of all things;
when the cognition of non-difference has arisen, what talk can there be of delimitation? (42)

370) When it is understood through the analogy of the space within a jar that difference is merely adventitious (aupādhika), and when the cognition of non-difference has become firm, the cognition of difference— which serves as the cause for the delimitation of the reality— becomes weakened.
The meaning is that there is no discourse whatsoever regarding delimitation. || 42 ||
Now, having revealed that non-duality, he concludes the section on the arrival of the bodiless state:
"For one who possesses the all-pervading realization, 'I am Śiva,' how could there be any connection with a body for that immeasurable Self? (43)

For that yogi of Śiva who possesses the realization of the non-duality of Śiva—pervading all things in the form "I am Śiva"—how could there be a connection with a limited body for him whose self is immeasurable? The meaning is: not in any way whatsoever. || 43 ||
Thus is the stage of the scripture on the bodiless; now,
the stage of the scripture on the non-existent.
One should not hold the mind above, nor in the middle, nor anywhere below;
one should always keep it free from internal mental states and without any support.
Thus, in accordance with the statement of the Devīkālottara, [the author] describes the locus of the scripture of non-manifestation for the Śiva-yogin who has attained the Nirdeha-āgama:
"Because of the distinction from one's own nature, and because of the exclusion of other states of being..."
Existence free from modification is called the arrival at non-existence. || 44 ||

The meaning is that because its own nature—which is a bodiless nature—is distinct, that is, separate from other states of being (bhāva), and because it excludes other existences, the state of mind (manobhāva) is free from modification; being liberated from the modifications of the senses, it is called the arrival at the state beyond existence (nirbhāvāgama). || 44 ||
371) Now, he demonstrates that characteristic of its manifestation through five sūtras:
"The state of 'I am Brahman' has two entities as its substratum."
The absence of that [duality] is certain for one who has become unified within the space of consciousness (cidvyoman). || 45 ||

The notion "I am Brahman" would imply two distinct entities: the "I" and "Brahman. However, for that state which has become one with and attained a single flavor within the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), the absence of such [duality] is certain; the meaning is that the absence of the implication of two entities is definitively ascertained. || 45 ||

Now, because the state of "I am Brahman" involves immersion in two poles and is thus constituted by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), whereas the singular state of "I" is free from conceptualization, it is said that for one who abides in that singular state, there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) of illusory distinctions such as caste and so forth: [The verse continues: "For one who has become one with the Self, there is no distinction of caste, nor lineage, nor even the notion of 'I'. (1.23) The meaning is as follows: when one has attained identity with the Self through the realization "I am Brahman," there is no longer any distinction of caste (*jāti*)—such as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra—nor any distinction of lineage (*gotra*), nor even the notion of "I" (*ahampratyaya*). This is because the state of being one with the Self is devoid of all conceptual construction. Since the state of "I am Brahman" is composed of dualities, it is permeated by conceptualization; however, the state of "I" alone is free from conceptualization. Therefore, for one established in that singular state, the impressions of illusory differences do not exist. Thus, the author says: "For one who has become one with the Self, there is no distinction of caste, nor lineage, nor even the notion of 'I'. (1.23) This means: when one has become identical with the Self through the realization "I am Brahman," there is no longer any distinction of caste, nor lineage, nor even the notion of "I. Thus, the author says: "For one who has become one with the Self, there is no distinction of caste, nor lineage, nor even the

For one who is firmly established in the singular state within the stainless sky of consciousness, where is the connection to the latent impressions of birth, and where is the wandering existence as an embodied being? (46)

For the Śiva-yogin who has ascended through identity into the stainless space of consciousness (cidākāśa), where is the connection with the latent impressions of caste, class, and stage of life? Where is embodiedness—the state of possessing a body?
And where is the wandering within the wheel of saṃsāra? This is the meaning. || 46 ||

If this is so, what then is the destination of meditation and the like? To this he says: "In the empty space of consciousness, the place far beyond the path of speech and mind, the great yogi whose self has dissolved—what could he possibly meditate upon, or by what means? (47)

Since the Śruti declares, "From whence words return along with the mind, failing to reach it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1), how or what object could a Śiva-yogin— who has attained identity with that station of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), which is beyond the range of the paths of speech and mind and is devoid of forms such as blue or yellow— possibly meditate upon? By no means.
The meaning is that there is no object whatsoever that cannot be made an object of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) by some means. || 47 ||
(372) Now, one might object: "If there is an absence of the latent impressions of injunctions and prohibitions, would it not result in censure? To this he says:
"Just as the radiance of the sun is the same whether the ground is impure or pure,"
Thus, one who maintains equanimity toward all things always falls [into error], even if they profess non-duality.

Just as the radiance or light of the sun, Ravi, falls upon both pure and impure ground alike, so too does the non-dualist of Śiva, always maintaining an even disposition—that is, possessing an equal mental state—move through all things; this is the meaning. || 48 ||
Regarding how he moves about, it is said:
"He does not fear old age or death, nor does he fall under the power of hunger;
experiencing his own perfectly full bliss, he is one of great happiness. (49)
The meaning is that, having become one possessed of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he moves about. The remainder is clear. || 49 ||
Thus is the stage of the scripture of non-existence;
then the stage of the lost scripture;
and thus, for one endowed with the scripture of non-existence, due to the absence of the knowledge of duality.
That [text] elucidates the locus where the scripture has vanished:

"In the Great Awakening, which is devoid of duality and free from the triad of the knower and so forth, because of the disappearance of knowledge, it is here called 'the vanished scripture' (naṣṭāgama). (50)

In this context, regarding the knowledge of Mahāśiva which is devoid of duality, because it is empty of the phenomenal world consisting of the triad of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object known,

there is the state of the destruction of "knowledge"— that is, of dualistic knowledge— within the scope of the Śiva-yogi who has attained the realization of the scripture that is free from objective manifestation.
The meaning is that because it has perished, it is called "the arrival of what was lost. || 50 ||
(373) Now, one might ask: how can Śiva-yogins possess the state of being empty of the phenomenal world consisting of the threefold division? To this he says:
"For the supreme yogins whose minds are permeated by the latent impression of non-duality..."
Otherwise, how could there be the state of being a knower for one who perceives the inner self? (51)
Otherwise, "knowership" means the state of being a knower of an object other than oneself; "within" means within one's own heart. The remainder is clear. || 51 ||
Now, one might ask: "If he lacks the status of a knower in any other way, what is it that shines forth? To this, he says:
"For one who contemplates: 'I am a non-doer, I am a non-knower, I am bodiless, I am stainless,' consciousness itself shines forth directly. (52)

For the Śiva-yogin who reflects in this way, although he is devoid of knower, knowledge, and the known, the very knowledge of the non-duality of the distinguished Śiva (viśiṣṭa-śivādvaita-jñāna) shines forth after effecting the destruction of the phenomenal world consisting of the triad [of subject, object, and means], according to the scriptural statement: "It is always knowledge. This is the sense of the phrase "the light of the destroyed scriptures" (naṣṭāgama-prakāśa). || 52 ||

Now, he states that for him there is indeed no further object of knowledge: "For one who has cast off all discursive thought of differentiation, who is effortless and tranquil, and who is dissolved in his own majesty—what other object of knowledge can be spoken of? (53)

For one who has cast off the chatter of duality, who perceives fear only in the second [the other], and whose dualistic speech has been refuted by both the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* Śruti and by reasoning; who is tranquil, free from passion and aversion, dissolved in his own greatness through self-reflection, solely intent on that, and devoid of worldly effort— [for such a person, there is no fear].
For the dispassionate Śiva-yogin, what else remains to be known that is worthy of being known? The meaning is: nothing at all.

If it is asked, "What is the reasoning here?", it is said: there are three possible alternatives regarding what is called "difference" (bheda)—is it mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), or dissimilarity (vaidharmya), or the essential nature of the thing itself (vastusvarūpa)? In the first case, therein "otherness" (anyatva) would be either the intrinsic nature of an entity...

There is a twofold alternative: [is it] based on a difference, or is it some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)? Of these, the first is not [the case], because it would entail the consequence that an entity (*bhāva*) is a non-entity (*abhāva*), due to its being something other [than itself].

Because it is well-established that non-existence (*abhāva*) is distinct from existence (*bhāva*) due to its having the nature of existence; for if it is argued that, because existents are manifold, the very nature of an existent is its difference from other existents, let that be so, since such [difference] is constituted by specific qualities (*viśeṣa*). However, in this case, [we refer to] the difference that has entered into the definition of the universal (*sāmānya*) of distinction.

That cannot serve as the answer to the question, because it occurs only after the difference [between entities] has been established. Furthermore, regarding the rule that the distinctness of one entity from another entity is its very nature (*svabhāva*), is this caused by those respective entities themselves, or is it caused by a Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) distinct from them? It cannot be the first, because an entity such as a jar is insentient (*jaḍa*).

Because there is an absence of agency. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because prior to the conceptual construction, due to its non-difference, it is impossible for difference—which is merely intermediate—to constitute its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If it is argued that "it was not created by anyone, but is self-established," then it would also have to be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), like Brahman.

Because it is established by itself (*svataḥsiddhatvāt*). Now, one might object: "Brahman is also established by other means of knowledge (*māna*); therefore, it cannot be said to be self-established. This is not so, because, being eternal, the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) is impossible with respect to it; and because, being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), the operation of a cognizer (*jñāpaka*) is impossible, otherwise the consequence of its being insentient (*jaḍatva*) would follow. Nor is it something else.

There cannot be some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as the basis for the distinction, because that would entail fallacies such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Nor can it be the second [alternative], for the cognition "there is no cloth-ness in the jar" and "there is no jar-ness in the cloth"—that is, the determination of their dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—occurs only after the difference between the jar and the cloth has already been established. And furthermore...
It should not be said that the difference between a jar and a cloth is already established by their respective natures of being made of clay and being made of threads; for that specific cognition—

that the jar alone possesses the nature of being made of clay and the cloth possesses the nature of being made of threads— is dependent upon the establishment of the difference between the jar and the cloth.

Even now, it remains within the scope of what is yet to be proven. Furthermore, the difference between being composed of threads (*tantumayatva*) and being composed of clay (*mṛṇmayatva*) is due to the difference in their respective parts;

thus, upon examining the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), since no difference can be apprehended due to their partlessness (*niravayavatva*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that destroys the very root [of the argument]. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, for the nature of a thing (*vastusvarūpa*) is indeed...

It must be admitted that [the nature of an object] does not follow into the nature of other objects, otherwise there would be the consequence of a confusion of essential natures (*svarūpa-sāṅkarya*). Furthermore, in the case of the cognition "this is silver," if it were held that the mother-of-pearl itself is determined in the form of silver, it would follow that erroneous cognition (*bhrānti-jñāna*) is impossible. [The appearance occurs] in such a way due to defects such as distance.

If it is argued that [the object] is ascertained [as silver], then why is a piece of iron or the like not also ascertained as silver? Nor should it be said that the causal complex for perceiving the specific difference (*viśeṣadarśana*) acts as an obstacle; for since the causal complex for not perceiving the specific difference exists even in the case of mother-of-pearl, it would follow that no superimposition could occur there either.
If it is argued that superimposition is possible due to the predominance of the causal complex for perceiving non-difference,
we say no; for since one must admit that the nature of one thing has entered into another thing,
it is impossible to say that it has not entered, and thus the resulting confusion of natures (*svarūpa-sāṅkarya*) is unavoidable.

Because it would entail the consequence of the doctrine of difference being annihilated, and because it would entail the previously mentioned faults. Furthermore, regarding the difference appearing in an entity, would that difference be non-different from the essential nature of that entity, or would it be different? Not the first, because of absolute contradiction, as it is impossible for difference to possess the state of non-difference. Nor the second; for what kind of difference would that be?
Thus, when examined further and further, it leads only to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the absence of any final resting point.

Nor is difference (*bheda*) the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of non-difference, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). There is no counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) for unity, because there is an absence of a counter-correlative for oneness itself, and because duality and the rest are rooted therein. Nor is it disjunction (*vibhāga*), because of its...

Because, if [direction] were preceded by conjunction, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of difference between the eastern and western directions, as well as between the eastern and western mountains, since they never possess conjunction; therefore, (p. 375) [it is not so].

Since there is no other possible mode of existence, for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of difference, one must accept that "difference" is merely an imagined division— resolved ultimately in non-difference through the power of the will of Maheśvara, whose nature is the perfect equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of all things, and which functions according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves; thus, non-difference alone is established.
Thus should the wise investigate that such is the reasoning of those who maintain the doctrine of Śivādvaita. || 53 ||

Now, he further specifies the meaning of the three previously mentioned sūtras: "When one's own form has become unified with consciousness that is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), what is to be known by whom? Who can be designated as the knower? (54)

When one has become unified with one's own form, one's true nature, through consciousness free from conceptual proliferation—that is, through the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva—and when there is a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya), what object could possibly be known or cognized? Who is designated as the knower of that, and who is the knower of the object of knowledge by means of that knowledge? For beyond this, there is indeed nothing further to be known.

The meaning is that for Śiva-yogins, there is no perception of the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of the illusory triad (tripuṭī)—composed of distinctions based on mutual non-existence—due to the scriptural statement from the Śruti: "There is nothing whatsoever to be known. || 54 ||
Now, stating what the perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would be like in that case, he concludes the section on the disappearance of the scriptures:
"The Great Being, the Great Consciousness, whose form is the universe, shines forth."
Apart from that, there is not a single entity for one who abandons the cognition of difference. (55)

In the case of "a sky-flower" (*gaganakusuma*) and so forth, because there is a conjunction consisting of the mere combination of two meaningful words, and because it possesses meaningfulness through the application of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) upon them, a sky-flower must be accepted as existing.

Because it pervades all things, both existent and non-existent, it is called "Great Being" (*mahāsattā*). Because the conventional usage of the term "sky-flower" is impossible without a mental representation (*hṛdayollekha*), it is called "Great Consciousness" (*mahāsaṃvit*). Thus, it is to be compared to the impossibility of overstepping the shadow of one's own head—[cf. *svapadā svaśiraśchāyām*].
Just as one who desires to leap over it would find that his head does not reach the region of the feet, so too is this *baindavī* digit (*kalā*).
It has become the pervader of the universe, both manifest and unmanifest.

For the Śiva-yogin who has abandoned the notion of duality— the realization that it is Brahman-consciousness alone that appears in the form of the universe and that nothing exists apart from it— there is no one thing that is distinct from another, except for the consciousness that is the radiance of Great Being (mahāsattā), according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves.
Because that cognition rests upon non-difference. || 55 ||
Thus ends the section on the disappearance of the transmission;
now follows the section on the original grace.
To Him who created Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him—
to that Mahādeva, the light of self-awareness...

"In accordance with the Śvetāśvatara mantra, 'I, desiring liberation, indeed take refuge,' it is said that one who possesses the grace of Śiva— the primordial source of all— and who is fit for Śiva through the recovery of lost scriptures, is called a *prasādī*; such is the context regarding him."
He explains:
Śambhu is the presiding lord of all; by his grace, he is called "the one whose grace is primordial" (ādiprasādī), established in the state that is free from modification. (56)

Because he is the foundation of the universe and its controller, Śambhu is the primordial cause of the fivefold cosmic functions, such as creation and the rest. By the grace of that Śambhu, who is the source of all,
this Śiva-yogin stands in the state of changelessness— a place where modifications cease and there is neither loss nor gain— and is thus one who has received the primordial grace.
The meaning is: "one who possesses initial faith. || 56 ||
Now, he demonstrates his greatness through four aphorisms:
"The Primordial God is pleased with one who has been purified through many births, who dwells in a state free from egoism, and who is beyond phenomenal proliferation, for the sake of liberation. (57)
Of one whose self has been purified through many births, who is devoid of the conceit of a limited body and so forth, and who is free from the phenomenal world (aprapañca).

For the Śiva-yogin who is devoid of worldly distinctions, Śiva—the primordial god, the god of all—becomes gracious for the sake of liberation, that is, for supreme release. This is the meaning. || 57 ||
When one has attained the state of Śiva through the perfection of Śiva’s grace, the web of the world, other than Śiva, is neither seen nor unseen. 58.

When the object has attained the state of Śiva through the acquisition of Śiva’s grace, the web of the world—the entire collection of the universe—is seen as "other than Śiva" in the sense that it appears as an object of perception (*idantvena*); yet, because duality has been negated, it is not seen [as truly other], meaning it is perceived as non-different according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves. || 58 ||
By the grace of Śiva, which severs the bonds of saṃsāra, the discerning ones pierce through the knot of delusion and attain liberation. (59)

The meaning is that those who discern between the eternal and the non-eternal, having torn asunder the knot of ignorance through the grace of Śiva alone—which brings about the severance of saṃsāra—attain supreme liberation. || 59 ||
To the objection that liberation does not exist without the grace of Śiva, he says:
"Without the grace of the Lord, transmigratory existence does not cease;
for in the world, how could there be the dissolution of darkness without the rising of the sun? (60)
This is clear. || 60 ||
378) Now, having indicated Śiva’s grace and favor through His impartial compassion toward all beings, he concludes the section on the "favored" (prasādistha) category:
Śambhu, the Lord who bestows grace upon all, out of pure compassion alone, shall liberate all living beings; there is no other cause for this in this world.

The Lord Śambhu, who is independent, the benefactor of all, and the well-wisher of all, would liberate all living beings— rendering them free from their bonds— by his grace alone; for in this matter of releasing beings from their bonds, there is no other cause whatsoever on the part of Śambhu, since his essential activity consists in bestowing grace upon everyone.
Because it has that as its intrinsic nature. || 61 ||
Thus concludes the section on the intermediate stage of clarity;
now follows the final stage of clarity.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest,
the Self is hidden in the heart-cave of this living being;
free from sorrow, one beholds that desireless One.
"Through the grace of the element (dhātu), [one attains] the greatness, the Lord" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.2.20).

In accordance with the manner stated in this Kaṭhavallī Śruti, he describes the section on "the one who has attained the grace of the final [state]" (antyaprasādisthala)— being the support of all by means of the very grace of that [element] and others, and possessing the grace of the experience of the final one, Śiva:
The wise declare that dissolution (laya) is the final state of all objects;
its experience is serenity (prasāda), and one who possesses that is said to possess infinite serenity.

The dissolution (*laya*) of all categories (*padārtha*), from the earth (*bhūmi*) up to Śiva, has its locus of dissolution in Paraśiva alone; thus, he is called by the wise the "final" (*antya*) and the "end of all" (*sarvāntya*). The grace (*prasāda*) of that Śiva, who is the end of all, is precisely his direct realization (*anubhava*, *sākṣātkāra*); one who possesses that [grace] experiences it.
The meaning is that one who possesses faith at the beginning is said to possess faith at the end. || 62 ||
379) Now, he explains the manner of the dissolution of all categories with two sūtras: "The conceptualization of worldly conventions such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth..."
When others are created by māyā within the supreme reality, their destruction occurs upon its dissolution. || 63 ||
The meaning is that "tallaye" signifies the abode of Māyā. The remainder is clear. || 63 ||
Regarding how this is the destruction of illusion, he says here:

"When the supreme reality, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, has been directly realized, where is there any thorough knowledge of objects, and from where could the state of being a knower arise? (64)

When the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is Sat-Cit-Ānanda, has been directly realized, since Māyā has ceased to exist, where is there any thorough knowledge of objects imagined by it? And where is the possibility of being a knower,
or the manifestation of a knowerhood that is distinct from the object of knowledge and the act of knowing— considering the dependence on such objects and so forth?
The sense is that this is because the state of being a knower is merely imagined. || 64 ||
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Just as no object whatsoever appears to one who is in deep sleep, so no object whatsoever is seen by the liberated soul. (65)
"Of the liberated soul" (muktasya jīvasya) means "of one who is liberated while living" (jīvanmuktasya). The rest is clear. || 65 ||

In this regard, one should not suspect that the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) possesses the perception of objects, because he perceives only through non-difference from Śiva; nothing whatsoever is seen as being material (prākṛta). Now, by means of two aphorisms, he explains what the nature of the one liberated while living is like:
Just as space is uninterrupted and changeless by its very nature,
so too does the true nature of the liberated soul remain.
"It remains" means "it shines forth. The rest is clear. || 66 ||
Now, regarding what such a liberated one knows, what he does, and how he abides, it is said: "For the liberated one, there is nothing whatsoever to be seen, nor anything to be done;
his state is described as an unwavering stability consisting of the manifestation of bliss. (67)
This is clear. || 67 ||
Now, explaining why there is no longer any visible duty for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), he concludes the section on the final state of grace:
"For one whose attachment to all things has been loosened by the thorough realization of the non-duality of Śiva..."
For one who perceives only the radiance of pure consciousness, who could be whom?

For the Śiva-yogin— who, through the thorough realization of the non-duality of Śiva, has ceased all perception of differentiated objects and thus beholds only the play of consciousness— what could possibly occur, or what purpose would there be, through any activity of the organs of knowledge or the organs of action? None at all.
By means of the principle of the beginning and the conclusion, the identity of these two—the initial "kiñcit" and the final "prasāda"—should be investigated. || 68 ||
Thus ends the section on those who inspire confidence through their final state;
now follows the section on those who inspire confidence through their service.
This very [reality] exists within the body and is not situated outside;
this grace of great bliss shines forth everywhere.
In accordance with this statement from the *Sarvajñānottara*,

he explains through three sūtras that one who has attained the grace of the Guru Śiva— who is to be served— is indeed "one who has attained the grace of the one to be served" (*sevyaprasādī*), being one for whom grace is the final [goal].
The Guru is to be served by all as Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
His grace is proclaimed to be the manifestation of supreme bliss. (69)

The venerable Guru is Śiva himself, the one to be served by all; of this there is no doubt. His grace is indeed the grace of Śiva in the form of the venerable Guru, and it is celebrated as the manifestation of supreme bliss. (69)
Indeed, the Guru is traditionally held to be served by him; his grace is considered to be direct experience.
Through the form of exclusive absorption in that [Guru], he becomes possessed of that [grace]—one who possesses the grace of the one to be served.

It is traditionally taught that the Guru alone, who is the venerable Guru whose very nature is Śiva, is to be served. The realization of this venerable Guru, whose form is Śiva, is understood to be nothing other than the realization arising from his instruction; this is what is meant by "grace" (prasāda). Through the state of exclusive absorption (*ekāveśa*)—that is, through the unification of those two, the Guru and grace—one who possesses that [realization] is indeed one who possesses the ultimate grace.
The meaning is that he is well known as "one who possesses the favor of the one to be served" (sevyaprasādavān), that is, "one who has the grace of the one to be served" (sevyaprasādī). || 70 ||
The Guru is the supreme reality; the Guru is remembered as the highest truth.
Through the experience of oneness with him, nothing remains [unrealized]. (71)

Through the relationship of power and the possessor of power between the Guru and Śiva, and by means of contemplating their unity, nothing remains to be known, because the entire universe consists of Śiva and Śakti. || 71 ||

Now, with three aphorisms, he explains that for one who possesses supreme bliss and whose mind is pacified by what is to be cultivated, there is no attachment anywhere: "The Self-abiding, which is indivisible and beyond the reach of speech and mind..."
For those men who behold Ānanda, what other pleasure could there be? || 72 ||

The meaning is that for the Śiva-yogins who perceive their own nature— which is devoid of limitations, beyond the scope of speech and mind, and supreme bliss— through direct experience, there can never be any attachment or desire for any other objects. || 72 ||
For one satisfied by the nectar of knowledge, what need is there for other objects of enjoyment?
Through knowledge alone does the true Śiva manifest supreme bliss. (73)
For the yogi of Śiva who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge (*jñānāmṛta*), what is the use of other edible objects apart from the nectar of consciousness? The meaning is: nothing at all.
True Śiva—namely, the attributes of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*)—are like the heat and luminosity of fire; they are inherent to Śiva.
Śiva, whose very nature is such, reveals supreme bliss—the eternal bliss that constitutes his own essential nature—through knowledge alone, that is, through his own innate knowledge. || 73 ||
Now, he clarifies that very point:
"Liberation alone is the supreme satisfaction, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
For one who is eternally satisfied and liberated, what need is there for other means of enjoyment? (74)

The meaning is: of the Śiva-yogin who is eternally satisfied—that is, liberated, possessing supreme liberation, and characterized by eternal satisfaction such as omniscience and so forth. The remainder is clear. || 74 ||
Now, he demonstrates that for one who has attained supreme liberation, there is no action whatsoever, either internally or externally:
"For one who is established in the knowledge of identity with Śiva and who abandons the delusion of the body, there is no external action, nor any internal, nor indeed anywhere at all. (75)

For one who has ascended to the knowledge of oneness with Śiva through a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with those of the same class— beyond any loss or increase of one's own essential nature— and who has abandoned the delusion of the body,
there is no external ritual of worship performed according to rules, nor any internal [ritual] within the inner self, for he is graced by the One to be served.

The meaning is that nowhere at all does there exist any action such as meditation being performed, nor is there even the bond of karma characterized by *bindu*, *tirobhāva*, *mala*, *māyā*, and so forth. || 75 ||
383) Now, he concludes the section on "The State of Serenity":
Neither in the bondage of karma, nor in specific ascetic practices...

Likewise, for those who partake in the supreme yoga, there is no mental activity directed toward the practice of mantra and yoga, nor toward meditation, nor toward awakening, nor even toward the reality of the self. 76.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Liṅgas Pertaining to the Stage of the Prāṇaliṅgin," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a Determination of the Vīraśaiva Dharma, composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the Six Stages (*ṣaṭsthala*).
The meaning is that for those who partake in the supreme yoga— those who possess the most excellent yoga of Paraśiva and who have attained grace through their service—

the activity of the mind, the fluctuation of consciousness, does not exist in the practice of mantra-yoga, specifically in the practice of the *so'ham* mantra in the form of the *ajapā-gāyatrī*. It is exactly the same regarding the bondage of karma.

It is not in the haṭha-yoga consisting of the six acts and the three bonds, nor in the specific austerity, nor even in the distinguished rāja-yoga, nor in meditation, nor in laya-yoga which consists of meditating on the unstruck Brahman;
rather, it is in that reality of the Self, in the awakening which is the nature of consciousness of those four types of yoga, that is, in the knowledge of one's own true nature.
The meaning is that the activity of the mind (*manaḥpravṛtti*) would [thus] occur. This is the intended sense:

having first purified and bound the hands, feet, and private parts of the other body through the instruction of the Guru, one subsequently [binds] Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and the others, who are of the nature of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.
Through the application of the mantra-yoga of the sovereign king of the three deities, one should gradually join [the breath] to the ears, eyes, nose, and tongue of the upper body; thereafter,
having rendered motionless the skin and speech— which are the effects of *māyā* and the nature of the *bindu* that serves as the pillar for the front and back parts of the body—

The meaning is that, having served the field of liberation— which is the ground for generating all yogic knowledge— under the names of the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Śiva, and the Supreme Liṅga (which are synonyms), one becomes graced by that which is to be served by one's own essential nature. These are the three liṅgas.
One should sequentially connect the three limbs of the *prāṇaliṅgin*; this is the stage of the "one who has attained grace" (*sevyaprasādi*). || 76 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Liṅgas in the Section on the Prāṇaliṅgin," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇivyākhyā* known as the *Tattvapradīpikā*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇḍadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences (*padavākyapramāṇa*).
The Nineteenth Chapter: Now, the Section on the Place of Refuge (Now, the Section on the Water for Washing the Feet of Initiation).
Now follows the question of Agastya. Agastya said:
"The various divisions of the sacred sites (sthalas) based on the Prāṇaliṅgas have been fully described.
Tell me now the division of the sacred sites pertaining to the Śaraṇa-sthala."
This is clear. || 1 ||
Then, Śrī Reṇuka speaks this reply: Reṇuka said— "Having taken refuge in the place of shelter, I shall speak of the twelve places;
O ascetic, hear the names of all these places. (2)
The meaning is "of the stages" (sthalānām), that is, of the intermediate stages. The remainder is clear. || 2 ||
Therefore, he indicates those stages by means of three verses:

first the water from the feet of initiation (*dīkṣā*), then the water from the feet of training (*śikṣā*), then the water from the feet of knowledge (*jñāna*), and thereafter that which results in the perfection of action (*kriyā*). || 3 ||
Then there is that which consists of the perfection of being, and thereafter that which consists of the perfection of gnosis;
then the station of the space of the body-mass, and thereafter the station of the space of the drop.
Then there is the great expanse of space and the illumination of ritual action;
after that, the illumination of existence, and then the illumination of gnosis.
I shall describe their individual natures in due order. || 5 ||
This is clear. 3-5 ||
Then, according to the manner stated in the Śruti— “The teacher is the prior form, the pupil is the subsequent form, and knowledge is the junction” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2–3)—
[the teacher leads him] from this extensive bondage which obstructs the state of the Supreme.
Initiation first liberates him and leads him even to the abode of Śiva.
In accordance with this statement of Svāyambhuva, he describes the place where the water from the feet of the Guru— who has been propitiated by service— is easily obtained for initiation:
"That knowledge which, through initiation, has transcended duality between teacher and disciple..."
The oneness with Ānanda by means of this is known as the water from the feet of initiation (dīkṣāpādodaka).
The oneness of bliss between the teacher and the disciple—that is, the teacher who is to be served and the disciple who serves—is the state of having become one with innate bliss (*nijānanda*).
Through initiation (*dīkṣā*), duality has been removed;
that knowledge which exists is the bestowal of wisdom, whose form is imperishable, and through the initiation of consciousness and action (*cit-kriyā-dīkṣā*), duality is warded off.
By means of this knowledge, the water from the feet of the Guru— which bestows grace upon those worthy of service—
is known as the "easily accessible water from the feet of initiation.
Just like the non-dual knowledge attained through Śiva-initiation, it is the very oneness of the bliss of the Guru, the disciple, and one's own self.
The meaning is "the water from washing the feet of the Dīkṣā."
387) Now, he states another position, namely that the very oneness of the guru and the disciple produced by initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed the "water from the feet" (*pādodaka*) of initiation:
"Alternatively, by the word 'foot' (*pāda*), the guru alone is designated."
The disciple is indicated by the word "water," and their identity is achieved through initiation.

Alternatively, if that is not the case, by the word "foot" (pāda) the venerable Guru alone is meant, and by the word "water" (udaka) the disciple is designated; through initiation— specifically the initiation in the form of the breath (ghrāṇa) performed upon the head of the disciple born from one's own hand— their oneness is indeed established.

The meaning is that the oneness of the guru and the disciple, which is denoted by the term "water for the feet" (pādodaka), is traditionally known as "initiation water for the feet" (dīkṣā-pādodaka). || 7 ||
Now, he explains by way of another perspective that the very unity of truth, knowledge, and bliss revealed through initiation is indeed the "water from the feet" (pādodaka) of initiation:
"The stainless supreme bliss itself is expressed by the word 'foot'."
Knowledge is denoted by the word "water," and their unity is achieved through initiation.
By the word *pāda* (foot), the bliss of the supreme Brahman free from impurity is expressed; by the word *udaka* (water), the knowledge of the essential nature of Brahman is expressed.

Through initiation—that is, the initiation of consciousness (*ciddīkṣā*) residing within the center of the heart-lotus—there is the unification of these two, according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.28).

The meaning is that the oneness of knowledge with the bliss of the essential nature of both the property and the substratum is traditionally known as the "water from the feet" (pādodaka) of initiation.
Now,
when one knows the bliss of Brahman, from which words turn back along with the mind, having failed to reach it, one fears nothing whatsoever. [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.9]

Thus, in accordance with the statement of the *Brahma* (or *Taittirīya*) Upaniṣad, he specifically characterizes that very knowledge-bliss: "Having attained the contemplation of supreme bliss, whose nature is the light of supreme consciousness, the great yogi does not perceive any duality anywhere. (9)

The great yogi, perfected through initiation by the water from his [the Guru’s] feet, is a Śiva-yogi whose nature is the manifestation of supreme consciousness; being one whose very essence is the light of the knowledge of the nature of the Supreme Brahman,
he attains the contemplation of supreme bliss and transcends duality— the duality between eternal, perfect knowledge and bliss.
One does not perceive it anywhere else, because there is no external location [for it]. || 9 ||
For this very reason, he says that one does not desire anything else:
"It is devoid of limitations such as place and time, and is eternally pure."
Having attained bliss through awakening, the self-controlled one desires nothing else.

The self-restrained Śivayogin, having attained through awakening— that is, by the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman— the eternal and stainless bliss of Brahman-joy which exists without limitation by space, time, and other conditions, and which persists without interruption throughout all forms of space and time, desires nothing else.
Because there is no other entity distinct from that. || 10 ||
Now he concludes the section on the water for washing the feet at initiation:
"Having tasted even the pure nectar of knowledge, which arises solely from the Guru, the yogi, freed from the maladies of saṃsāra, rejoices. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 3.17)

The meaning is that the Śiva-yogin, having tasted the stainless nectar of the knowledge of Brahman arising from the grace of the Guru, and being perfected by the water used for washing the Guru’s feet during initiation, becomes free from the disease of worldly existence and sports in his own true nature. || 11 ||
Thus ends the section on the water for washing the feet of initiation;
now follows the section on the water for washing the feet of instruction.
This duality is merely composed of illusion; in the ultimate sense, it is non-dual.
If it were imagined by anyone, then that conceptual construction would cease.
This discourse, beginning with instruction, exists [only so long as there is ignorance]; once [reality] is known, duality does not exist.
In accordance with the *Muṇḍaka* Upaniṣad, he describes the water from the feet of the initiation of that Śiva-yogin—[the water] which has become perfected—by means of two sūtras: p.
389) ... [as stated in the Muṇḍaka-śruti], he explains the water from the feet of the instruction of the Śiva-yogin, who is endowed with the water from the feet of his initiation, through two sūtras:

Knowledge consisting of the teacher and the disciple is taught as the practice for the yogin; indeed, the state of their essential equality is remembered as the water from the washing of the feet of the practice.

That training which consists of the knowledge of teacher and disciple— as previously described— is the knowledge in which both teacher and disciple have become one with that [reality], denoted by the term *pādodaka* (water for the feet);
it impels (*īryate*) the yogin, that is, the Śiva-yogin who has been perfected through that initiation and the *pādodaka*.

The meaning is that the state of being of one flavor (*samarasatva*) between those two—their training and their knowledge—is indeed *sāmarasya*, which is traditionally remembered as the "water of the feet of training" (*śikṣāpādodaka*). || 12 ||
Now, as to the question of by whom, through what means, and from where this nectar of knowledge of such a nature is obtained, he says:

"From the ocean of the scriptures, churned by the power of the churning-stick of reasoning—[compare: 'Like ghee hidden in milk, consciousness dwells within every single being; it must be constantly churned with the mind']..."
By means of the Guru, who acts as the churning stick, the nectar of awakening is obtained by the hosts of those with well-disposed minds. (Brahmavidyopaniṣad 20)
From the ocean of the Vīraśaiva scriptures— consisting of the Vedas and Āgamas— which has been churned by the power of the churning-stick of reasoning through the majesty of the *Yuktimanthana*,
the preceptor (Guru), acting as the instructor, [extracts] the nectar of consciousness, the ambrosia of the non-dual knowledge of Śiva, for those of noble mind.

The meaning is that it is obtained by the assemblies of Śiva-yogins whose minds are purified by receiving the water from the feet of their initiators (dīkṣā-pādodaka), just as the nectar was obtained by the gods through the churning of the ocean under the guidance of the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati). || 13 ||
Now, he specifies the true nature of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), which consists of both attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmi*), for that Śiva-yogin by means of three aphorisms:
"The moonlight of supreme bliss, arisen from the moon of knowledge..."
Those of great intelligence behold liberation in the supreme space during the night. (14)

The great-minded Śiva-yogins of subtle vision attain liberation at night— in the supreme ether characterized by the dense darkness of supreme liberation, within the heart-ether of the Supreme Brahman which is the nature of existence— manifested upon the wall of the moon of consciousness from the moon of knowledge.
The meaning is that they behold the moonlight consisting of supreme bliss as their own true nature, perceiving it as such. || 14 ||
Then, when this moonlight of boundless supreme bliss has been seen, he says that there is nothing else remaining to be seen or heard:
"When that supreme bliss, which is devoid of space, time, and so forth, has been seen..."
Nothing else exists to be seen, nor anything to be heard, or even to be known.
When that supreme bliss, which is undivided by space, time, and other such factors, is perceived, there remains nothing else to be seen—
that which ought to be seen with the eye— or to be heard— that which ought to be heard with the ear— or even to be known— that which is fit to be known;
for every object whatsoever is an effect of that [bliss].
The meaning is: because it is non-different from that. || 15 ||
Now, he says that one desires nothing else: "For one who is satisfied by the bliss of the Self, what longing can there be for the pleasure of sense objects?
For one satisfied by the water of the Ganges, how could there be delight in the water of a well? (16)
"By the bliss of the Self" means by one's own innate bliss. The remainder is clear. || 16 ||

Now, as to whether there is any limitation for the supreme yogi who is satisfied by his own innate bliss, he says: "When the great yogi sinks into that ocean of bliss whose waves have not yet been reached due to his state of equanimity (sāmarasya), how could there be any limit for him? (17)
This is clear. || 17 ||
(391) Now, one might ask: "Is it not possible that this yogin could sometimes or somewhere experience the delusion of duality?
Addressing this, he concludes the section on the water of the training rules:
For one whose mind-lotus is perpetually awakened by the stainless and beautiful moon of the Guru’s grace, how could there be any delusion? (18)
The meaning is that it is "constantly awakened," which is to say, perpetually blossomed. The remainder is clear. || 18 ||
Thus ends the section on the water for the feet of the Śikṣāpāda; now follows the section on the water for the feet of the Jñānapāda:
"It is neither perceptible, nor inferential, nor even verbal, yet it belongs to Śaṅkara."
Pure knowledge shines forth in every way regarding all things.
Thus, in accordance with the words of Mṛgendra, he reveals that the water from the feet of knowledge is easily obtained by one who has received the water from the feet of his teacher’s instruction:
"The Guru of Knowledge is considered to be the knowledge consisting of the bliss born from the perfection of union with That."
The wise know that state of their union to be the water from the feet of knowledge for the disciple. || 19 ||

The bliss-consciousness (ānandajñāna)—which is the very bliss-consciousness of Brahman as established in the Vedic scripture, "Bliss is knowledge; knowledge is bliss; Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28)—is considered and accepted as the Knowledge-Guru (jñānaguru).
Through the attainment of identity with him—that is, through the attainment of identity between that [Guru] and bliss-consciousness—there arises their state of essential harmony (sāmarasya).

The state of their being of one flavor (*samarasabhāva*) is known as the true water from the feet of knowledge belonging to the Śiva-yogin who has been perfected by the water from the feet of the disciple’s training; the meaning is that they truly know it. || 19 ||
Now, he teaches that light of the moon of knowledge by means of three verses:
The moon of knowledge, utterly stainless, is liberated from Rāhu, which is ignorance.
He of the great splendor of supreme bliss shines in the supreme ether. || 20 ||

The moon of knowledge— the moon of the non-dual knowledge of Śiva— is devoid of contact with Rāhu, which is characterized by ignorance; it is utterly pure, meaning it is untouched even by a trace of the latent impressions of impurity, and it possesses the great radiance of supreme bliss.
Being possessed of the light of the Great Kalā, whose nature is supreme bliss, he shines—that is, he is resplendent—in the Supreme Space, which is the most excellent space of the Heart. || 20 ||

To the question, "What then does this moon of knowledge cause to increase? he says: "Free from the clouds of ignorance, the full moon of the nectar of knowledge shines forth, beholding the swelling of the ocean of bliss. (21)

The meaning is that, being liberated from the veil of ignorance by the realization "I am not Śiva," one shines forth as the full moon of all-encompassing knowledge— pervasive everywhere through the analogy of the essence of the cosmic egg— perceiving the increase of one's own abundance of innate bliss characterized by absolute freedom. || 21 ||
Now, regarding the question of who sees what when such a moon of knowledge rises, he says:
"When the moon of knowledge has arisen, yogins—whose mass of darkness consisting of delusion has been destroyed—behold the supreme pinnacle, which is the very nature of bliss. (22)

The meaning is that when the rising of the moon of the knowledge of Śiva has occurred, the Śiva-yogins— the mass of whose darkness of ignorance has been destroyed— behold their own abiding nature, which is the supreme pinnacle consisting of the essence of ultimate bliss. || 22 ||
Thus, having described the knowledge of Śiva as the moon, he now demonstrates its wondrous nature by describing it as the sun:
"When the night of Māyā has ceased and the sun of consciousness has been made to shine..."
Having cast aside all activity, the self-controlled one sleeps in wonder.
Just as in the world, when the night has ended and the sun has risen, everyone becomes awakened and engaged in their activities;
so too, when the sun of consciousness (cidāditya) shines forth at the end of the night of the form of Māyā, the self-controlled one (saṃyamī) [becomes active].

It is remarkable that a yogi, having cast off all activity, sleeps. This very point has been stated in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā: "That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake."
"That in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. (Bhagavad Gītā 2.69) || 23 ||

Now, regarding when that manifestation of supreme bliss occurs, he says: "At the moment of the destruction of beginningless ignorance, for the supreme yogi, supreme bliss shines forth, divested of the phenomenal world. (24)

The meaning is that at the moment of the cessation of beginningless ignorance, there occurs the manifestation of unconditioned supreme bliss, which is entirely free from the phenomenal world produced by the illusion of Māyā. || 24 ||
Now, one might object: "Since Śiva-yogins exist within the phenomenal world (prapañca) itself, how can there be the manifestation of unconditioned bliss?
To this, he says:
"In the eternal bliss, which is one's own form, stainless and the supreme splendor..."
For those whose minds have dissolved, how could there be conceptualization of the universe? || 25 ||

The meaning is: for those virtuous men, the yogis of Śiva, whose minds have dissolved into the sun of consciousness—the supreme light which is of the nature of eternal bliss, stainless, pure, possessing its own form and its own essential nature—how could there be any conceptualization of the universe? || 25 ||

394) Now, by means of two sūtras, he explains that for the Śiva-yogin who has attained the water from the feet of [Śiva’s] knowledge and who is full of bliss, even the bliss of Brahmā and the other gods is not equal to his own:
Whence Brahmā, whence Viṣṇu, whence Rudra, whence Ravi?
For one who has directly realized the light of supreme bliss, all such conceptualizations are equal. 26.

The meaning is that because the bliss of Brahmā and the others is but a minute fraction of the bliss of the Śiva-yogin who has directly realized the light of supreme bliss; for the Śruti declares, "Other beings subsist on a mere portion of this very bliss," and because there is non-difference between the yogin and Śiva. || 26 ||
He clarifies this very point: "For the Great Soul, who is the play of immediate supreme bliss, the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu are merely particular drops of happiness. (27)
The meaning is: of the great-souled Śivayogin who is endowed with the water from the feet of knowledge. The remainder is clear. || 27 ||
Now, having distinguished that very bliss of knowledge, he concludes the section on the water from the feet of knowledge:
"What man in this world does not desire that supreme, immeasurable bliss, which is sought after by people along with even the slightest portion of worldly objects? (28)

In this world, people desire worldly pleasure accompanied by only a small measure—a mere fraction of that consciousness-bliss; yet who would not desire its immeasurable counterpart? Who would not desire that immeasurable, limitless, supreme bliss, the bliss of Brahman? Indeed, everyone [desires it].
The meaning is that they desire. || 28 ||
Thus,
[this is] the place for the water used for washing the feet of knowledge; now follows the place for the accomplishment of ritual action.
Now,
for the yogi endowed with devotion to non-duality,
every action remains like the analogy of a burnt cloth; for it is merely action, yet not true action.

In accordance with this statement from the *Vīra-tantra*, he clarifies the locus of the accomplishment of ritual action (*kriyāniṣpatti*) by showing that this very one, who has attained the water for washing the feet of wisdom (*jñānapādodaka*), possesses the accomplishment of imagined ritual action through the analogy of the rope-snake:
"The attainment of ritual action in another's body appears as something purely imagined."
For this person brings about the accomplishment of action like a snake upon a rope. || 29 ||
In the body of the Supreme Brahman, which is perfected by the water for washing the feet of knowledge, the Śivayogin possesses the perfection of action;

because, just as a rope appears as a snake [only through mental construction], it is merely imagined that appears, therefore this Śivayogin, perfected by the water for washing the feet of knowledge, possesses the perfection of action—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
For this very reason, he establishes through six aphorisms that there is no fruit of action for the wise: "The actions of the wise do not cause rebirth;
they are like seeds burnt by fire, which are no longer a cause for sprouting. (30)
The meaning is that for the wise, the seeds of karma are burnt by the fire of knowledge; like seeds consumed by fire, they are no longer a cause for sprouting. || 30 ||

Regarding this point, there is the statement of the Blessed One: "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes, O Arjuna" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37). Therefore, he says that for the knower, there is no purpose served even by performed action:
What can even performed action do to the wise man who is free from egoism?
What change can it produce in the reflection of the moon upon water? (31)

For one who possesses the knowledge of Śiva and is devoid of the fundamental egoism that thinks "I am the doer," there is no purpose served even by action performed; the sense is that just as a modification occurring in a reflection does not affect the moon which is the original object (bimba), so too for the knower, because his nature is consciousness that is not a reflection. || 31 ||
Now, regarding the point that action perceived in the Knower is merely imagined, he provides an illustration:
"Just as the imagination of movement [is attributed] to the moon due to its connection with clouds, so too, due to its connection with the body, action may be superimposed upon the Self. (32)
This is clear. || 32 ||
Now, he provides an illustration for the fact that even while performing action, the knower is not smeared by the taint of action:
"The knower, though established in action, is not smeared by the fruits of action;
just as the tongue, though it is the enjoyer of ghee and other such things, is not smeared. (33)
"Established" means intent upon that; the rest is clear. || 33 ||
Now, one might object: since the tongue consists of the water-element (*jalatattva*), it does not have any smear of ghee or other substances, just as a finger or similar object does not;
why then is there no smear of the fruits of action for the knower? To this, he says:
"In the individual soul (*jīva*) whose connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) has been discarded, whatever state of activity may exist..."
Each of those, being merely a mental perception, dissolves here without yielding any fruit. || 34 ||

The meaning is this: for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), whose connection with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has ceased and who is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), whatever state of activity remains exists merely as a perception—like the analogy of a burnt rope—and, being fruitless, dissolves back into its own self. For the knower of Śiva, the root of the taint of karma is the ego-sense; since that is absent, [karma does not bind].
The meaning is that there is no "staining by karma" (karmalepa). || 34 ||
Now, one might ask: "If it is said that there is no attachment to action for the knower, why is it not said that he has no action at all? To this, [the Lord] says:
"Whether walking, standing, or even sleeping, there is no one who is without action."
The nature of embodied beings is karma, but for the wise, that is fruitless.

By this "rope-snake" analogy, the objection that the accomplishment of action is merely superimposed upon Śiva-yoga is refuted, because it has been stated that action is the inherent nature of embodied beings. || 35 ||

Now, asserting that even though the completion of action possesses the nature of all bodies, there is no taint of karma for the knower, he concludes the section on the completion of action: "For one whose mind is pure and who abides in the state of perfect great bliss..."
There would be no wretchedness of action that yields various enjoyments as its fruit. || 36 ||

For the Śiva-yogin, whose internal organ is stainless and who experiences the eternal, ever-perfect supreme bliss, there occurs no affliction from karma characterized by merit and demerit—which yields various kinds of fruits of enjoyment; this is the meaning. || 36 ||
Thus [ends] the stage of the accomplishment of action; now, the stage of the accomplishment of existence—
The steady state of an emotion being gradually accomplished by actors who have transcended the sequence of its stages is called the perfection of the emotion (*bhāvanispatti*).

In accordance with the statement from the *Kiraṇatantra*: "Thus, the Śiva-yogin who possesses the accomplishment of that action is one who possesses the accomplishment of the [intended] object through the logic of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell," he demonstrates this.
Although a state of being is perceived, it is merely imagined in another's body;
for this [perception] brings about the manifestation of a state of being just like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. (37)

Since an entity perceived within the body of consciousness—which possesses the accomplishment of action (*kriyāniṣpatti*)—is imagined like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, therefore this Śiva-yogin possesses the accomplishment of action;
the meaning is that he possesses the accomplishment of existence (*bhāvanispatti*). || 37 ||

Now, with five aphorisms, he demonstrates that even though there is an absence of connection with objective entities for the practitioner of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayogin*), their consciousness should be established in the Supreme Śiva, whose form is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*).
"Affectionate attachment (*bhāva*) has no connection with the one who possesses pure knowledge (*kevalajñānayogin*)."
Nevertheless, one should cultivate devotion toward Śiva, the liberator from saṃsāra. || 38 ||
This is clear. || 38 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the use of devotion for one who possesses complete knowledge?
To this he says: "Even when full awakening has been attained, one should not abandon devotion to Śambhu;
for devotion placed in Him is that which carries one across the ocean of worldly existence. (39)
One should not abandon devotion toward Śambhu, whose essential nature is perfect and eternal bliss-consciousness. Why?
To this he says: the meaning is that it is well known that devotion established in that Śambhu is the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra. || 39 ||
By this, it is indicated that this entity, through its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), is distinguished from the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Therefore, the implication is that the state of being [the nature] must be stabilized within Śambhu. If so, then that state is eternal.
To this he says:
"Having turned back the suffering born of birth, the Śaiva state ceases;
just as fire, having consumed wood and the like, itself subsides. (40)
The meaning is that the suffering born of birth is the disease of existence (bhavaroga). The rest is clear. By this, one becomes eternally liberated. || 40 ||
Now, following the cessation of the disease of worldly existence (*bhavaroga*), he speaks regarding whether there is any further purpose for [the state of] being or not:
"When the bliss of Śiva has been revealed, what is the purpose of those states?
When that which is to be accomplished is already accomplished, what is the purpose of means, even after a long time? (41)

Once the disease of worldly existence has been cured and eternal bliss has been manifested, there is no further need for the states of Śiva. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as when a long-term goal has been accomplished, there is no further need for the means by which it was achieved; such is the meaning. || 41 ||
To the question, "In that case, how does the yogi shine forth after the dissolution of all objective existence? he says:
"When the state of Śiva has been unified through knowledge, the practitioner of restraint, with his soul immersed in wonder, shines forth within the state of Śiva. (42)
The destruction of the effect is simply the persistence of the cause; thus, when the state of being has become one with Śiva through the knowledge of its functional manifestation, the yogin of Śiva,
possessing the accomplishment of that state and immersed in his own essential nature as willed by wonder, shines forth in the realization "I am Śiva."
This is the meaning. || 42 ||
Having thus established the non-difference between existence and knowledge, he concludes the section on the locus of the perfection of existence:
400) There is no knowledge without existence, nor is there existence without knowledge.
The cause for liberation has been declared; therefore, one should rely upon both.

Without *bhāva* there is no knowledge of the *vṛtti*, and without that knowledge of the *vṛtti* there is no *bhāva*; thus, it is stated that *bhāva* and knowledge are mutual causes for one another. Therefore, for the sake of liberation, one should rely upon both. || 43 ||
