Thus [ends] the stage of the accomplishment of cultivation; now,
the stage of the accomplishment of knowledge— here begins [the next].
Just as the mind, having attained its mark in the supreme reality, dissolves,
so too does all cognition come to destruction.
Thus, according to the *Niśvāsakārikā*, he explains that this very [consciousness], though perfected as an objective entity, possesses the perfection of knowledge like a dream:
"Even in the empirical usage of knowledge, by its very nature there is an absence of an object of knowledge."
Because he has perfected knowledge like a dream, he is "one whose knowledge is perfected. (44)

The meaning is that in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because the knowledge of all worldly phenomena is by nature stable, there is an absence of the object of knowledge and an absence of objects; thus, this Śiva-yogin, possessing the perfection of existence, is said to possess the perfection of knowledge through the perfection of a knowledge resembling an unstable dream. || 44 ||
401) Now, he demonstrates that very point:
Just as cognition produced in a dream ceases together with its objects, [so too does waking cognition].
Likewise, when knowledge is luminous within the self, the object of knowledge ceases to exist. || 45 ||

The meaning is that just as knowledge arising in a dream ceases along with its own objects, so too, when one's own true nature is revealed, the universe of knowable objects ceases along with the knowledge of the waking state.
Now, to the question "When one's own nature is revealed, why does the knowable cease?", he says:
When the Great Bliss, characterized by the supreme space, is fully realized, for one whose mind has dissolved into Śiva, what talk can there be regarding any other object of knowledge? (46)
This is clear. || 46 ||
Now, as to what kind of knowledge belongs to the Śiva-yogin who has attained the perfection of knowledge, he says: "Brahman alone is of the nature of undivided bliss-consciousness;
everything else is false—this established conviction is here called knowledge. (47)
Brahman, known as Paraśiva, is Brahman whose very nature is the consciousness of absolute, indivisible bliss.

That which is other than this—the web of the world appearing as something distinct from Him—is indeed false; such is the established truth. This is what is called "knowledge" here; the meaning is that the locus for the perfection of knowledge is being described. || 47 ||
Now he demonstrates the definition of the particular (viśeṣa): "That which indeed persists through the nature of existence (sattā) in jars and other such things is the ultimate [particular].
The state of being turned away as false is here called knowledge. || 48 ||

According to the Vedic scripture, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), that which exists as the essence of Being—Brahman, who is the supreme and immutable—is the reality that persists and permeates all things such as jars and the like. Therefore, whatever name and form exist therein are false; thus, in this context, "staying" refers to that which is being excluded and set aside.
The meaning is that it is called "knowledge. || 48 ||

If this is so, one might ask: what is the distinction between this non-duality of independent Śiva (*svatantraśivādvaita*) and the non-duality of Brahman characterized by ignorance (*avidyaka-brahmādvaita*)? To this, he says:
"That which is without cause, without effect, and devoid of all attributes..."
"That is Brahman, and that am I"—this firm conviction is declared to be knowledge. (49)

"Of that entity which is not an effect, no cause is found; neither its equal nor its superior is seen" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8). According to this Śvetāśvatara Śruti, that Brahman is devoid of cause and effect and is free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi); and I am that very Brahman, having long been this.

The meaning is that the firm conviction—“the manifest universe, consisting of the five elements and comprising all that is moving and unmoving, is thus [of this nature]”—is called knowledge because of its excellence. || 49 ||

Now, stating that for the Śiva-yogin who has achieved the knowledge of identity within the Brahman whose nature is consciousness, there is no worldly transaction consisting of the threefold duality (tripuṭī) as something separate from himself, he concludes the section on the attainment of knowledge:
How can there be the conventional usage of "I am the knower" and "this is the object of knowledge," when all things have been discarded and the non-dual Brahman alone prevails? (50)

Since there is no duality whatsoever here, according to the Śruti text, "There is no diversity here at all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19), when one has attained identity with the non-dual Brahman in whom all worldly distinctions have been eliminated, how can there be the conventional usage of "I am the knower" and "this is the object of knowledge"? Why should such linguistic usage exist? It cannot.
The meaning is: "from whatever [cause]. || 50 ||
Thus ends the section on the accomplishment of gnosis;
now follows the section on the space of the body.
Now, indeed, there is only one Self of all beings, dwelling in every single being;
it is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water. [Brahma-viṣaya Upaniṣad 12]

In accordance with the statement of the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*, he describes through three aphorisms the nature of the space within the body (*piṇḍākāśa*), which has become easily accessible for one who has attained the perfection of knowledge:
"Just as space resides within the body, so the Self is said to be all-pervading."
Those who discern this meaning know it as the space within the body. || 51 ||
Just as space is full within a physical body, so too is the Self said to be "full" when residing within that body—the word "of him" being understood as the ellipsis.
For this Śiva-yogin, who is perfected in the accomplishment of knowledge, there exists this discernment of the meaning:
namely, that he knows that locus of the space within the body to be truly existent. || 51 ||
Then he states it by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"Just as space, though limited by a jar, is complete in its own nature, so indeed the Self, though situated within a body, shines forth as completely full. (52)

Just as space conditioned by a jar is full in its own essential nature, so too the Self residing in the body shines forth, being perfectly full in its own nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; this is the meaning. || 52 ||
Now he speaks of that which possesses the separation from the space of the *piṇḍa*:
404) "The supreme space situated within is Śiva, characterized by non-duality."
He who meditates with a well-disposed mind is called Piṇḍākāśa.

He who meditates with a mind free of support upon that Supreme Śiva—who, according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3.2), "Rudra alone exists, there is no second," and thus is non-dual; and who, as established by the Atharvaśikhā Upaniṣad, is the one Śiva to be meditated upon—and who is the very nature of the great space of consciousness situated within the space of the heart; he [attains liberation].
The meaning is that he is called "having the nature of the space of the body. || 53 ||
Now, the body is the abode of Śiva; therein dwells Supreme Śiva himself. This state of firm conviction is called the "liṅga known through the body" (piṇḍajña-liṅga).

In accordance with this statement from the *Vātulottara*, the two [following] sūtras explain that for one who meditates in this manner, the body itself is the temple of Śiva, and Śiva shines within it: "This body, illuminated by consciousness, is declared to be the temple of Śiva."
The lotus-throne of the mind is composed of the thirty-six principles.

The meaning is that this very body is called the temple of Śiva; it is constructed with pillars, walls, and so forth composed of the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, it is provided with a lotus-pedestal characterized by the heart-lotus, and it is illuminated by the lamp of knowledge. || 54 ||
The Supreme Lord, whose nature is light, shines as the supreme ether;
merged within the cave of the heart-ether, He is perceived within embodied beings. (55)

The meaning is that the Supreme Lord, manifesting as the very nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is perceived by those who have attained perfection through instruction, while remaining dissolved within the cave of the heart of living beings. || 55 ||
To explain how it is perceived, he states another perspective:
"This city of Śiva is said to be enveloped by the seven constituent elements (dhātus)."
Here, the lotus of the heart is the dwelling, beautiful with its subtle garment.
There, Śiva—whose nature is eternally established as light—is present in person, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, like the space within water. (57)

The meaning is that this very body, filled with the seven constituents (*dhātu*), is the city of Śiva’s capital. Within this royal seat of Śiva characterized by the physical aggregate (*piṇḍa*), the heart-lotus alone is the inner palace, delightful with the subtle elements and the internal space. Therein, he resides as one who has attained perfection through eternal fullness.

The meaning is that Paraśiva, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss, abides as the direct manifestation of light within the heart due to its transparency, like the sky reflected within water. || 56-57 ||
Now, addressing the question of how the Supreme Lord, who is indeed unlimited, can reside within the limited lotus of the heart, he concludes the section on the space of the body:
"Situated within the reflection of the inner space, He is devoid of all limiting adjuncts."
One should contemplate Śiva, who consists of consciousness, as being limited, like the space within a jar.

The meaning is that one should contemplate Śiva—who is composed of consciousness and free from all limiting adjuncts—residing in the space of the heart as if partitioned, like the space within a jar. || 58 ||
Thus is the space of the mass; now,
the space of the drop.
The supreme, all-pervading cause of the principles beginning with Sadāśiva is Śiva in the form of the Bindu;
he is the object of meditation and is thus called the Bindvākāśa (the Space of the Bindu).

406) In accordance with this statement from the *Kiraṇāgama*, [the author] describes the state of the space of the bindu, which has become easily accessible for one who has attained the state of the space of that piṇḍa:
Just as space is to be known as all-pervading and situated above all living beings, so too is the Self; thus they know the locus of the space within the bindu for the purpose of illustration. (59)
Just as space, which pervades all living beings, is worthy of being known in its omnipresence, so too the Self of this Śiva-yogin— who has attained the state of the "space within the body"—
is worthy of being realized as having become all-pervading, like the space that pervades all living beings.
Thus, they know—that is, they understand—the space of the drop (bindu) solely for the purpose of analogy; such is the meaning. || 59 ||
Or else, just as the one wind, having entered the world, becomes the counterpart of every form,
so too the single inner self of all beings becomes the counterpart of every form, both within and without.
Thus, by means of four sūtras preceded by the illustration stated in the Kaṭhavallī Śruti, he establishes that very point:
Just as one wind is described as pervading all living beings, so too the Self is directly pervasive, itself present within all living beings. (60)

Just as the single, all-pervading wind is said to have entered the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all living beings, so too the Self (*ātman*), being itself directly present within all living beings, is all-pervading;
this is the meaning. || 60 ||
Just as fire, though its nature is immeasurable, shines as one everywhere,
so too is Śambhu, whose self is everything and who is devoid of all limitation.
Fire, which possesses an infinite nature, is one, yet it exists in the forms of the essence-fire, lightning-fire, terrestrial-fire, submarine-fire, and the fire of time (kālāgni).

The meaning is this: being all-pervasive, the Supreme Lord—who is of the nature of universal consciousness and is the form of the fire of consciousness—shines forth as one alone; he resplendent, pervading all beings, whether gods, demons, humans, animals, or immobile things, in both manifest and unmanifest forms as the "I. || 61 ||
Because consciousness exists within all embodied beings, it shines forth from them;
within that, the omnipresent Self, Śiva, reflects like an image in a mirror.

Within all embodied beings, the mind—known in lexicons as *citta*, *cetas*, *hṛdaya*, *kamala*, *salila*, and *jala*—is the lotus of the heart which shines like a mirror. The meaning is that Śiva, as the pervasive Self, reflects within that mirror of the mind. || 62 ||

Though he is one, the sovereign, whose nature is the light of consciousness, higher than the highest, and resides within all living beings, he nevertheless shines forth and is called the All-pervasive Lord (Vibhu). || 63 ||
The meaning is this: in comparison with the supreme power (parā-śakti) that is superior to all else, Śiva alone—whose essence is the light of consciousness—is the most excellent;
having entered the lotus-heart of every living being, He shines while becoming limited by it, and because He is thus woven through everything, He is called "Vibhu" (the Pervasive). || 63 ||
Now, he concludes the section on the space of the *bindu*:
"Just as the sun alone, omnipresent, shines by means of its radiance, so too Śiva, the Self, becomes omnipresent through the differentiation of his powers. (64)
Just as the sun alone shines while pervading all with the power of its own rays of rain, cold, and heat,
so too the Self, whose nature is Śiva, pervades the universe through its own powers of will, knowledge, and the rest.
The meaning is that they have sat down. || 64 ||
Thus [ends] the stage of the space of the drop; now,
the stage of the great space.
He who does not meditate upon that which has the form of space, which is exceedingly subtle and all-pervading,
shall remain a transmigrating being in this world, like a worm inside a seed-capsule.

In accordance with the statement from the *Devīkālottara*, he explains by means of two aphorisms that the station of the Great Space (mahākāśasthala) is easily accessible for one who has attained the station of the Point-Space (bindvākāśasthala) characterized as previously described: "Just as the space contained within the cosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa) is not distinct [from the infinite space], so it is with the Self."
They know the undivided Supreme Self as the locus of the great ether (mahākāśa).

Just as the space contained within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and the individual egg (piṇḍāṇḍa) is not divided, so too, for this Śiva-yogin who has attained the space of the Bindu, there is no difference between his own self-consciousness and the Supreme Self; thus, they know that the state of the Great Space (mahākāśasthala) is indeed non-dual. This is the meaning. || 65 ||
Just as space is not divided within jars or within huts, so too the Self, though situated within cosmic eggs and physical bodies, is indeed not divided. 66.
This is clear. || 66 ||
Then, with three sūtras, he explains that the Great Liṅga itself is the Great Space (mahākāśa):
409) It is indefinable, incomparable, and beyond the sphere of speech and mind.
It is endowed with faces on all sides, consisting of blissful existence, and having consciousness as its essence. || 67 ||
Beyond time, beyond parts, devoid of sequential order and the like, it stands upon the authority of one's own direct experience; it is the place of the rising of all lights.
The supreme Brahman, known as Śiva, whose characteristic is the supreme ether, is called the *liṅga* by the wise; without which the stability of the world does not exist. (69)

"Beyond the thirty-eight *kalās*," meaning transcending the thirty-eight *kalās*; "devoid of the sequence of yoga," meaning free from the sequential process beginning with *utpatti* (origination) and so forth; "the place of the rising of lights," meaning the source of the arising of the sun and other luminaries—"I" am that, which is to say, it is accessible through the means of valid cognition consisting of one's own direct experience (*svānubhūti*). The remainder is clear. (Verses 67–69)
Now, he further specifies that very meaning with two verses:
"The supreme ether is unmanifest, characterized by the bliss of awakening;
they call it the light-filled *liṅga*, wherein yogis dissolve. (70)

The meaning is that the wise declare that the Great Space— in which the yogis of Śiva are absorbed— is the unmanifest Liṅga, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, consisting of light, and impossible for those of meager fortune to reach. || 70 ||
Consciousness alone is the supreme goal, whose nature is supreme bliss;
those sages who have cast off all doubt call it the supreme ether.

The sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, who are free from doubt, call that which they term "Great Space" (mahākāśa) by what name? To this, the meaning is that they say that Great Space is none other than Consciousness (cit), which is of the nature of supreme bliss and is the most excellent of all. || 71 ||
410) Now, he demonstrates the non-difference of the web of the world from that Great Space by means of an illustration: "Just as waves and the like are not distinct from the nature of the ocean."
In the same way, this entire universe is not distinct from Śiva, the space of consciousness. || 72 ||
This is clear. || 72 ||
Then, moreover, he states another illustration:
"Just as flowers, leaves, and so forth are not distinct from the form of the tree, so there is no difference between the world and Śiva, the supreme space. (73)
This is clear. || 73 ||
Now, one might ask: since the sky of consciousness is partless, how can the universe abide within it and yet be manifest? To this, he says:
"Just as the luminaries shine individually within the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa)..."
In that same way, the cosmic eggs shine especially in the supreme ether. || 74 ||
The luminaries mean the constellations; the rest is clear. || 74 ||
Now, he concludes that very section on the specific nature of bondage concerning the great space (mahākāśasthala):

"The relation is stainless, consisting of consciousness, and its nature as a limiting adjunct (upādhitva) consists in being occasional while simultaneously differentiating it from others, once all adventitious adjuncts have been discarded."
The supreme space is the foundational wall for the playful manifestation of the variegated universe.
The meaning is that the supreme space (*parākāśa*), characterized by the aforementioned qualifications, serves as the substratum for the variegated play of the web of the universe.
These three signs—the lump, space, and so forth—are to be joined with the three limbs of refuge. || 75 ||
Thus [is] the section on the Great Space;

then the section on the Illumination of Action, according to the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* scripture which states: "Those who possess action, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and are established in Brahman."

And according to the statement in the Yogaja Āgama: "The ritual action dedicated to Śaṅkara is truly the best of all, bestowing liberation as well as worldly happiness," it is said that only one who is fit for Śiva, whose nature is the Great Space (mahākāśa), is possessed of the light of the practice consisting of the contemplation of His true nature.
Because of the realization of Śiva— the perfect one whose nature is the space of consciousness—
as one's own self, the self-restraining one becomes possessed of the illumination of action.

The meaning is that the Śivayogin, whose nature is the great ether (mahākāśa), possesses the activity consisting of the contemplation of Śiva— who is of the nature of the great ether of the perfectly full form of consciousness— as his own self; thus, he is said to be "possessed of the manifestation of action" (kriyāprakāśanavān).

Now, in accordance with the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.8), which states: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and it is innate," that [power] as well,
being of the nature of knowledge and action, is real and possesses eternally manifest radiance.
She would be non-different from Śiva; in reality, she alone is the embodied form of the Lord.
And according to the statement of the Pauṣkara, he establishes that very act of contemplation through three sūtras:
"Of Him whose form is like the stainless sky of consciousness-bliss..."
And the function of the perfect Śiva is of the nature of consciousness.

The function (*vṛtti*) of Śiva, who has been described in such a manner, is the state of being "I am," which takes the form of action; it consists of consciousness, meaning it has the nature of pure awareness just like Śiva himself. || 77 ||
412) Now, he states that even the activity of the Śiva-yogin’s self-reflection is of such a nature:
"In the stainless, formless, eternal, and supreme light..."
Likewise, the power of one whose mental fluctuations have dissolved is called action (kriyā). || 78 ||

The meaning is that for the Śiva-yogin whose mental activity has dissolved into the aforementioned splendor of Paraśiva, that creative power (kriyā-śakti) which consists of his continuous contemplation is said to be of the nature of that very splendor of Paraśiva. || 78 ||
To the objection, "What is the use of such contemplation?", he replies:
"The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and omnipresent;
through the meditation on his identity, the yogi shines as one whose self has become like that. (79)

According to the Vṛddha-Jābāla Śruti, "The All-Knowing One, perfected in the fivefold acts, the Lord of all, the Sovereign"— having thus understood that the Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervading,
the yogi becomes a Śiva-yogin through meditation on the unity of equalized and identical essence, becoming himself of such a nature.
The meaning is that it shines forth as possessing the very nature of those modes. || 79 ||
Now, one might ask: since the activity of the senses exists for a Śiva-yogin, how can he be said to "see Śiva"? To this he says:
"Even while the activity of all the senses is present, the self-controlled one [sees Śiva]."
Beholding Śiva with a mind turned toward him, he rejoices. || 80 ||
The meaning is: "with a mind turned toward," that is, facing the western wheel. The remainder is clear. || 80 ||

Now, as to what kind of Śiva he is and how perceiving him he rejoices, [the author] says here: Perceiving the Śiva-principle by its own nature—unshakable, immovable, wise, beyond the qualities (guṇas), yet transcending the qualities—the yogi rejoices. (81)

p. 413) Superior in qualities—that which is preeminent through qualities such as knowledge and dispassion; the wise one; the healthy one; the immutable one; that which is designated by such names as the inner self (pratyagātman) that witnesses the fourth state (turyasākṣin); and that which transcends the qualities (guṇātīta).

The meaning is that the Śiva-yogin, perceiving by his own nature—that is, by his true self—the immovable Śiva-tattva which transcends qualities such as illusory existence (māyika-sattva) and the like, rejoices. || 81 ||

Now, stating that for the Śiva-yogin who is perfected in his own nature as the form of conscious activity, all activity is as unstable as a city of Gandharvas appearing in the expanse of the sky, he concludes the section on the "Manifestation of Activity" (Kriyāprakāśasthala), which was previously mentioned:
It has been stated that all activity, whether directed toward another or oneself, appears like a city of Gandharvas; such is the manifestation of activity. (82)

The meaning is that all activity regarding the supreme Self—the yogi whose nature is Śiva—manifests like a city of Gandharvas in the sky; thus, the manifestation of activity is called the "locus of the manifestation of activity. || 82 ||
Thus ends the section on the manifestation of action;
now follows the section on the manifestation of being.
When that very [Self], whose nature is full of self-relish and who is honored by Himself alone, shines forth in the state of objective manifestation, He is this primordial Great Lord.

In accordance with the statement of the *Yogajāgama*, [the author] describes the easily accessible locus for the manifestation of the inner state (*bhāva*) for the Śiva-yogin who has perfected the illumination of those practices: "Just as waves and the like are not distinct from the ocean, so [they are not distinct] from the Self."
All entities, such as cognition and the rest, are that which is the manifestation of being.

Just as entities such as waves and foam are not distinct from the ocean, so too all entities beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) are not distinct from the Śiva-yogi’s consciousness, which is endowed with action and luminosity within the Self; this is the meaning of the phrase "the manifestation of that state" (*tadbhāvaprakāśanam*). || 83 ||
414) Now, he qualifies that meditation with five aphorisms:
"The entire world is Śiva alone; I too am Śiva alone."
The supreme yogin, practicing this meditation, is not afflicted by the defects of worldly existence. || 84 ||
The meaning is that by contemplating, "The entire world is indeed Śiva; therefore, I too am indeed Śiva," the great yogi of Śiva becomes unassailable by the defects of worldly existence. || 84 ||
When the state of Śiva has become firm for the great-souled one who is untainted, whatever states arise are remembered as being composed of Śiva. || 85 ||
"Of one who is untainted" means of one who is free from attachment to sense objects; the rest is clear. || 85 ||
Now, as to what those states are, he says:
"By the Great-Souled One, whose karma has been destroyed through the meditation on the form of non-dual Śiva, nothing whatsoever other than Śiva is directly meditated upon. (86)
The sense is that for a Śiva-yogin of such a nature, whatever is meditated upon, all that is composed of Śiva (śivamaya). Now, as to how this is so, he says:
"For one whose bond of ignorance has dissolved and who experiences only the Self..."
Wherever there is attachment of the senses, in each of those places there is the nature of Śiva.

The meaning is that for the yogin of the aforementioned type, wherever there is attachment of the senses to objective entities (*bhāva*), in each of those places, his nature becomes that of Śiva consisting of those very entities. || 87 ||
(415) Now, one might ask: since states such as attachment and aversion are causes of bondage, how can they be identical with Śiva? To this, he says:
States such as passion and aversion are the causes of the afflictions of saṃsāra;
where there is their cessation, there the state is of the nature of Śiva. (88)
Where there is the cessation of states such as attachment and aversion which serve as the causes of bondage, in that Śiva-yogin, the state is of the nature of Śiva; this is the meaning. || 88 ||

Therefore, stating that the power of tamas does not overcome such a Śiva-yogin, he concludes the section on the *Bhāvaprakāśa*: "Just as darkness can never prevail when the sun has taken possession [of the sky]."
In the same way, self-luminous consciousness does not itself come under the sway of ignorance.

Just as darkness is not capable of obscuring the sun, so too, the darkness characterized by ignorance is not capable of obscuring the luminous Self—the Śiva-yogin whose nature is pure light; this is the meaning. || 89 ||
Thus ends the section on the manifestation of existence;
now follows the section on the manifestation of knowledge.

Just as the milk of cows of many different colors is of a single color, so too does the knower perceive knowledge to be like the milk, while the possessors of marks are like the cows. (Brahma-bindu Upaniṣad 19, p.
According to the statement in the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*:

"The remembrance of Śiva and others is knowledge; from knowledge, existence (*sattā*) is manifested. Through existence, there is the attainment of bliss (*ānanda*); and from bliss alone comes the bestower of perfection."
And in accordance with the statement from the *Yogajāgama*, he describes how the illumination of knowledge is easily attained by the Śiva-yogin who has perfected the manifestation of that state:
"When the primary meaning becomes impossible, one resorts to the application of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through yoga."
That which is the application of that knowledge is called the illumination of knowledge. (90)

When the primary meaning of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and the members (*aṅga*) becomes impossible— that is, when it is unestablished— there occurs the application of knowledge through the recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā-yoga*). This consists in resorting to figurative indication for the members and the indicative marks known as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which are qualified by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of effect and cause.

The conjunction of the two types of knowledge established in the limbs and the liṅga by way of a state of equalized flavor (samarasa) is said to be the illumination of knowledge for that Śiva-yogin who is perfected in the manifestation of the power of that [knowledge]. This is the intended meaning:

Just as between the space delimited by a jar and the great infinite space, the meaning of "definition" (lakṣaṇa) is simply the eternal relationship of the immutable supreme consciousness with [the individual]. Just as between the space delimited by the water in a jar and the space delimited by the water in a cloud, the primary meaning is merely the limiting adjunct (upādhi), like the finger and its mark; and that is precisely the knowledge of the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya) of that consciousness.
"Jñānaprakāśa" (The Illumination of Knowledge). || 90 ||
(p. 417) Now, he qualifies that very point with three verses: "The liberated one’s connection with knowledge is, by its very nature, the absence of an object of knowledge."
Knowledge accompanied by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) does not transcend differentiation. || 91 ||
The connection between the characteristic and the object-knowledge of one who is liberated and supremely liberated is, by its very nature, an absence of an object of knowledge;
this means it is devoid of an object of knowledge and devoid of anything to be cognized, due to being free from defects such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
As for the knowledge accompanied by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that belongs to him who is supremely liberated.
Knowledge qualified by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the primary object, the subtle body (liṅga), and the limbs (aṅga) does not transcend duality; it exists without transcending duality.
The meaning is that the very destruction of the limiting adjuncts is the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya) of knowledge. || 91 ||
The wise declare that knowledge is indeed the discernment of an object;
if there is no discernment of the Supreme Self, how could knowledge possibly exist? (92)

The discernment— that is, the fragmentation— of an object, which is to say an entity possessing characteristics, limbs, and form, is called "dualistic knowledge" by the wise, the virtuous persons. However, in the case of non-differentiation— in the undivided Supreme Self, the unconditioned Great Consciousness— there is indeed the possibility, that is, the arising, of knowledge as it is conventionally established in duality.
Why? Because it does not exist; this is the meaning. || 92 ||

Regarding that reality called Śiva, which is the self-nature of consciousness and bliss and is beyond the scope of [empirical] knowledge, the wise declare that the contemplation of the oneness of the Self is what is termed "knowledge. (93)

Because knowledge is self-luminous, it is the realization of the oneness of the Self— the contemplation of the unity of one's own self— within that reality known as Śiva or Paraśiva, which is the essence of consciousness-bliss (cidānanda), the nature of conscious happiness (citsukha), and which is not an object or a sphere for any other consciousness distinct from itself. This is what is meant by "knowledge."
The meaning is that it is spoken by the wise, that is, by the learned. || 93 ||
(On page 418) He explains with three aphorisms that this very knowledge of Śiva is the knowledge of Brahman: "It is unlimited bliss, the form of pure existence, and identical with the universe."
"Brahman" is the definition; knowledge [of it] is here called "knowledge of Brahman. || 94 ||

The meaning is that because the universe does not transcend existence (*sattā*), it is composed of that [existence]. For it is impossible for that which is non-existent by its own nature to have a connection with existence; whereas that which exists by its own nature has no need for another existence.
Thus, the conclusion is that it is simply of the nature of the existent (*sadrūpa*). The remainder is clear. || 94 ||
When the knowledge of Brahman has arisen, which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), everything shines as consisting of pure consciousness, and nothing other than that is seen. 95.

When the knowledge of Brahman—which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and free from all differentiation—has arisen and become manifest, the entire universe shines as consisting of consciousness; that is, it shines as being composed of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). Because there is no difference between Śiva and Śakti, nothing other than that is seen; the meaning is that nothing exists apart from Brahman. || 95 ||
Therefore, the knowledge of non-duality is the cause of liberation;
by constantly cultivating it, the yogi is not stained by worldly existence. || 96 ||

Therefore, the meaning is that the Śiva-yogin, by constantly cultivating the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva—the cause of liberation, both supreme and subordinate—is not defiled by worldly existence (saṃsāra). || 96 ||
Now he concludes the section on the illumination of knowledge:

In that eternal light, which is the self of pure being, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, which is supreme, free from latent impressions, partless, and situated in the state beyond all, and which is united with stainless *sattva*.

With his heart dissolved in the auspicious void of consciousness, the self-restrained one shines forth directly as all-pervading, with the universe melting away, due to his turning away from the perception of duality.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Discussion on the Twelvefold Liṅgas in the Context of the Stage of Seeking Refuge," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a determination of the Vīraśaiva doctrine composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*).

In that which is eternal, continuous, and joined with stainless beings; in that which exists preeminently among those possessing the quality of pure being; in that which is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*) and devoid of the impressions of objects of knowledge; in that which is partless, without divisions, the state transcending all, the ground that has risen above everything, and consists of both the moving and the unmoving.

With his heart dissolved in Śiva— the supreme Śiva who is the sky of consciousness, the light manifesting as the ultimate reality whose nature is the power of the sky of consciousness (cidambara-śakti), characterized by the activity of consciousness that serves as the material cause for the phenomenal world of moving and non-moving beings, and whose essence is existence (sattātman)— he turns away from the perception of difference, [realizing] that there is nothing other than Śiva.
Because he has become turned away [from duality], the self-controlled Śiva-yogin is all-pervading, encompassing the universe;
being one for whom the universe has dissolved—meaning one for whom the power of the distinction between the universe [and the Self] has dissolved—he shines forth, manifests directly and specifically.
This is the meaning. Because Śiva and the refuge possess the nature of being the "Sat" (Being) and so forth, those three marks belong to the refuge, which consists of the three limbs.
It should be applied. || 97 ||

Thus ends the section on the illumination of knowledge, in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Śrīmaritoṇḍadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Twelve-fold Signs Regarding the Domain of the State of Taking Refuge";
the twentieth chapter (now, the state of oneness).
Now follows the question of Agastya:
"O Lord of Gaṇas, you have described the various types of *sthala* (sites) situated within the *śaraṇa-sthala* (the site of refuge);
tell me now, O Lord of Gaṇas, about the various types of *sthala* that pertain to the *aikya-sthala* (the site of unity)."
"Differences of sections" (sthalabheda) means differences within intermediate sections; the same applies further on. The remainder is clear. || 1 ||
Now he states the answer to this question:
"In this single locus, a group of nine loci is proclaimed. (2)
This is clear. || 2 ||
Now, he indicates the subdivisions of that [subject] by means of three aphorisms:
First, the stage of the oneness of grace accepted by Him is proclaimed;
then the stage of the boiled rice of the disciples; and then the stage of the dissolution of the moving and the unmoving. || 3 ||
Then the place for vessels is proclaimed, followed by the excellent place for utensils;
after that, the place for applying unguents, and then the place for the knowledge of oneself and others.
Then there is the destruction of existence and non-existence, and the state of emptiness through knowledge;
O ascetic, listen as I describe their characteristics in due order.
This is clear. || 3-5 ||
421) Now, regarding the state of oneness accepted as the locus of grace:
"Then, with the clarity of knowledge, one whose being is purified beholds Him who is partless."
In accordance with the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* (3.1.8), which states "meditating," it is proclaimed:
"Action is declared to be the cause for the arising of knowledge;
having abandoned yoga with an object, one should contemplate that which is free from phenomenal proliferation. (*Dvikramatattvabhāvanā*, 25)

And according to the statement of the *Devīkālottara*, one who is endowed with the illumination of that knowledge is indeed a *śivayogin*; for by accepting the grace of knowledge, he is described as "one who has accepted grace" (*svīkṛtaprasādī*). Thus [the author] explains:
"In that conscious Self, there is neither the primary meaning nor the secondary (indicative) meaning."
Through his unrestrained nature, his favor would have been accepted. || 6 ||

In that Śivayogin who is the conscious self (cidātman), endowed with the light of knowledge, there exists neither the primary meaning— namely the primary sense of the separation of the individual soul (jīva) from the Lord (Īśvara)— nor the secondary (lakṣaṇa) meaning—
namely the secondary sense of the eternal non-separation of the unconditioned Śiva and the Self. Of that Śivayogin...
The meaning is that by being "viśṛṅkhala" (unfettered) and "niraṅkuśa" (unrestrained), the grace—the grace of perfect knowledge—would be "svīkṛta," that is, accepted or taken up. || 6 ||

Now, he clarifies this very point with two verses: "Having attained the direct realization of consciousness that moves within the conventional transactions of the knower, the known, the means of knowledge, and so forth, the yogi abides in his own self. (7)

The meaning is that the yogi, having attained the direct realization of the full consciousness while delighting in the initial worldly transaction consisting of the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, becomes a Śiva-yogi endowed with the light of wisdom and abides in his own true nature, which is characterized by self-accepted grace. || 7 ||
(p. 422) Now, regarding the fact that for a Śiva-yogin of such a nature there is no bondage by the fetters (pāśabandhana), he says:
"For the yogi whose immersion in duality has been shaken off by the realization of non-duality..."
For one who has directly realized the light of Great Consciousness, where is there any bondage?

For the Śiva-yogin—who has warded off the penetration of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) through the realization of the non-duality of Śiva, and who has directly realized the stainless light of consciousness—how could there be bondage by the elements arising from the fivefold fetters? The meaning is that it does not exist. || 8 ||
Now, he explains with three verses and an illustration that for that one of full knowledge there is no perception of phenomenal diversity (prapañca):
"This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is placed within the auspicious Self of Consciousness."
All that is known to be composed of that [Brahman], just as wood and other materials are in fire.

Just as wood and other materials cast into the fire are seen to be composed of fire, so too the universe established in Śiva is seen as consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*); the sense is that Śiva’s nature is the fire of consciousness. (9) Now, one might object: "The universe has not been placed in Śiva by anyone—like wood in a fire—but by Śiva himself."

To the question, "How can that which is imagined appear as being identical with that [Reality]?", he says: When Śiva, the conscious Self, is perceived, neither earth appears, nor water, nor fire, nor air; neither space, nor the supreme principle appears. (10)
Just as when clay is known, everything such as jars, bowls, and the like is understood to be merely made of clay—[compare:
"O gentle one, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth"].

It is known that nothing exists apart from That; likewise, when the auspicious Śiva, who is the conscious Self, is perceived, the earth and other elements—being His effects—do not appear as distinct from Him, but appear only as being of His very nature. This is the meaning. || 10 ||
(423) Thus, reflecting that the universe, whose nature is Śiva, is dissolved right there, the yogi is not defiled; regarding this, he says:
"In the light-liṅga, which is the form of consciousness, blazing incessantly within..."
Beholding all reality as dissolved, the yogi is not stained.

When the great Liṅga, the Liṅga of consciousness, which is of the nature of light, blazes and shines incessantly within the eight-petaled lotus in the form of the heart, the Śiva-yogin— perceiving all reality from Śiva down to the level of Bhūmi as dissolved and merged into that great Liṅga— is no longer stained by worldly taints.
The meaning is that he is not tainted by the thirty-six principles (tattvas) consisting of the body, the instruments [of perception], the worlds, and the objects of experience. || 11 ||
Now, for this very purpose, he specifies [the practice] in the form of an oblation:
"Offering all objects of experience into the light of his own Self, which consists of consciousness, with a mind turned inward, the yogi rejoices. (12)

The meaning is that the Śiva-yogin rejoices while offering all objects of experience into the luminous fire of his own essential nature— which is composed of consciousness— by means of an inward-turned mind and a mind directed toward that [reality], thereby surrendering them through identification with it. || 12 ||
Now he concludes the section on accepting the state of grace:
"Having offered all [objects] into the auspicious Self, which is his own nature—a stainless ocean of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—he enjoys the objects of the senses by its grace. (13)

The stainless Śiva-yogin, having offered all objects such as sound and the rest into his own self— which is Śiva, the ocean-born source of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and whose nature is self-luminous— enjoys them through that grace, in the form of that very grace. || 13 ||
Thus,
having accepted the stage of being gracious,
he then [proceeded to] the stage of the instruction of the learned.

Now, in accordance with the scriptural statement, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10): "From the knot [of Māyā] arise, in sequence: Kalā, Kāla, Vidya, Rāga, Nṛ (Puruṣa), Mātra (Buddhi), Guṇa (Ahaṃkāra), Dhī (Manas), Garva (the senses), Citta, the Mātrās, and the elements. (Mṛgendra-tantra-vivaraṇa, Pāda 10.1)

And according to the words of the *Mṛgendra*, he explains through four sūtras that for the Śiva-yogin who has accepted the grace of that [Lord], it is precisely the *māyā*-tattva that constitutes the remaining food:
"That *māyā* which shines forth for all [beings] is itself the form of the food."
That in which [the world] dissolves is proclaimed as the remaining subtle sign (cilliṅga). || 14 ||

That Māyā which is mixed with the pure path (śuddhādhvan), taking the form of the bodies, organs, worlds, and enjoyments of those who dwell therein, exists as the lower Māyā; it is that very same [Māyā] which manifests and dissolves for all beings.
That Māyā-tattva, consisting of the thirty principles from Kalā down to Earth, is indeed present in the "liṅga of consciousness" (cilliṅga), the sign of knowledge.

In that context, regarding the object accepted by Him as pure, the meaning is that it is proclaimed to have the form of the remaining rice, like the appearance of the rice left over [after consumption]. || 14 ||
When the body of the world is consumed and the expansion of the noose of Māyā has ceased, through awakening, that one alone remains within the light of one's own Self. 15.

In the light of one's own Self— the body of the universe, which possesses a cosmic form and is bound by the noose of Māyā consisting of the thirty principles from Kalā down to Earth, manifested through the expansion of the noose of Māyā— one should [abide] through awakening, that is, through the knowledge of one's own Self.
The meaning is that when [everything] has been swallowed up and overcome, only that single *māyātattva* remains.
Now, one might ask: since the nature of the embodied self is pervaded by consciousness, how can the principle of *māyā* remain? To this, he says:
For the wise one who is liberated while living and whose nature is the supreme Brahman— indivisible existence, consciousness, and bliss— Māyā speaks only of service (to him).

The meaning is that for such a wise Śivayogin— one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), whose essential nature is the Supreme Brahman characterized by indivisible existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who has conquered his senses— Māyā remains as one who speaks of service, proclaiming a state of servitude. || 16 ||
In such a state,
the illusion that deludes the universe— unrestrained and possessing manifold powers—
is no longer able to stand before one who has attained oneness with Śiva. (17)

The meaning is that Māyā, which deludes the world and is unrestrained by her manifold powers, does not desire— that is, is unable— to stand before the Śiva-yogin who has attained a state of equalized aesthetic flavor (samarasa) with Śiva, acting as a source of delusion. || 17 ||
Now, he describes the destruction of the objects of that oneness with Śiva through three aphorisms:
"When the great-souled one is immersed in the light-liṅga, which is the form of consciousness, the objects of the senses perish by themselves according to their respective fitness. (18)
This is clear. || 18 ||

Now, as to how they undergo dissolution, he says: "Even the objects, such as sound and the rest, when being experienced by their respective senses, dissolve into the Self alone, just as rivers [dissolve] into the ocean. (19)
The meaning is that, apart from any other cause, they dissolve by themselves alone, according to the analogy of a river merging into the ocean.

The meaning is as follows: having accepted grace, one becomes like oil—the essence consisting of consciousness and bliss—whereas the remaining food is like oil-cake, being essence-less *māyā*; thus, the enjoyment of that [food], being essence-less, perishes. || 19 ||
Now, explaining how the Śiva-yogin remains once the entire collection of objects has thus perished,
he concludes the section on the "remnant of boiled rice" (śiṣṭaudana): "Swallowing the entire multitude of objects, the yogin becomes tranquil."
Established in its own self, the Sun emits its entire web of radiance without exception.

The Śiva-yogin, swallowing the entire multitude of objects into his own essential nature—just as the sun, while setting, withdraws its entire web of radiance, that is, its whole collection of rays, until nothing remains—becomes tranquil; the meaning is that he becomes established in his own self. || 20 ||
Thus ends the section on the "Place of the Food of the Learned";
now follows the section on the "Place of the Dissolution of the Moving and the Non-moving," beginning with:
"He, my dear, cuts asunder the knot of ignorance here" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.10).
In accordance with the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "Just as the potency associated with poison is neutralized by mantras,
and just as that [poison] is rendered ineffective, so too is the destruction of the impurity of the person."
And according to the statement of the *Kiraṇāgama*,

by accepting the grace of pure consciousness alone, the Śiva-yogi— having consumed the remaining food of *māyā*— destroys the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) that pervades each and every moving and non-moving being, according to the degree of its ripening.
Regarding the term "destroyer of the moving and the unmoving," he says:
"When the identity of the *liṅga* has been attained and movement and non-movement have ceased, that yogi becomes bodiless, a destroyer of the moving and the unmoving. (21)

When movement and non-movement have ceased, when the manifestation of the moving and the unmoving has reached unity with the *liṅga*, and when identity with the Great *Liṅga* (*mahāliṅga*) has been attained, that yogi—endowed with the remaining *odana* (the subtle body)—becomes a Śiva-yogi who is bodiless;
the meaning is that he becomes the destroyer of the impurity and power residing in both the moving and the unmoving. || 21 ||

427) Now, he demonstrates with six aphorisms that that Śiva-yogin does not perceive the phenomenal expansion of Māyā by means of removing the impure power (mala-śakti) that pervades all things moving and unmoving:
For this perception of the worlds has its root in beginningless ignorance;
when that [ignorance] is destroyed through the realization of the oneness of one's own Self, how could there be the manifestation of the universe? (22)

The perception of the universe as restricted and determinate—such that one thinks "this is such-and-such"—is indeed Māyā, fashioned from beginningless time by the power of divine play (*līlāśakti*), and having the root cause [of impurity] as its basis.

Through the awakening to the fact that it is nothing but one's own self—that is, through the knowledge in which the self alone is predominant—the destruction of that [Māyā] occurs; and upon the destruction of the power of impurity (*malaśakti*), there is the manifestation of the entire universe.
The meaning is: why does the vision of the world rooted in that [ignorance] not exist? || 22 ||
To the question, "Where does this universe go to dissolution? he says:
Just as clouds that have arisen dissolve into the expanse of the sky, so too do the objects of experience dissolve into the Self. (23)

Just as clouds, having gathered in the expanse of the sky, dissolve away, so too for the Śiva-yogin who experiences his own true nature, the objects—namely the objects of sound and so forth—which have arisen or come into being within the consciousness of the Self, dissolve; this is the meaning. || 23 ||

Now, regarding how this universe perishes through the realization of its identity with one's own Self, he says: "Just as an object seen in a dream undergoes dissolution upon waking, so too everything pertaining to saṃsāra perishes in the knowledge of the Self. (24)

The meaning is: "when self-knowledge exists. Now, one should not raise the objection that if the universe is thus admitted to be similar to a dream, it follows that it must be false; for even in a dream, there is the perception of results and non-results, as well as the perception of seminal emission and so forth, which proves its very reality. The rest is clear.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
"For one who has attained the supreme state beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep..."
What is the means of valid cognition? What is the object of knowledge? And what is the instrument for attaining knowledge? || 25 ||

For the Śiva-yogin who has attained— that is, reached— the supreme state, the most excellent fourth state (turyāvasthā) easily accessible through the Khecarīmudrā which transcends the states of waking and so forth based on the three bodies (tanu-traya), what indeed is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa)? What [is there]?

What is the object of knowledge, or what is the means of knowledge? The sense is that because it transcends the manifold world consisting of the triple division [of knower, known, and knowing], there is no perception of it. || 25 ||
Now, he clarifies that state which transcends the fourth (turyātīta):
"That state which transcends the fourth is far beyond the path of speech and mind;
having entered it, the yogi no longer perceives the universe. (26)

That state which transcends the fourth (turyātīta), which is the station of the Turyātīta easily attained through the seal (mudrā) that is the culmination of silence, which lies far beyond the paths of speech and mind, and which is not the object of praise or meditation— having entered that station of the Turyātīta, the yogi who possesses the yoga of the Turya station becomes a Śiva-yogin and no longer perceives the universe again.
The meaning is "he sees. || 26 ||
To the question "Why?", he says here:
"The lord of yogis sees nothing else, knows nothing else, and hears nothing else, once Śiva, who consists of consciousness and bliss, has been perceived. (27)

When Śiva, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, is perceived—this being the ellipsis; when He is directly realized—the lord of yogis, the master of Śiva-yoga, established in his own true nature, does not see any other form apart from himself, does not hear any such web of sounds, and knows nothing else besides Him. This is the meaning.
The meaning is that due to the exhaustion of the power of impurity (mala), there is no perception of forms and so forth produced by māyā. || 27 ||
429) Now, clarifying the meaning already stated, he concludes the section on the locus for the destruction of the impurities of the moving and the immobile:
"The entire world, though non-existent, appears as if it were existent."
When Śiva is known, that ignorance is established as being his very own nature. || 28 ||

The entire world is indeed non-existent apart from Śiva; it does not exist at all, yet it appears as if it were real due to the power of impurity (*mala*). Apart from that [Śiva], it appears as if real. When the Supreme Śiva—characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss—is known and directly realized, that ignorance which is the cause of the perception of duality, the root-ignorance, [is destroyed].

The meaning is that the lost essential nature attains or goes toward the form of the causal power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Therefore, the meaning is that for the yogin of Śiva, there is no self-reflection apart from Śiva;
thus, this is the place where all things mobile and immobile undergo dissolution.
Now, regarding the place of the vessels:
furthermore, this eternal Aśvattha tree has its roots above and its branches below.
That alone is the pure, that is Brahman, and that alone is called the immortal.
"In that all worlds are contained; no one transcends it"—according to this *Kaṭhavallī* scripture:
"Just as the Kuṇḍalinī power follows after Māyā and karma, so its effects consist of Nāda, Bindu, and the rest; such is the constitution of the world. [Kaṭhopaniṣad 6.1]

Furthermore, in accordance with the subsequent statement from the *Viśvasāra*, he demonstrates that for the Śiva-yogin—who destroys the impurities of both the mobile and immobile worlds—the Supreme Bindu (*parabindu*), which consists of discernment (*vicāra*), is indeed the "place of the vessel" (*bhāṇḍasthala*). (p. 430)
That reflective awareness which serves as the locus for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of hundreds of millions of cosmic eggs is called the "site of the vessel" (bhāṇḍasthala).

The meaning is that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which serves as the foundational support for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of many millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), and which constitutes the contemplation of the nature of the *Śabdabrahman* of this Śiva-yogin who destroys all moving and unmoving things— that is called the "vessel-place" (*bhāṇḍasthala*). || 29 ||

Now, he clarifies the nature of that reflective awareness (vimarśa): "The supreme power called reflective awareness, which causes the manifestation of the universe, the witness of all beings, blazes forth in all directions. (30)

The supreme power called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), characterized by the expansion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*), is intent upon investigating the meaning of words; she is pure *māyā*, the cause of the manifestation of the universe,
illuminating the entire world through her own effects such as knowledge (*jñāna*), and the witness of all the *tattvas*.

Being omnipresent, she blazes; the meaning is that she manifests in the form of the bodies, instruments, worlds, and enjoyments belonging to those who dwell on the pure path (śuddhādhvan), characterized by the principles (tattvas) of Para-Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā. || 30 ||
Now, he further specifies that very power of reflective awareness (vimarśakalā):
"That power consisting of reflective awareness is the one in which the universe dissolves and wherein the Self, whose form is consciousness, shines forth directly as composed of eternal bliss. (31)
This is clear. || 31 ||

Now, indicating the location for the vessels, he establishes through two sūtras that this very *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) is the substratum for both Śiva— who is the form of the limbs of the Linga well-known as reality— and the individual soul (*jīva*).
Possessing the fullness of reflective awareness through immersion in the supreme I-consciousness, he is the omniscient, omnipresent witness and the great lord who is the creator of all. || 32 ||
Maheśvara, the Supreme Lord, possessing the fullness of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through immersion in supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*),
becomes possessed of full reflective awareness by ascending to the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*) which is common to both Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*).

He must be omniscient, the creator of all, omnipresent, all-pervading, and the witness of all actions; otherwise, he would be insentient like a crystal or other such objects—as it is said: "Without having the nature of luminosity, an object would remain unmanifest as it was before; nor could the luminosity of an object be distinct from the self."

"Thus, they know that the nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, even if it were colored by an object, light would be like an insentient thing such as a crystal. (ĪP 1.5.11). This is the intended meaning. Now, what is its essential nature? To this he says:

They call the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the Supreme Self that which consists of the supreme I-consciousness (parāhantā), completely filled with the light of the Great Consciousness that is the support of all. 33.

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "I am the first-born of the Supreme Self, the navel of immortality before the gods" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.6), and because of the Lord's own statement: "For I am the source of the gods" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.2) and "I am the origin of all; from me everything proceeds" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.8).

The Supreme Śiva, whose nature is supreme consciousness (parasaṃvidrūpa) and who is the Self (ātman), is filled with the light of great consciousness (mahāsaṃvitprakāśa), that is, filled with the light of Great Intellect (mahācitprakāśa). He is the support of the universe,

the substratum of the lower Māyā characterized by nescience (avidyā) which takes the form of the universe, and consists of supreme I-consciousness (parāhantāmaya), just as [the space within] a jar [is a reflection of the universal space].
The possession of a conch-like neck and so forth is not distinct from that [universal form]; likewise, the state of the "I" (aham) as "I-ness" (ahantā)—

according to the root *pṛ* meaning "to protect" and "to fill"— is, by way of the analogy of the essence of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍarasa*), the totality of the universe characterized by the impure, mixed, and pure paths.

Those proficient in the Śivādvaita scriptures declare that the upward-moving form of *māyā*, which consists of the supreme *ahantā* (I-consciousness) that is the fullness of life, is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness); the meaning is that they declare it with excellence. This is the intended sense:
according to the Vedic scripture, "A quarter of Him are all beings" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 8.4.17), the entire phenomenal world of moving and non-moving things [is His].

Because it consists of the expansion of the mobile form characterized by the consciousness and activity of Maheśvara, the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) itself— which manifests as the upward-moving form of *māyā*—
becomes a modification of a single part according to the analogy of the worm in ghee.
Vāgīśvarī is the supreme Vidyā; Kuṭilā and Kuṇḍalī are supreme;
Śuddhamāyā and the supreme Bindu—this is called Śabdabrahman.
Thus,

by the instruction of the Guru, she should be understood as the "Mother of the Six Paths" (*ṣaḍadhvajananī*), possessing synonymous names well-known from the words of the *Pauṣkara*. Because her nature is consciousness (*cidrūpatva*),...

Even though [the Absolute] is partless, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, because the differentiation of parts is possible through its own sovereignty, which is capable of bringing about the impossible by virtue of its skill in accomplishing the unachievable. || 33 ||
With the expansion of the principles of the universe deposited within the vessel of his discernment, looking to no other face for support, he remains liberated, established in his own self. (34)

The meaning is that the Śiva-yogin, liberated and released from the multitude of the snares of *māyā*, having placed within the vessel of his own reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) all the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *Śakti* and ending with *Earth* as so many bubbles, remains established in his own essential nature, facing inward toward his very self. || 34 ||
Thus [ends] the section on vessels; now, the section on receptacles.
His supreme power is vast and transformative;
it is innate and possesses qualities equal to those of Rudra,
manifesting in thousands of forms such as knowledge, action, and will.
"May that mind of mine be of auspicious intent. [This hymn is not found in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.
Thus, in accordance with the Śivasaṅkalpa-śruti—

That auspicious power of Maheśvara which bestows grace upon all is metaphorically designated as "bond" (pāśa) precisely because it follows after [the individual's] dharma. (Mṛgendra-tantra-vṛtti, Pāda 7.11)

And in accordance with the words of the *Mṛgendra*, he establishes through two aphorisms that for the Śiva-yogin who has attained the state of that vessel, it is indeed the power of concealment (*tirobhāva-śakti*)—which serves as the locus of his reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—that constitutes the vessel: [The two sūtras follow: 1. *tirodhānaśaktir eva bhājanaṃ tasya* (The power of concealment alone is his vessel). 2. *tadāśrayo hi vimarśaḥ* (For reflective awareness has that [power] as its locus).
That in which the reflective awareness (vimarśa) shines— which is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and end of all cosmic eggs— is here called the "vessel" (bhājana).

That supreme point (*parabindu*), which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) serving as the cause for the creation and other processes of the entire cosmic egg (*bhuvanāṇḍa*), shines forth within the power (*śakti*) that is conjoined with Śiva in the form of concealment (*tirodhāna*); that very nature of His power is here called the "vessel" (*bhājana*) in reference to the Śiva-yogi who has attained the state of the "vessel-place" (*bhāṇḍasthala*). This is the intended meaning: [The provided text ends here.]

The concealment of Śiva’s power (śakti) within the consciousness that is associated with the five sheaths (pañcakañcuka) and designated as the "Person" (puruṣa), which follows the three bonds (pāśatraya), is a metaphorical designation. || 35 ||
The supreme power called Vimarśa (reflective awareness) is the cause of the manifold diversity of the universe;
that Brahman in which she is established is this very vessel of the universe.

That Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and action (*dṛk-kriyā-svarūpa*), in which the supreme Kuṇḍalinī power called *vimarśa*— the cause of the manifold diversity of the universe— is established as the power of concealment; that very Brahman, whose nature is Brahman,
is like the heat of fire or the whiteness of a cloth (just as the heat of fire is not separate from the fire).

Or rather, just as the whiteness of a white cloth is not different from the cloth itself, so too power (śakti) is not distinct from the possessor of power (śaktimān). The meaning is that the vessel of the universe has as its essential nature perception (dṛk) and action (kriyā), which are powers inherent within it that remain concealed. || 36 ||
Now, he elucidates the slight mutual blending of concealment (*tirobhāva*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through two aphorisms:
"By way of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and by way of being the sprout of the universe (*jagad-aṅkura*).
In whom the power of consciousness shines forth, he is said to have become Brahman.

The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), characterized by the concealment of gross objects of knowledge and possessing inherent powers, shines within that Supreme Bindu in the form of the sprout of the universe— by way of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which serves as the cause of the cosmic sprout, and in the form of the root-ego (*mūlāhaṅkāra*).
The supreme bindu known as *vimarśa*, having become Brahman, is called Paraśiva, who is named the Supreme Brahman;
the meaning is that this very supreme bindu, possessing the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*), is the Great Linga (*mahāliṅga*). || 37 ||
To the question, "Since it is mixed with the ego (ahaṅkāra), why is it not false?", he says:

"Just as the steady moonlight, which illuminates all things, exists within the moon, so too does the power whose essence is reflective awareness (vimarśa) abide within Brahman in its various modes. (38)

Just as the moonlight, which is constant in the moon, illuminates all things— the entire universe— both in its entirety and in part, so too does the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-mayī*) and established as a stable power within the Supreme Śiva who is the nature of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā-ātmaka*), illuminate the entire universe of objects.
The meaning is that she is the illuminator who manifests the world in its various forms as portions fashioned by her own sovereignty.
She is known as the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) because she remains hidden from ordinary beings due to being beyond the reach of mind and speech;
she is the power of consciousness-action (*cit-kriyā-śakti*) whose nature is the manifestation of the reality of objects.
The distinction is that names such as Parabrahman, Paraśiva, and Paraliṅga are primary [designations] for the Mahābindu and so forth, while others are secondary. || 38 ||
Now, one might ask: how does Brahman, which is essentially the primary light and whose sole nature is power (*śakti*), exist? To this he says:
"The letter *A* is declared to be Śiva, and the letter *Ha* is said to be Śakti.
Brahman, consisting of Śiva and Śakti, abides as the one within the word *aham* (I). (39)

She is of the nature of consciousness, according to the Lord’s statement, "Among letters, I am the letter 'A'," and the Vedic revelation, "The letter 'A' is indeed all speech" (Ai. Ā. 2.3.6), as well as the scriptural tradition stating, "The seventeenth letter is called Śiva," "The letter 'Ha' is Śakti," and "The final letter 'Ha' is the form of Kalā."

It is called the power of vision and action (*dṛkkriyāśakti*). Thus, that which consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose nature is Śiva and Śakti—the Brahman, the Supreme Brahman, being one—resides in the word "I" (*ahaṃpada*).

The meaning is that [the Self] exists as "I" in its own nature (svarūpa) throughout the three periods of time. By this, those followers of Vyāsa who claim that Brahman is of the nature of the "I" are refuted; for if Brahman is admitted to be eternally immediate (nityāparokṣa), then nothing other than that could ever be perceived in any way whatsoever. || 39 ||
Now, it is said that having attained such an egoity (*ahantā*), the Śiva-yogin appears as the universal form:
"Having attained the supreme, stable egoity consisting of the power of Śiva, the yogin, having reached the state of Brahman, manifests as the soul of the universe. (40)

Having known and contemplated that supreme *ahantā* (I-consciousness), which transcends space, time, and form, consists of the power of Śiva (*śivaśaktimayī*), is composed of the power non-different from Śiva (*śivābhinnaśaktimayī*), and is the seventeenth digit of consciousness (*saptadaśīyacitkalā*)— having realized it as stable and firmly established through non-difference from one's own self— one attains the state of Brahman, the very nature of Brahman.
The Śivayogin, having gone [to that state], being the self of the universe, appears as the form of the world; the meaning is that he manifests and shines forth.
Now, as to how the Śivayogin, while being the universal form, shines—here [it is said]:
Just as the great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of the *nyagrodha* tree...
In this way, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.
Thus, speaking in the manner taught in the *Śrī Parātriṃśikā-śāstra*, he concludes the section on the locus of the vessel:

"Just as leaves, flowers, and so forth residing in a tree are contained within the seed of a banyan, so too this entire universe resides within the seed of the Heart of the Supreme Self. (Compare: *yathā*...)

Just as the great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of the banyan, so too does this entire world of moving and non-moving beings reside within the seed of the Heart. (Parātrīśikā 25) || 41 ||

Just as all the leaves, flowers, and so forth residing in a tree— specifically those in a banyan tree— exist within the banyan seed, so too this entire universe resides within the seed of the heart of the Śiva-yogin, who is the Supreme Self (parātman), whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, and who has attained the state of being a vessel for the world. This is the portion [of the teaching].
The seventeenth [digit] is to be known as that in which the moving and non-moving are internally dissolved, according to the statement of the Āgama.
Now, all the initial lunar days (tithis) consist of the vowels ending with the bindu;
by virtue of the conjunction of time within them, they are proclaimed as the Moon and the Sun.
O virtuous lady, the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa are located respectively in the consonant groups beginning with Ka and ending with Ma.
There is a tetrad of concentrations (dhāraṇās) on air, fire, water, and earth;
above that, the group beginning with Śa is renowned, and further ahead is the pentad of Brahmā.
"From the rootless, through that sequence, it should be known; emanation is said to end with *kṣa*.
According to this method taught in the *Śrī Parātriṃśikā-śāstra*, because the fifty phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* possess the nature of space, time, and form, [they constitute the universe].

"According to the established doctrine of the *Pañcāśikā-śāstra*: 'That supreme Speech (Parā Vāk), which is consciousness whose nature is reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) and flows by its own inherent savor, is the true I-consciousness (satyāhaṃtā) in which the entire collection of phonemes has been withdrawn from beginning to end. Thus, by virtue of the letter *kṣa* being a combination of *ka* and *ṣa*..."

Because the letter *ha* alone is the final [letter], it encompasses the entire alphabet which expresses space, time, and form; thus, within the union of Śiva and Śakti— manifested as the letters *a* and *ha* brought together by this contraction— it shines forth the object of knowledge contained therein.

The meaning is that [the Self] abides in a state of identity with the seed-syllable of the Heart (hṛdayabīja), which is characterized by the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the activity of consciousness (*citkriyā*) whose nature is the reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) consisting of Śiva, the power of Nara, and the vibration (*spanda*) of the drops (*bindu*) that are the characteristics of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

Herein, the reflective awareness— which consists of the subtle powers of speech beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *ha*— is contained within the word "I" (*ahaṃpada*), which is of that same nature.

The secret is this: the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which consists of the supreme power of speech (*parāvāk*) characterized by the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) that appears as something beyond the range of ordinary people, is the power of concealment (*tirodhānaśakti*).
There is no cognition in the world that exists without the accompaniment of sound.
"Every cognition is as if permeated by sound; it is apprehended (or appears) as such"—this is according to the statement of the Grammarians (*Vākyapadīya* 1.115). || 41 ||
Thus [ends] the section on the vessel;
now follows the section on the medicinal paste.

Now, according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (4.14.3), which states, "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling [to him]," the actions performed by such a yogi— [are not tainted.]
They proceed without being stained at all, as their merits and demerits reach total exhaustion.

And according to the statement in the *Yogajāgama*, he explains through three sūtras that for the Śiva-yogin— who possesses the capacity for vision and action characterized by concealment (*tirobhāva*)— karma does not become a "staining" factor of the limbs [of yoga]; thus it is called "non-staining of the limbs" (*aṅgālepa*).
He whose form is renowned as this great one, consisting of consciousness and bliss, unconditioned by space, time, and the like—he is here called Aṅgālepa. (42)

That Śiva-yogin who has attained the state of being a vessel for that [reality]— whose nature is known as the Great One, which is devoid of limitation in all three respects of direction, place, and time, whose essence is consciousness and bliss, and which manifests in the form of vision and action— is the one whose very form and essential nature is that [Great One], even while he remains a vessel for its concealment.
The meaning is that he is said here to be "free from the taint of bodily actions. || 42 ||
Regarding this, he provides an illustration:

"Even though the Great-Minded One, whose nature is consciousness, is the self of the entire world, he is not at all defiled by the cycles of existence, just as the sky is not defiled by smoke and the like. (43)

Being the self-consciousness of the entire universe, the great-minded Śivayogī, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is not tainted by the sinful actions of saṃsāra, just as the sky is not tainted by smoke, clouds, and the like;
this is the meaning. || 43 ||
To the question "Why?", he says here:
"There is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither alternative nor latent impression."

[This belongs] solely to that whose nature is pure consciousness and whose material self has dissolved: "There is no cessation and no origination; there is neither one bound nor a binder; there is neither one desiring liberation nor one liberated—this is the ultimate reality" (Pañcadaśī 6.35).
"Galita" means that for the Śiva-yogin, whose nature is pure consciousness and who has ceased all effort toward ordinary karma, there is no injunction (*vidhi*).

There is neither the action prescribed by injunction nor the prohibited action; there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "it exists" or "it does not exist," nor is there any latent impression (*vāsanā*), meaning that even the impression of such [constructions] does not exist. || 44 ||
Now, by means of two aphorisms, he specifies with an illustration the non-dual knowledge of the Śiva-yogin who is free from latent impressions (vāsanā):
"Just as space, though appearing separate within jars and other objects, is not divided."
In the same way, Brahman, though appearing in various forms when associated with limiting adjuncts, is not divided. || 45 ||

Just as the ether within jars, huts, and so forth is not distinct even though it appears separate, so too Brahman—though appearing in manifold forms when conditioned by limiting adjuncts such as gods and demons—is not divided; this is the meaning. || 45 ||
Just as the imperishable and indescribable ether shines forth, so too does Brahman shine as consciousness; herein lies its distinctive feature.

Just as space (*vyoma*), which is devoid of destruction, incomparable, and eternal, shines forth, so too does Brahman shine forth. Within this Brahman, consciousness (*caitanya*)—consisting of the forms of perception and action—is the specific faculty (*vaiśeṣikī kalā*); it is called the "specific faculty" in relation to the insentient elemental ether (*jaḍabhūtabhūtākāśa*), and its nature is that of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
The meaning is "Brahman. Here, it should be understood that non-perishability and partlessness do not imply eternity, because [the latter] would entail insentience. || 46 ||
(p. 439) Then, having declared that the Śivayogin, whose nature is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is "complete," he concludes the section on the application of ashes to the limbs:
Neither divinity, nor humanity, nor the state of an animal, nor anything else—
