this "state of being all forms" is declared for the yogin who is liberated while living.
For the yogi who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), because he is free from the bonds of karma, there is no divinity attained through the fruition of meritorious deeds;

nor is there human birth, which arises from a mixture of merit and demerit; nor is there the state of a subhuman creature produced by sin. Beyond these, he does not even exist within the womb of *māyā* in a state of torpor caused by impurity (*mala*).
However, it is declared that everywhere there is the nature of the all-pervading sky of consciousness (*paripūrṇa-cidākāśa*).
For the Śiva-yogin who possesses the grace of the eternally perfect consciousness,
the bondage of the five fetters— consisting of *māyā*, *mala*, *bindu*, *tirobhāva*, and *karman*— as well-known in the Siddhānta [tradition], [is dissolved].
The meaning is that it does not exist. || 47 ||
Thus, there is the stage of the application of ointment,
and then the stage of recognizing oneself and others;
just as one embraced by a beloved woman perceives nothing external whatsoever.

"There is no interval; even so, this person, closely embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman), knows nothing external and nothing internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21). According to this Śruti:
"To oneself, there is indeed no other that is superior, nor does any other exist for oneself."
Thus, even when that which is to be maintained has dissolved, there is indeed nothing for him to be known.

And because of this statement from the *Sarvajñānottara*, [the author] demonstrates that the Śiva-yogin who has applied the unguent (*aṅgālepa*) does not know himself or another due to his freedom from the five fetters (*pāśapañcaka*) as explained in the first section on the five stages (*pañcasthala*).
When dissolved in the immeasurable form of consciousness—the non-dual majesty of Brahman—what indeed does one know, whether as one's own self or as another? 48.
According to the Vedic scripture, "Brahman is one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), it is of an immeasurable and non-expanding nature.

Within this context, "internal difference" (*svagata-bheda*) refers to distinctions within a single body, such as "these are the two hands, these are the two feet. "Difference among similar things" (*sajātīya-bheda*) refers to a cow being distinct from another cow.

The statement "different from a white horse" refers to a distinction based on a different genus (*vijātīya-bheda*). Having attained a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) within the void of the Supreme Brahman, does one who is free from attachment (*aṅgālepa*) know himself or another? The meaning is that he knows neither. || 48 ||
(p. 440) Now, he elucidates this very point with five aphorisms:
"Where, due to the absence of the application of duality, there is no delusion of 'I' and 'you'..."
There is neither union nor separation, nor the conceptualization of the object of knowledge and the knower. 49.
There is neither bondage nor liberation, nor the conceit of being a god or the like;
there is neither happiness nor suffering, nor ignorance, nor even knowledge. (50)
It is neither superior nor inferior, neither above nor below;
it is neither behind nor in front, neither far nor at any distance.
In that stainless, supreme Brahman, which consists of the ultimate ether, which is eternal, whose form is truth, and which is the bliss of consciousness in all its aspects; (52)
For yogins who have attained oneness with the Supreme Self, how could there be talk of derision regarding the thorough knowledge of the higher and the lower? 53.

In that Brahman, which possesses the glory of non-duality, there is no delusion of distinction such as "I" and "you," because— through yoga— the two perspectives attain a state of equalized flavor (*samarasa*) like two eyes, since both have come to rest in the oneness of the notion of "I. Furthermore, neither conjunction nor separation exists there.
Where there is no conceptualization of the known or the knower, where there is neither bondage nor liberation,
where there is not even the conceit of being a deity and so forth; where there is no pleasure— that is, no sensual pleasure—
and likewise no such suffering, no knowledge born of the senses, and neither superiority nor inferiority.

Neither the upper part nor the lower part, neither the western part nor the eastern part— [in that] Brahman, which is not far but slightly distant, whose nature is all things, whose form is consciousness-bliss-truth, eternal, stainless, and consisting of the supreme space; for those who have attained oneness with it, for this very reason...

"How could there be occasion for the joke that 'I know the supreme and my own self-nature' regarding the Śiva-yogins who are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman? The meaning is that because they are all-pervading and one, such [distinctions] do not exist. (49–53)
441) Now, further specifying this very point, he concludes the section on the locus of self and other-knowledge: "Because it rests upon a form of light that is unconditioned by space and time."
Due to the absence of knowledge regarding self and other, the wise know this to be the state of ignorance concerning self and other.
"Of the nature of splendor" means having the nature of the light of consciousness; the remainder is clear. || 54 ||
Thus ends the section on the ground of knowing self and other;
now follows the section on the dissolution of existence and non-existence.

"In accordance with the Kaṭhavallī Śruti: 'The wise person does not grieve, having realized the Great, All-pervading Self, who perceives neither the end of sleep nor the end of waking. [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.21]
Those who know reality recognize that reality as transcending the duality of existence and non-existence, surpassing both dreaming and waking, and being entirely free from death and life.
And according to the statement of the *Yogajāgama*, he establishes that for the Śiva-yogin who is devoid of the cognition of self and other, neither existence nor non-existence exists:
"In the sky of consciousness, which is like a void, being entirely free from 'thou-ness' and 'I-ness'..."
For one who has become unified and perfected, whence can there be talk of existence or non-existence? || 55 ||

For the Siddha Śivayogin—who has become of one flavor within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), which is devoid of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and resembles the void, being distinguished from a delimited body, and who is empty of the cognition of self and other—how could there be any occasion for existence or non-existence? The meaning is that it does not exist. || 55 ||

442) Now, he explains the nature of the dissolution of the existence and non-existence of that [ego-sense] by means of two aphorisms: "Because of the emptiness of the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva), and likewise because of the non-existence of the self (ātman)..."
Freed from both existence and non-existence, the one liberated while living shines forth.

Due to the absence of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva), and because of the non-existence of this self as the well-known Supreme Self—according to the Upanishadic teaching, "This Self is Brahman" (Ai. U. 5.3)—as well as due to such emptiness, the Śiva-yogin, being liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and devoid of the knowledge of self and other, remains established in the mudrā of mental stillness and physical languor.

Being free from both existence and non-existence— where "existence" refers to the limited bodily ego-sense of "I am," and "non-existence" refers to the notion that the Self does not exist— one who is void of such forms of existence and non-existence shines forth in one’s own true nature.
This occurs by means of the sense of being the experiencer of all suffering, wherein the root-ego that tends toward deep sleep and dissolution exists as a state of being.

The meaning is that consciousness, which manifests without limitation even throughout the three states as the witness of all, is indeed distinct from both existence and non-existence, being devoid of both being and non-being. || 56 ||
In states such as pleasure and pain, there exists neither non-existence nor existence for the Great Self, whose nature is consciousness and who is untainted. (57)

The meaning is that for the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), whose nature is consciousness and who is free from the taint of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) characterized as previously described, there exists neither non-existence nor existence in relation to pleasure, pain, and so forth; this is because he is untainted and all-pervading. || 57 ||

To the objection that nothing whatsoever is seen in that which is empty of both existence and non-existence, he says: "In that light whose nature is consciousness, wherein nothing at all is seen—neither of the nature of being nor of the nature of non-being—for one who has abandoned both existence and non-existence. (58)
This is clear. || 58 ||
443) Now, he concludes the section on the dissolution of existence and non-existence:
Existence and non-existence, as they are perceived, do not exist anywhere at all.
When there is identity of the gender (liṅga), that which arises from it is the place of dissolution of both existence and non-existence.

The meaning is that since manifest existence and non-existence do not exist— that is, they are not found— anywhere in relation to the Supreme Being who has become one with the essence of the Śiva-liṅga, it is therefore called "the place of the dissolution of existence and non-existence. || 59 ||
Thus, [one should contemplate] the stage of the dissolution of existence and non-existence;
then, the stage of the void of knowledge.
Then, one should perceive water within water, fire within fire, wind within wind, and space within space.
In this way, a person is liberated when the mind has entered within, according to the Maitreya-śruti:
"All is empty and devoid of appearance; it becomes a state of uniformity (sāmarasya), just as ghee poured into ghee, or milk into milk."

And following the statement of the *Sarvajñānottara*, he describes— by means of three aphorisms— the state of voidness of knowledge, which is easily attained through non-duality, for the Śiva-yogin who has achieved the dissolution of existence and non-existence by virtue of the voidness of the knowledge of self and other:

The discernment of existence and non-existence, which depends upon the relative distinction between the higher and the lower, does not exist in Brahman; the wise know that state to be devoid of [dualistic] knowledge.

The knowledge that discriminates between existence and non-existence, which is joined with the desire for higher and lower knowledge, does not exist in the Brahman—which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman—nor in the Śiva-yogin who has attained the dissolution of both existence and non-existence;
they know this as the "state devoid of knowledge" (jñāna-śūnya-sthala). This is the meaning. || 60 ||
To the question "In that case, how does he remain?", he says:
"Like water poured into water, or fire cast into fire, his self merged in the Supreme Brahman is not perceived as distinct. (61)

Like water mixed with water, or like fire placed within fire, the Śiva-yogin— having dissolved all states of existence and non-existence through effort into the Great Liṅga which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman— is not perceived by means of differentiated perception. Nor is he [not perceived].

The meaning is "it remains," because it is devoid of dualistic cognition (*dvaitajñāna*). Here, in the non-duality of Śiva who is void of dualistic cognition, the analogy of water and fire is employed; it is of a nature that is an equalized equilibrium (*samasamara*), like the union of the visual forms of the watery and fiery elements, and not like the ocean and its water, which causes the loss or increase of their own essential natures (*svarūpa*). || 61 ||
In the supreme reality, which is the self of all and devoid of any suspicion of duality, how can knowledge arising from the conventional usage of "knower" and so forth be conceived? (62)
This is clear. || 62 ||
Now, he qualifies that very [Brahman] with three verses:
"Changeless, formless, eternal, and devoid of boundaries—supreme Brahman, like space, abides in a state of non-conceptuality. (63)
There are no primary elements such as earth and the rest, no planets, nor indeed stars;
there are no gods, no humans, no animals, and none others.
In that state, whose sole characteristic is the existence of pure consciousness and bliss alone, by what means could a consciousness rooted in "thou-ness," "I-ness," and so forth, be conceived? (65)

Like clay and other substances, the Supreme Brahman remains free from modification, devoid of forms such as blue or yellow, and without limit; it abides like the sky, in a state of non-conceptuality and freedom from duality. Therefore, the elements such as earth and the rest, which appear to be distinct, as well as the nine planets beginning with the Sun, do not [exist as separate entities].

Neither the stars beginning with Aśvinī, nor the deities beginning with Viṣṇu, nor humans, nor animal beings, nor others exist [in that state]. Therefore, in Brahman, whose nature is pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss, by what could the specific cognition arising from conventional designations such as "you" and "I" be produced? By nothing at all.
The meaning is that it is cultivated. || 63–65 ||
p.

445) Now, according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (1.12), which states: "This alone is to be known, eternally established in the Self; beyond this, there is nothing further to be known," it is said that [the Self] is the sole object of knowledge.

And following the statement of the Goddess in the *Kālottara*, "Nothing whatsoever is to be known," he demonstrates through five aphorisms that for one who knows their own true nature, there is no cognition of the phenomenal world consisting of the triple-fold (tripuṭī).
Due to the absence of an object of knowledge, it is specifically perceived as being like a void;
it is empty of the knower, the known, and so forth, and empty of qualities such as cognition and the rest. (66)
Empty at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle—empty everywhere and at all times;
it is realized as empty because it is empty of any second entity. (67)

Because there is an absence of objects of knowledge—due to the absence of cognition whose object is every entity—and because it is devoid of the categories that constitute knowable things, the venerable consciousness itself is the sole refuge for the apprehension of the existence of objects;
since this is accepted even by the Prābhākaras, it is understood that "knowledge is as if void" (śūnyakalpa). This is the remainder [of the argument].

Therefore, it is empty of the manifold expansion consisting of the triad of the knower, the known, and so forth; it is empty of cognition and other qualities such as knowledge and desire; it is empty everywhere and at all times—in the beginning, the middle, and the end. By what is it empty? It is empty of a second entity. Therefore, it is the Void (śūnya).
The knowledge of emptiness is cultivated. || 66-67 ||
Now, as to what that is, he says: "Only the Supreme Brahman shines forth, characterized by the non-dual light of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, appearing like a void, the supreme space. (68)

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman—which is the non-dual mark of the void characterized by the manifestation of pure Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—shines forth as reality, being of the nature of the great ether and therefore resembling the void. || 68 ||
446) Now, it might be argued that the arising of conceptual cognition is not possible for one who has attained identity with Brahman of such a nature; to this, he says:

When one has attained oneness with that which is of the nature of consciousness, self-luminous, unsurpassed, the form of light, the emblem of the Liṅga, the means for accomplishing all goals, and the conceptualization of the knowledge of emptiness and so forth— how could there be the possibility of [dualistic] knowledge? (69)

How could there be the arising of knowledge—the manifestation of functional cognition—for a Śiva-yogin who has attained oneness with that which possesses the volitions of void, knowledge, will, and so forth; which accomplishes all objects as the void; which is devoid of anything superior to itself; and which is the self-luminous form of consciousness in the nature of the light of the supreme Śiva-liṅga? It could not.
The meaning is "in any way whatsoever. || 69 ||
Now, according to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.9.26), "Not this, not this; neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither shadow nor darkness," it is indeed inexpressible,
without support, ungraspable, and devoid of all objective existence.
"One who is joined to the state beyond the principles (nistattva) is liberated"; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Thus, according to the *Niśvāsakārikā-tantra*,
there is the yoga of the bound soul (*paśu*) and the Lord of Souls (*paśupati*), the practice of the unity of the two eyes,
the region of space and the locus of space, and the region of the ocean and the ocean.

He whose nature is the flavor of absolute equality, yet whose form appears as diverse and distinct; at night, he is beautiful through the embrace of his beloved, who is the very essence of that equal flavor.

Thus, having stated the supreme definition according to the words of the learned who are proficient in the logic of the three Vedas (*trayītantra*), he concludes the section on the locus of the void of knowledge (*jñānaśūnyasthala*):
"That which has no state of being an effect, nor even the state of being a cause..."
He possesses neither the state of being subordinate nor the state of being the principal; he is called the liberated supreme one.
For him from whom everything has been negated as "not this, not this," who has transcended all categories of reality and is established in his own true nature,
there is no state of being an effect; nor, conversely, is there for him any causality,
he who is endowed with his own essential nature and whose names are synonymous with the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Śiva, the Liṅga, and so forth.

The meaning is that he for whom there is no state of being a subordinate (śeṣatva), no state of being a remainder (avaśeṣatva), no state of being a principal (śeṣitva), and no state of possessing subordinates (śeṣavattva)—he is eternally perfect and is said to be truly liberated by nature as the essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).

The meaning is as follows: "The self, being powerless, is bound due to its state as an enjoyer; by knowing God, it is released from all fetters" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.8). Thus, according to the Śvetāśvatara Śruti, the statement in the Vīrāgama that "the individual soul (jīva) is bound by fetters, while Paraśiva is liberated from fetters," and through the instruction of the teacher and one's own direct experience.
[To be compared with: from scripture, from the Guru, and from oneself (Taṃtrāloka)].

Furthermore, supreme liberation is precisely the manifestation of one's true nature, which is denoted by the term *paraśiva* (Supreme Śiva) when liberated from the bonds of *māyā*, impurity (*mala*), the *bindu*, concealment (*tirobhāva*), and karma. These three *liṅgas* correspond respectively to the three limbs of the unity with the *śivaliṅga*.
That which is conducive to fetters. || 70 ||
Thus ends the section on the ground of knowledge-emptiness (followed by the description of the conclusion of the instruction).
Now, the teacher Śiva, who has composed this compendium of the scripture, [addresses] his own disciples and grand-disciples.
Indicating the conclusion of this scripture, the Lord of the Gaṇas, Reṇuka, remaining without further reply, stayed silent;
this he declares with two sūtras:
"Having said this much, [he remained] in supreme awakening, the non-dual light of blissful Śiva."
When this was previously spoken by the Lord to the Goddess, the leader of the Gaṇas became silent and absorbed in meditation.

In ancient times, Gaṇendra, the lord of the Gaṇas of Reṇuka, was told by the Supreme Lord a secret to the goddess Pārvatī— a well-spoken teaching that reveals the bliss of Śiva, whose nature is the non-duality of Śiva,
and which constitutes the supreme awakening throughout its introduction, conclusion, and intermediate reflections.

Having thus spoken in this manner and taught up to this point the Vīraśaiva scripture— which culminates in the knowledge of the body and so forth that illuminates one’s own true nature— he became silent, meaning he remained in a state of silence, absorbed in meditation upon his own true nature. || 71 ||
Having spoken thus, the sage, with palms joined in reverence, looked at Reṇuka— who was seated there, devoted to the yoga of Śiva— and addressed him.
"Babhāṣe" means he began a hymn of praise; the rest is clear. || 72 ||
448) Then, with seven sūtras, Agastya offers a hymn of praise to Śrī Reṇuka, beginning with:
"O Knower of the specificities of Śiva-yoga, O Great Ocean of the Knowledge of Śiva!"
O bearer of the burden of all worldly activity regarding the Vedas, Shastras, and other sciences!
O Śiva, whose every bond of saṃsāra has been shaken off by mere light, who delights in the play of free movement, and who is like the self-luminous Self! 74.
Having heard this faultless treatise descended from your mouth, my mind rejoices; may I behold the light named Śiva.
An expert in the specific yoga of meditation on Śiva, an ocean of Śiva-knowledge,
the bearer of the burden of the practical application of all the scriptures such as the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas,
one who has severed the bonds of saṃsāra for all people by the mere sight of him, and one who manifests his conduct according to his own will.

O Lord of Gaṇas, having heard this Vīraśaiva scripture—free from defects and manifesting the very nature of Śiva through its own self-luminous consciousness—my mind rejoices; may I behold the light of Śiva! 73–75.
Today my birth has become fruitful; the delusion of my mind has passed away.
The severing of the noose has occurred, and my ascetic penances have borne fruit.
The phrase "today for me" is to be connected with every [verse]. || 76 ||
Just now has the most excellent of the best kings of sages been born to me;
from this point forward, there is no one equal to me in the three worlds.
The meaning is that the lords of sages, the best of seers, possess the state of being the highest of the high;
this is because of the non-difference between the attribute (dharma) and the possessor of the attribute (dharmī). The rest is clear. || 77 ||
This scripture, the supreme tradition of the non-duality of Śiva, has issued from your mouth;
who else in the worlds, apart from me, possesses the auspicious merit of penance sufficient to hear it? (78)
O highly fortunate one, through the ripening of your austerities and by the grace of Śaṅkara, you have come with your speech to fulfill my purpose. (79)
"Udgīrṇa" means that which has emerged or gone outside. "Śāstra" refers to the Vīraśaiva scripture. "Mahābhāga" means "O excellent one. The rest is clear. (78–79)
Then the compiler, the venerable Śrī Reṇuka, spoke regarding how the teacher Śiva offered praise to the pitcher-born Agastya:
"To Agastya, the preeminent among sages, who was thus praising him with humility..."
Having gazed upon him with a compassionate look, that Lord of the Gaṇas spoke.
"From discipline" means "out of devotion. The rest is clear. || 80 ||
O Agastya, tiger among sages, whose desires have been fulfilled through asceticism, who else but you has the authority to hear the scriptures of Śiva? (81)
"One hundred and one varieties of initiation were previously declared by me;
among these, one who has been initiated by a Guru and is devoted to this [system] possesses the requisite authority."
Thus, according to the statement from the Yogaja-āgama, the meaning is that in this scripture there is no one qualified [to practice] except for you.
"You alone, and no other, are the vessel for the grace of Śiva;
having thus resolved, I have taught this tantra to you. (82)
The meaning is that such is the Vīraśaiva Tantra. || 82 ||
O Sage, let this tantra be established by you throughout all the worlds;
for nowhere else exists such a means for the realization of Śiva. (83)
This is clear. || 83 ||
The omniscient Śiva, the benefactor of all, the Lord of Pārvatī, has declared this secret for the spiritual perfection of all the worlds. (84)
"For the sake of accomplishment" means for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. "This secret" means the secret of Vīraśaivism. The remainder is clear. || 84 ||
This is the most excellent among the essences of the Śiva-siddhānta; it is the entirety of the Vedas and Vedāntas, and the promoter of knowledge and right conduct. 85.
This [work], which reveals the non-duality of Śiva and is to be received by heroic devotees of Maheśvara,
should be given to disciples who have been tested, and never otherwise.
This scripture, which establishes the path of Śivayoga through the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*) of Vīraśaivism,
is the most excellent among the essence of the twenty-eight divine Āgamas beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Vātula*;
it is the very soul of the four Vedas and the thirty-two Upaniṣads, illuminating both knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*).
This scripture, which establishes the non-duality of Paraśiva, must be accepted by the heroic devotees of Maheśvara;

for according to the Aitareya Śruti: "One should teach so many Saṃhitās to a pupil, but not to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year; the teacher is not a true expounder [to such a person]."
To one who is devoted, a disciple of the self, dispassionate, and of great intelligence,
the Guru who possesses knowledge should impart that which is overflowing with the essence of bliss.

And because of this statement from the *Yogajāgama*, the sense is that [this knowledge] should be given to disciples who have been tested, but one should not speak it to those who lack the qualification. || 85-86 ||
By the mere hearing of this, there is the destruction of all sins for everyone.
451) I have descended to the earth for the sake of setting this scripture in motion.
You too should propagate such knowledge as this, which is the non-duality of Śiva.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Liṅgas Concerning the Stage of Unity with Śiva," in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a definitive exposition of the Vīraśaiva dharma, composed by the venerable Reṇukācārya, known as Śivayogin, a Brāhmaṇa of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). || 20 ||
This is clear. || 87 ||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Occurrence of the Ninefold Liṅgas Concerning the Section on Unity with Śiva," in the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇḍadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences. 20.
The Twenty-first Chapter: The Granting of the Desired Object to Vibhīṣaṇa;
now, by Revaṇasiddheśvara, to the Pot-born Sage (Agastya).

The teacher known as Śivayogin, having composed the *Vīraśaiva-saṅgraha*— which begins with the *piṇḍa* and ends with the teaching on the knowledge of the state beyond [the body]— and having made it renowned among his own disciples and grand-disciples, subsequently [composed] the *Reṇuka-vibhīṣaṇa-saṃvāda* and the *Revana-siddheśvara-ekya*.
Having summarized [the matter] in fifty-five sūtras, he says:
"Having spoken thus, even as he was looking on, Reṇuka vanished right before him, while reflecting upon Mahādeva within his inner self. (1)
This is clear. || 1 ||
He who listens with a pure mind to this supreme Vīraśaiva doctrine, the Śivasiddhānta, attains the highest goal.

That person who, with a pure mind and a stainless heart, listens to this Śiva-siddhānta— which is the Vīraśaiva doctrine consisting of the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*) and the *aṅga-liṅga*, which is the excellent and supreme determination of the Vīraśaiva dharma, and which is in accord with the Vedas— he...
The meaning is that one goes to the supreme goal, which is supreme liberation. || 2 ||
Then, having vanished, Reṇuka entered Laṅkā; thus it is said:
"Delighting in the practice of independent conduct and assuming a form created by his own will, Reṇuka, the leader of the Gaṇas, reached the city of Laṅkā. (3)
The meaning is: one who delights in the practice of stainless self-will. The rest is clear. || 3 ||
Seeing that illustrious one, who was an expert in all the scriptures, arrive,
Vibhīṣaṇa led him into his own home. (4)

"Mahābhāgaḥ" means the most excellent one, proficient in all the scriptures (āgamas), specifically skilled in the divine scriptures beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Vātula; the rest is clear. || 4 ||
Having seated the Lord of the Gaṇas upon his own beautiful and auspicious throne,
he worshipped him with all the ritual services, beginning with water for the hands and feet.
"On his own auspicious seat" means on his own lion-throne; the rest is clear. || 5 ||
Having been honored by the pleased Reṇuka,
he was invited and sat down near him, taking his own seat.
That Vibhīṣaṇa, having been commanded by the illustrious Renuka—who was pleased with his worship—took a seat near him on another throne and sat down; that is the meaning. || 6 ||
Then Vibhīṣaṇa addressed that lord of the hosts with palms joined in reverence—
he who was endowed with a human form, like another Śiva in person. (7)

Vibhīṣaṇa—[the rest of the sentence implies] as if he were another Śiva himself in human form—to that lord of the Gaṇas, Reṇuka, with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), addressed him; that is to say, he uttered words of petition in such a manner as was appropriate for the occasion. || 7 ||
(454) O Reṇuka, you who are the lord of the Gaṇas and devoted to the knowledge of Śiva,
I have heard correctly that you have descended to this earth. || 8 ||

"O Śrī Reṇuka, leader of the Gaṇas, devoted to the knowledge of Śiva— I have heard this news from the mouths of people that you have descended to this earth, to the world of mortals. By the greatness of my merit, you have come today to this city."
How could those like you be easily obtained by those who are devoid of good fortune? || 9 ||
This is clear. || 9 ||
"In all the worlds, there is no one equal to me in the excellence of my fortune,
since you, Maheśvara himself, have come to my very home."

O Reṇuka, you are the Great Lord (Maheśvara) himself manifest before my eyes upon this earth; since you have come to my royal palace of your own accord, the meaning is that by virtue of such extraordinary fortune, there is no one equal to me in all the worlds. || 10 ||
Then, to the objection that it is not merely that much, he says:
"This city of mine has indeed achieved its purpose; the lineage of the Rākṣasas has achieved its purpose;
and my life has achieved its purpose, since you have come within the range of my vision. (11)
"O Reṇukā, since you have come within the range of my vision, therefore this city of Laṅkā has fulfilled its purpose for me," and so forth. || 11 ||
To the auspicious lord of the Rākṣasas who was speaking thus, Gaṇeśvara,
smiling, spoke these auspicious words that bring joy to the entire universe.
"Sasmitaḥ" means being endowed with a gentle smile; "viśvollāsakarīm" means that which causes joy for all, i.e., bestowing bliss upon everyone. The remainder is clear. || 12 ||
(p. 455) Now, he describes that manner [of conduct] in four verses:
"O illustrious Vibhīṣaṇa, I know you to be an expert in dharma."
In all the worlds, whose devotion such as this could arise without you? (13)
This is clear. || 13 ||
"O Lord of Rākṣasas, they say that you are one who knows the essence of all scriptures, who is devoted to all dharmas, and who is intent upon the science of the supreme self. (14)
"O Vibhīṣaṇa! You are one who knows the essence of all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas;

you are devoted to, that is to say, the ultimate refuge in all the dharmas of Śiva. They say you are a constant practitioner of the spiritual science (adhyātmavidyā) consisting of the yoga of the knowledge of the non-duality of Śiva. || 14 ||
For this reason—
having heard of the perfection of your dharma, my mind filled with wonder—
I set out for Mount Kailāsa and have now arrived in your presence. (15)
The meaning is: "While traveling to Mount Kailāsa, having heard of the excellence of your auspicious dharma, my mind filled with wonder, I have come into your presence. || 15 ||
I am pleased with your excellent conduct, renowned throughout the world;
I shall grant you a boon in person—ask for whatever you desire.
This is clear. || 16 ||
(456) While the Lord of the Gaṇas was speaking thus with a face bright with grace,
Vibhīṣaṇa, having bowed down with supreme affection, spoke.
"Vyājahāra" means he uttered a petitionary statement; that is the sense. || 17 ||
Having thus demonstrated that method through six aphorisms,
he now indicates his own intention as expressed by Rāvaṇa through eight aphorisms: "Precisely through the favor of the scriptures, you are a Śiva-yogin."
Prosperities that are difficult for all people to obtain came to pass.

O Lord of the Gaṇas, O Śiva-yogin, by the very grace of your arrival, all prosperities—which are difficult for all people to obtain—have come to pass; that is to say, they have been attained. || 18 ||
Nevertheless, O Lord of the Gaṇas, there is something I must request;
for when one's merit has reached full maturity, what is desired is accomplished of its own accord. (19)
"Me" means "to me. The remainder is clear. || 19 ||
For Rāvaṇa was my brother, the crest-jewel of the devotees of Maheśvara;
indeed, he ruled over the three worlds without having encountered the perils of enemy forces.
The meaning is that he ruled—that is, protected—the three worlds as they are well-known, in such a way that there was no encounter with enemies. || 20 ||
All the gods, beginning with Indra, being unable to endure his incomparable majesty, were deprived of their royal fortune.
This is clear. || 21 ||
But he, through the reversal of his own conduct as if by the power of time,
was slain in battle by Rāma, an incarnation of Viṣṇu. (22)
This is clear. || 22 ||
Pierced by Rāma’s arrow, his life-breath faltering in his throat, he looked at me who remained there and spoke, deeply distressed. (23)

The meaning is that Rāvaṇa, having been wounded by Rāma’s arrow and with his life-breath reaching his throat, saw me— the only survivor remaining among the slain Rākṣasas— and being exceedingly distressed, he replied. || 23 ||
Now he provides the justification for what Rāvaṇa had said:
"O Vibhīṣaṇa, you who possess specialized knowledge, O one of great intellect, O most righteous one!
You alone remain of the lineage of the Rākṣasas due to the weight of your good fortune. (24)
This is clear. || 24 ||
Filled with ignorance, we committed acts of malice toward the great;
having attained such a state, it is clear that the course of destiny is indeed difficult to overcome. (25)

Being possessed of ignorance, we have committed offenses against the great in the domain of the great, and thus have attained such a state. For such is the nature of destiny; its course is dependent on fate, and it is indeed difficult to cross—that is, impossible to overcome. || 25 ||
"Nine crores of lingas were previously resolved by me to be installed here on this spot; that remains to be done. (26)

(458) At this place, on this site of the city of Laṅkā, it was previously resolved by me that nine crores of liṅgas were to be installed; the meaning is that something remains yet to be completed there. || 26 ||
Regarding how much remains, he says here:
"Sixty million liṅgas have been properly established by me;
therefore, thirty million liṅgas must be installed by you. (27)
Therefore, the meaning is: "for the sake of fulfilling that resolve. || 27 ||
Having heard these words of that dying man, whose mind was despondent,
I likewise promised him, saying, "I shall do so."
This is clear. || 28 ||
It was my firm conviction that three crores of unsurpassed Śiva-liṅgas should be installed simultaneously according to the scriptures. (29)
This is clear. || 29 ||
In this rite for the simultaneous installation of three crores of liṅgas, not knowing a single preceptor, I have remained in this state. (30)

The meaning is "here in Laṅkā. The sense is that, having failed to obtain a principal teacher regarding the simultaneous establishment of the three categories of evidence (*liṅga-trikoṭi*), I remain in this state. || 30 ||
O knower of the specific teachings of Śiva, you who are a treasury of the knowledge of Śiva;
having assumed the state of an Ācārya, fulfill my desire.
O Revanasiddha, you who are an expert in the specific teachings of Śiva, you are a treasury and a repository of the knowledge of Śiva; therefore, having attained the status of a teacher—
The meaning is: "Having attained the state of being a teacher for the three crores [of beings] simultaneously, fulfill my desire. || 31 ||
Then, having fulfilled the desire of that [king], the illustrious Renuka vanished; this he demonstrates with five verses, beginning with:
"Having heard those words of the wise lord of the Rakshasas..."
"So be it," replied the omniscient leader of the hosts.
"Pratiśuśrāva" means he promised or accepted; the rest is clear. || 32 ||

There, for the sake of attaining his desired goal, the mind of the descendant of Pulastya was filled with contentment; he then, at that very moment, installed three crores of Liṅgas according to the scriptures and according to the prescribed rites, through the agency of thirty million preceptors.
In that Laṅkā, [it belongs] to Paulastya, meaning Vibhīṣaṇa; the rest is clear. || 33 ||
Beholding such majesty of hers, Vibhīṣaṇa, filled with wonder, bowed repeatedly with devotion at her feet. (34)
This is clear. || 34 ||
Having bestowed his grace upon the lord of the Rākṣasas, who was bowed down, full of humility, and greatly delighted, Reṇuka vanished by his own majesty. || 35 ||
This is clear. || 35 ||
Bibhīṣaṇa also, his soul gladdened by the grace of Reṇuka and devoted to the essence of devotion to Śiva, protected his stable kingdom. (36)
This is clear. || 36 ||
Now, he reveals the greatness of the renowned Revaṇasiddheśvara in the eight directions by means of eight aphorisms in brief:
"Even Reṇuka, possessed of great splendor, while wandering upon the circle of the earth..."
Both secret and manifest, he is permeated by the state of supreme non-duality. || 37 ||
Some he [graced] with a glance that rained down the essence of compassion,
and others with instruction that touches upon auspicious non-duality.
And by dwelling together with others, he fulfilled the purpose of all people—those who were skillful and whose karma was ripened—by removing every stain. (39)
Having displayed his own superiority, he who was longing for the vision of Śiva destroyed the wicked practitioners of heresy and those of divergent views.

Having conquered by his own power those who were hostile to him— those perfected in the arts of machines and mantras, as well as those established in the circles of the Siddhas— and having established the Śiva-āgamas,
he returned to his own residence, the city named Kollipāka.

And he remained hidden for a period of seven hundred years—this is the remainder [of the sense]. Then, having become manifest, he fulfilled the aims of some people with side-glances filled with the essence of compassion;
others he fulfilled through instruction that reveals the non-duality of Śiva; and still others through pure association.

Making all remaining people fulfilled— those who were already accomplished, skilled in all arts, and whose karma was matured— and being himself one whose bonds of impure *māyā* were fully ripened, the holy Revanasiddha, longing for the vision of Śiva and devoted to the discipline (*samaya*) of Śiva, [proclaimed] his own superiority and his many wonderful and diverse personal greatnesses.
Having displayed various sectarian views, he refuted the heretics who adhere to other systems such as Vaiṣṇavism and others,
those bearing other marks such as the conch and discus, and those of wicked conduct;
[he then established] those endowed with the accomplishments of the sixty-four arts, including the mastery of yantras and mantras.

Having conquered by his own power the maṇḍalas established by the doctrines of the Kāpālikas and others, as well as the nine crores of Siddhas beginning with Gorakṣa, and having established the Śiva-siddhāntas such as the Kāmika and others, he returned to his own residence, the city named Kollipākya; that is to say, he arrived there. (37–41)
There, highly esteemed by all people devoted to Śiva,
he reached the temple of the Lord Śiva known by the name Somanātha. (42)
"Esteemed" means honored. The rest is clear. || 42 ||
While all those devotees and Śiva-yogins were watching,
he, evoking wonder through his states of being, praised the Supreme Lord.
"By states" (bhāvaiḥ) means by stainless qualities; "extending wonder" (vismayam) means spreading astonishment. || 43 ||

Then, with seven verses, he offers praise to Someśvara: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Cause of the cause of the world, whose lotus feet are being worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods! (44)
Here, by the word "jagat" (the world), the worlds are meant; the meaning is that he is the cause even of the bindu, māyā, and so forth, which serve as the causes of those worlds. || 44 ||
O you who bring to completion the illusory performance of the drama of saṃsāra;
O you whose majesty is fully awakened by all the Vedas and Vedāntas! 45.
The meaning is that he bestows victory over the illusory artifice of the drama of saṃsāra. || 45 ||
O Physician of Saṃsāra, Omniscient One, possessing all power without restraint;
O Being-Consciousness-Bliss, the All-in-all, whose form is the supreme ether! || 46 ||

The meaning is that Brahman has the nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman has space as its body" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.6.2). The remainder is clear. || 46 ||
O manifestation of the Jyotirliṅga that is the support of the entire universe;
O bearer of the portions of the many divine forms beginning with Sadāśiva! 47.

The meaning is that he expands in the form of the *jyotir-liṅga* (the light-linga), according to the Vedic scripture: "Salutation to the Jvālā-liṅga" (*Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* 14.9). The meaning is that he possesses the divine forms and *kalās* (aspects) beginning with the *sakala-niṣkala Sadāśiva*, according to the Vedic scripture: "With steady limbs, he is many-formed and fierce" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.33.9). In this regard—He is one...
"He is Rudra, he is Īśāna, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavān), he is Maheśvara, he is Mahādeva"—thus says the Śruti (Aitareya Upaniṣad 3). || 47 ||
O you who have transcended the three qualities (guṇas), O destroyer of the three impurities (mala), O soul of the splendor of the three worlds, O you whose eyes are the three Vedas! 48.
Transcending the states of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas,
He is the uprooter of the three impurities known as āṇava, kārmaṇa, and māyika,
and is intent upon the playful manifestation of the fivefold cosmic acts— creation and so forth— of the three worlds characterized by heaven, earth, and the netherworld.
The meaning is that he has the three Vedas, known as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, as his eyes. || 48 ||
Protect me, O Supreme Lord; protect me, O Lord of Pārvatī!
By your command, for this duration of time alone, I have remained upon the surface of the earth.
I have practiced for the sake of establishing the scriptures spoken by you. || 49 ||
This is clear. || 49 ||
Therefore, O Śaṅkara, desiring to attain your true nature hereafter, grant me some interval out of your special compassion. (50)

O Śaṅkara, O bestower of happiness, O renowned Someśvara! From this point forward—that is, beyond this—desiring to attain your true nature, I pray: grant me space within; show me special compassion, that is, act with mercy. || 50 ||
Then, with three verses, he establishes the propitiation of Śiva and the identity of the *liṅga* of Revaṇasiddheśvara:
When this was said by the leader of the Gaṇas, suddenly from that *liṅga* of Śaṅkara...
"O child, come! O one of great majesty, I am pleased with your devotion.
Thus he spoke these words aloud; at that time, it was a marvel for all embodied beings:
a divine drum resounded in the sky and the hosts of attendants rained down flowers.

When the leader Gaṇanāyaka, Revanasiddheśvara, had spoken thus and made this request, at that very moment, suddenly from that Śāṅkara Liṅga— the Someśvara Liṅga— [a voice spoke]: "O noble one, O child named Revanasiddha, you who possess a mind of great certainty regarding the Vedas and Āgamas!"
"O you, I am pleased by your devotion—by this ninefold devotion; come, do come!
Thus Śiva spoke these words aloud. At that moment, there was wonder and curiosity among embodied beings, and a divine drum resounded in the sky.
He roared everywhere; the Gaṇas—the hosts of Pramathas and the hosts of gods—showered flowers, meaning they rained down a rain of blossoms. || 51 ||
Having heard those compassionate words spoken by Śaṅkara through his divine form,
Gaṇapati, his soul thrilled with joy, then blazed forth with light.
Then, being praised by his supreme attendants and yogis who were filled with longing,
he entered the self-luminous supreme jyotirliṅga.

Then, immediately after the rain of flowers, Gaṇapati— the Lord of the Gaṇas of Śiva, the venerable Revanasiddha— with a thrilled soul and a contented mind, shining and radiant with the light of Śiva,
rose up from the *liṅga*, the Someśa-liṅga, [manifesting] that which had arisen with compassion.

Having heard the compassionate words of Śaṅkara— the speech concerning Śiva, the previously mentioned utterance— he was then, at that time, being praised to the highest degree by his attendants and companions, the Śiva-yogis, who were filled with longing and struck with wonder; [he was praising] that which is supreme and most excellent.

The meaning is that, entering the *jyotirliṅga*— which is of the nature of self-luminous light, as established by the Śruti passages, "By its light all this shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15) and "Everything shines following Him who shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15)— he has entered into a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), free from any decrease or increase in his essential nature. || 52 ||
When that self-luminous Renuka, the Lord of Siddhas, who possesses a divine form, had dissolved into Śaṅkara,
all the world was then filled with wonder.
Devotion to Śiva became established with authoritative proof. || 53 ||

When that Śiva-liṅga— the self-luminous Lord of Revanasiddha, the Siddhanātha Reṇuka, who possesses divine forms and a captivating nature— had merged into the Someśa-liṅga and attained oneness, all the world, every person, was struck with wonder and filled with amazement. At that time, the Śaiva...
Devotion related to Śiva—devotion accompanied by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), meaning existing together with authority—came into being; that is to say, it existed. || 53 ||
The path of the Śrī Vedāgama Vīraśaiva, the rising jewel of the six sacred sites (ṣaṭsthala), the lotus-raft for the union of the individual soul and the Lord, the secret wish-fulfilling gem.

He who causes the Śrīsiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi to be written, and having written it himself, hears it from others or causes others to hear it, attains stainless worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation. || 54 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Context of the Unity of Reṇuka and the Śiva-liṅga," within the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, a definitive exposition of the Vīraśaiva dharma, composed by the illustrious Brahmin of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*), the Śiva-yogin named Reṇukācārya, in the dialogue between Reṇuka and Vibhīṣaṇa. || 21 ||
And the Śrīsiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi is completed.

The meaning is: he whose sole refuge is the path of Śrī Veda-Āgama-Vīraśaiva—the path of Vīraśaiva propounded by the *Uttara-Vedāgama*, which is superior to all other scriptures and brings about auspiciousness; [he who is] the jewel arising from the six *sthala*s.

The jewel polished on the whetstone of the *Śāṇollīḍha* [treatise], which illuminates the path of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthalamārga*)—consisting of the one hundred and one auspicious sites (*maṅgalātmakaikottaraśatasthala*) that are the limbs of the *liṅga*; the lotus-like boat of the venerable Jīveśvara-yoga; the sun that causes the blooming of the lotus characterized by the beautiful, supreme non-duality (*paramaikya*) of the individual soul (*jīva*); the venerable Gopyacintāmaṇi.
He who, having written this *Śrīsiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, the Vīraśaiva scripture which is a wish-fulfilling gem for illuminating the auspicious meaning of the *Śivarahasya*, causes others to write it;
or he who, having heard it, causes others to hear it— he attains pure devotion and supreme liberation.
The meaning is that he attains it. || 54 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Context of the Unity of Reṇuka and the Śiva-liṅga," within the *Tattvapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Maritoṇḍadārya, who is preeminent in crossing the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences, in the dialogue between Reṇuka and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Section Twenty-One.
